News.title: How Kemi hopes to neutralise any blowback that her bid to cut benefits is cruel with a plea to our hearts
News.content:
POLITICS FIX How Kemi hopes to neutralise any blowback that her bid to cut benefits is cruel with a plea to our hearts







Next

KEMI Badenoch thinks she is on to a winner by hammering Labour over the eye-watering benefits bill.

Seizing on a relatively quiet political period, the Tory leader will once again go on the offensive over Britain’s monster welfare spending.



Of course, she will highlight the £180billion annual spend on handouts to working-age adults and vow to cut that by £36billion.

But today she will also try to shift the argument beyond just the raw numbers and look to take the moral high ground too.



Ms Badenoch will argue there is nothing kind about writing off people and dumping them on the dole scrapheap.

She will say: “If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself. That is what our welfare system is currently doing.



“Conservatives believe in a system that looks at people through the lens of what they can do, not what they cannot.”

So far much of Ms Badenoch’s position has been to appeal to people’s heads: that bloated welfare spending is a drag anchor pushing up all our taxes.

It is interesting she is now making a plea to our hearts too, hoping to neutralise any blowback that her bid to cut benefits is cruel.

This is an argument likely to be fleshed out by the government’s own welfare adviser Alan Milburn in a long-awaited report next week.



The jobs tsar has been warning that too many youngsters especially are being consigned to a life on welfare rather than pulling themselves up by the bootstraps and getting a job.

But Mr Milburn’s recommendations are unlikely to make any savings in the long-run, leaving an opening for Ms Badenoch to continue punching the bruise.

Meanwhile Andy Burnham is preparing to once again jet out of the country to the COP climate summit later this week.

Yet his commitment to Net Zero is rubbing up against his pledge to ease the cost of living for Brits.

Despite looking to burnish his climate credentials ahead of the summit, the PM is expected to weaken his environmental clampdown on car manufacturers in the coming weeks.

News.title: I can breathe easier now, says murdered James Bulger’s father after killer Jon Venables’ freedom bid REFUSED
News.content:
Next

THE father of murdered toddler James Bulger last night told of his “huge relief” after one of his son’s killers was refused parole.

Ralph Bulger said he could breathe easier after Jon Venables, 44, lost his freedom bid following a three-day hearing last month.



Ralph, 60, and ex-wife Denise Fergus, 59, were blocked from attending the private review.

Builder Ralph said: “I’m hugely relieved the Parole Board has seen sense and kept this vile child killer behind bars.



“I can breathe easier now I know he will not be free to harm other children.

“But the trauma never ends. In another two years, he will be eligible for parole again.

“Jon Venables knows he will never stop his sick lust for children and so do I.

“Why the parole board insists on this ridiculous cat and mouse game every two years is beyond me.”



Venables was ten when he and accomplice Robert Thompson abducted and killed James, two, in February 1993.

He was freed in 2001, recalled in 2010, then re-released in 2013, and jailed again in 2017 for 40 months over more child abuse images.

He was kept in jail this time round after the panel heard concerns about “how open and honest he would be in supervision”.

He also told parole staff ­dealing with his latest review that he was not seeking release.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said: “I welcome the Board’s decision.”

News.title: Burnham MUST listen to message from his own backyard and not give away our sovereignty…or public fury would be seismic
News.content:
Brexit betrayal







Next

ANDY Burnham claims opinion about Brexit has shifted in the ten years since the historic referendum.

But the Prime Minister says a lot of things — often without proof, or much prior thought.



Just four months ago, when Burnham was standing to become an MP, he solemnly promised he would never rerun the toxic Brexit debate.

Yet, next Friday, our PM without a mandate will head cap-in-hand to Brussels to surrender vital UK powers on food standards, Net Zero and car tariffs.



He’s even expected to let them dictate how many European criminals we can deport. How’s that for toxic?

It would not only be a Brexit betrayal.

It would be an insult to democracy for Burnham — who the public could never have expected to become PM when they voted Labour in 2024 — now to hand over power to unelected EU officials.

And, as a poll reveals today, it would also be a kick in the teeth for the patriotic voters of Makerfield, the only people who HAVE actually voted for him.

Two-thirds of his constituents backed Brexit and even now three-quarters are opposed to relinquishing power to set our own food standards.

That means not allowing meddling Eurocrats to ban smoky bacon crisps, for starters.



Whatever happened to the “Makerfield test” that Burnham proudly promised to apply to all his big decisions?

If the PM persists with his sneaky, backdoor plot to reverse Brexit by stealth, public fury would be seismic.

The message from his own backyard is deafening: don’t give away our sovereignty again.

Just the job

KEMI Badenoch is rolling up her sleeves and doing the hard graft to prove she is a serious Prime Minister-in-waiting.

While Andy Burnham ducks the big decisions, the Tory leader has been drawing up a detailed plan to fix Britain.



Today she unveils a blueprint to slash a staggering £36billion from the soaring benefits bill.

Her “Welfare that Works” package is a serious, common-sense plan to reform a system dragging the nation towards financial ruin.

And it is exactly the right place to start.

Britain currently hands out a mind-boggling £180billion a year in benefits to working-age adults — more than we spend on our army, police and schools combined, and costing £4,000 for every taxpayer.

Unlike our dithering PM who hides behind endless “reviews”, the plain-speaking Tory is ready to deliver action.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

She wants to clamp down on handouts for foreign nationals and call time on claims for low-level mental health conditions and routine aches or pains.

It’s time to stop the welfare ride that rewards staying at home, and get Britain back to work.

News.title: How Nvidia boss’s affair with ‘Chinese spy’ sent shockwaves across globe as UK pensions exposed & tech markets plunge
News.content:
Next

IT sounds like the plot of a classic spy thriller: A suspected Chinese agent has an affair with the American boss of the world’s most valuable company, sparking fears of a security breach.

And US tech chief Jensen Huang’s fling with businesswoman Alice Huang might also have huge consequences for the future of artificial intelligence — as well as the global economy.



That’s because his chip-making business Nvidia supplies two-thirds of the world’s AI computing power, and the storm over the company brought about by his conduct is likely to spook investors who already fear the boom in the new technology is coming to an end.

Shares in the huge firm crashed eight per cent in early trading yesterday, wiping out $335billion from its market value, amid fears the tech titan could be forced to quit — with no obvious successor in place.



Famed for his trademark leather jacket, 63-year-old Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife Lori and apologised for hurting his family, adding that he supports an investigation into his actions which his own board is now carrying out.

In a message to staff on Sunday, Huang confessed: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

He added: “Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together.

“To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.”

Huang’s friend US President Donald Trump backed the microchip mogul as Nvidia insisted there was no evidence its security had been compromised as it battles Chinese rivals for global AI domination.

The workaholic CEO — whose fortune is estimated at £116billion — has flown on Air Force One with Trump on Chinese trade missions.



Marco Rubio, the US Secretary of State, was reported to have warned that dark–haired Ms Huang, aged in her late 30s, was a spy recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security.

She was alleged to have gathered information regarding US artificial intelligence chips and encouraged the Nvidia boss to push for looser export restrictions on sale to China.

Tech markets propping up the global economy were braced for a crash in trading later today which could hit investments, including UK pension funds.



Shares in Nvidia, valued at a staggering £3.35trillion, crashed early yesterday but rallied later on Wall Street amid continuing market jitters.

The shock news triggered an immediate share price drop, aggravating a sell-off already under way following the rout of Trump’s Republicans in last week’s mid-term elections as Democrats seek to place greater control on the development of AI.

British tech firms are also braced for fallout from the sex scandal.

Liz Upton, co-founder of British computer business Raspberry Pi, told a conference amid laughter yesterday: “I do hope Jensen’s wandering penis doesn’t bring down my share price.”

Online wags were also quick to poke fun at the Nvidia boss’s fling with copycat memes of the famous Coldplay Jumbotron moment when the affair between US executives Andy Byron and Kristin Cabot was exposed in 2025.

But serious concerns intensified that a burst of AI bubble stocks could trigger a global recession as the scandal played out yesterday.



The International Monetary Fund and central banks across the globe fear over-investment in AI tech stocks could herald broader financial turmoil.

Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Broadcom account for an unprecedented chunk of the market value of listed companies and prop up many investment and pension funds.

The UK Pensions Regulator recently warned British retirement pots were at risk and urged investors to test for “hidden AI exposure”.



US spy chiefs have been eyeing Ms Huang, who works for Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, which buys AI semi- conductor chips from Nvidia.

Megaspeed is suspected of helping Beijing boffins to gain access to Nvidia’s world-leading technology built into microchips banned from export to China.

Nvidia’s board ordered an independent investigation amid concerns that its charismatic boss may have fallen victim to a Chinese “honey pot” sting.

He said that he was fully co-operating and would continue as chief executive until the investigation concluded and issued a statement in a bid to calm shareholders.

Mr Huang said: “You deserve better from me. Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”



China branded the spying claims “entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China”.

But Tory Shadow Foreign Secretary Tom Tugendhat warned yesterday that “it wouldn’t at all surprise” him if the Chinese state had recruited Alice Huang.

He added that it “would not be beyond the Chinese state” to threaten sending Ms Huang’s family to prison if she did not co-operate.



Ms Huang — no relation to the Nvidia boss — worked as a TV reporter in China before becoming a chip buyer at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

It is unclear when the alleged spy met the tech supremo but they were photographed together in 2024 at a bar in Taiwan’s capital Taipei.

Megaspeed swiftly became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers after the illicit affair was kindled.

In the past two years, the company has bought more than £3.6billion worth of microchips from the US firm.

Taiwan-born Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has become one of Donald Trump’s closest “tech bro” pals and claims the US president often calls him late at night.



He has also met British PM Andy Burnham and attended a summit with the King in September.

Trump said yesterday that Mr Huang was “an honourable guy”, adding he had not spoken with him about the affair.

He said: “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but, you know, so does everybody else. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on.”

Trump was reported to have been briefed in October 2025 that Ms Huang was spying for China.

Asked by reporters whether he now wished he had “acted on the intelligence” at the time, Trump replied: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honourable guy. He probably has an excuse for it.”



Trump’s inaction last night is said to have “raised eyebrows” among former national security officials.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Tracy Walder, a former CIA officer and FBI special agent, told the American cable network NewsNation: “It’s even more disturbing to me that President Trump knew about this information and personally allowed him to stay that close.”

AI firm stocks were hit last week by the Republican mid-term election flop which triggered fears that Trump’s support for his big tech pals would begin to wane.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch will urge the anxious to show a can-do spirit as she sets out £36bn benefits blitz plan
News.content:
Next

KEMI Badenoch is to set out a £36billion benefits blitz plan — urging the anxious to show a can-do spirit.

The Tory leader wants to make big inroads into the £180billion a year going to working-age adults.



She is aiming to draw a distinction from PM Andy Burnham — who is unable to guarantee the bill will be slashed before the next election.

Her Welfare that Works package looks to inspire — by highlighting what others in adversity achieve.



The proposals will take away claims from 2.5million people for what are called “low-level” problems such as mild mental health issues and bad backs.

She will say in a speech today: “Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful, creative work from home.

“People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world.

“If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself.”

Plans include £13.7billion of cuts from reforms to disability and sickness benefits — including for mild mental health conditions and routine back and joint pain.

A further £9.5billion will come from ending benefit claims for foreigners without EU settled status.



Limiting child benefits to two children per family will save £3.1billion.

Ms Badenoch will add: “The weight of this welfare burden is crushing our economy and plunging us deeper and deeper into debt.

“There is no world in which the current system is sustainable and not just because of the cost.”

A Labour spokesman said: “The Tories let the welfare bill soar on their watch. Now they have the audacity to pretend it was nothing to do with them.”

News.title: School phone ban set to be tightened by Labour in bid to stop pupils from scrolling throughout the day
News.content:
Next

LABOUR is tightening school rules to keep pupils off their phones throughout the day.

Headteachers will be urged to ban mobile phones during school time from September 2027 — and sooner if possible.



Education Secretary Lucy Powell said: “Children should not be using smartphones at any point during the school day, full stop.

“That’s why we’re strengthening our guidance to take the next leap towards truly phone-free schools.



“School is for learning and friendship, not scrolling.”

For more than a year, the Tories have called for a ban on mobile phones in schools.



Labour has at times resisted calls to go further but new guidance will go beyond the “not seen, not heard” policy where some children still have phones in their bags.

Polling shows 40 per cent of nine to 16-year-olds were not going out socially in order to spend time online.

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said: “I am delighted that Labour have finally listened to us.

“But this is the same Government ploughing ahead with unevidenced AI tutors for the most disadvantaged children.”

News.title: Woman in her 20s ‘raped’ in popular park late at night as locals wake to find cordon and police launch urgent appeal
News.content:
PARK ‘ATTACK’ Woman in her 20s ‘raped’ in popular park late at night as locals wake to find cordon and police launch urgent appeal







Next

A WOMAN in her 20s has allegedly been raped in a popular park, as cops launch an urgent appeal.

Cops raced to Hollow Way Recreation Ground in Cowley, Oxfordshire, late on November 8.

All entrances to the park were sealed off as an investigation got underway.

Cops have now confirmed they are looking into a reported rape which is thought to have happened around 10pm near the junction of Horspath Road and Rupert Road.





A Thames Valley Police spokesperson said: “Officers are investigating a reported rape of a woman in her 20s, that occurred at around 10pm yesterday (8/11) near the junction of Horspath Road and Rupert Road.

“We are in the early stages of our investigation and officers are carrying out a number of fast-time enquiries to establish exactly what happened.

“The victim is being supported by specially trained officers.”

Neighbourhood officers are patrolling the area in an effort to reassure residents.



A police scene remains in place at the park.

Locals said they were “anxious” and “concerned” after they woke to find the popular park had been sealed off, reports the Oxford Mail.

A number of uniformed officers, cop vehicles and plain-clothes detectives were spotted in the area throughout Monday.

Residents say they heard fireworks in and around the park late on Sunday evening.



Police are appealing for anyone who was in the recreation ground near Hollow Way or on surrounding roads at around 10pm to come forward if they saw anything suspicious.

Officers have also requested any CCTV, doorbell, dash-cam or mobile phone footage recorded in the area around that time.

Anyone with information should contact police quoting investigation reference 43260585129.

News.title: FBI probes billionaire Nvidia boss’ affair with ‘Chinese spy’, Trump says as company board also launches investigation
News.content:
Next

THE FBI has launched a probe into Nvidia’s CEO’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Donald Trump told reporters today.

Billionaire boss Jensen Huang confessed to cheating on his wife with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang – and the sex scandal has sparked a massive espionage investigation.



Nvidia supplies two-thirds of the world’s AI computing power – and its leather-jacket clad boss is one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley.

Referring to Huang’s spy scandal, the president said: “I know the FBI is looking into it” adding that “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”



The tech titan was left red-faced by the public sex tryst – and has been summoned to appear in front of congress over “significant national security concerns” after it emerged that his mistress was under investigation over spying claims.

The billionaire boss is one of several AI chiefs circling Trump’s orbit in a bid to turboboost US tech and artificial superintelligence.

The US president revealed that he had spoken to the humiliated Nvidia boss earlier that day “just to see if he’s feeling all right”.

He told reporters: “I asked him about that and he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”



Secret memos from US intelligence suggest that Alice entrapped Huang into an affair to smuggle confidential information to Beijing.

Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped from Nvidia’s value after the firm’s stocks plummeted following news of the salacious affair.

It comes just days before Trump is due to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping next week – but the president suggested he would skirt the spy claims.

Asked whether he would discuss the Nvidia espionage scandal he replied: “No, I don’t think so” before adding “I mean, maybe.”

He said: “I’m sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man.”



The leather-jacket clad CEO previously told staff: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

The tech boss has previously denied having but a “normal” relationship with Alice, according to Bloomberg.

China has denied allegations that it sent Alice to ensnare Huang and has slammed the claims as “entirely groundless”.



Nvidia said on Sunday it had opened an investigation in light of worrying claims that its CEO had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.

Jensen Huang is still in charge of the chip-making giant – whose cutting edge tech make it a leading player in the AI boom.

But the tech CEO may have fallen prey to a honeytrap plot – with leaked surveillance footage showing his mistress passing on information to China.

Top secret memos circulated through the White House – and seen by the New York Times – suggest that US officials were aware of a potential spying threat linked to Huang’s extramarital affair.

The tech titan’s relationship appears to have been risque in more ways than one – with US Secretary of State overseeing a memo into the tryst – and its potential threat to US security.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Trump himself was told of the scandal – which also involved Alice allegedly nicking AI chips – before visiting China in May.

British spy chiefs have previously warned about mounting spy operations from Beijing – but the government nonetheless green-lighted China’s new mega-embassy in London earlier this year.

News.title: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of violence and abuse against her
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.

Goldsmith, who dated the disgraced entertainer for roughly a year around 2014, alleged that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

In a lengthy statement on social media, the 52-year-old said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison earlier on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

He was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

The judge at the sentencing hearing told Brand that he harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

News.title: What happened inside court as Brand was sentenced
News.content:
Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan said Brand harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you".

The 51-year-old was sentenced on Monday to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for sexual assault.

The former comedian was found guilty by a jury last week of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

Senior UK correspondent Sima Kotecha was inside the Southwark Crown Court during the sentencing.

More on this story.

News.title: Hundreds more offenders to leave jail on Tuesday
News.content:
Around 650 more offenders will leave jails in England and Wales on Tuesday in the third phase of the government's plan to end the prison population crisis.

The group will include offenders serving up to three years and two months for their crimes.

Under the new rules, they are leaving jail after serving no more than a third of their sentence behind bars, rather than a half.

At least 1,350 offenders have left jail early since 1 October under the first two waves of the scheme.

By the end of the year officials project that at least 2,500 will have been let out to spend two-thirds of their sentence on a licence in the community.

Tuesday's third stage continues the process of releasing batches of offenders serving increasingly long sentences - culminating next June with those serving more than 12 years.

The cohort will include people convicted of affray, which has a maximum sentence of three years, burglary and fraud.

Some violent offenders convicted of wounding, grievous bodily harm with intent or lower-end firearms charges could also be released.

Offenders convicted of one of more than 70 offences are exempt from the earlier release scheme, including manslaughter, rape, sexual and grooming offences and those on life terms.

Weekly prison population statistics show that the early release programme is having an impact - for now - on the population crisis inside jails.

On Monday the latest release of weekly data showed there were 86,982 people in jail, with enough spare spaces to take in 2,076 additional offenders if needs be.

That is 500 more cells available at any one time than was the case on the eve of the programme beginning in October.

News.title: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under stricter rules for schools in England
News.content:
Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders union, said phones could raise "safety issues" and be an "unhelpful distraction" during the school day. But he said the more robust measures recommended under the new guidance would "come at a cost".

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said the latest guidance "does at least provide some clarity", but added that school leaders "cannot simply make mobile phones disappear".

"If all schools are going to be expected to have lockable pouches or other secure storage facilities for every pupil, the cost involved will be very significant indeed," he said.

"This is not feasible unless the government puts in the funding required to meet these costs."

Dame Rachel de Souza, Children's Commissioner for England, said she welcomed strong action to stop phones distracting pupils and disrupting the school day.

Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of campaign group of Generation Focus, similarly welcomed the changes, saying "no see, no hear" policies were not working and pupils were still "TikToking in the toilets".

"Ultimately, we need to get to a point where it's not normal for every single child to have a personal internet-enabled device in their pockets with them 24/7," she said.

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said she was "delighted that Labour have finally listened to us and agreed to properly ban smartphones in schools".

She said it was also the "right thing to do" to have a review of safety standards around the technology used in schools, which the government has also announced on the back of calls for improved guidance.

But she criticised what she called a lack of "joined up thinking" over what new tech was being allowed in classrooms.

Because education is devolved, the approach to phones in schools varies across the UK.

In Scotland, external, the government has said it will introduce a new law to restrict the personal use of phones in schools, and launched a consultation on the issue over the summer.

In Wales, external, the Senedd recently voted against a motion to introduce a national statutory ban on phones in classrooms. Schools are still encouraged to restrict the use of phones during the school day, but heads have flexibility over how to implement their own rules.

And in Northern Ireland, Education Minister Paul Givan launched a 12-week consultation in August on whether to ban mobile phones from schools by law, calling for "a stronger and more consistent approach across our education system".

Rules around phones in schools are separate from the UK's upcoming ban on social media for under-16s, due to be introduced in March.

Children will be barred from accessing platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Vinted and eBay could also be included in the list of platforms set to be banned, the culture secretary has said.

Additional reporting by Beth Rose and Nathan Standley

News.title: Trump says Iran war is 'effectively over' militarily with further strikes unlikely
News.content:
Donald Trump says the Iran war "militarily is effectively over" declaring that there is "positive momentum" behind negotiations to end the Middle East conflict.

"We're just keeping it the status quo," the US president said on Monday. "And we're doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours."

Addressing reporters from the White House press briefing room, Trump said that renewed US attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" but that the US was "locked and loaded" should the circumstances change.

Iranian officials have repeatedly expressed doubts about the US president's prior comments about resolving the conflict.

Responding to a question over why he would not officially declare an end to the conflict, Trump said that some of the Gulf allies could still face Iranian aggression.

"We have some great allies there and we have to make sure they're not hurt," Trump said, suggesting that the US naval blockade on Iranian ports was helping to make the region more secure.

Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani in the Oval Office earlier on Monday, saying they had an "excellent conversation" about negotiations to end the war.

In a post on X, the Qatari prime minister said he held "positive discussions" with Trump and Vice-President JD Vance on "reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region".

Efforts to broker a peace between Washington and Tehran have largely been held indirectly through mediators since the war first broke out following joint US-Israeli strikes in February.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar and United Arab Emirates are among the US's Gulf allies that have been hit by Iranian strikes over the course of the war, in addition to threat of strikes that have led to major air travel disruptions in the region.

This is not the first time that Trump has said Iran war is "militarily" over, but the circumstances for him are different now.

Trump has hinted at de-escalation in Iran after a bruising set of midterm election results for the Republicans last week, which senior figures including Vice-President Vance blamed on the Iran War.

In an interview with 60 minutes that aired on Sunday, the president said he did not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war.

Ahead of the midterms, Trump said US forces conducted what he described as "minor strikes" on an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Post-election recriminations over the US war in Iran are already placing pressure on members of the Trump administration.

Republican congressman Thomas Massie launched a strong attack against Trump's Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday over the war in Iran, requesting a vote in the House of Representatives to impeach him.

Trump has backed Hegseth, who says he is "not worried" about the looming impeachment threats, calling Massie's effort a "sham".

While the move is unlikely to succeed with Republicans still in control of Congress until January, Democrats have expressed willingness to impeach Hegseth once the new session begins and they have control of both the House and the Senate.

News.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
News.content:
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.

In January, it could jump by more than a quarter â around Â£460 extra a year for the typical UK household â according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.

For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.

Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.

Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard â and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.

Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

News.title: 'Baffling but brilliant' post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything wins Booker Prize
News.content:
The story follows a man and his aunt who must muddle through on the south-east English coast in the aftermath of an unexplained disaster and the arrival of mysterious alien beings.

The author has said he deliberately omitted as much explanation about the background to the events as possible, in order to make readers feel the same disorientation as the characters.

He has said: "The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It's a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend."

He added: "I've passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien."

That approach has led to a mixed reaction. The Guardian praised the book but said, external "it won't be for everyone", while the New York Times said, external: "The more we learn about the conditions of this novel's broken world, the harder it is to grasp."

The Literary Review described it as, external "a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts", while the Telegraph said, external "you feel you're not so much reading as dreaming".

Another Telegraph critic wrote, external that it was "ultimately, in both skill and humour, a cut above" the other shortlisted books.

"And in an age when AI overlords keep threatening to kill us, and the Government has told us to stockpile tinned food and bottled water, it is, for once, a novel that you can genuinely call 'timely'."

News.title: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
News.content:
A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.

An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management.

"Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said.

"But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement."

A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost Â£285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions.

"This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account."

The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers".

Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue.

He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark.

Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home.

The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered Â£500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months.

Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her Â£2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it.

At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer.

Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence.

News.title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault
News.content:
Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag. His sentence will not be included in the early release scheme. Sex offenders, along with murderers, are exempt from the scheme.

The judge also paid tribute to the bravery of the women who gave evidence during the trial.

News.title: Civil servant who secretly held five jobs found guilty of fraud
News.content:
The prosecution argued that he used sick notes to cope with his impossible schedule. In March 2023, he was on sick leave from four of the organisations he worked for. But he kept working at the Home Office and did not tell them he was ill.

His line manager at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023. By this point he'd been off sick for three months and she wanted to make a plan to get him back to work.

She told the jury that at the start of the call he was coughing a lot and waving tissues up to the camera. She also told the jury that he had been wearing white make-up to try to look ill.

Adams told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."

Chowdhury told the jury this was a smear and that he had not been wearing make-up.

After the call, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it he blamed a technical error.

Adams grew suspicious. ''I believed he was lying,'' she told the jury. She escalated her concerns up the chain at the UKHSA.

But his fraudulent behaviour went on for several more months until he left the civil service in September 2023.

He was finally caught in 2024 by the government's National Fraud Initiative, which conducts searches of civil service databases such as payroll every two years to look for anomalies.

Chowdhury has also been accused by his siblings of bullying their mother into increasing his share of the family home days before she died.

In a case at the High Court, Chowdhury's two brothers and sister allege that he put "undue influence" on Faijun Nessa to sign documents that meant he would inherit half of her home.

The four-storey, six-bedroom home in east London has been valued at Â£2.1m.

His siblings say their mother could not have understood what she was signing because she was "desperately unwell". In January 2023 she was given a terminal diagnosis of stage four metastatic colorectal cancer.

The claimants also allege that Mrs Nessa, who was nearly blind and could not speak English, was unaware of what she was signing because the documents were not translated into her native Bengali at the time they were signed.

Kashim Chowdhury denies the claims. That case is ongoing.

News.title: Poundland unable to buy new stock as fears over collapse grow
News.content:
Poundland is unable to buy new stock to fill its shelves after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

The discount chain is on the brink of collapse with one insider describing it as "running on fumes". It has until Thursday to secure a rescue deal.

About Â£50m has been frozen by its American owner Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning its 600 shops are running out of stock.

Pressure is building on Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for Â£1 last June, after the owner rejected a takeover bid that could have saved the thousands of jobs currently at risk. Gordon Brothers has been approached for comment.

Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until Thursday.

Access to funds was limited because of a tension between Gordon Brothers' dual role as both creditor and shareholder, a source said, but added they expected a relaxation of funds in the next two days.

Last week, Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4% last week, which included Halloween, but said this was Â£1.5m ahead of budget.

He said the business made a profit of Â£18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where the business made losses of Â£68m.

The latest annual accounts have yet to be audited.

News.title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
News.content:
Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost Â£6,000.

She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.

But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action.

Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.

Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.

After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.

Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.

This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.

Within weeks she had generated almost Â£6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process.

"I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."

Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.

In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.

After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending Â£455 in court fees.

News.title: Man jailed over racist Badenoch death threats
News.content:
A man has been jailed for sending the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch emails threatening to shoot her dead.

Ex-teacher Kieran Kyle sent three emails on 2 May to the Tory party leader in which he made racist references and claimed to have been in the IRA, the court heard.

The 43-year-old, from Gillingham in Kent, pleaded guilty on 22 September at Westminster Magistrates' Court to two counts of sending communications of an indecent or offensive nature.

Kyle was sentenced to 20 weeks in prison at the same court on Monday.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, Badenoch and her husband Hamish said the "malicious communications and targeted harassment" not only had an effect on them, but also undermined "a healthy democracy".

In two of the emails, Kyle had made racist references and written: "I'm ex-IRA, so Bloody Sunday references from you are going to give you trouble," the court heard.

The messages were sent on the day Badenoch apologised for footage from Bloody Sunday being mistakenly used in a social media clip to criticise a parliamentary Bill on legacy issues in Northern Ireland.

The Tory leader had said she did not sign off the video and that it was sent out by "very young people".

The video criticising the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, posted to her social media channels on 28 April, showed Badenoch saying the Labour legislation would "drag" Troubles veterans back to court.

Thirteen unarmed civilians were shot dead when members of the Army's Parachute Regiment opened fire on civil rights demonstrators in the Bogside area of Londonderry on 30 January 1972, a date that became known as Bloody Sunday.

The court heard Kyle had also sent an email to Badenoch's husband Hamish on 29 April, which used a racist term and said she had a "big mouth" and he should "put a leash on her".

News.title: Ground Force and Homes Under the Hammer star Tommy Walsh dies aged 69
News.content:
Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert known for starring on TV shows including Ground Force, Homes Under the Hammer and Challenge Tommy Walsh, has died at the age of 69.

Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the BBC's Ground Force from 1997 to 2005.

He went on to also front popular programmes including Clean It, Fix It, and Cowboys and Angels, and joined daytime TV favourite Homes Under the Hammer in 2021.

Walsh's agent told BBC News he died "peacefully after a long illness surrounded by his family", and asked for privacy for the family.

Walsh was previously reported to have had surgery for throat cancer in 2022 and lung cancer in 2023.

News.title: Prince William wants more protection from harassment for service women
News.content:
"I want to play my part in making the military feel like the welcoming, open and professional place I enjoyed and make it feel like that for everyone," writes Prince William, in his first intervention on this subject.

"At the moment, I don't feel that we meet those standards and, as a former serving officer, I really mind it when those who wear the uniform now don't feel safe, respected or valued."

According to royal sources, Prince William has been holding his own fact-finding meetings with service women of all ranks, across the Army, Royal Navy and the Royal Air Force.

He has now raised some of those concerns about the issues concerning women in the armed forces, in the article he commissioned for Country Life.

It cites a survey from the Ministry of Defence that found 67% of service women had faced unwanted "sexualised behaviour" every year and that 30% had considered leaving the armed forces because of such behaviour.

The article also references the experiences of Royal Artillery Gunner Jaysley Beck, who took her own life at Larkhill Camp in Wiltshire in 2021.

Gunner Beck had faced months of unwanted attention and had reported a sexual assault and an inquest heard about a complaints system that failed to adequately respond.

Earlier this year, four young women told the BBC they were sexually assaulted and harassed at an Army training college for teenagers - the Army Foundation College at Harrogate, North Yorkshire - with one saying she was raped by fellow junior soldiers in an attack that lasted hours.

News.title: Detective stole more than £85,000 from police force
News.content:
A former police detective who stole more than Â£85,000 from her own force while working in a team that investigated high-level drugs gangs has been jailed.

Acting as the exhibits officer and one of only a small number of people with access to a safe that contained hundreds of thousands of pounds, Michelle Kirsty Reason began siphoning off cash in January 2022, Derbyshire Police said.

According to the force, the 54-year-old spent the money - which had been seized from criminals - on a car, a holiday, and tickets to events.

On Monday, Reason pleaded guilty to theft and misconduct in public office and was jailed for four years and two months at Mansfield Magistrates' and County Court.

Detectives said Reason, of Church Lane in Buxton, was a police exhibits officer based in Ripley.

From about January 2022, the force said Reason began siphoning cash after she dealt with a large cash seizure in the region of Â£350,000.

She initially stole Â£15,000 and told officers that, once she found that nobody had noticed, began taking money on a regular basis until she left the force in December 2025.

However, officers then began to review the stored exhibits ahead of an upcoming court case, and began to question where the cash had gone.

Knowing she had been caught out, Reason went to St Mary's Wharf police station to confess to taking the cash.

News.title: Scientists discover the likely cause of one in eight cancers – and it’s not smoking, diet or alcohol
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Around 12% of the world’s total cancer cases in 2024 were likely caused by an infection, according to new research from the World Health Organisation (WHO).

The study, published in The Lancet Oncology, analysed the frequency and causes of different cancers, specifically examining the role of infections.

It linked 2.3 million new cancer cases to an infection. Most were caused by just five pathogens: Helicobacter pylori (4%), human papillomavirus, or HPV (4%), hepatitis B (2%), Epstein-Barr virus (1%) and hepatitis C (under 1%). These infections can cause more than 20 different types of cancer, including stomach, liver, blood and cervical cancers.

So, how can an infection cause cancer? And does this mean these cancers are preventable?

Did we already know about this link?

Some of the study authors have been researching this field for around thirty years. Their previous work investigated cancer cases caused by infections in 1990, 2002, 2008, 2012, and 2018.

The proportion of cancer cases caused by infections may appear to have dropped during those years (from a high of 18% in 2002), but the authors stress these comparisons cannot really be made confidently, as the sources and quality of the data have changed over time.

open image in gallery New research from the World Health Organisation analysed the frequency and causes of different cancers ( AFP via Getty )

In fact, the latest study wasn’t trying to compare between the years. Instead, it aims to highlight where controlling and preventing infections can help to reduce cancer rates.

To make sense of this, it helps to know how infection is linked to cancer. Extensive research has dissected the molecular mechanisms behind this link, and we now know there are various ways infections can cause cancer.

How can a virus cause cancer?

A virus can (directly or indirectly) change the genes of the cell it infects (the host cell), making that cell more likely to grow out of control and eventually become a cancer.

There are three main ways viruses can do this.

The first is by turning off the ability of a cell to destroy itself (for example, by inactivating the TP53 protein) or to stop dividing (for example, by inactivating the RB protein). A healthy cell would normally try to do these things if infected by a virus.

The second way a virus can cause cancer is by inserting its own DNA into the host cell’s DNA, which can accidentally disrupt genes that control cell death or division (like those above).

The third way is when the virus itself carries a gene that causes cancer (an oncogene). In many cases, the virus has picked up these by accident from another organism.

The link between viruses and cancer is actually foundational to modern cancer science, and has helped scientists uncover the direct link between genetics and cancer we now take for granted.

What about bacteria and parasites?

It’s not just viruses that cause cancer. Infections from bacteria or parasites – such as Helicobacter pylori (best known for causing stomach ulcers), or Opisthorchis viverrini (a liver fluke, a type of parasitic worm) – can also lead to cancer.

However, these work more indirectly than viruses. Long-term (chronic) infection by these types of organisms can cause significant stress to different tissues.

open image in gallery Infections from bacteria or parasites can lead to cancer ( Getty/iStock )

Inflammation, normally a part of the body’s immune response, can then become overactive, damaging the tissues further.

These stresses can result in cancer-causing DNA damage in cells, or lead to mistakes during cell division as the body tries to rapidly produce new cells to repair tissue damage.

In both cases, the cells acquire genetic mutations that put them on the road towards becoming cancer.

Many cancers are preventable

Of course, there may be other mechanisms linking infections and cancer that we don’t know about but, overall, the connection between infections and cancer is indisputable.

Critically, what this tells us – and what this new study into the rates of cancers caused by infections reinforces – is that many cancers are preventable.

In Australia, one of the best examples of preventing cancers caused by infections is the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine.

This vaccine protects against certain strains of HPV strongly associated with cervical cancer, and is available to adolescents in Australia.

About the authors John (Eddie) La Marca is a Senior Research Officer, Blood Cells and Blood Cancer, WEHI (Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research). Sarah Diepstraten is a Senior Research Officer, Blood Cells and Blood Cancer Division, WEHI (Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research). This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

Since the program began in 2007, HPV infections dropped by 90% among people eligible to receive the vaccine.

Because of its success, Australia could be on track to eliminate cervical cancer by 2035.

However, vaccination rates among 15-year-olds have fallen from 85.7% in 2020 to 79.5% in 2024, which is concerning. As is the case for all vaccines, a high proportion of the population need to be vaccinated to also protect those who, for health reasons, cannot be vaccinated. For HPV, the WHO and Australian target is to vaccinate 90% of 15-year-old girls by 2030.

Sadly, the new study also highlights that around 75% of cancers caused by infections were found in low- and middle-income countries.

Treating infections that can lead to cancer – such as HIV, H. pylori, and hepatitis B and C – is one way to reduce cancer rates. Preventative measures also play a major role, including vaccinations, condoms and disease screening.

However, the availability of these programs in poorer countries can be limited, and so access continues to be a major equity issue in combating cancer.

The authors would like to acknowledge the contribution of Amali Cooray from the Olivia Newton-John Cancer Research Institute to this article.

News.title: The £50 fine UK drivers need to know about as weather warnings come into effect
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

As weather warnings for fog come into place across parts of England, drivers risk a £50 fine for not observing a simple Highway Code rule.

The Met Office has issued a yellow fog warning across the Midlands, London, Wales, Yorkshire, the north west, east, south east and south west of England. The warning began at 6pm and will remain in place until 10am on Tuesday, meaning commuters will have to battle through the mist on their journey to work.

The forecaster warned that public transport and flights may be affected. Motorists also face the challenge of restricted visibility, but with the help of fog lights they should be able to make the journey into the office without too much difficulty.

open image in gallery A fog warning is in place until 10am Tuesday ( Met Office )

But when visibility clears, motorists should remember Rule 236 of the Highway Code: “You MUST NOT use front or rear fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced as they dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights. You MUST switch them off when visibility improves.”

Those who don’t switch off their fog lights when the fog clears risk a £50 fixed penalty notice, according to the AA.

The Met Office has warned drivers to check road conditions before driving and leave extra journey time. Drivers should be confident in switching on fog lights and check they are working prior to their journeys.

open image in gallery By Friday midnight, parts of the UK will see 0C temperatures ( Met Office )

It won’t be the first time Britons have woken up to fog this month with the Met Office issuing yellow warnings multiple times last week in Northern Ireland, London, and the south-east of England.

The fog is expected to give way to colder, frostier weather conditions in the south of England later this week. Meanwhile, parts of Scotland can expect wintry showers.

Met Office Chief Meteorologist Jason Kelly, said: "Snow showers could briefly fall on lower ground in northern Scotland and the Northern Isles, mainly Shetland, overnight on Wednesday and into Thursday. However, snow may only settle on higher ground and this is relatively normal for the time of year."

Temperatures are expected to fall below average widely by Thursday and Friday, as frost becomes more widespread. The far north east will also feel particularly cold in stronger winds, the forecaster said. By midnight on Friday, Manchester is expected to see freezing temperatures while parts of Scotland will see 1C.

open image in gallery The Met Office has issued a warning over fog (Will Meakin-Durrant/PA) ( PA Wire )

Met Office five day forecast:

Tonight:

Apart from showers in the far north, clear skies for northern and central areas allow frost and fog patches to form overnight, Rain and cloud pushes into the south and southwest. Milder in the far southwest, but feeling chilly elsewhere.

Tuesday:

Dense fog in central areas may linger tomorrow, but plenty of bright spells in the north when it clears. Cloud and rain pushes into much of England and Wales later.

Outlook for Wednesday to Friday:

Rainy across the south on Wednesday. Brighter further north, and drier and brighter for all towards the weekend. Becoming colder, with wintry showers possible in Scotland. Frosts become increasingly widespread.

News.title: China's trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year, according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing.

Exports in October surged 35.2% from a year earlier, the customs agency said. Exports have grown rapidly this year supported by high-tech goods like semiconductors and autos. Imports rose 41.6% year-on-year.

Between January and October, China logged a $1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to $105.3 billion from $133.5bn in September as imports picked up pace.

That puts China on track for surpassing last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus.

“We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics.

Overcapacity in many industries, excess domestic savings and weakened domestic demand are still forcing China to ship its goods abroad as some countries move to protect their own industries, said Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.

The situation is not sustainable, she said.

Businesses are feeling the pressure of ferocious competition as China’s economy has slowed, said Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in Linhai city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province.

“It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasingly the lack of it across the industry, since there’s significant homogenization,” said Zhou, whose company makes frames and lenses sold both in and outside China. “That has forced everyone to compete on price,” she said.

Trade curbs by the European Union pose an important risk at a time of heightened U.S. trade barriers and tariffs, Chia said.

Top Chinese officials insist Beijing is not seeking to expand the trade surplus but wants more balanced global trade.

China’s exports could be vulnerable to setbacks for the artificial intelligence industry, a concern that deepened with the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections given the public backlash against expansion of data centers.

“If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China’s exports hard,” Chia said.

Trade is among the top issues likely to be on the agenda in planned meetings between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit later this month in China’s technology hub Shenzhen.

A two-month extension of a trade truce until January has provided some relief to exporters, though it’s unclear how long that may last.

U.S. and European trade policies have added “a lot of difficulties” for Chinese businesses to expand in the markets, said Wang Xin, head of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, an industry group.

Strong exports have helped offset sluggish domestic demand in China, where the economy is forecast to meet Beijing’s official target of a 4.5% to 5% annual growth this year, slightly slower than last year’s 5% expansion.

News.title: How North Korean defectors view Kim Jong Un's daughter as his possible successor
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The teenage daughter of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has drawn intense international media attention as their frequent public appearances together fuel speculation that he is grooming her to succeed him one day.

There are debates about her status, but most experts expect Kim to eventually hand over power to one of his children and extend his family's rule into a fourth generation.

Here's a look at how North Korean defectors and others think about the girl, who is reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae, and the family's dynastic rule.

Tae Yongho

Tae, a former minister at North Korea’s Embassy in London, defected to South Korea in 2016 and later served as a member of South Korea’s parliament. Tae said it's deeply lamentable to observe what he believes are Kim's moves to prolong his family's rule.

“It's a wretched reality that unchecked power in an absolute monarchy is being passed down to a fourth generation in the 21st century," Tae said. “North Korea will likely fall further behind the outside world if it has a fourth-generation power succession.”

Kim Yumi

Kim fled North Korea in May 2023. She said many North Koreans are unhappy to see Kim’s daughter wearing her hair long down past her shoulders, walking around in high heels and dressing like a grown-up, because such styles aren’t allowed for ordinary teenagers in North Korea. But she said they have no choice but to keep their frustration to themselves out of fears of harsh punishment.

“People would now think Ju Ae would become their monarch,” she said.

Lee Si-young

Lee came to South Korea in 2013 and heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station. She said North Koreans wouldn't have complaints about the girl's hairdo and outfit because they've been so thoroughly brainwashed.

“They wouldn't know whether her clothes are designer brands but they think she can wear them because she's the daughter" of their supreme leader, she said.

Choi Song-juk

Choi, who fled North Korea in 2015, said that Kim’s daughter kissing her father on the cheek is “an extremely uncommon” display of affection between a father and his daughter in the North.

Living under a cult of personality centering on the Kim family, Choi said some North Koreans likely feel proud of such a scene, venerating Kim as “the father of all people," and "not a tyrant who killed even his uncle" in a series of brutal executions of his potential rivals.

Lee Young-hyeon

Lee is a defector and lawyer who runs a website meant to provide North Koreans with outside information. He said that given the North's deep-rooted male-centered hierarchy, North Koreans wouldn't readily accept a woman leader. Lee noted even South Korea has had only one female leader, President Park Geun-hye, who governed from 2013-2017.

“Even South Korea is a very patriarchal society where women find it difficult to hold leadership roles. I can't buy the idea of a woman becoming leader in North Korea, which is virtually a dynasty,” he said.

Oh Gyeong-seob

Oh, an analyst at Seoul’s Korea Institute for National Unification, cautioned against concluding that the girl is Kim's heir. But he said that if she's formally anointed as her father's heir, she could quickly cement her authority because members of the ruling elite with shared interests would rally around her and eliminate potential opponents.

“Whether the successor is a male or female doesn't really matter,” Oh said.

Ahn Kyung-su

Ahn, a researcher who has interviewed hundreds of defectors, said Kim would need to deliver economic improvements and raise living standards to make his people accept his succession plan in a more positive way. Ahn said that despite living under their country's repressive rule, younger North Koreans have changed how they think due to the spread of South Korean TV and other cultural content, posing a burden on Kim.

“North Korean people won't rise up against Kim. But what matters is whether he can have his people accept his plan happily or begrudgingly,” Ahn said.

Jo Sung-rae

Jo, who runs an online news site, said contacts in North Korea told him they weren’t yet sure if the girl is Kim’s heir. Jo himself believes she is, and that Kim’s concerns about his health have likely prompted him to rush the process of preparing her as his successor.

In late September, South Korea’s main spy agency told lawmakers that Kim showed no other significant signs of poor health, though he remained severely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease. Both his father and grandfather, who ruled North Korea before he inherited power in 2011, died of heart problems.

News.title: ‘Like gods reigning over humans’: Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.

Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family’s fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.

“My husband and I didn’t want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom,” said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.

North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.

This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.

Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she’s being groomed as her father’s heir.

The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.

North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.

To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country’s previous power successions, as well as several experts.

Most defectors believe the girl is Kim’s heir

Not much is known about Kim’s daughter except that she’s reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.

Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim’s “most beloved" and “respected” child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.

South Korea’s spy agency says she is Kim’s likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.

“During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un,” said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea’s Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. “They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un," when he accompanied his father as his heir.

Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea’s economy, said that her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.

Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.

Doubts remain about a woman becoming North Korea's leader

Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.

Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un’s influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.

“My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader,” said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.

Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family “are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter.”

Kim's push for hereditary power transfer faces little resistance at home

Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea’s spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.

North Koreans will passively "accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with,” said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.

During North Korea’s first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.

The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.

“A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system,” said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul’s Korea Institute for National Unification. “North Korea’s ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens.”

Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them “nonsense.”

Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.

Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.

“Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about the Kim family history," said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. “They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger.”

News.title: California voters reject measure to tax the wealth of billionaires
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

California voters have rejected a first-in-the-nation tax on the net worth of billionaires following a contentious ballot fight that generated huge spending by some prominent tech leaders eager to stop their taxes from going up.

The measure’s failure is a win for Democratic leaders who opposed it, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, who’s deciding whether to run for president in 2028. Critics of the tax, known as Proposition 40, said it would have prompted ultrawealthy taxpayers to leave the state.

The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone dumped more than $100 million into a political action committee working to defeat the measure.

The measure would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion. Most of the money would have been used to backfill federal funding cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone toward education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, which backed the tax, said it was necessary to replace an estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years.

Proposition 40 was the nation’s biggest test yet on an idea progressives have long championed: raising taxes on the ultra-rich by targeting the main way they make their money — through their investments as opposed to the paychecks they receive from work.

The measure attracted support from liberal leaders beyond the state, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who rallied in cities across California in the race’s closing weeks to urge voters to pass it.
