Sports.title: Can Hamilton and Verstappen fight back for F1 Brazilian GP victory?
Sports.content:
With Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen 20th and 21st on the grid of the Brazilian Grand Prix, Sunday’s Formula 1 race promises to be fascinating – regardless of weather conditions.

Hamilton and Verstappen happen to be two drivers who performed memorable recoveries at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace, a track where overtaking has always been easier than most.

Back in 2021, the seven-time world champion was excluded from qualifying results due to a technical breach, meaning he started the sprint from last; he fought his way up to fifth. With a five-place grid drop for a new engine, Hamilton was 10th on the grid for the grand prix but battled to the front and came out on top in a titanic duel against Verstappen.

Three years later, the Dutchman was eliminated in Q2 on a wet Sunday morning and also took a five-place grid penalty for his sixth internal combustion engine, ending up 17th on the grid. The rain also impacted the race, but Verstappen rose to the occasion and comfortably overtook Esteban Ocon for victory.

But the DRS device had facilitated Hamilton’s exceptional drives, and the overtake mode that now features on F1’s new power units instead isn’t as decisive; the Interlagos layout might actually make it worse.

When asked how easy overtaking would be compared to 2021, the Ferrari driver replied: “Harder, because back then we had, obviously, a very long straight, and if you got close, you had the DRS, and maybe a car wouldn't have it – whereas now, everyone is just opening up their wings.

“I think overtaking will be very, very, very hard. I'm not sure you're going to see the same sort of races that you've seen in the past. But maybe the wet conditions will change that.”

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“Now we don't have DRS anymore,” Verstappen concurred. “And the overtake mode is very limiting around here because of the long straight, everyone is draining the battery. So, your speed difference on the straight is going to be a lot less – a bit like Mexico, really. So, it will be quite a lot harder to pass than normal.”

So what will Hamilton’s strategy be? “I don't have one,” he responded. “Try to win, somehow.”

Verstappen, meanwhile, is banking on a number of incidents if he is to be a contender for victory. “Lots of safety cars, so they can't pull away, it keeps coming back to me,” the Red Bull racer said. “We'll see. I don't really think about it too much. I'll just go from lap one and see where I end up.”

He added: “I hope [with Lewis] we can clear the cars in front of us as quickly as we can.”

Across 19 grands prix so far in F1 2026, just two races have been won from outside the front row. Verstappen prevailed from fifth on the grid in Mexico, though he was virtually in the lead on lap one, and Antonelli remarkably triumphed from 19th in Italy. But if the expected rain impacts the race, then 2026’s dry-weather history will be meaningless.

Additional reporting by Isa Fernandes and Federico Faturos

Sports.title: The wet-weather challenges thrown up by Brazilian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
One hour, 23 minutes. You could've squeezed most of a football match into the rain delay during Formula 1 qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, and it looked for all the world like the session wouldn't actually get going again.

A repeat of 2024, where qualifying was squeezed onto Sunday morning, looked likely. Yet, a saviour arrived when a break in the clouds emerged, and the circuit had dried just enough for safety car specialist Bernd Maylander to give his approval of the conditions. It scarcely stopped a handful of drivers from having a moan about the visibility, but they soon accepted that they needed to lock in and focus up on getting around the track.

This meant the use of the lesser-spotted full-wet tyre, or the "x-wet" per the F1 lexicon. Often derided as a tyre only fit for bumbling around on behind the safety car, the blue-walled Pirelli was actually holding up pretty well and proved perfect for the level of standing water around the circuit. Aquaplaning, where the tyre struggles to break the surface tension of the water on-track, was nonetheless prevalent - but water dispersal as the rain held off soon brought the track to a more driveable state.

The downside of using the extreme wet tyre lies in the greater water dispersal (according to Pirelli, around 85 litres of water per second) which drastically cuts visibility as the spray rooster-tails out the back of the car. Yet, the dispersal is a necessary evil: without it, the circuit would just remain wetter for longer.

Although the rain lights ensure that the driver behind has at least some level of visibility, selecting your braking zone remains tricky; poor visibility means the driver must find a reference point in their immediate circle of vision. Stopping distances are also considerably longer, so a driver needs a different marker to their usual point of pedal application in the dry.

Considering all these climatic challenges, it's small wonder why race control takes a more tentative approach to wet conditions. Hence, it was a welcome surprise to see the session reopened - even if the circuit was still sodden with the afternoon downpour. Carlos Sainz reckoned that it was a "punchy" call from the FIA - but it only took a couple of laps to ensure the cars were more stable.

"It felt a bit punchy when we left on the x-wet because we were aquaplaning in sixth and seventh gear down the straights. And if you lose the car at those speeds, it's always going to be a big one," Sainz concluded after the session.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

"Also, very little visibility when you were running close to a car, but we were not forced to run close to cars in quali, so you can create a bit of a buffer to see. But it was very sketchy for two laps.

"Then we managed to create that little bit of dry line and the tyres started working, the aquaplaning started to go away. Everyone managed to keep the car on track until the end of Q1, which was a bit of a surprise, to be honest."

Liam Lawson agreed with Sainz's view of the session, stating that "when we started, it was extremely sketchy - I think we were definitely pushing it. But I like the fact that we were out there and not in the garage; I think obviously it is risky, but there weren't that many incidents."

As expected, the wet conditions delivered chances to those usually not accustomed to fighting at the top; the free practice performance-chasing was effectively rendered obsolete and the power units had slightly more parity as the effects of top-end performance and acceleration were mitigated by the low-grip track conditions.

This put a bit more of a premium on low-speed downforce and, crucially, keeping the tyres warm across Q1 - although Fernando Alonso nonetheless noted that "the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners, and we still have a little bit of an issue there".

The approach through Q1 was, initially, simply about trying to set clean laps and hope that the progression of the circuit and the tyres would yield a lap-on-lap improvement.

Of course, each driver was tested on their reaction times in the event aquaplaning occurred, and the 2026 power units and the control over the rear brakes added another hurdle to overcome. But each driver (largely) became increasingly dialled in, watched as the laptimes improved, and then started to push the braking zones a little bit more as the circuit dried up.

There was a transition point in Q2, however, as the intermediates soon became the tyre to be on. With less standing water, the full wet was starting to overheat and was giving up performance in the middle part of the lap, initially enough to perhaps offset the dampness through the first and final sectors, before all three became much more suitable for the intermediate overall.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

This meant that they could chase the track grip more, and it was evident that the times had begun to peak at the end of Q2 as the circuit approached its best conditions under the downpour. Getting the intermediate timing right, which Lawson reckoned he and his Racing Bulls team had nailed, was key to getting a couple of quicker laps in without risking the threat of falling off the circuit.

A few drivers struggled at this crossover, particularly with harvesting and braking into Turn 12 - Sainz and Ollie Bearman both had offs here, as newcomer Rafael Camara couldn't get the car to slow down enough before he careened into the barrier at the close of Q2.

With more rain impending during Q3, it was more about a mad dash to get a clean lap in, rather than watching the progression. That's perhaps when it felt most like 'normal' qualifying, as the tyres were effectively good enough for one lap with the expected downpour setting something of a timer.

It appeared that the majority of the drivers genuinely enjoyed the rare chance to tackle properly wet conditions, although some had a few qualms about the session restarting. George Russell surmised that "I love driving in the rain - but at some point, if that was a race, that was no way we should be driving in it - the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident is very, very high."

Perhaps there's a bit of a split of opinion between the younger and older drivers; both Lewis Hamilton and Nico Hulkenberg expressed their enjoyment of wet conditions, while new champion Kimi Antonelli labelled them "the wettest conditions I've ever driven [in]. So it was not the nicest of experiences"; both he and Bearman said that the circuit was over the limit at the Q1 restart, although the latter conceded that the early running did at least contribute to the circuit improving.

Regardless, it was valuable data for each of the drivers ahead of Sunday's race - where inclement weather is expected to play a role once again. And so begins the overnight discussions: does anyone risk a pit-lane start for a set-up change?

Andrea Kimi Antonelli looked on course to win his first race as the new world champion as he pulled out an eight-second lead over his pursuers over the opening 12 laps at Interlagos.

But he reported something felt wrong with his Mercedes’ handling soon after switching to slick tyres and spun off, allowing Lando Norris through into the lead. The two Red Bull drivers passed him and by lap 34 Antonelli was 17 seconds off the lead.

Antonelli’s exchanges with race engineer Peter Bonnington underline how he was mystified by his car’s handling. Bonnington kept him supplied with notes on where he could find more time but it was only after he swapped his flat-spotted set of slicks for a fresh set that he began to show more competitive pace.

Unfortunately for Antonelli, the rain returned soon afterwards. He pitted for intermediates again – collecting a penalty for an unsafe release as he did – and the early leader had to settle for a fifth-place finish.

Sports.title: Russell explains pit exit spin: ‘I took too much risk because I saw a chance to win’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell says he spun in the pit lane exit during the Brazilian Grand Prix because he thought he had a race-winning opportunity.

The Mercedes driver was running third early in the race as the track was drying. He was within 10 seconds of race leader Andrea Kimi Antonelli when he came in to swap his intermediate tyres for slicks on lap 17.

However Russell spun when he reached the pit lane exit. The error cost him around 16 seconds and dropped him behind several of his rivals.

“Obviously it was a bit of an up and down race,” said Russell, who eventually finished fourth. “I’ve no idea what happened on that pit exit, I probably just took too much risk because I was seeing an opportunity to go for the win at that point, but it happened.”

Russell was one of few drivers who only made two pit stops during the race, keeping his set of slick tyres on until the rain returned in the closing stages.

“Ironically, because that happened, I then didn’t pit for another set of slick tyres and it kind of put me back in the same position as I was before the incident,” he acknowledged.

The Mercedes driver set the second-fastest time in qualifying, and believed he could have been quickest had he not aborted his final run under instruction from his race engineer. He said he was satisfied with his performance.

“I’m probably more happy coming away from the weekend because the performance was good,” said Russell, who started seventh following a penalty for replacing his engine. “At this stage I care more about the performance and I care about the result because that’s what’s been my weak point.

“The performance yesterday was great, the performance on the soft tyre was really great today but obviously I did make that mistake. But it probably would have been a different picture if we’d have started P2.”

Sports.title: Piastri splits from Webber’s management team | Formula 1
Sports.content:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri has confirmed he is no longer being represented by Mark Webber’s management team.

Webber, who won nine grands prix during his 12 seasons in Formula 1 , has guided Piastri’s career since 2019. Piastri made his F1 debut with McLaren in 2023 and led much of last year’s championship before slipping to third place at the end of the season.

Piastri issued a statement saying he had split from the management team led by Webber and his partner Ann by mutual arrangement.

“I’d like to thank Mark and Ann for all their support and advice over the years,” said Piastri. “Their guidance has been invaluable, particularly in navigating the beginning of my F1 career. I wish them all the best going forward.”

Webber said he and Ann were “proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar’s career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early on.

“Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close. This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure, and for us to embark on our new ventures. We wish Oscar all the very best for a long and successful career.”

Sports.title: Stewards ruled Hamilton “gained no advantage” by passing Bearman off-track | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The Brazilian Grand Prix stewards ruled Lewis Hamilton did not gain an advantage when he overtook Oliver Bearman off the track during the Brazilian Grand Prix.

Hamilton slowed down and let Bearman overtake him on lap seven after the stewards began investigating the incident.

The stewards do not order drivers to swap positions but can issue penalties of five or ten seconds if they determine a competitor gained a place on a rival by going outside track limits. Teams often instruct drivers to surrender positions to avoid these potentially more costly penalties.

Hamilton passed Bearman at the exit of Descida do Lago on the first lap of the race. Bearman had gone off earlier in the lap at Curva do Sol.

The stewards ruled Hamilton had sufficient speed advantage over Bearman to make the pass and was forced off the track by his rival. However in explaining their decision not to penalise Hamilton they also noted he let Bearman past.

“In defending the position, car 87 [Barman] moved to the right and car 44 [Hamilton] was pushed off the track to avoid a collision. Car 44 clearly had the momentum for the overtake and gained no advantage by going off the track. We also noted that the position was subsequently given back by car 44. We therefore took no further action.”

There have been cases in which the stewards have declined to penalise a driver for overtaking a rival off-track and not giving back the position, notably when Yuki Tsunoda forced Lando Norris off during last year’s Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Sports.title: Willy Hutchinson Has the Belt and the Style Canelo Hates
Sports.content:
Willy Hutchinson offers Canelo Alvarez an intriguing path toward an undisputed crown at light heavyweight, along with the precise movement that historically gives Canelo fits. After Hutchinson claimed the vacant WBC belt against Joshua Buatsi, Chris Mannix proposed the pairing, prompting Sergio Mora to wonder about the logic behind it.

Mora highlighted Hutchinson’s slick jab, deceptive rhythm, and southpaw looks, arguing that if Canelo wants to spend twelve rounds chasing an elusive stylist, he might as well target Dmitry Bivol directly.

“It’s the movers, the guys that don’t engage, the tricky guys,” said Mora on Mannix’s YouTube channel, who pointed to Hutchinson’s jab, timing and habit of switching southpaw. If Canelo is prepared to deal with that style, Mora would rather see him fight Dmitry Bivol again.

Mannix’s pitch carries clear tactical purpose. Should Canelo defeat Hutchinson while Bivol retains the remaining straps, their second meeting would crown an undisputed champion. Capturing the WBC strap gives Canelo fresh leverage after dropped rounds in their initial encounter. The cost, however, involves chasing a rangier opponent who rarely plants his feet long enough for return fire.

Against Buatsi, Hutchinson demonstrated his ability to reset aggressive opponents. He scored with his lead hand from distance, slipped away before Buatsi set his base, and tied up on the inside. While Christian Mbilli offered Canelo a stationary target, Hutchinson could force him to spend full minutes fighting into close quarters, only to wrap him up before the Mexican star digs into the ribs.

Stylistically, Hutchinson brings every single attribute that gives Canelo severe problems. Canelo has always struggled against slick, disciplined movers with active lead hands and sharp ring generalship. Floyd Mayweather wrote the blueprint, Dmitry Bivol executed it with physical authority, and Terence Crawford exploited those exact gaps in mobility and lateral footwork.

Hutchinson takes that exact stylistic formula and backs it with genuine light heavyweight size. At 6-foot-1 with a 73-inch reach, he is not an undersized fighter moving up; he is a natural 175-pounder in his physical prime. As he proved against Joshua Buatsi, he can switch stances seamlessly, snap a long jab, control distance, and disengage before an opponent can set their base to load up power shots.

For an aging Canelo whose foot speed has noticeably slowed and who relies heavily on opponents standing in the pocket to trade, chasing Hutchinson around the ring for 12 rounds would be an absolute nightmare. From a risk-versus-reward perspective, it is even worse for Canelo.

Hutchinson possesses world-class talent and now holds a major belt, but he does not carry the mainstream American pay-per-view profile to deliver a massive blockbuster gate. If Canelo wins, critics immediately dismiss it by claiming he merely defeated an opponent without marquee status. If Canelo loses or gets thoroughly outboxed, his aura and marketability take another massive hit against a fighter most casual fans are just learning about.

If Turki Alalshikh put an obscene sum on the table for Willy Hutchinson, Canelo and Eddy Reynoso would probably have a private conversation behind closed doors that sounds very different from what they would say into a microphone.

Their internal calculation would break down into two stages. For starters, Reynoso would likely watch the tape and spot every red flag imaginable. Reynoso is a meticulous matchmaker who protects the Canelo brand with extreme precision. He knows Canelo’s legs are not what they were five years ago, and he knows how much trouble tall, athletic switch-hitters who move laterally cause his fighter. Reynoso’s immediate coaching instinct would be to steer Canelo away from a nightmare style that yields minimal glory.

From there, Canelo’s response would depend entirely on what that number looked like. Canelo has reached the point in his career where he views himself as an enterprise. If the money was merely “great” ($40 million to $50 million), Canelo would casually brush it off. He would tell Turki that Hutchinson brings nothing to the gate, has no real profile in North America, and does not deserve to share the ring with him. He would counter by asking for that same bag to fight someone like Chris Eubank Jr. or another name who actually comes forward to trade.

If Turki offered an absurd, once-in-a-lifetime figure, say, $100 million or more with full guarantees, Reynoso and Canelo would pause. But even then, they would attempt to alter the playing field before signing anything. They would push for a catchweight, demand strict rehydration stipulations, or try to impose terms designed to drain Hutchinson’s mobility and take the spring out of his legs.

If Turki insisted on a straight 175-pound fight with zero compromises, Canelo would almost certainly pass. At this stage of his career, with his financial empire secure, taking a guaranteed boxing lesson against a young, 6-foot-1 mover for any amount of money is not worth watching his aura evaporate in front of the world. Canelo would smile, thank His Excellency, and ask to fight a brawler instead.

Sports.title: Canelo Plans to Renew Turki Deal After March Fight
Sports.content:
Canelo Álvarez plans to renew his deal with Turki Alalshikh after his March fight, trainer Eddy Reynoso says. His decision win over Christian Mbilli may have strengthened the case for another deal, which would keep Saudi backing in play for a Terence Crawford rematch.

“It’s the last one [the fight in March], but we’re going to renew. There are very good plans for Saúl. He already spoke with Turki, and there are good plans to continue his career,” said Reynoso, in comments to La Afición translated and shared by EverythingBoxing’s Darshan Desai.

What Turki Could Get From Another Deal

Some fans saw the Mbilli win as Canelo’s best performance since he stopped Caleb Plant in 2021. Canelo still fought in bursts, but he had to keep finding clean shots against an unbeaten contender who pressed him for 12 rounds. That gave Alalshikh a fresh performance to judge alongside Canelo’s name and drawing power. Reynoso gave no indication of how much the win figured in their talks.

Crawford offers the biggest commercial reason to renew. The first fight gives the promotion an obvious question to sell. Can Canelo reverse the result? Saudi backing helped make the first fight happen, and a renewed deal would give Canelo a direct route back to the same financier. The boxing problem remains. Crawford could still use his jab and reach to score from outside and make Canelo follow him. Beating Mbilli, who came forward, tells us little about how Canelo would close distance on Crawford.

Hamzah Sheeraz offers a different kind of event at 168 pounds. His British following gives the promotion a second market, and his height and reach give it something to sell beyond Canelo’s name. Sheeraz has less experience at that level, though. Compare that with IBF champion Osleys Iglesias, a dangerous southpaw whose belt gives Canelo a sporting reason to fight him. Sheeraz gives Alalshikh an easier fight to market, especially if the aim is to put on an event that can draw in Britain as well as with Canelo’s audience.

A return to 175 pounds would open up two more fights. Dmitry Bivol already beat Canelo, so a rematch comes with a result to avenge and a clear question about whether Canelo can get past Bivol’s jab and footwork. Artur Beterbiev would be a first-time opponent. The sell there is whether Canelo can hold his ground against a naturally bigger puncher who can force him to work at a pace he would rather set himself. Both fights depend on Canelo being willing to go back up to light heavyweight.

Reynoso named no opponents for an extension and gave no terms. If the deal goes through, Crawford would offer the biggest event, while Sheeraz would give Alalshikh a way to build one around Canelo at 168. Bivol and Beterbiev only enter the picture if Canelo wants another fight at 175.

For Canelo’s camp, Crawford, 39, is the ideal financial play with almost zero physical danger. He is a smaller guy who relied on running, movement, and potshots to nick rounds. He was never going to walk Canelo down or smash him up. There is zero wear and tear on Canelo’s body in that matchup compared to getting in the trenches with a relentless slugger or moving back up to 175.

If Crawford came out on the back foot the first time, a full year sitting on the couch is not going to turn him into a pressure fighter. Ring rust makes guys even more defensive. If he gets pried out of retirement by a massive Saudi check, he will likely double down on the track shoes, look to survive on points from the outside, and avoid any inside trade.

For Reynoso and Canelo, it represents a massive payday without the physical toll. The only hurdle is whether Turki actually wants to cough up another nine-figure purse to finance a fight that already lacked real fireworks.

Sports.title: Alycia Baumgardner Outclasses Turhan, Then Gets Called Out By Caroline Dubois
Sports.content:
On Sunday night, November 8th, at MVPW07, in her lightweight debut, Alycia “The Bomb” Baumgardner put her boxing skills on display as she outclassed Elif Turhan (14-1, 8 KOs) and won the IBF world title.

Baumgardner was elusive; she touched the body, and her power shots were sharp and accurate. Turhan couldn’t find the range to land her right hand, and she failed to make any in-ring adjustments.

In the opening round, Baumgardner set the tone as she fired the jab and followed it up with a three-punch combination. Round two featured back-and-forth action as Baumgardner’s shots were landing and Turhan was missing wildly.

At the 1:05 mark of the third round, Baumgardner landed a big right hand that knocked Turhan off-balance. As the third round was coming to a close, Baumgardner hurt Turhan, but the referee prematurely stepped in to stop the action.

The referee made a significant error when she stopped the action because she thought the ten-second bell was the final bell, which is the one that officially ends the round.

During the first four rounds of the fight, the hard-hitting Turhan was routinely off the mark when she threw her power shots. In the 5th round, Turhan finally experienced success when she was able to land the uppercut.

The second half of the fight featured Baumgardner working off the jab and landing a variety of punches. Baumgardner exposed Turhan as she made it apparent that we were viewing a matchup between a highly skilled boxer and a one-dimensional fighter.

At the conclusion of the 10-round contest, the scorecards reflected the dominance that took place inside of the ring. All three judges scored the bout (100-90) in favor of Baumgardner.

With the victory, Alycia Baumgardner (19-1, 7 KOs) won the IBF title and became a two-division world champion. Following the impressive victory, Baumgardner was confronted by WBC/WBO lightweight champion Caroline Dubois.

After Baumgardner conducted her post-fight interview, Dubois left her ringside seat, grabbed a mic, and addressed Baumgardner. While standing by the ring, Dubois issued a challenge to the new IBF lightweight champion.

“I handle my business; you handled yours. Are we fighting?” Dubois asked. “Are we fighting champ? Are we fighting champ? Are we fighting champ? That’s all you got to say. That’s all you got to say. Why you’re not looking at me champ? Why you’re not looking at me champ? Let’s go. Undisputed.”

Caroline Dubois pulled a bold move based on the fact that she was scheduling a fight for undisputed status while her February 2027 opponent, the WBA lightweight champion Stephanie Han, was sitting one seat away from Dubois at ringside.

During the verbal exchange, Alycia Baumgardner was advising Dubois to focus on her next opponent as opposed to looking ahead to a fight for undisputed. However, if Dubois is successful on February 20th, a Baumgardner vs. Dubois bout would be the 2027 fight of the year for women’s boxing.

Sports.title: Dana White Says Zuffa Will Work With Sanctioning Bodies Case by Case
Sports.content:
Dana White plans to treat boxing sanctioning bodies as optional business partners, dealing with them when convenient and bypassing them when they become an obstacle. Denzel Bentley found out firsthand what that freedom costs the athlete, surrendering his WBO middleweight championship to face Shane Mosley Jr. under the Zuffa Boxing banner.

“We’re sort of dealing with that on a case-by-case basis, and if we can work it out, we’d like to for the fighters. If we can’t, then we won’t,” White said at Saturday’s post-fight press conference.

In mixed martial arts, White operates an enclosed system. He picks the challengers, dictates the schedule, and awards the internal championship hardware. Boxing strips away that total control. Zuffa can stage any pairing it likes, but an external regulatory body controls the hardware. That gives the sanctioning body immediate leverage over the athlete, even if it cannot stop the promoter from opening the arena doors.

Bentley attempted to negotiate a delay, asking the WBO to permit an interim defense against Mosley before facing mandatory challenger Yoenli Hernandez. The sanctioning body held all the leverage. Warriors Boxing had already claimed the promotional rights to the Hernandez fight with a $200,000 purse bid, guaranteeing Bentley a $150,000 payday. The WBO denied the exception and stripped Bentley on October 30. Zuffa staged the Mosley bout regardless, eight days later in London.

That sequence exposed the sharp divide between promotional convenience and fighter interest. Bentley walked away from a locked-in six-figure purse and the regulatory leverage of a world championship belt. While his London compensation remains undisclosed, losing the belt permanently damages his future bargaining position at the elite level. For Zuffa, the upside was immediate and clear. Keeping Bentley in London retained two in-house fighters for its own platform instead of sending its champion to perform on a competitor’s broadcast.

The WBO acted out of institutional preservation. Once a purse bid concludes, allowing a champion to pivot to an unapproved bout undermines the entire mandatory framework. Permitting Bentley to delay would have shelved Hernandez and made a mockery of Warriors Boxing’s winning bid. Enforcing the vacancy was the only way the organization could protect its authority and the credibility of its bidding process.

London proved Zuffa can run standalone events without the approval of an alphabet organization. The breaking point will arrive when White tries to stage an undisputed championship or a major unification. Stripping one titlist instantly evaporates the historical premise of a unification bout. When the hardware itself is the primary selling point for the global audience, White will either have to accept the rules of the boxing establishment or abandon the pursuit of true world titles altogether.

Sports.title: Anthony Yarde In Line For WBC Title Shot After Benavidez Knockout Loss
Sports.content:
Anthony Yarde was knocked out by David Benavidez and spent a full year on the shelf. Somehow, his reward could be an immediate crack at a world title. Frank Warren is considering using Yarde for Willy Hutchinson’s first WBC light heavyweight title defense in March, effectively granting him championship access without the burden of winning an eliminator.

Hutchinson had to go through the fire with Joshua Buatsi across two fights to capture the vacant belt. Yarde, meanwhile, might walk directly into the challenger’s corner coming off a stoppage defeat and twelve months of inactivity. What has Yarde done since Benavidez demolished him to justify cutting to the front of the line? Nothing inside the ring. His entire argument is built on name recognition and the equity of older wars.

Warren was open about the option on talkSPORT Boxing: “Anthony Yarde was in the ring. I don’t know where we’re going to go with that one. We’ll see if we can agree terms. That’s something we may consider as well.”

Casual British fight fans recognize Yarde from his past encounters with Benavidez, Artur Beterbiev, and Sergey Kovalev. That name value makes him infinitely simpler to sell to television buyers than a high-risk contender like Albert Ramirez. If the WBC blesses a voluntary defense and numbers make sense, Warren converts Hutchinson’s hard-won triumph into a profitable domestic event. If Hutchinson retains, he collects a marquee domestic scalp. If Yarde pulls it off, Warren crowns a long-tenured in-house headliner.

The timing also plays directly into Hutchinson’s hands. Yarde carries sufficient power to make Hutchinson pay if he retreats into the ropes, but Hutchinson possesses the footwork to keep Yarde turning. Forcing Yarde to reset his base prevents him from sitting down on heavy bursts. As the rounds wear on, Yarde faces the grueling reality of sustaining hard combination punching over twelve rounds after such a protracted layoff.

The commercial logic is obvious. The sporting logic is nonexistent. A tune-up win would establish what Yarde has left after the Benavidez beating. Under Warren’s plan, Yarde could skip that test and answer the question with a world title on the line.

Sports.title: Denzel Bentley Wants Zuffa to Skip the Line
Sports.content:
Denzel Bentley is calling on Zuffa Boxing to steer him straight back toward middleweight championship hardware. Giving up his WBO belt came as the direct cost of facing Shane Mosley Jr. instead of mandatory challenger Yoenli Hernandez.

With that bout behind him, Bentley is targeting two stablemates who hold the remaining pieces of the division: IBF champion Aaron McKenna and WBC titlist Carlos Adames.

Scoring a knockdown over Mosley helped Bentley secure a close unanimous decision during his promotional debut. The result delivered a recognizable name for his record, yet the real payoff hinges entirely on what Zuffa delivers next. Stepping straight into a voluntary defense allows Bentley to cash in on that narrow win without slogging through another eliminator. Zuffa controls all three fighters internally, leaving promotional squabbles out of the equation once sanctioning bodies give their blessing.

Bentley told The Ring that McKenna or Adames are the targets. He wants whichever man keeps their title next. “I think McKenna or Adames because they are the ones with the titles. I want to fight one of those two next. Next year, either one of those two; they’ve both got their belts. Whoever keeps their strap, I want them next.”

A clash with McKenna appears simpler to schedule. The newly crowned champion has yet to lock in his first defense, and Bentley publicly offered to travel across the Irish Sea. That willingness hands Zuffa an easy sell for a stadium or arena defense in Ireland against a proven puncher. McKenna cannot afford to march forward upright against someone who sits down on short counter hooks with sudden authority. If McKenna uses his jab and relentless output to keep Bentley backing up, those counterpunching lanes vanish quickly over twelve rounds.

Taking on Adames is asking for a beating. Adames has real power, switches stances smoothly, and loves tearing into guys who linger in mid-range. Bentley could get caught along the ropes, and once Adames starts letting fly with those heavy combinations, it turns into a short night.

Dodging Yoenli Hernandez was pure self-preservation. Hernandez is a sharp power-punching Cuban amateur gold medalist who would have put Bentley through a grueling fight for a modest purse.

Targeting McKenna makes complete sense if they want to stay on the path of least resistance: McKenna is tall, fights upright, and walks into range with his chin up. He throws good volume, but he lacks the one-punch explosiveness to terrify Bentley. Bentley can sit down, wait for McKenna to march forward, and drop those short left hooks that stunned Mosley. If Bentley wants a belt he actually has a puncher’s chance of taking, McKenna is the target.

The sanctioning body optics are an absolute circus. Bentley literally just treated a world title like a disposable bargaining chip. When a fighter turns his nose up at an ordered mandatory defense to chase an off-brand debut bout, why should the IBF or WBC reward him with immediate voluntary status?

Sanctioning bodies care about sanctioning fees, but they also hate champions who abandon obligations the second a tough Cuban contender turns up. Putting Bentley in with McKenna signals to the entire sport that mandatories mean nothing. If Bentley wins the IBF strap, there is zero guarantee he stays in line for their mandatory either. He has already shown he would rather drop a belt and wander off than face a high-risk challenger.

Zuffa might want to push Bentley into McKenna’s first defense because it sells well in the UK and Ireland, but it completely undermines the legitimacy of the rankings. Bentley’s handlers will inevitably steer him away from Adames, but handing him an immediate shortcut to McKenna makes a mockery of the system.

Sports.title: Diego Pacheco Risks Plenty for Little Against Fulghum
Sports.content:
Diego Pacheco takes a real knockout risk against Darius Fulghum on Saturday in Carson without a single guarantee waiting on the other side. Winning keeps his WBC Silver and WBO International belts while handing Eddie Hearn another top-fifteen name to sell.

What it does not do is force a world champion into the ring. Neither organization made this a final eliminator, creating a dangerous setup: real physical risk with almost no official leverage.

At 25, Pacheco has time on his side, but boxing crowds run out of patience fast. Matchroom previously walked away from two separate fights with Christian Mbilli, passing on an IBF eliminator and a WBC interim title bout. Pacheco then pulled out of a vacant WBO world title fight with Hamzah Sheeraz after a purse bid was called. That hesitation backfired once Sheeraz vacated.

Because Pacheco was already tied to Fulghum, the WBO bypassed its No. 2 contender entirely and ordered Janibek Alimkhanuly to negotiate with No. 3 Jacob Bank instead. Turning down official eliminators surrenders control. Contenders waiting around for better timing end up watching guys ranked beneath them step straight into world title shots.

Pacheco’s fight against Kevin Sadjo last December in Stockton exposed the exact survival reflex that makes the Fulghum matchup genuinely dangerous.

When Sadjo put Pacheco down in the eighth round, the technical game plan flew out the window. Pacheco did not regain his composure behind a stiff jab, move to create space, or use ring generalship to recover. He went into pure panic mode, wrapping both arms around Sadjo like a vice the second distance closed. It was excessive, blatant clinching designed to kill the clock rather than fight back, and on another night with a referee less tolerant of persistent holding, Pacheco loses points or faces a disqualification warning. The look in his eyes told everyone watching that he wanted no part of the exchanges once his chin was checked.

That survival instinct becomes a glaring liability against Fulghum. Fulghum is not a crude brawler who gives you room to rest. He is a heavy-handed, aggressive puncher who comes forward with bad intentions inside the pocket. If Fulghum connects and hurts Pacheco early, Pacheco cannot afford to clamp on like a sea lamprey and hope the referee lets him hold for four rounds.

Bringing that specific flaw into the Fulghum analysis exposes the real danger:

Pacheco’s chin and ring composure are already under serious question. When a fighter turns down Mbilli and Sheeraz to preserve a clean record for a Canelo Alvarez or Jaime Munguia payday, getting dragged into deep waters by a live dog like Fulghum is suicidal matchmaking. If Pacheco gets tagged on Saturday and reverts to the octopus routine, a sharp referee will take points, the crowd will turn on him, and any voluntary sales pitch Hearn has for Canelo evaporates before the final bell even sounds.

Hearn wants to bypass sanctioning body politics altogether in favor of high-profile voluntary matchmaking .“If we can get Jaime Munguia, we’ll beat him, then we’ll face Canelo Alvarez as well,” said Hearn to DAZN after Pacheco stopped Immanuwel Aleem. That roadmap sounds great on camera, but voluntary talks depend on rival promoters agreeing to play ball.

Canelo does not hand out voluntary paydays just to do Hearn a favor. Contenders get Canelo by bringing massive commercial demand, undisputed hardware, or pay-per-view leverage to the table. Jaime Munguia earned his shot because he had already held a belt at 154 and had the Mexican fan base to anchor a Cinco de Mayo weekend.

Beating Munguia for the WBA belt would give Pacheco real chips to play with, but Matchroom still has to get Munguia into the ring first. Fulghum is the landmine in the middle of it all. He has 13 knockouts in 15 wins, real amateur credentials, and heavy enough hands to wreck the entire script in one round.

Even an ugly, labored decision win hurts the sales pitch. Emphatic knockout or not, Pacheco still leaves the ring Saturday night depending on Hearn’s salesmanship instead of an enforceable title mandate. Pacheco already passed on fights that offered direct routes to a belt. Taking on that kind of danger for a bargaining chip is why Saturday is such a massive gamble.

Sports.title: Alycia Baumgardner Sweeps Elif Nur Turhan to Win IBF Title
Sports.content:
Alycia Baumgardner took away Elif Nur Turhan’s unbeaten record and her IBF lightweight title on Sunday night, using a sharp jab and quick counters to win all 10 rounds on each judge’s card. All three scored it 100-90 for Baumgardner, who became a two-division world champion in her lightweight debut.

Turhan (14-1, 8 KOs) spent much of the early going trying to get close enough to throw her looping right hand. Baumgardner’s jab made her start those attacks from farther out than she wanted. When Turhan committed to the overhand anyway, Baumgardner (19-1, 7 KOs) could step clear and catch her before she was set to punch again. Turhan kept bringing the fight to her, but Baumgardner landed the cleaner shots while giving the champion few chances to follow up.

The pattern held through the middle rounds. Turhan stayed busy and found openings with hooks and uppercuts when she shortened her punches. Baumgardner took those shots and went back to the jab, making Turhan, 31, work her way inside again. Turhan’s best punches came once she was close enough to throw without reaching. Too often, she had to risk a wide shot just to get there.

Turhan landed clean uppercuts in the ninth and kept pressing in the tenth, still looking for a big shot after spending much of the night behind. Baumgardner, 32, kept her composure and continued to make Turhan miss and pay for coming forward. The three shutout cards gave Baumgardner every round, even with Turhan landing some of her best punches late.

The win gives Baumgardner a belt at 135 pounds after her undisputed run at 130 and puts a potential unification with Caroline Dubois in play. Turhan gave her an immediate test at the new weight. She kept coming for 30 minutes, landed cleanly when she got inside, and made Baumgardner keep working to regain her distance. Baumgardner did it often enough that none of the three judges found a round to give the defending champion.

The fight headlined Most Valuable Promotions at College Park Center in Arlington, Texas. It was contested over 10 three-minute rounds at the 135-pound limit.

Earlier on the card, Ramla Ali won the vacant IBF and WBO super bantamweight titles by split decision over Mikiah Kreps, and Skye Nicolson retained her WBC belt at the same weight by unanimous decision over Miyo Yoshida.

Ghana News.title: ‘We have waited too long’ – Bunkpurugu MP on GH¢10m media fund
Ghana News.content:
Dr. Abednego Lamangin Bandim

The allocation of GH¢10 million as seed money for the Media Development Fund has come after years of waiting and calls for greater support for Ghana’s media industry, the MP for Bunkpurugu, Dr Abednego Lamangin Bandim, has said.

He said the announcement by President John Dramani Mahama had been welcomed across the political divide in Parliament, describing it as a significant commitment to an industry that had long looked forward to such support.

“We have waited for it for a very long time,” Dr Bandim said on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, November 9.

He said the President’s announcement had immediately triggered discussions among lawmakers, with members on both sides of the House expressing support for the initiative.

According to him, the GH¢10 million commitment marked the first time a President had made what he considered a substantial financial pledge towards the development of the media in Ghana.

Dr Bandim said the President’s professional background in journalism and communications had also raised expectations that he would take steps to support the industry.

“People are not surprised because it was expected that it will take President John Mahama to do this, to make this announcement, to make this commitment, because he is one of us, a journalist himself,” he said.

He pointed to Mr Mahama’s experience as a journalist, public relations and communications practitioner, former Minister of Communications and member of the Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) as factors that made the announcement unsurprising.

The Bunkpurugu MP, who holds a PhD in communications management, said the President’s understanding of the media landscape had helped shape expectations that the long-awaited commitment would eventually materialise.

He also disclosed that discussions had started in Parliament on the legislative process for establishing the fund.

Dr Bandim said he had discussed the matter with the Ranking Member of the relevant committee, whom he identified as Munam, and indicated that the committee would take up the bill when it was presented as a Private Member’s Bill.

He said lawmakers were awaiting the bill before proceeding with consideration of the proposed fund.

Ghana News.title: UG students reject hostel fee hikes as EFL raises academic freedom concerns
Ghana News.content:
The Economic Fighters League (EFL) has thrown its support behind students of the University of Ghana who staged a demonstration against increased hostel accommodation charges, describing the protest as a broader struggle to protect academic freedom and the right of students to organise and challenge university authorities.

The group said the demonstration on November 9, 2026, had brought renewed attention to concerns about rising accommodation costs, student representation and what it described as an increasingly restrictive environment for student activism on university campuses.

In a statement issued under the banner of its Students Command, the EFL commended members of the Concerned Students of the University of Ghana and allied groups for taking to the streets to oppose the proposed increases by the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL).

The university's initial proposal was to increase hostel fees by 26 per cent, but the adjustment was subsequently revised to between 15 and 19 per cent following engagements with stakeholders.

The students, however, rejected the revised charges, particularly the 15 per cent increase for standard four-in-a-room accommodation.

They are also demanding the abolition of the UGEL hostel management framework, the removal of its management and greater transparency and accountability in the determination of accommodation fees.

The EFL said the students' concerns were justified, arguing that they were being asked to pay higher charges without sufficient evidence of corresponding improvements in accommodation facilities or meaningful consultation.

It said the increases would further strain students and their families at a time when the cost of living was already placing considerable pressure on household finances.

The group also criticised the University of Ghana Students' Representative Council (UGSRC) and the Graduate Students Association of Ghana, University of Ghana (GRASAG-UG), for what it described as their failure to visibly support the demonstration.

According to the EFL, the two student representative bodies distanced themselves from the march, citing the organisers' registration status and cautioning students about the Public Order Act.

Although the bodies had acknowledged the financial burden of accommodation costs and ongoing negotiations with university management, the EFL said student leadership must go beyond expressing sympathy for aggrieved students.

It maintained that student representatives had a responsibility to defend the interests and rights of their constituents, particularly when those rights were being challenged.

The group further raised concerns about what it described as a climate of fear and victimisation that was discouraging students from participating openly in demonstrations and other forms of collective action.

Drawing on its engagement with more than 10,000 students through its platform, the EFL said there was considerable support for the campaign against the accommodation increases, although many students were reluctant to demonstrate publicly.

It attributed the reluctance to what it described as weakened student organising networks and fears of disciplinary action, surveillance and possible retaliation by university authorities and the state.

The EFL argued that academic freedom should not be confined to the rights of lecturers to teach, research and publish, but should also protect students' ability to organise, assemble, express dissent and participate in decisions affecting their university experience.

It cited student activism at universities such as Oxford, Cambridge, Yale and Columbia, where demonstrations over Palestine, government policies and other public issues had formed part of campus life.

The group said such demonstrations did not undermine the reputation of those institutions but rather contributed to their intellectual culture and traditions of debate.

It expressed concern that students in Ghana's leading universities increasingly felt unable to exercise similar freedoms, citing what it described as restrictions on student organising, disruptions to established student networks, limitations on hall celebrations and activities, and measures discouraging large gatherings.

The EFL also called for a review of the university's In-Out-Out-Out system, arguing that its implications should be assessed beyond administrative considerations to include its effects on student solidarity, participation and freedom of association.

"A university should cultivate independent thinkers, not compliant subjects. It should encourage students to question power, not condition them to fear it," the statement said.

The group said the Legon demonstration went beyond the immediate dispute over hostel fees, describing it as part of a wider struggle against the privatisation and commercialisation of university life and the erosion of students' democratic rights.

It commended students who participated in the protest, those who supported the action in other ways and individuals who continued to organise despite what it described as the risks they perceived.

The EFL called on students across the country's universities to defend their rights to organise, assemble and speak out.

It also urged university authorities to end practices it said intimidated students and undermined collective action, while challenging student representative bodies to reclaim their responsibility to defend the interests of those they represented.

The statement concluded that academic freedom could not be fully realised if students were afraid to express dissent or organise around issues affecting their welfare.

"A university without student activism is not a university at its best," it said.

Ghana News.title: New Economy raises questions over delivery of 24-hour economy – IPPA
Ghana News.content:
The Institute of Public Policy and Accountability (IPPA) has questioned the government's proposed $10 billion New Economy programme, demanding clarity on how it differs from the 24-Hour Economy initiative announced earlier as a major driver of job creation and economic transformation.

In a press statement signed by the Executive Director of the Institute ahead of the 2027 Budget Statement, the Institute said Ghanaians needed explanations about the new programme, particularly when several flagship interventions announced in the 2026 Budget had yet to demonstrate tangible results.

The proposed New Economy programme is expected to attract $10 billion in investment between 2027 and 2030.

However, IPPA said the government must first account for the implementation of existing commitments rather than introduce new programmes extending beyond its current mandate.

It argued that the 2026 Budget had raised expectations of a transition from macroeconomic stabilisation to investment-led growth, job creation and economic transformation, but questioned whether the promised outcomes were materialising.

The Institute cited a decline in non-oil GDP growth from 8.2% in the first half of 2025 to 5.9% in the corresponding period of 2026 as evidence of what it described as stagnating economic performance.

It also pointed to October 2026 figures from the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS), which it said showed that close to two million young people were neither employed nor in education or training.

"Where are the millions of jobs promised under the Big Push?" the Institute asked, questioning the employment impact of the government's investment commitments.

IPPA said the 2026 Budget provided for total expenditure of GH¢302.46 billion, including GH¢57.53 billion in capital expenditure, and committed GH¢30 billion to the flagship Big Push infrastructure programme.

It noted that the budget also outlined interventions across agriculture, energy, health, education, transport and housing.

However, the Institute maintained that the effectiveness of a budget should be measured by its delivery rather than the size of its allocations or the number of programmes announced.

On agriculture, IPPA said several interventions presented as central to the government's transformation agenda had yet to show significant implementation.

These include the Farmer Service Centres, Feed Ghana Programme, Oil Palm Development Programme, construction of 1,000 kilometres of agricultural enclave roads, a GH¢200 million food buffer-stock intervention and the provision of mechanisation equipment to farmers.

The Institute said the initiatives were intended to move Ghana from subsistence farming towards a more productive and commercially oriented agricultural sector.

"Little or nothing has been done to implement these agricultural policies," it claimed, adding that it expected the Finance Minister to provide updates on their implementation in the 2027 Budget Statement.

IPPA also raised concerns about the implementation framework for the 24-Hour Economy, which was presented as a key mechanism for expanding production and creating employment.

Citing its December 2025 assessment, the Institute said it had questioned whether the resources allocated in the 2026 Budget were adequate to support the programme's full implementation.

It also identified a lack of sufficiently clear targets and rollout arrangements as weaknesses that could undermine the initiative.

According to IPPA, the central challenge confronting the government is the gap between its policy ambitions and the financial, institutional and implementation capacity required to translate them into measurable outcomes.

It argued that the government was approaching its third year in office without demonstrating sufficient progress on several flagship policies announced in previous budgets.

Ghana, the Institute said, needed fewer ambitious programme announcements and greater accountability for existing commitments.

"Ghana does not need another budget filled with impressive project names and ambitious policy targets. It needs a government that can deliver what it has already promised," the statement said.

Ghana News.title: Nvidia, CEO Huang sued over disclosures related to suspected Chinese spy
Ghana News.content:
Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has overseen explosive growth

Nvidia and Chief Executive Jensen Huang were sued on Monday in a proposed class action accusing them of defrauding shareholders by concealing Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy.

According to a complaint filed in federal court in San Jose, ​California, the defendants misled shareholders about Huang's alleged ​affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based ⁠Megaspeed who is not related to him, and did ​not disclose that the matter raised national security concerns that ​threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.

The New York Times reported last month about the alleged relationship, and that US authorities had concluded Alice Huang ​was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to ​a request for comment.

Jensen Huang told Nvidia's employees, opens new tab he had been unfaithful to ‌his ⁠wife, without disclosing details of the alleged relationship.

He co-founded Nvidia and led the Santa Clara, California-based company as it became the world's most valuable chipmaker, making him one of the world's most prominent symbols of the artificial intelligence boom.

Nvidia announced a probe into the matter on Sunday. ​Its shares closed down 4.3% on Monday, reducing Nvidia's market capitalisation by about $190 billion. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after the US stock market closed.

Shareholders often ⁠sue companies after unexpected share price declines. ​Nvidia shareholders led by Mark Kistenmacher are seeking unspecified damages from the defendants.

Ghana News.title: Media houses must have accountability systems to receive grants – George Sarpong
Ghana News.content:
Executive Secretary of the National Media Commission (NMC), George Sarpong

Media houses seeking grants from the Media Development Fund must have accountability systems, the Executive Secretary of the National Media Commission (NMC), George Sarpong, said.

Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, he said transparent funding rules must be matched by accountability within the organisations receiving support.

“If we are going to give a grant to any media organisation, that media organisation itself must have systems that support accountability.”

His comments follow President John Mahama’s announcement of GH¢10 million in seed funding for the reactivated Media Development Fund in the 2027 budget.

The fund is intended to support journalists’ welfare, training, investigative journalism, digital literacy and safety programmes.

Mr Sarpong said the fund’s managers must establish clear procedures for deciding who receives support.

“That governance architecture that we create must also in turn develop very transparent mechanisms for grants or awards.”

He proposed using evidence of a media house’s work to assess its application. He pointed to the NMC’s Credibility Measurement Index, which tracked coverage of issues including children, agriculture and health.

He explained that the approach could help establish whether an applicant had demonstrated commitment to the area for which it sought funding.

“So, if somebody applies for support for, say, developing or improving their coverage of maternal health, we already know that this is a media house that is committed to that enterprise, and therefore, if we supported them, it could enhance their work.”

Mr Sarpong also cautioned against building a large administrative structure around the fund.

“We need to decide whether we want to create a bureaucracy around this fund. That won't be my best suggestion.”

Instead, he proposed a small committee of credible professionals, accountable to the profession through its stakeholders.

Members should understand fund management, the media’s changing needs and what would improve the industry. He also called for people with fundraising skills to help attract additional contributions.

For Mr Sarpong, the fund's operations should be underpinned by credible management, transparent grant decisions, and accountable beneficiaries.

Ghana News.title: Global Changemakers Conference 2026: Build Beyond Africa set to inspire young people to drive change
Ghana News.content:
With just a week to go, preparations are underway for the 2026 Global Changemakers Conference, which seeks to inspire young people to recognise their potential, embrace purposeful leadership and take an active role in driving positive change in their communities and beyond.

Organised by Build Beyond Africa, the conference is scheduled for November 21, 2026, at 9 a.m. at the GNAT Hall in Accra. It will bring together young people, speakers, development advocates and other stakeholders to explore the importance of youth leadership and the role of young people in shaping a better future.

This year's theme, “The Audacity to Change the World,” challenges young people to move beyond ideas and take practical steps towards creating meaningful impact.

A major highlight of the event will be the official launch of Build Beyond Africa, a youth-focused organisation founded and led by Andy Oppong Dankyi.

The organisation has operated for more than seven years under the name Empowerment Through Education, during which it has implemented initiatives centred on education, youth empowerment, leadership development and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Its formal registration under the new name marks a new chapter in its efforts to nurture and develop young changemakers across Africa.

The conference will also feature the launch of Mr Dankyi's forthcoming book, You Have Not, Because You Ask Not, a practical and inspirational resource that examines the importance of asking, pursuing opportunities and taking deliberate steps towards personal growth and success.

The 2026 Global Changemakers Conference is expected to offer participants an engaging platform for learning, inspiration, networking and action.

It will also reinforce the belief that young people are not merely leaders of tomorrow but have an important role to play in addressing present-day challenges and driving the change their communities and societies need.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s tourism economy: The gains, the opportunities and the road ahead
Ghana News.content:
Government performance should be examined through evidence rather than political sentiment. Progress deserves recognition where it exists, just as public institutions must remain accountable for the results they report.

Ghana’s tourism sector offers an instructive case.

The Ghana Tourism Authority’s 2025 performance figures reveal measurable expansion across several indicators, including international arrivals, domestic tourism and licensed business activity. These developments warrant attention, particularly as the country seeks to position tourism as a productive contributor to national economic development.

International arrivals reached approximately 1.31 million, while visits to tourist attractions increased by seven per cent to about 1.79 million. Licensed tourism enterprises rose by 6.1 per cent to 7,109.

The commercial indicators are equally significant. Travel trade enterprises expanded by 18.6 per cent, while food, beverage and entertainment businesses recorded 8.2 per cent growth.

These figures indicate expanding formal participation in tourism-related economic activity. They also establish a credible basis for assessing the sector’s development priorities.

It was against this background that IMANI Africa’s Centre for Policy and Education undertook a working visit to the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts.

Our delegation, comprising IMANI President Franklin Cudjoe, Vice President Selorm Branttie, and associates Princess Umul Hatiyya Ibrahim Mahama and myself, engaged Minister Abla Dzifa Gomashie in discussions covering tourism development, investment, cultural preservation and institutional coordination.

The Minister presented an integrated policy approach connecting tourism, hospitality, creative industries, cultural heritage and private enterprise.

The economic reasoning is persuasive.

Tourism operates through interconnected markets. Accommodation providers depend on transport operators, food producers, entertainment businesses and reliable public infrastructure. Cultural attractions generate additional economic opportunities when supported by professional management and commercially viable visitor services.

The Ministry’s approach recognises these relationships and the need for coordinated development.

Another encouraging dimension emerges from visitor experience data.

The 2025 Tourism Report recorded satisfaction ratings of 99 per cent for Ghanaian friendliness and 98 per cent for airport facilities and formalities. More than 60 per cent of international visitors were repeat travellers.

Business travel accounted for approximately 31 per cent of international arrivals, while the entertainment and conference segment expanded by 14.3 per cent.

These indicators point towards opportunities in business tourism, international conferences, hospitality services and organised cultural experiences.

They also suggest that Ghana’s tourism development strategy should address visitor retention, service quality and commercial diversification alongside destination promotion.

The Minister’s attention to cultural merchandise, textiles, trademarks and intellectual property is particularly relevant.

Ghana’s cultural economy contains substantial opportunities for local production, enterprise development and commercial ownership. However, the economic benefits of cultural promotion depend on whether producers and traditional custodians can participate meaningfully in the markets created around their heritage.

Appropriate intellectual property protections, quality standards and access to commercial distribution channels would help strengthen that participation.

During our engagement, IMANI also explored the potential application of augmented reality, digital heritage interpretation and historically authenticated storytelling.

These technologies could improve educational experiences at heritage attractions while creating opportunities for Ghanaian historians, filmmakers, animators and software developers.

Such possibilities demonstrate why tourism development increasingly requires cooperation across institutions and industries.

The Ministry’s policy direction provides an opportunity to strengthen these connections.

There is, however, an important distinction between recording sectoral growth and establishing the specific contribution of government policy.

Annual performance figures demonstrate changes in economic activity. They do not independently identify every intervention responsible for those changes.

That is precisely why institutional reporting matters.

IMANI sees considerable value in a comprehensive Ministry performance report covering January 2025 onwards. Such an assessment could document expenditure, implementation milestones, investment partnerships, institutional reforms and measurable economic outcomes.

It would provide policymakers, investors and the public with a clearer understanding of the Ministry’s achievements and outstanding priorities.

We also envisage a Reset Tourism Conference bringing together government institutions, traditional authorities, private investors and creative enterprises to translate development priorities into practical investment programmes.

The value of such an engagement would depend on clear responsibilities, financing arrangements and measurable commitments.

These proposals complement the Minister’s articulated policy direction and reflect the importance of constructive engagement between government and independent policy institutions.

The Ministry’s integrated approach recognises that tourism development requires more than attracting visitors. It requires the systematic development of businesses, infrastructure, cultural assets and commercial opportunities.

The sector’s recorded gains provide an encouraging foundation for that work.

The responsibility now is to consolidate progress through stronger institutional coordination, sustained private investment, competitive services and greater participation by Ghanaian enterprises.

Success should ultimately be reflected in employment, business profitability, visitor satisfaction, heritage conservation and the economic benefits retained within local communities.

Ghana’s tourism sector has recorded progress worth acknowledging. The next responsibility is to convert that progress into lasting economic value, supported by transparent institutions and measurable results.

That is the standard by which the Ministry’s development agenda should be assessed.

By Kay Codjoe | IMANI Africa

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
