World.title: Manchester United are becoming a club of survival rather than ambition
World.content:
The 4-4 draw against Aston Villa felt like a victory at Old Trafford, but the fact that supporters could celebrate a point while their club sits in the relegation zone tells a more troubling story about how far United’s expectations have fallen.

There was a time when a draw at Old Trafford felt like a defeat. Manchester United were a club built around winning, where anything short of three points could leave supporters disappointed, regardless of the performance. The expectation was not simply to compete but to dominate, to set the standards and to make winning feel like an obligation.

Those expectations seem increasingly distant.

On Sunday, Manchester United celebrated a 4-4 draw against Aston Villa with the sort of emotion usually reserved for a significant victory. Two goals in stoppage time, courtesy of Joshua Zirkzee and Patrick Dorgu, rescued a point after Michael Carrick’s side had twice fallen two goals behind. The comeback was extraordinary, the atmosphere was electric and the players had every reason to appreciate their resilience.

But perhaps the most revealing aspect of the afternoon was not the comeback itself. It was how much it meant.

Manchester United are now in a position where avoiding defeat feels like an achievement. A point against Aston Villa, under ordinary circumstances, would hardly have been considered a successful afternoon for a club of United’s stature. Yet the circumstances have become so desperate that the draw felt like a victory.

That is how quickly footballing standards can collapse.

United sit 18th in the Premier League with eight points from 10 matches. They have managed just one league victory, recorded against Ipswich Town in August, and Sunday’s result extended their winless league run to eight matches. It is a club-record sequence in the Premier League.

The numbers are alarming, but the deeper concern is what they reveal about the club’s changing relationship with success.

Manchester United have become a team defined by what they are trying to avoid rather than what they are trying to achieve. Instead of discussing title challenges, European qualification or the development of a convincing footballing identity, the conversation increasingly revolves around managerial uncertainty, defensive mistakes, relegation calculations and the possibility of another disappointing weekend.

Survival has become the immediate ambition.

And that is a remarkable development for a club whose history was built on refusing to accept anything less than excellence.

Sunday’s performance captured both sides of United’s current identity. There was the determination to fight back, the willingness to keep attacking and the refusal to surrender even when the game appeared beyond them. Coming back from 2-0 down, reaching 2-2, falling behind again and eventually recovering from 4-2 demonstrated a spirit that supporters have desperately wanted to see.

However, resilience cannot become an excuse for repeated carelessness.

United conceded twice inside the opening four minutes. They then surrendered their defensive organisation again immediately after half-time, allowing John McGinn to score from the penalty spot before Leon Goretzka extended Villa’s advantage. The attacking response was admirable, but the defensive problems that made such a dramatic recovery necessary were equally concerning.

There is a difference between fighting back from adversity and repeatedly creating adversity for yourself.

For Carrick, the challenge is no longer simply convincing supporters that his team can produce entertaining football. He must demonstrate that Manchester United can become dependable again. The occasional spectacular comeback cannot compensate for a team that struggles to manage the opening minutes of matches, protect advantages or maintain concentration.

There is also a wider question about the club’s direction.

Manchester United’s problems cannot be reduced to one manager, one transfer window or one poor run of results. The instability surrounding the club has created an environment in which every setback becomes another argument about leadership, recruitment and the footballing structure. The manager becomes the immediate subject of scrutiny, but the problems appear considerably deeper.

The danger is that United become accustomed to this existence.

When a club repeatedly lowers its expectations to accommodate its circumstances, mediocrity can gradually become normal. Supporters who once demanded victories begin celebrating draws. A team that once approached matches expecting to dictate proceedings now approaches them hoping to survive the next defensive crisis.

That is perhaps the most disturbing part of United’s current predicament.

The 4-4 draw against Aston Villa should not be dismissed. There was genuine character in the comeback, and the players deserved credit for refusing to surrender. Football supporters should be allowed to enjoy extraordinary moments, even in difficult seasons.

But one dramatic afternoon cannot disguise a deeply troubling campaign.

Manchester United have spent years searching for a return to the standards that made them one of football’s most formidable institutions. Now, with the relegation zone beneath their feet, the immediate concern is no longer how quickly they can return to the summit but whether they can first escape the bottom three.

A draw that once would have been considered two points dropped has become a reason for celebration.

Perhaps that is the clearest indication of how far Manchester United have fallen.

The problem is no longer just that United are struggling to win football matches. It is that a club built on ambition is beginning to look increasingly comfortable with survival.

World.title: 2027 And The Leadership Question
World.content:
REUBEN ABATI

“I appeal to each one of you to remember that political participation places obligations on those who organize others. Keep your engagements peaceful, and your message issue-based… reject violence, threats, intimidation, misinformation, and every form of electoral conduct”. These were the wise, fitting and relevant words by Vice President Kashim Shettima in the month of September 2026 while formally inaugurating the National Working Committee of Transporters for Tinubu/Shettima 2027. He could well have been talking to all supporters of the Tinubu/Shettima ticket and everyone else involved in the struggle for political office in the 2027 elections under whatever party platform. His admonition was also on all fours with the objectives of the National Peace Committee, which on August 18, 2026 got political parties, their chairpersons and presidential candidates to sign an accord to act after the fashion of gentlemen and respect the same principles outlined and reiterated by Vice President Shettima in September. In recent instalments in this column, (Oct. 27, Nov. 3, 2026), we have given a sketch of the resort to violence, threats, and intimidation by Nigeria’s combative political elite, noting the danger that this poses to the integrity and credibility of the 2027 general elections with corresponding impact on voter turn-out and post-election legitimacy questions that may arise. The additional note is the pervasive reign of abuse, competitive rhetoric, character defamation, absolute lack of respect for the other or political ethos which would appear to have overtaken the Nigerian landscape, 59 days to the first election, the Presidential and National Assembly elections having been scheduled for January 16, 2027. The closer we get to the elections, the more febrile the rhetoric. Political rhetoric is part of the condiments of electioneering or political campaigns, edifying when it is constructive, but lamentable when it collapses to the level of a street-fight with all decorum thrown to the winds. It then becomes difficult to know exactly what the politician is selling to the public, noise or reason, propaganda or issues, as in that mix, every participant tries to outdo the other. It is most unfortunate that this is where we are at the moment in Nigeria and even Vice President Kashim Shettima who has asked for an issue-based campaign, has found himself also descending into the arena of vitriol, a variant of “bolekaja politics” which was more or less elevated to the status of statecraft during the Obasanjo years.

The Presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Waziri Adamawa, Atiku Abubakar is a denizen of those old-time battlefields, and it should not be surprising that he was the first to set the stage for the current rise of combative politics. In August 2026, he fired up the space by dismissing Tinubu’s decision to remove fuel subsidy as a wrong-headed policy which has impoverished Nigerians, and were he to win the Presidency, fuel subsidy would be restored. He pooh-poohed Tinubunomics as a system of “fiscal sedation and rascality.” The Tinubu Presidency did not waste time in firing back, dismissing Atiku’s statements as “a demonstration of serious ignorance on governance and economy.” Atiku’s hitman, Phrank Shaibu, also fired back with his acidic pen. What could have been a robust debate of Tinubunomics, for the benefit of the public, and a necessary review of the administration’s reforms soon became a shouting match. In subsequent interventions, Waziri Atiku Abubakar began to refer to the President at every turn not as Tinubu or President Tinubu, but simply Bola. He affected a tone of familiarity, that was entirely dismissive, to convey the impression that he does not recognize Tinubu as President. When the commentariat observed that this was disrespectful to the office of the President, Atiku’s aides smeared pepper on an open wound by insisting that “the President’s name is Bola”, and those who found that offensive were guilty of illiteracy. Even in the United States, those who try to get familiar with President Trump, either call him Mr. President or The Donald, as he was known in “The Apprentice”, a 2004 television series on NBC. The attack on President Tinubu by the Atiku camp and the ADC was sustained. In African communities, respect matters a lot to the people, and certain positions attract specific levels of reverence which must be openly demonstrated. Besides, African leaders are monarchs of some sort, they relate with others as the overall boss, the ruler, not as equals. Each time Atiku refers to the President as “Bola”, he breaks the code. The Bolanization of President Tinubu has since placed the Tinubu team on a war-path with the Atiku camp. In October, Rotimi Amaechi, Vice Presidential candidate of the ADC following in his Principal’s footsteps, declared in Edo State that “only a mad man will vote Tinubu in 2027” He added: “If Edo people vote for Tinubu, that means Edo people are mad. If you are not mad, Tinubu should not win here.”

In this war of words, there has been quite a competition, as to who can outsmart the other. Senator Adams Oshiomhole, one of the key campaigners of APC extraction has been very vocal. He has described Peter Obi, the NDC Presidential candidate as “a trader” whose business is “to export jobs, and import unemployment to the country”, a shop-owner who wants to run Nigeria, and yet he could not fix Anambra state for eight years when he was Governor. He calls Rotimi Amaechi a “serial loser,” “failure”, “shallow and unreliable”. As he puts it: “Amaechi has been a serial loser, very, very stubborn. He was a Governor who came into office without winning an election…Amaechi is a failure. He cannot benefit from other people’s abuse and pass it off as his own achievement…. hungry, ruthless individuals, shallow, unreliable”. Amaechi has since asked Senator Oshiomhole to make his educational certificates available for public scrutiny, and that he, Amaechi led the team that kicked away Oshiomhole when he was Chairman of the APC and he was still a member of the ruling party. Oshiomhole could not have spared Atiku Abubakar, the ADC Presidential candidate who has become a thorn in the flesh of the APC and President Tinubu, and who despite a Justice Peter Lifu judgement nullifying his emergence as the ADC flagbearer, has continued to insist that he remains a candidate, and that no one can stop him from that happening. Oshiomhole says “Atiku is a serial loser. He has been felled four times and he is completely broken with internal pollical bleeding.” Chieftains of the two leading political parties have been the most vociferous in the combat of verbal assault in the 2027 electoral process, but other presidential candidates and their agents have been no less aggressive. Omoyele Sowore, leader of the African Action Congress (AAC), insists he is determined to take back Nigeria from the ruling class.

When he and his supporters were attacked recently in Ado Ekiti, on October 30, Sowore protested that “It was not just a random attack. Tinubu’s aide and inlaw were involved in my attack in Ekiti.” He has also refused to back down on his various characterizations of the President “as a criminal” , a matter that is in court and only just yesterday, his lawyers got Justice Mohammed Garba Umar, presiding judge in Sowore’s defamation case, to subpoena Tinubu’s election documents in 1999 and 2023, and for INEC to make same available to the Federal High Court in Abuja. The matter has been adjourned to November 11, 2026 for further proceedings. Adewole Adebayo, Presidential candidate of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) has dismissed President Tinubu in these words: “Tinubu is not a mistake, he is a punishment.” He adds: “Tinubu is not just breaking the pot. He wants to break the pot, cart the pieces away and set the entire kitchen on fire.” He also says: “Tinubu should wear a mask of shame”. Seyi Makinde, Governor of Oyo State, Presidential candidate of the Allied People’s Movement (APM), a former Tinubu supporter turned adversary, has joined the anti-Tinubu group by dismissing the APC campaign team as a “Necbuchadnezzar Coalition of discredited and failed politicians.” He says what he calls “Tigunomics” is nothing else but voodoo. He tells Tinubu “win fair and square if you can.”. There are other players also in this game of competitive rhetoric: There is former Governor, Senator, and Minister of Works, Dave Umahi who has rechristened himself “Lion of the South East, a fanatical Tinubu supporter, who tells us that “Peter Obi can never be South East’s best”. However, Mr. Peter Obi, candidate of the NDC has said publicly that he will never abuse President Tinubu or any other political office holder, but he has been consistent in tearing into the Tinubu’s administration’s policies. His slogan is that a New Nigeria is POssible. According to him: “I cannot abuse any governor. I cannot abuse anybody in government. I don’t need to abuse people in the Federal Government. I’ve never abused anybody. Who has seen me calling Tinubu’s name? Never! I will never do that. He’s the President of the country, he has all my respect… But I can argue on other issues, whether you’re doing well, or you’re not doing the right thing. That is allowed.”

Peter Obi is probably an exception to what has become the norm in Nigeria’s political discourse: the on-going competition to be the man with the most memorable attacks on the opponent. The prize for that at the moment should go to the Vice President, Senator Kashim Shettima, who is standing out as the man with the bon mot, and the most entertaining put-downs in the political arena today. In the lead up to the 2023 election, he had advised former Vice President Yemi Osinbajo to consider selling popcorn and ice cream because “nice men do not make good leaders.” He has overreached his own accomplishments in political rhetoric this time around and his main target is Peter Obi, the NDC Presidential candidate. Obi may be modest and less contrarian but he is backed by an army of irreverent, abusive foot-soldiers on social media and in the streets who make it impossible for even those who respect him to overlook his shortcomings. He receives much collateral damage as a result. At the inauguration of the APC Presidential campaign Council in Abuja in October, VP Shettima dismissed Peter Obi, “my very good friend” as “a master of bogus statistics and incoherent economic prescriptions”. He further said: “He seems convinced that a size 36 shirt tailored for Bangladesh will somehow fit Nigeria’s size 52 frame.” And that for claiming he won the 2023 Presidential election without evidence, “this is called delusion of grandeur.” Three days ago, at the APC Rally in Akwa Ibom, VP Shettima accused Peter Obi of squandering away his “political goodwill” with falsehoods and statistics.” In Port Harcourt on Saturday, November 7, Shettima dismissed Obi again as “having philosophised himself into political irrelevance”, with Obi’s reputation as Governor of Anambra State or Chairman of a Bank for being “at best mediocre.” The Vice President also didn’t leave out the flagbearer of the ADC, Atiku Abubakar whom he previously referred to as a “sanitary inspector”,, “Dubagari”, also a Kachalla and now, he says Atiku is “intellectually malnourished,”, receiving poor economic advice from “voodoo economists.” He had previously called Atiku a serial presidential election loser, comparing him to Kenyan politician, the late Raila Odinga. Shettima has also reminded Atiku Abubakar that the Presidency of Nigeria is not “a retirement benefit!”

The curious thing is that President Tinubu himself seems to have joined this strategy of insults to overwhelm the opposition. In his campaign rallies in Uyo and Port Harcourt, the President descended into the arena as he dismissed both Atiku Abubakar and Peter Obi in very uncomplimentary terms. He more or less called Atiku a thief. He dismissed Obi as incompetent. And he concluded by saying both men do not have enough ability to lead Nigeria. “They lack the leadership, character and traits.” He quipped, referring to Obi: “He ran away from erosion in Anambra, and he now wants to be President? President of where?” Nigerians tend to remember the tirades of the season trying to figure out which is more entertaining or more memorable. But this campaign should not be all about rhetoric. In the face of the expletives and strong personal exchanges, the key issues about the future of Nigeria and how best to move the country forward are swept under the carpet. An election campaign should not be a circus. It should be an opportunity for reasoned engagement which empower the people to make an informed choice in a credible and fair process. Nigerian politicians should learn from the recent American midterm elections. President Trump was very good at abusing his party’s opponents or those he disliked -in Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota, California, Georgia. When it came to the vote, Americans voted on the issues and gave control of Congress to the Democrats, including Rep Ilhan Omar who won in Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District and Abdul el-Sayed, the Senator-elect from Michigan. Nigeria’s 2027 election process raises many questions of leadership, the quality and non-quality. Nigerians should not get carried away with the drama of politics, because when the drama is over, what remains will be the realities of our lives.

World.title: Ken Saro-Wiwa: 31 Years of Begging the Question
World.content:
Nigeria has continued to evade, rather than confront, the issues at the heart of the Niger Delta agitation. Vincent Obia writes

Nigeria marks a bitter anniversary today. On November 10, 1995, the Nigerian state, under the military rule of General Sani Abacha, silenced one of the most powerful voices of justice in environmental rights history. Ken Saro-Wiwa, a celebrated writer, environmental rights campaigner, and leader of the Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni People (MOSOP), was hanged alongside eight other Ogoni activists after a trial that was widely condemned as designed to act out a script rather than deliver justice.

Saro-Wiwa, Barinem Kiobel, John Kpuinen, Baribor Bera, Felix Nuate, Paul Levula, Saturday Dobee, Nordu Eawo, and Daniel Gbook were accused of murder by the state, which also applied every known treachery to frustrate the efforts of the accused to prove their innocence.

But it was clear from the kangaroo trial that the crime of the Ogoni 9 was daring to challenge the environmental devastation and economic injustice visited on their homeland by decades of oil exploration and exploitation.

Many believe the murder of four Ogoni chiefs – Chief Albert Badey, Chief Edward Kobani, Chief Theophilus Orage, and Chief Samuel Orage (Ogoni 4) – in 1994, for which Saro-Wiwa and the others were tried, was conducted by the establishment to create an excuse to silence the Ogoni 9.

Abacha conducted the executions in Port Harcourt on a day the Super Eagles played against Uzbekistan in the second leg of the Afro-Asian Cup of Nations, at the National Stadium, Lagos, and the attention of the whole country was diverted. The celebratory mood that would have followed Nigeria’s 1-0 victory in the edgy game turned to national bitterness as news of the executions broke. The indignation flowed quickly across the world.

Nigeria was isolated by the international community, until it commenced visible efforts to return to civil rule in 1999.

Thirty-one years after, the questions Saro-Wiwa raised remain unresolved. And like the state under Abacha, successive administrations have seemed more zealous to apply cosmetics and divert attention from the real issues than address them. This begs the question of whether Nigeria is committed to justice and sustainable development in the Niger Delta.

The federal government launched the Hydrocarbon Pollution Remediation Project (HYPREP) in June 2016 following the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report findings on Ogoniland.

HYPREP was set up to clean up soil and groundwater contamination and restore shorelines and mangroves damaged by over 50 years of oil activities in the Niger Delta.

Under the scheme, some infrastructural projects have been established, including hospitals, potable water, environmental research centres, as well as educational and skills acquisition schemes.

In September, HYPREP commenced the development of a new five-year Strategic Plan, 2026-2031, focussing on completing outstanding projects, sustaining restored ecosystems, and safeguarding the gains of the Ogoni Cleanup Programme.

Minister of Environment and Chairman of HYPREP Governing Council, Balarabe Lawal, said at the 10th anniversary of the Ogoni Cleanup Programme that the plan will also focus on “preventing re-pollution and strengthening community ownership of completed projects”.

Lawal unveiled the remodelled Ogoni Cleaup Plaque and monument at the historic Patrick Waterside in Bodo City, Gokana Local Government Area, saying it is a permanent reminder of the Nigerian government’s commitment to the people of Ogoni.

But Executive Director, Health of Mother Earth Foundation(HOMEF), Nnimmo Bassey says the clean-up exercise in Ogoni does not address the continuing “environmental genocide” in the Niger Delta.

Bassey states, “There has been some throwing of money at the region through the NDDC, but that does not address the existential challenges of massive, persistent, and possibly irreversible damage done to the environment of the region.”

Nigeria has historically established interventionist agencies to try to tackle environmental degradation, poverty, and infrastructural deficit in the Niger Delta. They include Niger Delta Development Board (NDDB), established in 1961 following the Willink Commission report; Oil Mineral Producing Areas Development Commission (OMPADEC) set up in 1992 by the military government; Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC) created by the President Olusegun Obasanjo government in 2000; and Ministry of Niger Delta Affairs created in 2008 by the President Umaru Yar’Adua government to coordinate development policies and supervise federal development agencies in the region. There is also the Presidential Amnesty Programme initiated by the Yar’Adua government.

The derivation principle is also a major policy intervention in the Niger Delta.

But the regions under the Independence Constitution of 1960 and Republican Constitution of 1963 controlled their natural resources, and retained 50 per cent of revenue derived from such resources, while the rest went to the common pool and the central government. From 1970, the states were stripped of control over their natural resources by the military, which also created an onshore/offshore dichotomy that limited derivation to onshore production.

The derivation principle was reduced to as low as 1.5 per cent, before it went up slightly to three per cent, and to the current 13 per cent under the 1999 Constitution.

Successive governments have initiated intervention agencies and programmes for the Niger delta, but the fundamental questions of environmental justice and resource control remain largely unresolved.

Yet, the Niger Delta remains the economic lifeblood of a country whose fortunes have depended heavily on crude oil exports. But for many in the region, the wealth produced on their land has brought neither economic prosperity nor a healthy environment, as pollution from oil spills, gas flaring, blowouts, and other oil-related disasters continue to degrade the environment and destroy livelihoods.

The recent divestment of Shell’s onshore Nigerian subsidiary underlines a seeming alliance between the state and foreign capital in the continuing economic exploitation of the Niger Delta. It raises the question of whether international oil companies (IOCs) can walk away from decades of devastating operations without fully accounting for their environmental liabilities.

Bassey believes the divestment by IOCs should be revoked.

He says, “The IOCs must clean up their mess. They own their toxic legacy and cannot leave without addressing the gross harms.”

The issues that inspired Saro-Wiwa’s agitation appear to have become even more entrenched, with politicians hardly seeing the Niger Delta question as a serious topic.

The HOMEF director says, “Any presidential candidate who cannot enunciate his plans for addressing the Niger Delta genocide should not be voted for.

“The same goes for the Niger Delta candidates for the state Houses of Assembly, House of Representatives, and Senate.”

The persistence of the ugly circumstances in the region has raised fears of a possible return to agitation by the people.

Bassey says, “The issue is whether the people can survive and reasonably expect a future for coming generations.

“The region has been essentially sacrificed and the reign of life threatening health issues continue to be compounded by reckless and irresponsible exploitation and pollution of the area.”

Last year, President Bola Tinubu granted a posthumous pardon to the Ogoni 9 and Ogoni 4, ironically, recognising them as heroes, but refusing to exonerate Saro-Wiwa and his eight compatriots of the bogus charges for which they were executed.

Amnesty International Nigeria and many in Nigeria’s civil society community rejected the pardon as deficient, insisting that the government must grant the Ogoni 9 a full legal exoneration rather than a pardon that implies retention of guilt.

Bassey insists, “You don’t pardon persons who were not found guilty of any offense through a fair justice system.

“Saro-Wiwa and the other eight leaders were denied the right to appeal the sentence handed down to them by the kangaroo tribunal. They should be exonerated. Nothing short of that would come close to an admission of grave error.”

Paradoxically, amid the unfinished clean-up work in Ogoni, the federal government is pushing for the return of oil production in the area. And outside Ogoniland, the environmental devastation has continued, with burning oil wells, abandoned oil wells, and gas flaring.

Bassey says, “The federal government should declare an environmental state of emergency across the Niger Delta and urgently commence environmental auditing, remediation, and restoration.”

He says the push to resume oil production in Ogoni “shows a lack of understanding of the interwoven nature of the Niger Delta environment and would be the final nail sealing of the hopes of ever getting the Niger Delta environment cleaned up and restored”.

According to him, “Not one new oil wells should be drilled in the region. And Ogoni oil should be left in the ground. To drill that oil is literally to bleed the blood of the people and the land.”

Thirty-one years after Saro-Wiwa and his compatriots were executed, Nigeria still confronts the issues for which they died. The Niger Delta question remains alive and unresolved, and operators of the Nigerian state appear content to beg the question, with no indication of when – or if – they will ever provide a real answer.

World.title: Frank Aigbogun at 70: The TEXEM Alum Turning Vision into Institutions, Journalism into Impact
World.content:
By Dr Alim Abubakre





A nation’s future is shaped by the quality of its institutions and the courage of those who build them. Some leaders create successful enterprises. Others develop institutions that influence how societies think, make decisions and pursue progress. The latter leave something particularly valuable: opportunities for people they may never meet.

Following Frank Aigbogun’s 70th birthday celebration on November 1, 2026, which I could not attend, I take immense pride in honouring a distinguished TEXEM alumnus, an exceptional media entrepreneur, an accomplished journalist, and a remarkable Nigerian whose contributions to national development extend far beyond the newsroom.

Frank’s life offers an inspiring lesson in purposeful leadership. His journey demonstrates that intellectual curiosity, enterprise, perseverance and a commitment to the public good can combine to create enduring national value.

Beginning his journalism career at The Guardian in 1982, Frank subsequently worked with the Associated Press and Vanguard, where he rose to significant editorial positions. These experiences prepared him for an undertaking that would reshape Nigerian business journalism.

In 2001, he co-founded BusinessDay, recognising the need for a publication dedicated to serious economic reporting, corporate governance, financial markets and public policy.

What followed was an extraordinary exercise in institution building. BusinessDay developed into one of Nigeria’s foremost platforms for business intelligence and economic debate, helping executives, investors, policymakers and citizens engage with issues central to national prosperity.

Peter Drucker, the influential management thinker, observed, “The purpose of information is not knowledge. It is being able to take the right action.”

Few observations better capture the importance of Frank’s contribution. Reliable economic journalism informs investment decisions, improves public understanding and creates opportunities to scrutinise government policies. Where credible information flourishes, accountability is stronger.

Frank’s commitment to nation-building is equally evident in his involvement with the Nigerian Economic Summit Group. His 19 years of membership, including 10 years of board service, contributed to the sustained engagement between the private sector and government that Nigeria needs for meaningful economic reform.

His recognition by the NESG in October 2026 was especially fitting, acknowledging years of dedication to policy dialogue and institutional development.

His leadership as chairman of the board of trustees of the Impact Investors Foundation further demonstrates his interest in linking investment, enterprise and positive social outcomes.

Yet, perhaps, one of Frank’s most significant contributions is the professional talent he has helped develop. Through BusinessDay, journalists, analysts and editors have gained opportunities to sharpen their abilities and contribute to public discourse.

Albert Einstein famously observed, “The important thing is not to stop questioning. Curiosity has its own reason for existence.”

That spirit of inquiry is indispensable to responsible journalism. It encourages professionals to challenge assumptions, examine evidence and pursue understanding. Frank’s professional journey illustrates how curiosity, supported by discipline and sound judgement, can become a foundation for lasting institutional achievement.

His accomplishments also offer an important lesson about good governance. Independent journalism strengthens democracy when it encourages transparency, examines public decisions and gives citizens reliable information with which to hold institutions accountable.

Nelson Mandela expressed this responsibility powerfully: “A critical, independent and investigative press is the lifeblood of any democracy.”

As Nigeria confronts complex economic choices, this principle’s relevance cannot be overstated. Strong institutions require scrutiny. Responsible policymaking requires evidence. Sustainable prosperity requires citizens and leaders who understand the consequences of their decisions.

As founder of TEXEM, UK, I find Frank’s remarkable achievements particularly gratifying because he is a valued member of our distinguished alum community. His journey embodies the commitment to strategic leadership, good governance, intellectual development, societal responsibility and nation-building that TEXEM seeks to encourage. The TEXEM alum community is enriched by accomplished leaders such as Frank, whose professional contributions show what can emerge when expertise is matched with dedication to the wider public interest.

At 70, Frank’s achievements deserve admiration, but his example also invites reflection. How many institutions are we strengthening? Whose opportunities are we expanding? What knowledge are we passing to those who will lead after us?

These questions matter because enduring leadership is measured through the value that continues to benefit society long after individual achievements have been celebrated.

Dear Frank, on this magnificent milestone, I celebrate your courage, your intellectual contributions, your entrepreneurial accomplishments and your dedication to building institutions that matter.

May the years ahead bring abundant good health, happiness, renewed energy and deeper fulfilment. May you continue to inspire younger generations, shape important national conversations and enjoy the immense satisfaction of seeing the people and institutions you have supported flourish.

On behalf of TEXEM, UK, and our global alum community, I congratulate you wholeheartedly on your 70th birthday.

May your next chapter be your most fulfilling yet, and may the institutions you have strengthened continue to enlarge the possibilities of our nation.

Happy 70th birthday, Frank. Keep flourishing, keep inspiring and keep making a difference.

•Dr Alim Abubakre is the founder of TEXEM, UK

World.title: Monimichele Hails Flamingos, Attributes Victory to Good Preparations on Quality Turf
World.content:
Nigeria’s Flamingos victory at the just concluded FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup in Rabat, Morocco, has been attributed to proper preparations under very conducive atmosphere and facilities.

The Flamingos defeated Japan 2-1 in Saturday’s final at the Mohammed VI Football Complex in Rabat to emerge champions, becoming the first African nation to win the women’s U-17 global tournament.

Nigeria took the lead through Awawu Bashiru in the 39th minute, while Oluebube Umejiaku doubled the advantage two minutes into the second half. Japan’s Fuki Ito reduced the deficit in the 80th minute, but the Nigerian side held on to secure a landmark victory first time victory for Africa.

Speaking yesterday on Flamingos victory, Nigeria’s stadium facility expert, Ebi Egbe, attributed the team’s success to the result of training on quality turf under a good manager.

Egbe who is the Chief Executive Officer of Monimichelle Sports Facility Limited, the company that constructed the Remo Stadium turf in Ikenne where Flamingos honed their skills before leaving for the tournament in Morocco, Insisted that the facility played a major role in the success of the team.

“The Flamingos’ example illustrates the importance of proper preparation ahead of major competitions.

“The team spent several months training at the Remo Stars Stadium facility in Ikenne before travelling to Morocco for the youth championship.

“The point is that consistent training on a quality, well-maintained playing surface helps young players adapt, improve their technical abilities, build confidence and prepare better for competitive football,” observed Egbe one of the country’s best known groundsman.

The Monimichelle Boss restated his long held opinion that Nigeria teams will become better in continental and global competitions if they training longer on quality playing surfaces like the Flamingos have done.

“The pitches that the Flamingos played on in Rabat were exactly the same they have been used to at Remo Stadium. The ball movements were the same and so were better taking on opponents with relative ease,” continued the Bayelsa-born facility expert.

He however gave plaudits to the coach and the young players for making the country proud, becoming the first African women’s team to win a FIFA World Cup event.

“Nigeria has the talent. Providing our young players with quality facilities and adequate preparation time can help translate that talent into better performances and results on the international stage,” concludes Egbe.

Flamingos opened their campaign in Morocco on a shaky ground, losing 2-1 to Poland in their opening Group B match. They then won six games in a row. They defeated Puerto Rico 2-0 and two-time defending champions DPR Korea 3-1 to advance from the group. In the knockout stage, Flamingos beat Mexico 2-1 in the Round of 16 and Venezuela 1-0 in the quarter-finals. They then hammered Brazil 3-1 in the semi-finals to reach their first World Cup final.

World.title: NFF, Musawa, Oborevwori, Others Hail World Champions Flamingos
World.content:
*As heroines return to Abuja early hours of Monday with U17 World Cup trophy

Olawale Ajimotokanin Abuja and Sylvester Idowuin Warri

Nigeria’s cadet women’s team, Flamingos, returned to Abuja early hours of Monday from Rabat, Morocco where they won this year’s FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup after a pulsating final with Japan.

Speaking at the team’s hotel in Abuja yesterday, Nigeria Football Federation’s Acting General Secretary, Dr Emmanuel Ikpeme, MON, described the feat of the Flamingos as magnificent, as a joyous nation continues to celebrate the triumph of the young ladies in the Kingdom of Morocco.

Dr Ikpeme restated the appreciation of the NFF and the entire Nigeria football family for the hard work, discipline and dedication of the young players in ensuring that they triumph in the tournament.

He fed the team with words of encouragement and motivation, assuring them of the Federal Government and the good people of Nigeria’s appreciation for how they had improved the country’s position on the world football map.

The Ag. General Secretary reiterated that not only is Nigeria the first African country to win the FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup, Nigeria is also the first African country to win male and female titles of the FIFA U17 World Cup.

“There is no way the history of the FIFA U17 Women’s World Cup will be written without your names. The Federal Government is happy and the generality of Nigerians are happy about this accomplishment. Our prayer is that as a collective and as individuals, you will continue to improve your game to get even better and take your game to the next level.”

Ikpeme disclosed how FIFA President Gianni Infantino and the President of CAF, Dr Patrice Motsepe commended the Flamingos and spoke so highly of the team.

Present during the visit were the NFF’s Acting Deputy General Secretary, Dr Ademola Olajire; Director of Legal Services, Okey Obi, Esq; Director of Competitions, Ms Ruth David; Director of Finance and Administration, Mr Rajan Zaka; Director of Planning, Research and Statistics, Mr. Dayo Enebi Achor and; Head of Women’s Football, Hajiya Amina Daura.

Also yesterday, the Minister of Art, Culture, Tourism and the Creative Economy, Hannatu Musa Musawa, congratulated the Flamingos following their historic victory at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco.

In a congratulatory statement issued by her Special Adviser on Media and Publicity, Nneka Ikem Anibeze, the minister described the triumph as a defining moment for Nigerian sports and a significant milestone for African women’s football.

Musawa said the victory demonstrated the resilience, talent and determination of young Nigerian women, noting that the team had inspired the country and the continent with their remarkable journey to the title.

“This is more than a trophy. It is a story of young Nigerian girls who refused to give up, who rose after defeat, and who carried the hopes of a continent to the top of the world,” she said.

Musawa particularly commended Oluebube Umejiaku who emerged winner of the tournament’s Golden Ball award as the best player, as well as Awawu Bashiru for their crucial contributions in the final.

She also praised the entire squad for their teamwork, discipline and collective determination, which she said were instrumental to the country’s historic achievement.

The minister reaffirmed the commitment of her ministry to celebrating, protecting and promoting the stories of young Nigerians whose achievements inspire national pride and project the country’s positive image globally.

“Our girls have shown the world what Nigeria is made of. We celebrate you today, and we will continue to stand with you,” she said.

In his reaction, Delta State Governor, Rt. Hon. Sheriff Oborevwori, also congratulated the Flamingos on their historic victory at the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco, describing the feat as a moment of immense national pride.

In a congratulatory statement issued yesterday by his Chief Press Secretary, Sir Festus Ahon, Governor Oborevwori described the triumph as a remarkable achievement that had brought honour to Nigeria and the African continent.

He praised the players for their determination, discipline, resilience and fighting spirit, noting that their performance demonstrated the growing strength of women’s football and the abundance of sporting talents in Nigeria.

The Governor particularly celebrated Onyinyechi Opara of Delta Queens FC, who was part of the victorious squad, describing her contribution as another source of pride for Delta State.

He noted that Opara had reinforced Delta’s reputation as a leading contributor to sports development in Nigeria, following in the footsteps of other outstanding athletes who had represented the state and country with distinction.

Oborevwori said her achievement demonstrated the capacity of young Deltans to excel on the international stage when provided with the necessary opportunities, encouragement and support.

The Governor reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to sports development and youth empowerment through investments in sporting infrastructure, grassroots talent discovery and programmes designed to nurture emerging athletes.

He urged the Flamingos to sustain their winning mentality and remain focused on greater achievements, adding that their historic accomplishment would inspire young Nigerian girls to pursue careers in football and other sporting disciplines.

Oborevwori wished the team continued success in future competitions, stressing that their victory had secured a special place in Nigeria’s football history.

World.title: Praise Ugoh Wins Youth Olympic 400m Gold for Nigeria
World.content:
Nigeria’s remarkable run of success at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games continued on Monday as Praise Ugoh became the first Nigerian to win a 400m title at the competition, adding another gold medal to the country’s historic sprint double secured by Rosemary Chigozie Nwankwo and Gift Bright earlier on Sunday.

Ugoh produced a superb performance in the women’s 400m final, clocking a personal best of 52.76 seconds to claim gold in a closely contested race.

She finished ahead of Venezuela’s Osmary Pacheco, who took silver in 52.85 seconds, while Aisha Muhammed of the United Arab Emirates settled for bronze in 53.06 seconds.

The victory marks a major milestone for Nigerian athletics with Ugoh becoming the first Nigerian to win the 400m title at the Youth Olympic Games.

Her personal best performance also underlines the progress of the young athlete, who delivered when it mattered most to secure her place in the competition’s history.

Her triumph follows Nigeria’s outstanding achievement in the 100m events on Sunday, when Rosemary Nwankwo and Gift Bright swept both sprint gold medals to complete a historic Nigerian double.

Nwankwo stormed to victory in the women’s 100m in 11.16 seconds while Bright made history in the men’s event, becoming the first Nigerian to win the Youth Olympic Games 100m title.

Nigeria’s sweep of the men’s and women’s 100m titles marked the first time the country had won both sprint crowns at the same edition of the Youth Olympic Games.

With Ugoh’s 400m breakthrough now added to the sprint double, Nigeria’s young athletes have delivered a memorable statement in Dakar, demonstrating the country’s growing depth of talent and its capacity to compete for honours on the global stage.

World.title: Bendel Insurance Petitions NPFL over  Matchday 9 Clash with Rangers
World.content:
Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City

Bendel Insurance Football Club of Benin has petitioned the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF), demanding the cancellation of its 1-0 defeat to Rangers International FC in their rescheduled Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) Matchday 9 midweek encounter played at the Awka City Stadium on November 4, 2026.

The club accused league managers of double standards, insisting displaced goalframe invalidated Rangers’ winning goal.

The petition, signed by the club’s Chairman, Comrade Jarrett Tenebe, followed an earlier protest to the NPFL over a controversial goal scored by Rangers after the goalframe defended by Bendel Insurance was visibly displaced during an attacking move.

Tenebe is also threatening to withdraw Bendel Insurance from the league, going by the repeated unfair officiating of matches involving the team over some time and especially if the false goal awarded to Rangers is allowed to stand

In a significant development, the NPFL has acknowledged the grievance raised by Bendel Insurance, admitting that its review of the match footage brought it to terms with the club’s complaint.

However, the league declined to overturn the result, citing its inability under existing regulations to annul the outcome of a concluded match.

In its November 6, 2026 letter addressed to the Chairman of Bendel Insurance, the NPFL Chief Operating Officer, Dr Ayo Abdulrahaman, said the league had reviewed the video evidence submitted by the club and decided to refer the referee to the NFF Referees Appointment Committee for further examination of the decision.

The NPFL explained that its position was informed by the existing rules governing concluded matches and what it described as football’s longstanding tradition of not overturning decisions made by referees on the field of play.

The league, however, stressed that its decision was not intended to disregard the provisions of the Laws of the Game cited in Bendel Insurance’s protest.

Dissatisfied with the response, Bendel Insurance escalated the matter to the NFF Disciplinary and Appeal Committees, arguing that the NPFL’s acknowledgement of the irregularity of the goal should necessarily attract appropriate sporting consequences.

In its five-page petition dated November 6, the Benin Arsenal contended that the goal should never have been allowed because the crossbar and goalframe had become visibly displaced before the ball entered the net.

According to the club, the match officials were obligated under Law 1.10 of the International Football Association Board (IFAB) Laws of the Game to immediately stop play whenever a crossbar becomes displaced or broken, pending its repair or replacement.

The petition maintained that the referee’s failure to stop play constituted a breach of a mandatory provision of the Laws of the Game, rendering the goal invalid.

Bendel Insurance further argued that Law 10.1, which defines the conditions under which a goal is scored, could not be properly applied in circumstances where the goalframe and crossbar were no longer in their prescribed positions.

The club also rejected the anticipated reliance on Law 5.2, which generally makes referees’ decisions on facts connected with play, including whether a goal has been scored, final

It argued that its complaint was not about challenging the referee’s judgement on an ordinary incident but about the failure to enforce an express provision of the Laws of the Game requiring play to stop.

The petition also placed responsibility on Rangers International as the home club, citing Rules B4.1 and B4.2 of the NPFL regulations, which require home clubs to ensure that their match venues meet approved standards and satisfy applicable safety requirements.

According to Bendel Insurance, the displacement of the goalframe during normal play raised serious questions about compliance with those obligations.

The club consequently asked the NFF to review the NPFL’s November 6 decision, declare that the match officials breached Law 1.10, invalidate the disputed goal and annul the 1-0 result.

It further requested that the match be declared a draw, with one point awarded to each club, while Rangers should face appropriate sanctions for allegedly failing to provide a safe playing environment.

Other reliefs sought include an order compelling the NPFL to release the video footage reviewed by its officials and the match officials’ reports, as well as an investigation into compliance with the venue safety requirements at Awka City Stadium.

Beyond the disputed goal, Bendel Insurance raised concerns over what it described as inconsistent treatment by the league in its handling of disciplinary and match-related decisions.

The club recalled that on May 10, 2026, following its Matchday 37 encounter against Rangers International, the NPFL reportedly stripped it of points it had earned after disputed officiating decisions and subsequent acknowledgement of irregularities.

It argued that the league’s willingness to take retrospective action against Bendel Insurance in that instance contrasted sharply with its present refusal to intervene despite acknowledging the grievance surrounding the Rangers goal.

The petition also referenced December 12, 2025, as the date of an earlier retrospective action by the league, although the specific Matchday 37 incident was identified in the document as having occurred on May 10, 2026.

Bendel Insurance therefore urged the NFF to ensure that the league applies its regulations uniformly and without discrimination against member clubs.

The controversy has now placed the NPFL’s handling of disputed match outcomes, the responsibility of home clubs for stadium safety and the limits of retrospective disciplinary intervention under fresh scrutiny.

While the league has referred the referee’s conduct to the NFF Referees Appointment Committee, the final determination of Bendel Insurance’s appeal now rests with the appropriate NFF authorities.

The outcome could have wider implications for the enforcement of the Laws of the Game and the accountability of clubs and match officials in the NPFL.

During the match played over the weekend, November 8, 2026, between Bendel Insurance and Niger Tornadoes played at Dr. Samuel Ogbemudia Stadium, in Benin City, Insurance supporters staged protest against NPFL with various placards denouncing the football body. Insurance won Niger Tornados 2:1.

World.title: Ikpokpo Credits NDDC for Bright’s Youth Olympics Gold
World.content:
Sir Itiako Ikpokpo (KSM) has reflected on the gold winning performance of Gift Bright at the Youth Olympics in Senegal and declared that the Niger Delta Games (NDG) has already began to live up to the vision it was founded on.

Ikpokpo is the founder of Dunamis-Icon Limited, franchise owners of the NDG sponsored by the Niger Delta Development Commission (NDDC).

Bright was runners-up behind Chibueze Osama of Delta state, while Saturday Godswill finished third at the second edition of the games held in Benin, Edo State in February 2026.

Bright, who represented Akwa Ibom State, was scouted by athletics coaches from the National Sports Commission (NSC), and he went to dust an international youths line-up in 10.22 seconds.

“I am naturally delighted to see the realisation of one of the major planks on which the games was founded – which is to provide Nigeria athletes from the Niger Delta region who will bring honours to the country”, Ikpokpo told the media in his reaction to news of the feat.

He declared that “there’s going to be more celebrations of children of the Niger Delta region on the international podium for our country.”

Looking back, he expressed appreciation for the support of the games by the NDDC, the nine member State governments, the coaches, and members of the organising committee.

“As we celebrate the gold, it is very important to thank all those who, in one way or the other, made it possible. Our biggest appreciation is to the NDDC leadership led by Dr Samuel Ogbuku, whose financial backing enabled the games. The coaches and my team members in the organising committee are all contributors to this national success,” Ikpokpo concluded.

World.title: ‘I don’t bring them here’: Ouaddou reveals Orlando Pirates’ transfer secret
World.content:
Orland Pirates coach says his job is to work with the players the club has signed. He does not operate in the club’s player search and signings.

The Morrocan coach further added he does not utilise his established network on the African continent.

ABDESLAM OUADDOU EXPLAINS WHY HE DOES NOT SCOUT PLAYERS FOR ORLANDO PIRATES

The Buccaneers have developed an impressive reputation for identifying promising players before turning them into established stars. The list has included Mohau Nkota, Mbekezeli Mbokazi, Relebohile Mofokeng, Simphiwe Masilela, and most recently the league’s Player of the Month Thapelo Mokobodi.



The strategy has also delivered lucrative player sales. Nkota, Mbokazi and Mofokeng generated around R200 million in under two seasons.

Ouaddou provided an insight into the club’s recruitment structure following Pirates’ 1-0 victory over Sekhukhune United in the Carling Knockout Cup quarter-finals on Saturday.

The recently promoted Mpho Padime’s first-half goal proved decisive at the Orlando Amstel Arena, sending the Buccaneers into the semi-finals.

Speaking after the match, the lanky tactician was asked whether he would personally look for a prolific striker during the club’s upcoming CAF Champions League travels.

He explained that recruitment is handled by a separate department that understands the club’s identity and the type of players required.

“Look, I think the club has a very good scouting department,” Ouaddou stated when asked whether he would personally hunt for a prolific striker during Pirates’ upcoming CAF Champions League travels.



“They know exactly what they are looking for, the identity of the club, and the way they want to play. It’s no secret to anybody that I’m here to coach, and I’m not here to scout players.

“I have the players at my [disposal], and I play with the players that I have. Unfortunately, [signing of players] is not part of my duties. Let’s put it that way, it’s not part of my contract to look for players.

“It’s another department’s job to look for players. Of course, if you ask me about [searching for a striker], I have a big network across Africa, but I don’t bring them here.”

World.title: A slice of fashion: Roman’s Pizza serves streetwear [photos]
World.content:
Roman’s Pizza has made a stylish move into the world of fashion by launching a unisex streetwear brand.

The range includes oversized T-shirts, heavyweight hoodies and corduroy caps, all designed in Cape Town using locally sourced, high-quality fabrics.

ROMAN’S PIZZA BRANCHES INTO STREETWEAR

RP Knead, the new clothing brand from Roman’s Pizza, has dropped a limited-edition collection. This means shoppers can enjoy a sense of exclusivity, as the collection will not be restocked.



The T-shirts and hoodies are available in sizes ranging from small to double extra-large and come in only three colours: white, navy, and burgundy.

The collection features hand-drawn graphics inspired by comic characters, such as Running Man, Romaneer DJ, Stack A Friend, Chow Down, and Hands of the Slice.

Prices range from R399 to R899, and shoppers can purchase items via the RP Knead website, with delivery available countrywide.

THE STORY BEHIND RP KNEAD

The introduction of RP Knead proves that the brand isn’t resting on its laurels. Instead, it continues to evolve by tapping into new markets.



RP Knead describes the brand as:

“RP KNEAD is that story in streetwear form. Designs rooted in the craft, the characters, and the culture of pizza-making.”

“Graphics that pull from the kitchen, the street, and everything in between. Heavyweight tees, hoodies, and caps that carry real meaning because they come from a real place.”

“This isn’t merch. It’s a movement worn by people who know the brand runs deeper than the box.”

Since launching over three decades ago, Roman’s Pizza continues to be one of South Africa’s most popular pizza spots.

World.title: Informal structures in Cape Town have increased by 67% in nine years
World.content:
New data released by the City reveals a 67% increase in the number of informal structures in Cape Town over the past nine years.



The City’s latest Spatial Trends and Implementation Tracking report gives an overview of development and land use patterns in Cape Town from 2012 to 2026.

According to the document, the number of informal structures rose from 169 330 in 2016 to 283 379 in 2025.

The mapped footprint of areas of informality also expanded significantly. It grew by roughly 1 900 hectares, from about 1 200 hectares to more than 3 100 hectares.



“The scale of informal settlement growth has increased substantially since 2016,” the report says.

The figures highlight the growing scale of informal housing across the metro, as well as the amount of land occupied by these settlements.

It is important to note that this excludes areas of unlawful land occupation. The 283 379 figure is therefore not necessarily a complete count of all informal structures in Cape Town.

Informal housing growth concentrated in key areas

The report identifies clusters of informal settlements along major transport routes, including the N2, N1 and N7.

These are generally located within or close to lower-income communities.

Wallacedene, Delft, Gugulethu, Dunoon and the Khayelitsha/Mitchells Plain area are among the locations with particularly high densities of informal structures.



Several districts have also experienced notable growth.

In the Northern District, the number of informal structures increased significantly after 2021. Wallacedene and Klipheuwel were identified as areas showing clear growth.

In the Helderberg District, Macassar, Sir Lowry’s Pass, Lwandle and Nomzamo have also seen increases.

Khayelitsha remains an area with a particularly high density of informal structures. Image: Wikimedia

Pressure on land and infrastructure

The City warns that areas of informality sometimes occupy land unsuitable or unsafe for residential development.

These include biodiversity areas, floodplains, wetlands, road and rail reserves, and land affected by airport noise contours.

The report also highlights the relationship between informal settlement upgrading and government-subsidised housing, particularly in the metro south-east.

It notes that informal settlements can expand outwards or become more densely populated.

“Growth occurs through both outward expansion and increasing AOI (area of interest) net density,” the report states.

World.title: Could Starlink cut off some users in Zimbabwe?
World.content:
Starlink has tightened restrictions on international roaming, putting Zimbabwean users who rely on accounts registered in other countries at risk of losing their satellite internet connections.

The changes affect customers using foreign-registered Starlink equipment in Zimbabwe, particularly those who have relied on international roaming to access the service.

According to Starlink’s updated support documentation, customers on its Roam Unlimited package can use their service outside their registered home country for a maximum of 30 consecutive days.



The company previously allowed customers to use the service abroad for up to 60 consecutive days.

The new rules took effect for customers signing up from 14 July 2026, while existing subscribers transitioned to the updated policy on 17 August 2026.

Starlink tightens international roaming rules

Under the updated conditions, customers who exceed the 30-day international roaming allowance must either return their equipment to their registered home country, transfer their accounts to the country where they are using the service or upgrade to a Global Business package.

Starlink has also restricted international access for customers using other Roam packages.

Its 100GB and 300GB roaming packages are now intended for use within the country where the account is registered or an eligible regional grouping.

Customers requiring international connectivity must upgrade to Roam Unlimited or move to an appropriate business package.



Starlink’s Business service, currently marketed as Local Priority, allows up to 60 days of international use until 1 December 2026.

Thereafter, the allowance will also fall to 30 days.

Zimbabweans face potential disconnections

The changes could affect Zimbabweans who purchased Starlink equipment registered in countries such as Zambia, Mozambique, France and the United Kingdom.

Some customers turned to foreign-registered accounts when local residential subscriptions were difficult to obtain because of capacity constraints.

However, the latest restrictions make it increasingly difficult to use international roaming as a permanent alternative to a Zimbabwe-registered subscription.

My Zimbabwe News reported in September that some customers had already experienced service restrictions after exceeding the new roaming allowance.

Starlink has also introduced travel registration requirements for customers using their equipment outside their registered countries. These may include submitting a passport or other government-issued identification.

The company says the verification process helps ensure that international users comply with local regulations.

Zimbabwean customers using locally registered accounts are not automatically affected by the international roaming restrictions.

The changes, however, present a challenge for those relying on foreign subscriptions to stay connected.

Starlink advises customers to check their account status and applicable service conditions before travelling or continuing to use their equipment abroad.

World.title: ‘No different to last season’ – Khan’s verdict on Kaizer Chiefs
World.content:
Former Kaizer Chiefs assistant coach Farouk Khan believes Amakhosi have made little progress compared to last season.

During the 2025/26 campaign, Chiefs finished third in the Betway Premiership under co-coaches Khalil Ben Youssef and Cedric Kaze.

The Glamour Boys, however, have struggled for consistency this season, both in cup competitions and the league.



Speaking on SoccerBeat, Khan believes Sunday’s 2-1 Carling Knockout victory over Siwelele will give head coach Fernando Da Cruz some encouragement. However, he feels there are still several issues that need addressing.

“If I was Da Cruz, I will be happy after the derby loss; I’d be overjoyed with the result but if I had to be honest with myself as far as performance is concerned, there are a lot of loose ends that need to be tied up,” he said.

Kaizer Chiefs into the Carling KO semis

Khan was also critical of Chiefs’ playing style, arguing that their approach could work against them when facing defensively organised opponents.

“When Chiefs win possession, you know they are going to attack you at a 120km/h, which sometimes work but when teams are organised defensively, it can work against you because you give away possession.”

The former Kaizer Chiefs coach also questioned whether Da Cruz has made any significant improvements to the team compared to last season.

“I think this team is no different to the team we saw last season with co-coaches. They are very similar in their approach; I think that team was a bit more consistent if you look at where they finished,” Khan added.



Can Amakhosi win the Carling KO?

World.title: Mofokeng does something no other player has managed in the Europa League
World.content:
According to statistics platform Statz.ai, Mofokeng has created 15 chances in four UEFA Europa League matches. It has put him at the top of the rankings.

The 22-year-old is ranked first in the entire competition. Benfica’s Chiquinho lurks in second place with 13 chances created.

RELEBOHILE MOFOKENG LEADS EUROPA LEAGUE RANKINGS

Bayer Leverkusen midfielder Aleix García, Sebastian Szymański and Keito Nakamura complete the top five, each having created 12 chances.



The Sharpeville-born former Orlando Pirates star has averaged 4.20 chances created per 90 minutes, highlighting his creative contribution in the competition.

His numbers place him ahead of players representing some of Europe’s established clubs, with the rankings highlighting his influence in the final third.

Mofokeng’s performances have duly seen him linked with two German clubs Bayer Levrerkusen and SC Freiburg. The same reports revealed French side Lille and Dutch club AZ Alkmaar are also keen.



FAST RISE FROM THE SCHOOL OF EXCELLENCE

Mofokeng began his journey to the top at the renowned School of Excellence. During his time there, he developed his distinctive playing style, combining natural flair on the ball with intelligent movement.

Orlando Pirates soon spotted him at the under-19 Pirates Cup in August 2022. Mofokeng quickly made his name DStv Diski Challenge (DDC) ranks before making his senior debut for the Buccaneers in May 2023.

The following season saw Mofokeng win the PSL Footballer of the Year and PSL Young Player of the Year awards.



His development also translated to the international stage, where he made his Bafana Bafana debut before representing South Africa at the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

In July 2026, Mofokeng completed his highly anticipated move to Europe, signing a long-term contract with Belgian Pro League champions Royale Union Saint-Gilloise. The transfer was reportedly worth €3.5 million, approximately R65.3 million, marking a significant milestone in the career of one of South Africa’s most highly rated young footballers.

World.title: ‘He said I must protect him’: Matlala drops Sibiya bombshell at Madlanga Commission
World.content:
PRETORIA - Vusimuzi 'Cat' Matlala has accused former police deputy national commissioner for crime detection Shadrack Sibiya of coercing him to lie to Parliament.

Testifying before the Madlanga Commission of Inquiry on Monday, Matlala alleged that Sibiya did this through his lawyer

He claimed that Advocate Bronwynne Forbay would call Sibiya during breaks at the Ad Hoc Committee sittings and hand Matlala the phone.

READ | LIVE | Madlanga rejects Section 204 submission presented by Matlala's lawyer

He further told the commission that his wife, Tsakane Matlala, told him that Sibiya repeatedly contacted her from a private number, threatening that Matlala should not reveal anything about him at the Ad Hoc Committee.

Some of those threats, he said, were directed at his life and the safety of his family.

World.title: 36 years in igloo homes: Mdantsane residents fed up with broken promises
World.content:
MDANTSANE - For over 36 years, a community in Mdantsane has lived in igloo-shaped homes made of fiberglass.

Originally provided as temporary shelters, the domes now harbour fungus, posing a health threat to children and the elderly.

Some families are crammed with 12 people in a single room, living like sardines in a can.

READ | Bronkhorstspruit residents still waiting for clean water

They say politicians often show up just before elections to canvass for votes, but their living conditions never change.

"We’ve been voting all the time, and then after we’ve cast our votes, nothing changes. Politicians only come here because it suits their campaigns; it makes them look good. Because they use our situation as a promise to bring positive change."

These Nkomponi residents have had enough. They don't care who's elected into power anymore.

All they want is to be treated like human beings and provided with suitable homes.

eNCA's Ronald Masinda filed this story.

World.title: Police probe two brutal murders after bodies found in abandoned buildings
World.content:
THEUNISSEN - Police in the Free State have launched a manhunt for suspect(s) after two women were found murdered and their bodies discovered in separate abandoned buildings in Theunissen over the past weekend.

According to Free State police spokesperson Thabo Covane, the first murder incident was discovered on 7 November.

On the day, at around 03:40 am, members of the Neighbourhood Watch directed police to an abandoned building where they discovered the lifeless body of a woman.

READ | WC Anti-Gang Unit probes triple murder in Grassy Park

Covane said preliminary investigations confirmed that the 35-year-old woman had sustained multiple stab wounds.

“The victim was discovered half-naked with multiple injuries to the head and stomach. The victim was declared deceased on the scene by Emergency Medical Services personnel.

“Police are not ruling out the possibility that the victim may have been sexually violated,” he said.

According to Covan, on 8 November police attended a crime scene of a 25-year-old woman whose body was found in a decomposed state.

READ | Jabulile Ntimba murder: Suspects back in dock

“According to the report, children were playing at an abandoned building near the Day Care Centre in Masilo, Theunissen. The children were exposed to a horrific scene when they discovered the body of a half-naked woman inside a toilet with serious head injuries,” Covane said.

He said no arrests have been made in either case, but a multidisciplinary task team has been established to probe the murders.

World.title: Witness breaks down at tribunal against Eastern Cape judge accused of racial slur
World.content:
EAST LONDON - The Judicial Conduct Tribunal opened its investigation into allegations of gross misconduct against Eastern Cape High Court Judge Belinda Hartle on Monday.

Hartle is accused of using racist and derogatory language towards court employee Thozamile Semekazi in May last year, after reportedly growing frustrated with court file delivery delays.

Semekazi grew emotional while recounting the events of that day.

READ | High Court grants Selby Mbenenge impeachment interdict

In a report by Judges Matter, Semekazi complained that the events of the day constituted "humiliating and demeaning conduct", which caused him to "suffer a major depressive disorder and resulted in his being admitted to hospital for treatment".

The report further revealed that Judge Hartle’s stated that she used only one swear word, and that it was not directed at Semekazi, and accused him of grossly misrepresenting the interaction between them. Judge Hartle disputes ever using a racist word,

World.title: Carrim denies smuggling vehicles
World.content:
MUSINA - Suliman Carrim has denied any involvement in the car-smuggling plot.

Through his affidavit in court on Monday, Carrim claimed he was hospitalised when the alleged crime took place.

Carrim appeared in the Musina Magistrates' Court on charges of cross-border vehicle smuggling.

The state, which is opposing bail claim that Carrim allegedly instructed two employees to smuggle vehicles into Malawi, bypassing the bank's clearance by claiming his upcoming Madlanga Commission appearance blocked the paperwork.

READ | Suliman Carrim back in court over alleged vehicle smuggling

Carrim tried to distance himself from his co-accused.

But prosecutors said WhatsApp messages show frequent communication between them, as well as evidence that Carrim paid for the co-accused' rental accommodation.

The state also revealed the co-accused were working illegally on visitor permits, and that Carrim knowingly ran an unlawful operation.

Carrim has been remanded in custody until 16 November, when he'll find out his fate.

World.title: Former top cop's fraud and corruption trial postponed
World.content:
PRETORIA - The R54-million SAPS software corruption trial against former acting National Police Commissioner Khomotso Phahlane and his five co-accused has been postponed to12 November.

The accused appeared at the High Court in Pretoria, where the State requested a postponement to amend the charges they face.

READ | IDAC withdraws blue light tender case against Phahlane

The case involves two SAPS contracts worth approximately R54 million.

The State alleges that the procurement processes for the police monitoring software systems were manipulated.

The irregularities allegedly took place during Phahlane's tenure as acting National Police Commissioner.

Hlungwani says the lack of medical aid is a major concern, particularly when workers seek medical attention.
