World.title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over Chinese spy concerns
World.content:
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over allegations he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.

The allegations center around a Chinese business executive named Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency.

The CIA, NSA and ODNI did not immediately respond to CBS News requests for comment.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.

Two law enforcement sources confirmed to CBS News on Monday that the Justice Department's National Security Division is investigating Megaspeed. The investigation involves potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips, the sources said.

In a message to Nvidia employees Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and apologized for hurting her and their children, although he did not name the woman involved. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."

The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.

John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Monday, "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."

A company spokesperson said Jensen Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.

Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.

"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to The Times.

Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."

On Monday, President Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." Mr. Trump also said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday to see how he was doing, and that Huang "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.

World.title: California voters defeat billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats
World.content:
California voters defeat billionaire tax proposal that divided Democrats

toggle caption i Jae C. Hong/AP

Midterms coverage: Live results | Stories around the country

Stay connected: NPR Politics Podcast | NPR Politics newsletter | NPR app

California voters have rejected a proposal to charge billionaires a one-time 5% tax on most of their wealth, according to a race call by The Associated Press.

Proponents said the tax could raise $100 billion for healthcare. Led by a union that represents healthcare workers, the SEIU-UHW, advocates of the tax said the Republican-controlled Congress cut healthcare programs to give tax breaks to the wealthy, so it was time for the wealthy in California to fill the gap. The state has more than 200 billionaires, according to estimates, with some putting the number at a few hundred.

Sponsor Message

Opponents argued that the proposal, known as Prop 40, would just drive the wealthy out of California, costing the state revenue and harming its economy.

But the measure divided Democrats in a state where they heavily outnumber Republicans.

Loading...

The state's Democratic Party favored Prop 40, as did Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who went to the state to campaign for it. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed the tax, saying it would be better to have a national tax on the wealthy. The Democratic candidate for governor, Xavier Becerra, also opposed it.

A leading teachers union also opposed the proposal, which would have set aside just a small portion of the resulting revenue for schools. And Google co-founder Sergey Brin led other wealthy Californians in a surge of campaign spending opposing the measure. At least five times as much was spent opposing the measure as favoring it.

Brin also drove a campaign that put two other proposals on the ballot to block the billionaire tax from taking effect, had it been approved by voters.

World.title: France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks
World.content:
France accuses Iran of cyber 'sabotage' in fridge attacks

toggle caption i FRED TANNEAU/AFP via Getty Images

France is accusing Iran of having launched a series of destructive cyberattacks against its critical infrastructure in October.

According to the French National Cybersecurity Agency, ANSSI, Iranian military hackers took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France, from supermarkets to butcher shops, turning up the temperature in the middle of the night and spoiling millions of dollars' worth of food.

They also targeted several small hydroelectric power plants, resulting in "moderate effects," wrote ANSSI in its press release.

The hacking campaign was "unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression," said French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot. He said it "marks the first large-scale cyberattack aimed at sabotage on our national territory, and it constitutes a major attack on the nation's interests and the security of the French people."

Sponsor Message

The Paris Prosecutor's Office has opened its own investigation into the Iranian cyber unit, Shahid Kaveh, which the French government is linking to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The Paris Public Prosecutor's Office is requesting the issuance of international arrest warrants," the office said in a statement.

A trend of attacks on refrigeration systems

The attacks on French industrial controllers are part of a larger trend . In 2026 alone, hackers have targeted refrigeration controllers from Europe to Israel and the United States.

Grocery stores in European countries including Sweden and Ireland were hit in similar attacks last week.

In a separate incident in France, employees at a major French blood bank had to act fast to save blood samples from heating up when their refrigeration system was hit last week, prompting international calls for the health sector to protect its lifesaving products from spoiling.

In Israel in the spring, suspected Iranian hackers going by the name of "Cyber Isnaad Front" claimed responsibility for sabotaging an industrial food processing plant, including infecting its corporate computers with malware, taking over office printers to print out threatening messages and hacking office cameras for use in a propaganda video released in early October. That video included a taunt in French referencing ongoing education-related protests, and came just before the attacks on French supermarket fridges. Cyber incident response firm Profero attributed the Israel attack to a wing of Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps .

Sponsor Message

Over the summer, commissaries on U.S. military bases also went through something similar, when food spoiled after the temperature shot up inside refrigerators and freezers overnight.

The French government is the first to formally assign blame for the wave of destructive attacks.

They were able to identify the hackers through a series of digital clues, including digital infrastructure used by the hackers, connection to a propaganda outlet, and "traces" of the use of Farsi language in the attack, according to ANSSI .

While NPR and others have reported that U.S. officials suspect Iran may have been behind the attacks on U.S. military bases in August, the Pentagon has not made any official statement, even to conclude that the disruptions were in fact the result of a cyberattack.

"Consistent with our policy and to preserve the integrity of the process, the DOD [Office of Inspector General] Criminal Investigative Service does not discuss ongoing investigations," Mollie Halpern, a spokesperson for the Department of War Office of the Inspector General wrote in an email to NPR.

Attacks fit Iranian hackers' modus operandi

If Iranian hackers are behind the attacks across Europe, the U.S. and Israel, cybersecurity experts say that would fit with what they know about Iranian hackers' strategy and goals.

"Iran's cyberattacks against refrigeration systems likely represents the IRGC attempting to reassert Iranian power abroad through both physically and psychologically disruptive operations," Alex Orleans, the head of threat intelligence at cybersecurity firm Sublime Security, told NPR. "Such activities continue to provide tangible and cost-effect results given how Iran's national resources remain tied down in the war."

"Also, Shahid Kaveh, the IRGC cyber unit that the French specifically attributed the disruptive attacks to, is repeating a pattern here," Orleans says. He referenced a series of cyberattacks on American water treatment plants in August, which most experts believe were linked to Iran, as precedent. The U.S. government has still not officially attributed those attacks.

Sponsor Message

"This unit has once again refined its tradecraft through attacks on Israeli targets before shifting their targeting to the same systems in the West," Orleans says.

For those tracking Shahid Kaveh and the other Iranian cyber units that operate alongside it, these attacks fit squarely into their modus operandi.

"Shahid Kaveh group is an offensive cyber unit responsible for some of the greatest hits of Iranian offensive cyber [operations]," says Ari Ben Am, an adjunct fellow at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies' Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.

One group tied to Shahid Kaveh is the Cyber Av3ngers, he explains, which the U.S. government linked to cyberattacks on Israeli-made systems in U.S. water treatment facilities in the winter between 2023 and 2024. The French government also cited other cyberattacks carried out on behalf of the IRGC against French interests, including against the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo and another against digital kiosks used at the Paris Olympics in 2024.

Challenges in securing operational technology

Cybersecurity experts say the attacks on refrigeration controllers have highlighted a yearslong difficulty with securing operational technology, the machines that control physical processes in the real world — from water pumps to cooling systems.

These machines are often outdated and riddled with vulnerabilities, and are very difficult to patch because operators can't afford to shut them down and disrupt critical services including healthcare and transportation. Additionally, the machines are often left exposed to the open internet — often at least in part due to contractual requirements with vendors that want to maintain those systems remotely. That combination of factors makes it a complicated problem to solve .

Iran has yet to respond to the accusations. However, Monday's accusation by the French government may lead other affected countries to take action as well.

During Monday's G7 meeting in Paris, Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked by journalists whether the U.S. shared information with the French to help with their attribution of the Iranian hacks. Rubio said he couldn't comment, but noted that the "French are quite capable."

Sponsor Message

"What kind of sickos are these people?" he asked. "They attack refrigerators. France is not even involved in this, really," referring to the war between the U.S. and Iran, which began in February. "[These Iranians] do terrible things around the world … the news today doesn't surprise us," Rubio concluded.

Rebecca Rosman reported from Paris.

World.title: Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas
World.content:
Supreme Court says border wall construction can continue in west Texas

toggle caption i Carlos Morales



/for NPR.

The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the Trump administration to continue with its plans to construct hundreds of miles of border barrier and security infrastructure in west Texas, while a court hearing over the effort moves forward.

The federal government's plans have stirred bipartisan backlash for its inclusion of Big Bend National Park, a beloved stretch of public land known for its sweeping canyons and unspoiled desert landscape.

In a five-page decision issued Monday , the high court wrote that the federal judge who ruled on the order didn't have the authority to weigh in.

Sponsor Message

"The injunction thus impedes the Government from advancing its 'compelling interests' in border security and integrity," reads the unsigned decision. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenter in the decision.

The court wrote that federal law allows the Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to waive environmental protections and conservation laws, which they called a "clear preference for expeditious border construction over the very harms respondents assert."

In an emergency application to the high court in late October , the federal government urged the justices to intervene and allow the work to begin again, saying that a gap in "border defenses" in the Big Bend region "would act as "a dangerous magnet for cartels and other bad actors."

toggle caption i Carlos Morales/for NPR.

A federal judge in El Paso issued the temporary injunction that halted the construction of 30-foot-tall steel barriers, patrol roads, surveillance systems and other border infrastructure.

The Center for Biological Diversity, an environmental advocacy group, brought forward the lawsuit, along with an area nonprofit working to preserve a historic church near the U.S.-Mexico border and a landowner who stands to lose his border property.

"This decision greenlights the contractors and allows the bulldozers to come roaring back into the region," said Laiken Jordahl with the Center for Biological Diversity. "It allows the dynamiting of national park canyon walls, the bulldozing of pristine desert."

Sponsor Message

The lawsuit argued that the Department of Homeland Security's plans are unconstitutional and that Big Bend residents would be "irreparably harmed" if the construction continues.

The Trump administration's plans for the beloved Big Bend region of Texas have provoked an unusual bipartisan backlash. People across the political spectrum say a wall isn't needed in the Big Bend––a region known for its sweeping canyons, tough terrain and unforgiving desert heat. They worry about the threats a wall or any other kind of infrastructure poses to the region, from the impact on the environment and Indigenous sites to the effect on the region's tourism-based economy and on wild animals .

In the Trump administration's emergency relief request to the Supreme Court , Solicitor General John Sauer called the injunction "baseless" and "unprecedented" and said any pocket of the Big Bend without a barrier would "become a funnel point for illegal alien crossings that are thwarted by barriers elsewhere."

Historically, the Big Bend area's rugged landscape has meant fewer people attempting to cross into the U.S. through this pocket of the border. And while the Big Bend Sector, a nearly 500-mile stretch covered by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, makes up over a quarter of the U.S.-Mexico border, it regularly sees the fewest number of encounters along the Texas border, according to CBP data .

World.title: Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
World.content:
Thomas Massie files articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

toggle caption i Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images

Rep. Thomas Massie has reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, setting up a vote in the House of Representatives in the next two days.

The Kentucky Republican's resolution accuses Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors and lists eight specific charges against him.

The allegations include:

3 charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution

1 charge for ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties

1 charge for overseeing "extrajudicial killings" in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean with strikes on alleged drug boats

1 charge for suppressing free speech, brought in connection to the effort to punish Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for a video telling service members they can refuse illegal orders

1 charge for the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization

1 charge for illegally waging war against Yemen in violation of the War Powers Resolution

toggle caption i Finn Gomez/Getty Images

Hegseth defended his record at the Pentagon in a video released last Thursday, dismissing Massie's effort as "sham articles of impeachment."

Sponsor Message

"Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me," Hegseth said.

Speaking to reporters during an impromptu press briefing on Monday, Trump expressed support for his embattled Defense Secretary.

"I'll stand by him," Trump said. "He won two wars. He was in charge. We all won."

Massie has long been a staunch critic of Hegseth. During the GOP primary, Hegseth campaigned on behalf of Ed Gallrein, who went on to defeat Massie.

In response to Hegseth calling him a "disgruntled defeated congressman," Massie told reporters on Monday: "Well, he's right about one thing — I'm a defeated congressman. I'm not disgruntled."

He added: "I'm being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing someone, really. You don't go to prison, you don't go to jail, you don't pay a fine. When the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious."

Massie said the effort also underscores the need to litigate whether Congress has real war powers or not. The war powers resolution has largely been ignored by presidents of both parties.

"What's at heart here is the balance of power between the executive branch and Congress," he said.

Massie first sought to bring the impeachment resolution to the floor before the midterm elections, prompting Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to call an early recess to avoid the vote. That caused the resolution to expire, which is why Massie reintroduced the resolution Monday.

Sponsor Message

Presumptive next House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has already signaled support for an impeachment push against Hegseth.

Even Republican members who oppose impeaching Hegseth have said the Trump administration could do a better job making the case to Congress and the public about what the plan is for the Iran war going forward.

Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio., indicated to NPR that impeachment would be hypocritical given that administrations going back to the Korean War have largely ignored Congress' war powers efforts.

"I think trying to scapegoat Pete Hegseth is just the status quo politics in Washington," he said. "I think it would be a mistake to impeach."

Davidson said lawmakers who want changes are better off trying to leverage the power of the purse to withhold money from the conflict.

There could be sufficient votes to impeach Hegseth in the House, with the support of all Democrats, Massie, and a handful of Republicans. However, it is unlikely to clear the higher Senate threshold for convicting and removing Hegseth from office — which requires two-thirds of the Senate.

NPR's Eric McDaniel contributed to this report.

World.title: Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution
World.content:
Thick smog shrouds New Delhi after Diwali firecrackers add to seasonal pollution

toggle caption i Manish Swarup/AP

NEW DELHI — A thick blanket of smog shrouded India's capital Monday after firecrackers lit up the skies over New Delhi during Diwali celebrations, compounding dangerously high pollution levels and intensifying the seasonal air pollution crisis that grips the city every year.

Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents in New Delhi celebrated the Hindu festival of lights with firecrackers on Sunday evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the atmosphere. The air quality index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital on Monday morning, reaching the severe category and posing significant health risks.

Monitoring stations across the city recorded similarly alarming levels, while visibility deteriorated as a gray haze blanketed streets and high-rise buildings.

Sponsor Message

India's Supreme Court in October had sought to limit Diwali pollution by restricting conventional firecrackers and allowing only approved "green firecrackers" under specified conditions for three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. The crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. They still release particulate matter and other pollutants, adding to the city's already hazardous air.

Isyad, a New Delhi resident who uses one name, said the worsening smog was taking a toll on his health.

"Because of the pollution there is irritation in the throat and itching in the eyes," he said.

New Delhi and its metropolitan region, home to more than 30 million people, regularly rank among the world's most polluted areas during winter. Pollution worsens as Diwali fireworks coincide with cooler weather and smoke from crop-residue fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana.

After harvesting rice, farmers often burn leftover stalks to clear their fields for the next planting season. The smoke drifts toward New Delhi, adding to pollution from vehicles, industries, construction dust and other local sources.

The problem becomes particularly acute in late October and November, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing. The result is a thick haze that can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

toggle caption i Manish Swarup/AP

Authorities in New Delhi have implemented a set of measures to curb pollution, which include limits on construction activity and restrictions on diesel generators, while courts have sough restrictions on firecrackers. But the measures have not prevented the return of severe pollution each year.

Sponsor Message

Environmentalists say long-term solutions, such as cleaner energy and stricter controls on vehicle emissions, are needed to prevent the annual crisis.

Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, described the government's response so far as "knee-jerk" and "temporary."

"A lot of interventions happen only because the government is pressured or pushed in a corner to do something," she said.

World.title: British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault
World.content:
British comedian Russell Brand sentenced to over 10 years for rape and sexual assault

toggle caption i Elizabeth Cook/PA/AP

Russell Brand, the raunchy, irreverent British comedian who became a celebrity darling in the early 2000s, has been sentenced to over 10 years in prison after being found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"The total sentence is one of ten years, six months," said Judge Justice Bennathan on handing down the sentence at Southwark Crown Court in London on Monday.

Brand, 51, was a career chameleon who went from stand-up comic and MTV host to a political analyst esteemed by Britain's left, only to become a conspiracy theorist and Christian convert beloved by the U.S. right.

Sponsor Message

But critics of Brand said there was always a clear thread of misogyny running through his comedy routines, and that his mistreatment of women had been an open secret for decades.

Over the past four weeks, six women testified against the comedian in court in London, in a trial that garnered massive media attention.

A jury found Brand guilty last week on four of the seven counts against him. He was found guilty of raping a woman he'd met at one of his shows in 2009 and of sexually assaulting three women — at a bar, a radio station and a TV studio — between 2004 and 2009.

Brand denies all charges and said he never had non-consensual sex.

Before the judge handed down the sentence, four of the women who brought the case against Brand gave victim impact statements to the court. Three of the statements were read out by the prosecution, while one woman appeared in court behind a curtain to read her own.

None of the women have been publicly named and the trial was not televised.

Victim impact statements read

The prosecution read out an impact statement from the one complainant, who Brand was found guilty of anally raping at his home in 2009. In her statement she said: "It's something I carry with me every day and it often feels never-ending."

Sponsor Message

"I doubt my ability to make good decisions and no longer trust my instinct in the way I did," her statement said, adding that because of Brand's fame she didn't think she'd be believed if she reported him.

toggle caption i Matt Sayles/AP

Another complainant, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting at a bar in 2004 when he grabbed her breasts, said the confusion of what she "should" or "could" do had stayed with her for over 20 years.

The complainant, who spoke in person from behind a curtain in the courtroom, said she felt "physically sick" seeing Brand in the press afterwards as his fame rose.

Another of Brand's victims, who he was found guilty of sexually assaulting in 2005, said the assault had "a lasting impact on her life" and that over the years "hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump."

A fourth woman, who Brand was found guilty of sexually assaulting when they worked together at a TV studio, said she was badly affected and afterwards felt her working environment was unsafe.

Brand holds rosary and prays

British media who were in the court for the sentencing said Brand, who had spent the weekend in prison, was in the suit he was convicted in on Thursday and sat holding a set of white rosary beads as the victim statements were read. Brand's wife Laura, who had supported him throughout the case, was in court, as was his father.

After the victim statements, the defense and prosecution teams had the opportunity to make their last statements.

The prosecution called for a long sentence, saying there were aggravating circumstances in the anal rape case, such as Brand removing a condom. The defence meanwhile said Brand was "a fundamentally different person" from who he was at the time of the crimes.

Sponsor Message

After considering the victim impact statements and those by the defence and prosecution, the judge handed down the sentence live on camera.

In his remarks, he said Brand had become "a sexual predator" and paused "to pay tribute to the determination and bravery" of the women who'd come forward.

He then ordered Brand to be taken down to the cells.

World.title: Congress is back after GOP's midterm defeat. And, Trump appoints new chief of staff
World.content:
Congress is back after GOP's midterm defeat. And, Trump appoints new chief of staff

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

President Trump has appointed Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. It's Trump's first major personnel change since the Republicans' defeat in the midterms. Miller, who was deputy chief of staff, has been key in shaping many of Trump's controversial policies, particularly on immigration. Voter data indicates that the Democrats gained support partly due to Trump's immigration enforcement.

toggle caption i Alex Wong/Getty Images

🎧 Miller supports unchecked executive power. By selecting him, Trump is signaling his readiness to confront an opposition Congress, NPR's Mara Liasson tells Up First. The president has also posted on social media that he offered the White House Press Secretary job to Dana White, the CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. He later said it was a joke. As president, the public takes his words seriously, and the fact that people cannot take his statements at face value poses a challenge for the U.S., Liasson says.

The 119th Congress is reaching its final weeks before a new Democrat-controlled House and Senate step in. Lawmakers' key agenda item is keeping the federal government open, as funding runs out on Dec. 11. They will likely use a short-term continuing resolution to extend funding, because they lack the time and political will to negotiate the typical 12 appropriations bills.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Attendance could be a problem for many of the Republicans defeated in the midterms, NPR's Eric McDaniel says. With only a two-vote majority in the House, any absenteeism could jeopardize Republican plans to end their time in power on their own terms. McDaniel says Senate Republicans will likely want to confirm as many judges and Trump appointees as possible before Democrats take over in January. Once the Democrats take control, McDaniel says those confirmations won't happen without significant compromises from the White House.

Massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia is launching an internal investigation after reports that its CEO was involved in a close relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. The New York Times reported that a Chinese intelligence operation targeted Jensen Huang to send advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. NPR reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment but has not received a response. China denied the allegations on Monday in a press briefing.



🎧 Nvidia plays a crucial role in the U.S. economy as a leading company at the center of the AI revolution, NPR's John Ruwitch says. Huang has significant access to Trump, communicating frequently and even traveling to China with him. When asked about Huang and the incident, Trump said he thinks "Huang is a fine person." The U.S. restricts exports of advanced chips to China, including Nvidia's best chips. Huang has argued that allowing China to buy these chips would slow the growth of its chipmaking industry and benefit America. Despite ongoing investigations, Nvidia believes that neither national security nor its secrets are compromised. The House of Representatives has requested a closed-door briefing from Huang regarding his interactions with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.

Sponsor Message

Deep dive

Connie Hanzhang Jin/NPR

Climate change is transforming the vibrant colors of nature, from Arctic landscapes to coral reefs. The effects of these color shifts are complex, and scientists are racing to understand them. Here's how climate change is altering the colors of the world:

➡️ Every summer, climate-driven wildfires blanket Arctic ice in soot. These dark particles from oil and gas operations, commercial shipping and tourism absorb heat from the sun, accelerating melting ice and contributing to sea-level rise.

➡️ As permafrost thaws deeper into the soil, nutrients become more available, enabling larger vegetation to take hold and turning the landscape greener. A 2020 study in Nature Communications found that about 38% of sites in Alaska, Canada and western Eurasia showed greening.

➡️ Thawing permafrost can also mix soil with lake water, turning them darker. A 2021 study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America (PNAS) found green wavelengths in lakes in the boreal Arctic zone declined by 15% from 1984 to 2019, making these lakes appear darker to the naked eye. The darker a lake gets, the more heat it can store.

➡️ Some insects have changed color due to warmer climates. North American male dragonflies are losing wing color, according to a study in PNAS. This helps them stay cooler but also reduces the coloration that attracts females.

Picture show

toggle caption i Tamera Merino for NPR

The Atacama Desert in Chile has transformed into a vibrant patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples, thanks to the El Niño super cycle. This floral bloom has been the largest and most colorful in at least 30 years. The phenomenon followed unprecedented rainfall that caused flash floods, damaging homes and forcing evacuations. The rain reached deep into the parched ground, awakening millions of dormant seeds, bulbs and tubers. Now, more than 200 species have burst into color, creating a breathtaking spectacle where every crevice is streaked with hues.

Sponsor Message

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Alastair Grant/AP

Comedian Russell Brand faces a "significant" prison sentence as a London court is set to announce his punishment today after a jury convicted him on three counts of sexual assault and one count of rape. Brand has denied all charges. The U.S. homeless population decreased by more than 6% in 2025, according to the Department of Housing and Urban Development. This marks the second consecutive year of decline. Pope Leo XIV arrived in South America on Friday for a 12-day trip across three countries. This will be his longest and most significant journey to date, as well as his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Why a South Korean city is turning to a U.S. college to outsmart AI?
World.content:
Why a South Korean city is turning to a U.S. college to outsmart AI?

toggle caption i Anthony Kuhn/NPR

CHUNCHEON, South Korea — "Is the Frankenstein monster human?" a teacher asks students at the Toegye public elementary school in Chuncheon city, some 50 miles east of Seoul, as they discuss Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein.

"I think we can call it a human being with no soul," ventures student Ma Yeonwoo.

The Toegye school has adopted the " Great Books" educational model used by St. John's College, whose main campus is in Annapolis, Md.

The class's discussion then shifts to whether artificial intelligence is human.

"No," Ma Yeonwoo responds, because humans created AI, and although it is intelligent, it "has no creativity."

Sponsor Message

In the "Great Books" model, teachers do not lecture, they only guide discussions. There are no majors or elective courses. Students do not seek answers from outside sources such as the internet and rely only on their readings, their own reasoning and class discussions with their peers.

That suits Ma Yeonwoo, who says he enjoys debating with his classmates.

"If only the teacher talks we can have one idea, but if we all debate together, like, we can get many ideas together," he says.

This nascent educational movement addresses several concerning trends. One is that international tests such as PISA have shown a post-COVID drop in South Korean reading skills, after decades in which South Korean and other East Asian students outperformed their American counterparts.

Another is South Korea's rapid adoption of AI in education. 51% of South Korean students say they use AI chatbots to study at least once a week, according to Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) figures. Students also face intense competition to pass college entrance exams, which piles pressure on them down to the pre-K school level and prompts many South Korean families to send their children to cram schools to gain a competitive edge, or to foreign schools to escape the system.

toggle caption i Anthony Kuhn/NPR

"We all feel that this system leaves students with no time to read and think," because they're too busy memorizing facts to pass tests," says Lee Yonghwa, a professor of English language and literature at Incheon National University, where he co-founded South Korea's first "Great Books" program in 2019.

Sponsor Message

But now, Lee laments, "Korean students are even losing their old capacity to memorize facts because they collect facts and ideas mainly from A.I."

And if they can't reason and think independently, he adds, they can't judge the quality of the results that AI generates for them.

The limitations of their educational system motivates many South Koreans to look for alternatives, from education overseas, to educational experiments at home.

"As someone who went through this system, I felt those limitations keenly," Chuncheon Mayor Yook Dong-han said in an interview at city hall. "When I became mayor, I wanted to introduce a different kind of education and a distinct educational philosophy to the city of Chuncheon."

Chuncheon draws visitors from neighboring Seoul to enjoy its mountains, lakes and rivers, and dakgalbi, a local dish of grilled or stir-fried marinated chicken.

Chuncheon's government established an academic partnership with St. John's College last year to promote the "Great Books" educational model.

There are now 120 college students and some 770 younger students taking the "Great Books" program in South Korea, and 40 teachers in training, according to Lee Yonghwa.

Although the program is still in its infancy, Yook says it represents a "small but revolutionary achievement — a breakthrough that challenges established practices," and generated interest among participating students that has exceeded his expectations.

South Korean students following the "Great Books" model read Aristotle, Shakespeare, Euclid, and Korean authors including Nobel laureate Han Kang .

toggle caption i Anthony Kuhn/NPR

In one Chuncheon high school, students read Martin Luther King Jr.'s 1963 Letter from Birmingham Jail.

They discuss King's ideas about what kind of laws are just and unjust, and which laws citizens should obey or disobey.

Lee Yonghwa says he's impressed that students connected King's letter to their own country, such as in 2024, when citizens and lawmakers defeated former President Yoon Suk Yeol's attempt to put South Korea under martial law.

Sponsor Message

That fits the purpose of the "Great Books" model, in which "each seminar table really becomes a miniature republic, where ideas clash but people cooperate," St. John's College President J. Walter Sterling wrote last year in an opinion essay .

Through civic participation and liberal education, he adds, "we quietly stitch the fabric of our democracy…before it unravels beyond repair."

NPR's Se Eun Gong contributed to this report in Chuncheon and Seoul.

World.title: Federal government budgets record $12M for Justin Trudeau's archives — the most for any former PM
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian taxpayers could pay $12 million for former prime minister Justin Trudeau's records from his decade in office — the most the government has ever paid for the archives of any prime minister.

A single line in the federal budget tabled on Thursday reveals that the government has budgeted $3 million a year for the next four years to enable Library and Archives Canada (LAC) to "acquire, preserve and provide Canadians with access to the records of Canada's 23rd Prime Minister Justin Trudeau."

While Trudeau's official photographer, Adam Scotti, donated files to the federal agency, the archives has not yet acquired Trudeau's records, said Patrick Boissonneault, communications adviser at Library and Archives Canada.

Boissonneault said none of the $12 million would go to Trudeau.

There is an established tradition of prominent politicians donating their private records.

Typically, Library and Archives Canada assesses the material that is being offered and determines its monetary value. If LAC decides to acquire the records, the donor then receives a tax receipt for that amount, since the records are considered a gift of cultural property.

Boissonneault said the amount of the tax credit is considered a private matter between the Canada Revenue Agency and the donor.

Over the years, LAC has acquired the records of every former Canadian prime minister with the exception of R.B. Bennett, who served from 1930-35 and John Diefenbaker, who was prime minister from 1957-63, he said.

The cost of archiving prime ministerial papers has varied over the years.

LAC paid a total of $1.4 million to acquire and process the records of four prime ministers — Brian Mulroney, Joseph Clark, John Turner and Kim Campbell, Boissoneault said.

The records from Jean Chrétien's decade in office cost $3.8 million while his successor Paul Martin's roughly two years of archives cost $1.7 million.

The archives spent $8.3 million to acquire, process and preserve the archives of Stephen Harper, Trudeau's predecessor.

Harper served from February 2006 to November 2015 — four months longer than Trudeau.

Boissonneault said the difference in costs is based on a few factors.

"The resources needed to process and make accessible the records of a former prime minister depend on the volume and the complexity of the records, as well as increases due to inflation," Boissonneault said.

Library and Archives faces budget cuts

The funding for Trudeau's records comes as Library and Archives has been hard hit by budget cuts under Prime Minister Mark Carney's government. In its most recent planning report, the archives said it has to reduce its spending by $11.1 million in 2026-27 and another $14.7 million in 2027-28 — the year the new funding for the Trudeau archives is set to begin.

A third cut of $22.1 million is expected for 2028-29.

By the end of the cuts, Library and Archives Canada expects to eliminate the equivalent of 161 full-time positions.

In the report, it says it plans to find the money by discontinuing the Documentary Heritage Communities Program, which helps smaller archives across the country, and gradually reduce its access to information and privacy (ATIP) functions and its proactive review of historical records.

"These changes to its budget and workforce will directly affect LAC's operations and its ability to fully deliver on its expected results," the archives wrote.

Former prime minister Stephen Harper's archives cost taxpayers about $8.3 million. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)

The budget for Trudeau's records comes after Harper celebrated the launch of his records collection earlier this year.

Harper's records include 49.2 metres of textual records and 1.2 million digital photographs, sound recordings, digital moving images and video cassettes. They were the first time that a prime minister's records consisted of a large number of digital files.

During the event to launch Harper's collection, Jennifer Schofield, Library and Archives Canada assistant deputy minister of collections, said LAC invested considerable effort to preserve the records.

"We have a long-standing tradition of acquiring the private records of former prime ministers — photographs, audiovisual materials, paper files and in Mr. Harper's case, terabytes of digital records," she said.

Schofield said Harper's files "marked the largest digital archival acquisition ever undertaken by Library and Archives Canada at the time."

Since leaving office, Trudeau has been travelling the world, carrying out a number of speaking engagements.

In September, he launched a new production company called Hope & Hard Work with his former chief of staff Katie Telford.

On Friday, the University of Oxford's Blavatnik School of Government announced that Trudeau was named a distinguished fellow and a member of the school's World Leaders Circle. Other members of the circle include former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern, former U.K. prime minister Rishi Sunak and former Colombian president Iván Duque.

In a statement accompanying the announcement, Trudeau said the challenges facing governments around the world require thoughtful leadership.

"I look forward to contributing my experience, exchanging perspectives with fellow leaders and engaging with the next generation of government and policy leaders as we consider how governments can respond to change and build a more hopeful, inclusive and prosperous future for everyone," he said.

World.title: Premier Doug Ford suggests 'ass whooping' for 2 boys connected to alleged assault of Hamilton cadet leader
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford had some choice words for the parents of two boys allegedly involved in the assault of a commanding officer for the Royal Canadian Air Cadets who was handing out poppies.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the parents of two boys allegedly involved in the assault of a Hamilton cadet leader should "give your kids a little ass whooping in the wood shed."

Ford's comments at a news conference come a week after the Hamilton Police Service said it charged a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman with assaulting a 59-year-old commanding officer for the Royal Canadian Air Cadets.

T he cadet leader was supervising the distribution of Remembrance Day poppies at the Centre on Barton mall when two boys approached them and blew a loud air horn in the ears of young cadets he was with, police said in a release. The man followed the boys into a nearby restaurant to confront them and "a struggle ensued."

Police said a woman — who they later told CBC News is named Estela Quintanilla — jumped in to assist the boys and assaulted the cadet leader, causing him to fall. The 12-year-old hit him several times, police said.

The family of the cadet leader has identified him as Capt. Kenneth Kunkel. On Nov. 5, his daughter Kimberly Dietrich told CBC's Hanomansing Live that Kunkel was unable to walk.

Dietrich said her family was "taking it a day at a time," and her dad was "trying his hardest to recover."

WATCH | Daughter of cadet leader says he is unable to walk: Cadet leader faces life-altering injuries after ‘senseless’ attack | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 6:23 Capt. Kenneth Kunkel, commanding officer for the Royal Canadian Air Cadets, is suffering from life-altering injuries and is unable to walk for the foreseeable future after an alleged assault by a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman. Kunkel was helping young air cadets collect donations for poppies in Hamilton, Ont., just before the attack. His daughter, Kimberly Dietrich gives Hanomansing Live the latest.

The 12-year-old boy faces aggravated assault and assault level one charges, police said. The second boy was not arr ested, police said, after officers were able to review footage of the incident.

The woman faces aggravated assault charges.

The charges have not been tested in court.

Ford has a history of commenting on criminal cases. Some lawyers have told CBC News that public officials should be careful about such comments, as they ri sk prejudicing juries and contributing to misinformation.

"I just don't know how to process it," Dietrich said of the incident Thursday. "I don't know why someone would even think of doing something like that."

She said it's important to support veterans by wearing poppies.

Hamilton mayor-elect Keanin Loomis issued a statement about the incident Thursday, saying he is "deeply troubled" by it.

"My thoughts are with Kunkel, his family and the cadets during this difficult time. We wish him strength, healing and a full recovery," Loomis said.

World.title: Could Nvidia survive without its ultra-powerful CEO, Jensen Huang?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Jensen Huang, the leather-jacket-wearing and autograph-signing co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, has made himself a seemingly inseparable part of the AI chipmaker.

But now that an investigation is underway into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, that tight control at the company's helm is creating worries about whether he could actually be replaced, if such a move were deemed necessary.

The investigation comes after the New York Times reported late last week that Huang had a close romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive who is accused of spying on behalf of China. It's unclear when he met the executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, but the two were photographed together in 2024.

Nvidia's board said Sunday it had no reason to believe that state or company secrets were compromised, but was undertaking an independent investigation in light of the reports. U.S. House Republican committee leaders have also called on Jensen Huang to sit for a briefing on his relationship with the woman.

In a message to his staff, Huang admitted to having an affair and apologized to his family and colleagues for breaking their trust.

"I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence," he wrote.

Huang will stay on as CEO while the investigation takes place. But if the board were to oust him, or if he changed course and stepped down, tech analysts like Dan Ives say finding someone to take his place would be nearly impossible.

"In my opinion, Jensen is a one of one," said Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., a New York-based modern merchant bank. "Nvidia is here because of Jensen."

'The king of tech'

Nvidia began as a graphics card maker in 1993 until company leaders — Huang in particular — realized that its graphics processor units could power more than just games. The company pivoted to making chips for supercomputers in the early 2010s, betting on an artificial intelligence boom that wouldn't come for many years.

An early partnership with OpenAI led to a long-term relationship with the ChatGPT creator, which still relies on Nvidia's chips to power its technology today. Amazon , Meta , Google and virtually every other company building AI tools rely on the chipmaker's hardware to power their systems.

Worth about $4.5 trillion US today, Nvidia is the second most valuable company in the world, and invaluable to the AI ecosystem as a whole, according to Ives.

From his place atop the massive company, Huang became something of a rock star, routinely signing fan autographs at public appearances. One of his signature leather jackets sold for more than $1 million at an auction earlier this year.

"He's gotten to the point where he's sort of like the king of tech. Everybody listens to what Jensen has to say," said Bob O'Donnell, president and chief analyst at Technalysis Research.

Outside of his own company, Huang has also championed the AI buildout, financially backing companies like cloud computing company CoreWeave and Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot. He has also dismissed fears about an AI bubble and challenged apocalyptic warnings about the technology's existential threat to humanity, and has forged a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump .

WATCH | Nvidia shares drop amid investigation into Huang: Nvidia shares tumble as company investigates CEO Jensen Huang | Duration 2:13 Nvidia is conducting an internal probe following a media report that CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing. Nvidia's shares fell nearly six per cent in early morning trading. At the current levels, the chipmaker would lose around $280 billion US in value from its last closing price.

Ives says the loss of Huang's advocacy would be a major hit to the industry if he had to step away.

Meanwhile, within the company, Huang created an unusually flat chain of command, with many employees reporting directly to him rather than to high-level executives. On a podcast earlier this year, Huang said as many as 60 people reported to him directly.

The company's site lists only a handful of high-ranking executives aside from Huang.

Two of Huang's children are also on staff at the company — his son Spencer is director of product for robotics, while his daughter Madison is senior director of product marketing.

No clear successor

With Huang having held control at Nvidia for so long, analysts say there is no clear successor.

"There's no one person or two people or three people that could replace Jensen. And that's a scary thing for investors, given this … black-eye moment that we're seeing," Ives said.

If Huang were forced to step down, Ives worries Nvidia would never fully recover from the loss of his leadership, given his integral role in the company's growth.

But others say with a firm as big as Nvidia, there are others who could take on the top job.

WATCH | A look into the spying scandal: The falling star of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang | About That | Duration 2:58 U.S. tech giant Nvidia's shares tumbled after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a woman accused of spying for Beijing. Andrew Chang breaks down what we know so far and what the scandal means for the world’s most valuable AI chipmaker. Images provided by The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images

"You don't create a company that large by yourself, right? It's just not possible. There's a huge team of very strong, smart, capable people," O'Donnell said.

While he agrees that Huang's loss would be massive, he says the company's technology roadmap — used to plan the next few years — is already laid out, making any potential successor's job easier.

O'Donnell expects Nvidia is on track to keep its leadership position among chipmakers for now, and doesn't expect a shakeup at the top would change that.

Furthermore, with the board saying it has confidence in Huang , O'Donnell says he doesn't expect those members would try to oust him.

Still, if Huang does stay on as CEO, his grip on the company likely won't be so tight going forward, O'Donnell says, as other high-ranking executives are likely to take centre stage as spokespeople and dealmakers at least some of the time.

"It's hard to replace an iconic figure who just lights up a room," he said. But "if the board is smart, and I'm sure they are, they recognize they're going to have to address this so people can regain confidence in the company."

World.title: $276 for hair ties? Skims offers advent calendar refunds after online backlash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The contents of the Skims 2026 accessories advent calendar have been described as what you might find in the bottom of your purse, on the floor of a car, or behind your dresser when you pull it away from the wall.

After intense customer backlash, Kim Kardashian's apparel brand is offering refunds to anyone who purchased the calendar. The package costs $276 Cdn (or $148 US — a relative premium), is advertised as "12 fun days of surprises" and contains an assortment of hair ties, bobby pins and key chains.

Viral unboxing videos posted over the weekend by disappointed customers have called the pricey calendar "a mess" and a scam.

"Are we serious right now?" exclaimed influencer Kayla Ryan as she opened the package for Day 4 to reveal three pink bobby pins. She called it "the worst advent calendar I have ever seen" in her Saturday video which accrued more than 20 million views as of Monday morning.

" I’m hoping this is a prank and the last one is a $150 gift card for all my money back," she added, after opening Day 9 to reveal an ornamental keychain comb that can't actually comb hair.

"This is the last one and it better be made of gold," another content creator says in a TikTok video with nearly 65 million views before opening Day 12 to reveal a furry compact mirror on a key chain and then grimacing.

"So, basically, everything that falls between my car seats," one person commented on the video; another described it as "wild for maybe $20 worth of stuff."

A composite of three screen grabs from TikTok unboxing videos for the new 2026 Skims advent calendar by, from left, @wetsloppyswollen, Brittany Shaw, and influencer Kayla Ryan. (@wetsloppyswollen/TikTok, @kaylaryan/TikTok, @brittanyshaw2.0/TikTok)

In statements provided to multiple media outlets, a Skims spokesperson said the company was " aware of the feedback" about the advent calendar and acknowledged that "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations."

The company told told Page Six they "personally contacted every customer who purchased the calendar" and offered either a full refund or credit towards their other products.

CBC News reached out to Skims for further comment but has not received a reply.

WATCH | Chanel dragged for $1,025 advent calendar: Chanel advent calendar lambasted on social media | Duration 2:07 Chanel’s limited edition advent calendar, priced at $1,025, has become the subject of backlash online after it left some consumers unimpressed. Strategists say it could serve as a reminder of how to market to a Gen Z audience.

'Disappointed they got what they paid for'

This is far from the first advent calendar controversy. In 2021, Chanel was roasted online for a $1,025 calendar full of stickers, a magnet, a keychain and other miscellaneous branded items in addition to a miniature lipstick, hand cream and small bottle of perfume.

A year later, Dior was slammed for a nearly $5,000 advent calendar that mostly contained candle accessories and scented soaps in addition to small bottles of perfume.

Some commentators have criticized high-end advent calendars for being little more than luxury status symbols driven by the unboxing craze. Last year, for instance, Dior sold an $11,000 calendar. In 2019, Tiffany & Co. released a limited advent calendar that contained 24 pieces of jewelry and cost $158,000.

The Skims advent calendar is currently sold out with a waitlist. Some people have noted, the product description online details exactly what can be found in the calendar each day: a bear keychain, hair elastics, scrunchies, bobby pins, a squishie, bra elastic hairbands, more bobby pins, a comb keychain, a logo keychain, more scrunchies and a faux fur compact mirror keychain.

"W hile I agree the contents are ridiculously overpriced, we need to have a conversation about personal accountability as consumers," one person wrote on Threads.

LISTEN | Extravagant advent calendars: Radio Noon Manitoba 18:11 Extravagant Advent Calendars and the Evolution of Adult Holiday Traditions Rob Warren, marketing professor at the University of North Dakota, speaks with host Marjorie Dowhos about the rise of high-end advent calendars for adults and why retailers are capitalizing on childhood nostalgia.

" If the contents were disclosed, you ignored the description, spent $148 [US], and then acted completely blindsided by what you received, some of that responsibility belongs to YOU."

A Toronto influencer who goes by the name Glamzilla online defended the advent calendar in a TikTok video, where she argued it's about the experience of opening something leading up to the holidays rather than a "big gift."

She was dragged in the video's comments, with some accusing of "gaslighting" and being insensitive to the price.

World.content:
The National | U.S. Republican moves to impeach Hegseth

News

LIVE

Nov. 9, 2026 | An outgoing Republican representative introduces articles of impeachment against embattled U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. Stellantis sells a major Ontario assembly plant to a Canadian armoured vehicle maker. And, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is investigated for his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

World.title: Roshel to buy Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton for undisclosed amount, automaker says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian armoured vehicle maker Roshel Inc. will buy the Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., the two companies announced Monday. CBC’s Dana Roberts breaks down what we know.

Canadian armoured ⁠vehicle maker Roshel Inc. will buy the Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., the automaker announced Monday.

Roshel will acquire the idled facility and associated equipment from the automaker for an undisclosed amount, Stellantis said.

The companies said they are also exploring future collaboration across vehicle technologies and related services in the defence industry.

In a news release, Stellantis said the announcement will "create a path to return Brampton Assembly Plant to productive industrial use."

The news comes after Unifor, which represents Canadian workers at Stellantis, said it met with Stellantis on Friday to ask about reports that the plant had been sold and said the company would not confirm or deny if a sale had been finalized.

'Stellantis has betrayed our members': union president

Unifor national president Lana Payne said Monday that the sale is an "unacceptable outcome" for the union and its members, calling it the "worst-case scenario." Closing and selling the plant cuts Canada's auto vehicle production capacity by 10 per cent, she said.

"Selling an auto assembly plant and losing vehicle production capacity is devastating for the Canadian industry, for our country, but mostly for the workers who have given so much to this company over so many years," Payne told a news conference.

"Because once that capacity is gone, it's often gone for good, and along with it, thousands of good union jobs and thousands more along the supply chain," she added.

Unifor national president Lana Payne said Monday that the sale is an 'unacceptable outcome' for the union and its members, calling it the 'worst-case scenario.' (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

"Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers. Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of our national auto strategy and breaks the federal government's promise to protect auto workers from this U.S. trade war."

Payne said the union urged the company to keep the plant in a "ready state for future work" despite U.S. tariffs.

"Stellantis has walked away from its obligations to Canadian workers in Brampton. Roshel upfitting trucks for the military is not the same as building vehicles from the ground up," she said.

The union will meet later this week with company and government officials, she added.

Automaker committed to 'fair resolution' for workers

Stellantis said it acknowledges its obligations to workers under their collective agreement and is prepared to engage with Unifor to negotiate a settlement.

"Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution,” Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa said in the release.

A handful of Unifor members gathered outside the Brampton assembly plant on Monday to show support for the union after the sale was announced. (Dana Roberts/CBC)

The move opens "new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry," Filosa added.

Roshel founder and CEO Roman Shimonov said the company's plan is to create a new centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing "which will allow Canadian companies to better serve customers at home and export into allied markets."

"Aligned with Canada's defence industrial strategy, it will strengthen our sovereign industrial capabilities, drive local economic growth and bring much-needed manufacturing space and jobs to the Toronto area," Shimonov said in the release.

In an interview on CBC's Hanomansing Live on Monday, Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov said the company plans to lease some of the site's space back to Stellantis, but added Roshel is not assuming responsibility for obligations made by Stellantis.

Shimonov said it is in the best interests of Roshel to utilize as much of the plant as possible, adding it hopes to bring in a major European automaker that he declined to name. Roshel has a letter of intent from the automaker and the plant will not simply manufacture defence vehicles, he said.

"Our goal is to employ thousands of people and we'll definitely give the first priority to Brampton people," he said.

In September, Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel for a potential sale of the facility.

Over 2,000 workers laid off when plant idled in 2023

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023.

In August, the union said it received notice that Stellantis was considering the closure and sale of the plant. The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025.

WATCH | 'Punch to the gut': Brampton's mayor comments on Stellantis moving production: Stellantis moving production to U.S. ‘punch to the gut’: mayor of Brampton, Ont. | Duration closed caption 7:17 Mayor Patrick Brown says retaliatory tariffs need to be back on the table after automaker Stellantis announced plans to move Jeep production slated for the plant in Brampton, Ont., to south of the border.

It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to the U.S., in what the union called a violation of its current collective agreement, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

The news of the sale comes as contract talks between Stellantis and the union representing more than 9,000 of its workers in Canada remain at an impasse.

The two sides have clashed over the future of the Brampton site as well as issues around job security. Last month, Stellantis workers in Canada voted to give their union a mandate to strike, with 97.3 per cent of members in favour of authorizing a potential job action.

Unifor said at the time a strike was still its "last resort" and that it hoped to reach a deal with the automaker.

Federal ministers call for return to bargaining talks

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a statement posted on social media platform X on Monday that the decision to sell the plant doesn't "erase the commitment" that Stellantis made to its workers.

"We remain focused on finding solutions for the more than 2,000 affected workers and their families. They deserve answers, respect and, above all, a secure future," Joly said.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, pictured here during question period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Nov. 4, said Monday that the decision to sell the plant doesn't 'erase the commitment' that Stellantis made to its workers. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

Joly said the parties involved must return to the bargaining table. She said she has reached out to representatives from Stellantis, Unifor, Ontario government and the Brampton plan to hold a meeting later this week.

"I expect them to come to the table with a single focus: protecting good-paying jobs in Brampton," Joly said.

"For Brampton's auto workers, walking away is not an option. We are unequivocal in our efforts to defend and grow Canada's auto sector in Brampton and across the country."

'Families deserve answers,' minister says

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, also MP for Brampton East, said in a post on X that he support Joly's call to a return to the bargaining table.

"More than 2,000 Brampton assembly workers and their families deserve answers about their future," Sidhu said.

"This plant has been part of our city’s auto industry for generations. Stellantis made commitments to these workers, and it must honour them.

Sidhu said the federal government will continue to advocate for the plant to deliver good-paying jobs in Brampton.

'We're angry today in Brampton,' mayor says

Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown said in an interview that Stellantis has a legal obligation to Canadian taxpayers for the production incentives it received to produce cars in the city and a moral obligation to members of Unifor Local 1285 who worked hard for decades at the plant.

"We're angry today in Brampton," Brown said on Monday. "Stellantis has an obligation that they cannot renege on."

Brown said the announcement contained few details about what exactly will be produced at the plant. He noted that the land on which the plant sits is zoned for automotive production.

"If we allow Stellantis to cut and run in Brampton, don't think for a second there's not going to be more of this across this country. This is ground zero for Canadian automotive production. I worry, if we allow Stellantis to run, with no consequences, we are really accepting automotive production to leave Canada entirely," Brown said.

Brown said he is calling on Roshel to work directly with the union local to identify hiring and training opportunities for the laid-off Brampton autoworkers.

The transaction is expected to close by the end of this year, subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.

World.title: Booker Prize goes to post-apocalyptic, sci-fi novel The End of Everything
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

English author M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for his novel The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic adventure that explores what it means to be human in a shifting world.

The £50,000 (approx. $94,893 Cdn) prize annually recognizes the best original novel written in the English language and published in the U.K.

The End of Everything is set in a slow-collapsing, near-future landscape along the Kent coast of the U.K. Years after an obscure, world-altering crisis, governments across the world barely function and the seas teem with strange new life.

Harrison becomes the first sci-fi author to win the award.

Harrison is an author and literary critic. He sold his first story in 1965, and in 1969 joined the staff of the U.K. speculative fiction magazine New Worlds, where he edited the books pages until 1978.

His novels include Climbers, which won the Boardman Tasker Prize for Mountain Literature in 1989; Nova Swing, which won the Arthur C. Clarke Award in 2007; and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again, which won the 2020 Goldsmiths Prize for innovation in fiction.

A collection of short stories, You Should Come With Me Now, was published in 2017, and a volume of selected stories written between 1970 and 2020 was published under the title Settling the World.

This year's Booker Prize jury is comprised of poet, writer and educator Raymond Antrobus, musician, writer and broadcaster Jarvis Cocker, journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and poet and essayist Patricia Lockwood.

The jury is chaired by English classicist, writer and broadcaster Mary Beard.

The shortlist also included Jamaican author Marlon James's The Disappearers, Scottish author Douglas Stuart’s John of John, U.K. poet and writer Luke Kennard's Black Bag, English writer Rebecca Perry's May We Feed the King and American author Elizabeth Strout's The Things We Never Say.

The six-book shortlist was whittled down from a longlist of 13. Shortlisted writers will receive £2,500 (approx. $4,692 Cdn) and a specially bound copy of their book.

There are no Canadians on this year's list.

Since 2013, authors from any nationality have been eligible for the Booker Prize.

In 2025, Montreal-born author David Szalay won the Booker prize for his novel Flesh.

Two other Canadians have won the prize since its inception in 1969: Michael Ondaatje in 1992 for The English Patient and Yann Martel in 2002 for Life of Pi.

World.title: Mother testifies police killing of autistic son in Surrey, B.C., left her 'broken'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story mentions threats of suicide.

The mother of a 15-year-old autistic boy who was fatally shot by an RCMP officer in Surrey last year says her son's death has "broken" her.

Crystal de Balinhard was testifying at the B.C. Coroners Service inquest into the death of Chase de Balinhard, who died on a Surrey street corner during a confrontation with police. Chase was carrying a pellet gun that, at the time, police believed was a handgun.

De Balinhard said Chase lived with multiple challenges, including XYY syndrome, autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, anxiety disorder and intellectual disability.

De Balinhard said on Feb. 9, 2025, she drove a niece to the airport before stopping at a pub to meet her husband at a multi-family Super Bowl party on her way home.

Chase had opted out of the party to stay home, saying he was tired.

De Balinhard said at the pub she received texts from two friends asking if she knew what was happening at the school near their home. One of the friends said there may be a school shooter.

De Balinhard became worried that Chase may have left the house to video the incident.

"He'd do these videos pretending that he was a YouTuber, but they were just for us," said de Balinhard.

The IIO published this image of the pellet gun Chase de Balinhard was carrying when he was shot and killed by police. (IIO B.C.)

She said she checked Chase's location on an app and it showed two addresses near a corner. When she tried to drive to where his phone was pinging, the roads were blocked off.

"So I started walking but a nice lady officer said, ‘You can't go there.' I said my 15-year-old autistic boy's phone is pinging up there. You could see the reaction on her face," said an emotional de Balinhard. "[The officer] said why don't you go sit in your car."

De Balinhard said she and her husband were prevented from getting close to Chase's body.

"We tried to get by police but they held us back," she said. "I just wanted to see him. I wanted to say goodbye."

Police responded to the Clayton Heights neighbourhood after Chase called 911 saying he was armed with a gun and threatening to harm himself.

According to a report by the Independent Investigations Office of B.C. (IIO), police attempted to apprehend the boy for 22 minutes. The report says Chase pointed what appeared to be a handgun at himself and police several times before two officers shot at him. The Grade 10 student was hit by a single bullet.

The gun was later discovered to be a pellet gun Chase had taken from the family home. De Balinhard said the pellet gun was kept locked in a location that she wasn't aware he had access to.

Chase de Balinhard, 15, was fatally shot by police in Surrey, B.C., on Feb. 9, 2025. (GoFundMe.ca)

De Balinhard said Chase could become dysregulated or upset if overstimulated by things like loud noises or people yelling at him.

"He didn't respond well," she said. "He told me loud noises hurt his body. It made him want to flee."

She also said in addition to his normal triggers, he was dealing with the aftermath of surgery on a painful cyst on his buttocks that wasn't healing.

She said the morning of his death, Chase was in good spirits after a pancake breakfast with his cousin and grandmother.

"It was the first time he cut his food with a fork and knife by himself and he was so happy," she said.

The site of the fatal police shooting, near 185 Street and 70 Avenue in Surrey, is photographed on Monday, Feb. 10, 2025 — one day after the incident. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

De Balinhard said she'd like to see first responders receive better training around dealing with people with autism.

"I wish officers could learn some of the signs," she said. "With autistics, when everything goes sideways for them they can't communicate. Why not give people the tools to do their job better?"

De Balinhard testified that Chase was a sweet, kind boy who loved Terry Fox, superheroes and playing jokes on his family. He loved his cat Ava and learned to paddle a kayak. She said his superpowers were identifying anything to do with the Titanic and mastering arcade claw machines.

"He would win all the time and would usually give his prizes away," she said. "He had a big heart."

De Balinhard said Chase did well in elementary school with the extra support provided, but once he moved to high school the support dropped off. She said in his Grade 10 year, despite the school receiving funding to help him, he received no support and had stopped attending altogether.

"Surrey started this thing where funding goes into a big pool and it wasn't going to him," said de Balinhard. "He regressed."

Dr. Patricia Frew, a psychiatrist who worked with Chase, said the teen had developed chronic suicidal thoughts, although not to the extent that he needed to be apprehended under the Mental Health Act.

A coroner's inquest is a public process involving a jury that does not find fault. At its conclusion, the jury and presiding coroner can make recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
