World.title: Ladies in White Leader Released After Two Days in Detention
World.content:
Berta Soler was injured in her right foot as a result of violence during her arrest. / Facebook/Ángel Moya

Berta Soler was subjected to violence during her arrest, confined to a dark cell, and interrogated by State Security.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Berta Soler, leader of the Ladies in White, was released on Monday after being held by State Security for 46 hours, during which her whereabouts were unknown. Her husband, Angel Moya, announced the news on social media: “Released bearing the marks of violent repression.”

Moya reported that Berta Soler was released at around 10 a.m. “on a public street, near the headquarters of the Ladies in White,” in the Havana neighborhood of Lawton. In his post, Moya provided details about an injury the activist sustained to her right foot as a result of the violence during her arrest.

Soler was taken to the Aguilera police station in Diez de Octubre and later transferred to the Cotorro police station, where, according to the activist, she received medical attention before being confined to a dark cell.

According to Moya, before her release, Soler was interrogated by an officer from the State Security Investigation Department at Villa Marista. The officer questioned her about what had happened during the peaceful protest at which she was arrested, reminded her that she was under a precautionary measure of house arrest and that the measure could be revoked, and warned her that she would soon be summoned for questioning.

The post included photographs of the injury Berta Soler sustained to her foot during her arrest. Hours earlier, Moya had denounced her detention, saying he had overheard police officers mention that they had seen his wife “walking with a painful limp.”

According to activist Blanca Reyes, Moya went that same day to the Revolutionary National Police (PNR) station on Aguilera Street, in Lawton, in Havana’s Diez de Octubre municipality, to find out where the opposition leader was being held, “since she was beaten and no one knows whether she is at a police station or in a hospital.” Reyes stated: “Our sister’s situation is worrying.”

According to Moya’s account, on Saturday, two days after Soler had been arrested for several hours alongside fellow Lady in White Mara Cristina Labrada — the same Thursday that Yoani Sanchez, director of 14ymedio, was also arbitrarily detained — Berta Soler joined a “public and peaceful protest” with about 20 women from Lawton who were suffering from a lack of water.

The water shortage, Moya claims, is “intentional,” caused by the state-run company Aguas de La Habana to harm the Ladies in White headquarters and the area “within a 50-meter radius.”

Shortly after 10 a.m. that day, “several high-ranking State Security repressors” arrived at the scene and spoke with the protesting women, while the security operation was reinforced over the following hours.

“At noon, representatives of the state-run company Aguas de La Habana arrived and offered an explanation that also failed to convince the protesting women,” Moya recounted. His impression was that the authorities “had no intention of resolving the underlying cause of the problem, which is the deliberate manipulation of the water supply valve.”

With no satisfactory response, half an hour later the demonstrators blocked traffic on Porvenir Avenue, “using their own bodies as barriers.”

Moya said he did not witness the end of the protest because he had already been arrested by the political police and taken to the Aguilera station, where he overheard that his wife was walking in pain and that she had subsequently “been taken in a patrol car to another location,” which was not identified.

After an eight-hour interrogation, Moya was released, but his wife was not. The activist also clarified that “with the exception of Berta Soler, none of the women participating in the protest belong to organizations opposed to the Cuban communist regime. They are working women.”

The regime has intensified its persecution of activists and journalists on the island in recent weeks. Also on Saturday, dozens of residents took to the streets in El Cobre, Santiago de Cuba, to demand the release of Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano, a young activist known for his community work who had been detained hours earlier by State Security in an operation involving armed agents.

As for independent journalists, before Yoani Sanchez’s detention, Adelth Bonne Gamboa and Camila Acosta, both contributors to CubaNet, had also been arrested during the same week.

Meanwhile, Rolando Pérez Lora, an evangelical pastor known as the Preacher of Christ, was forcibly transferred from Havana to Las Tunas, where he was released on Monday, with a pending police summons.

According to reports from the Cuban Observatory for Human Rights and the Alliance of Christians of Cuba, Perez Lora had been detained while providing pastoral support to a young Christian member of the religious organization, who was also arrested.

In mid-September, State Security also detained Henry Constantin, director of La Hora de Cuba. In his case, rather than being released like the other journalists mentioned above, he was transferred to Kilo 7 prison in Camagüey, where he remains in pretrial detention on a charge of disobedience.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times,

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Serbia’s Student Movement: From Protest to Power
World.content:
By Andrew Firmin (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – On the night of 25 October, tens of thousands filled the streets of Belgrade and other cities, as they’d so often done in protest over the past two years. But this time they came out to celebrate. In that day’s National Assembly election, Student List, a slate of political newcomers, defeated Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), in power since 2012. The student-led movement behind the protests, which rose up against corruption, has given Serbia the opportunity for a democratic reset.



From grief to protest

Serbia became steadily more autocratic under Vučić. Public institutions served ruling-party interests amid a web of corruption, patronage, coercion and impunity. Public media became a ruling party mouthpiece.



Civic freedoms deteriorated dramatically. In 2018, the CIVICUS Monitor rated Serbia’s civic space as narrowed, meaning that fundamental rights were broadly respected. By the end of Vučić’s rule, the rating had collapsed to repressed, meaning that criticizing those in power carried severe risks. The state used violence against protests and treated civil society as a security threat, targeting it with spyware and subjecting organizations to raids and police investigations.



The seismic shift began in November 2024 with the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city. Sixteen people died. The government insisted it was a tragic accident, but the station had only recently been renovated and, with construction contracts shrouded in secrecy, many suspected corners had been cut. For protesters, this was a lethal symbol of the costs of corruption, negligence and impunity. No one has been held accountable.



Students held vigils and mass protests on a scale unseen since 2000, when demonstrations ousted Slobodan Milošević, the infamous authoritarian leader and accused war criminal. This time, their most effective tactic was a months-long education strike in which they blockaded and occupied universities.



As the protest movement grew it connected with existing groups, including environmental and legal aid organizations, independent media and, crucially, academics, university administrators and education unions, who took solidarity strike action. This built wider public support, backed by a ‘students in every village’ campaign that saw students meet with rural communities to ask about what mattered most to them.



State attempts to suppress the movement failed, including mass arrests, violence by security forces and gangs of ruling-party supporters and an extensive campaign of disinformation and smears. Vučić vilified protesters as agents of foreign powers bent on subversion and the government fired education sector employees for taking part in strikes.



Change on the cards



Ultimately, the protests forced Vučić’s hand. Constitutionally barred from seeking a third term as president, he announced an early parliamentary election in June and stood down as president in September, making clear his intention to hold onto power as prime minister. He presumably gambled that a skewed playing field, characterized by intimidation and biased coverage, would let him win again and unleash an even fiercer crackdown.



The gamble failed because of the movement’s discipline and the smart choices it made. Throughout, students resisted opposition parties’ attempts to co-opt them, insisting that deeper change was needed to re-establish the rule of law, free public institutions from political capture and tackle corruption. From its early days, the movement practiced internal democracy, taking decisions in university plenums, open assemblies where people debated, learned and decided together. When it decided to field a slate of candidates, it used the same method to select them. Students didn’t put themselves forward, choosing instead public figures untainted by association with established politics and likely to command broad support. Those who’ve won seats include academics, actors, former sports stars and medical professionals.



The result surpassed all predictions. According to projections based on the preliminary count, Student List has around 53 per cent of the vote, which would give it a clear majority of 141 of the National Assembly’s 250 seats. The SNS-led bloc trails on around 39 per cent. The margin was such that Vučić had to concede quickly.



Challenges of power



After the euphoria comes the challenge of moving from protest to power. A movement that has refused to have formal leaders must now unite behind a prime minister. Once the National Assembly convenes, Student List will have 90 days to form a government. Its deliberately broad campaign focused on major questions of national renewal but offered little detail. This strategy papered over political differences among representatives who range from nationalist to more liberal, which can be expected to surface if the incoming government succeeds in restoring the space for normal political debate. There’s also the question of how those elected will relate to the student movement.



As in Hungary, where long-term autocratic leader Viktor Orbán finally fell to electoral defeat in April, the new government will face the difficult task of reorienting state institutions that have bent to the former ruling party’s interests. An early sign of change came when the public broadcaster apologised to viewers for its bias towards the SNS, something that also happened in Hungary. The government will need to repay voters’ faith by rooting out corruption, which will mean overhauling institutions including the judiciary and police. All this will unfold alongside a presidential election that’s due by the end of the year.



Challenges lie ahead, but a population that has rediscovered the power of collective action can face them with confidence. Serbia also offers a vital source of international inspiration. Together with Hungary’s example, it shows there’s nothing permanent about autocratic rule. The world’s many Gen Z-led movements that have self-organised to demand a fairer distribution of economic and political power, and civil society more broadly, can take heart. Serbia has shown that organising and protesting works, and change is possible.



Andrew Firmin is CIVICUS Editor-in-Chief, co-director and writer for CIVICUS Lens and co-author of the State of Civil Society Report.

Read more feature articles here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Monday, November 9, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Monday, November 9, 2026.

Democrats Build on Sweeping Gains in Midterm Elections, Claiming 254 House Seats

Nov 09, 2026

Democrats are continuing to build on their sweeping gains in last week’s midterm elections as votes continue to be counted. They can now claim 254 House seats, compared to 162 for Republicans, with 19 House races yet to be decided. Democrats will also control at least 30 governorships and will control both legislative chambers and the governor’s office in 23 states — up from 16 before the election. Democrats also broke Republican “trifectas” in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and in Texas, where 87-year-old Houston Democrat Senfronia Thompson says she has the votes to become the first woman and first Black speaker of the Texas House of Representatives. Retired Navy Vice Admiral Nancy Lacore, who was abruptly fired from her post as chief of the Navy Reserve by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in August 2025, won election to the House of Representatives, flipping a seat in South Carolina held by the GOP. According to Axios, the House is poised to impeach Hegseth this week.

Meanwhile, Houston, Texas, Mayor John Whitmire announced Friday the city would start limiting the collaboration of local law enforcement with ICE during traffic stops. The announcement comes amid pressure from activists and as Republican Governor Greg Abbott prepares to leave office. Abbott previously threatened to revoke more than $110 million in public safety funding to Houston over a policy granting officers discretion over whether or not to contact ICE. Houston has seen mounting violent incidents involving ICE agents during traffic stops and car pursuits, including the fatal shooting of Mexican father Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July. This is Houston Mayor Whitmire.

Mayor John Whitmire: “This morning, I have directed the chief and HPD, through an executive order, that we will change our policy in regarding contact with ICE. I do this to begin a healing process, reduce fear and anxiety across our community. I also do this knowing that elections matter.”

Trump Replaces White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller

Nov 09, 2026

President Trump has replaced White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the chief architect of his mass deportation policy, days after Republicans lost control of Congress. In a statement, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, Democratic Congressmember Robert Garcia, said, “Just days after the American people rejected his corrupt and lawless presidency, Donald Trump is doubling down. Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families. Stephen Miller should lawyer up.” Attorney General Todd Blanche responded on Fox News that quote “Stephen Miller has a lawyer, it’s me”. This is Blanche on CNN.

Attorney General Todd Blanche: “The Department of Justice represents members of the executive who are brought in front of Congress, so there is nothing unique to me saying that every attorney general in history represents members of the administration. And this idea that Congressman Garcia comes out and says, ‘Oh, no, no, Stephen Miller needs his own personal lawyer,’ I would suggest he read the Constitution.”

In that interview, Blanche also repeatedly dodged questions about whether he’d investigate Democratic members of Congress, after President Trump ordered probes against congressional Democrats for calling for the impeachment of certain Cabinet officials. Soon after, Democratic Congressmember Robert Garcia issued this response to Blanche.

Rep. Robert Garcia: “We have the attorney general saying to the American public that somehow he’s going to defend administration officials, when his job is to defend the Constitution and the Department of Justice to be the people’s lawyer.”

Meanwhile, President Trump offered the press secretary job to Ultimate Fighting Championship, UFC, chief Dana White. Trump later said that he was only kidding, but White is set to meet with Trump today at the White House.

Former Top Federal Health Official Accuses Wiles of Putting Lobbyists and Campaign Funds Ahead of Public Health

Nov 09, 2026

Calley Means, a top federal health official who resigned two weeks ago, went on Joe Rogan’s podcast to accuse outgoing Chief of Staff Susie Wiles of prioritizing lobbyists and campaign funds over public health initiatives. Means claimed Wiles refused to back his push for healthier children’s diets because she wanted the sugar industry’s money, and says her team pushed for more flavored vape approvals and looser restrictions on the largely unregulated drug kratom. Means said, “Susie said to me many times: ‘We need money for the midterms, Calley. We need money for the midterms.’” Calley Means also alleges that companies hiring Wiles’s daughter, a lobbyist, got special priority.

Petition Urging Jeffries to Remove Himself from Race to Become House Speaker Surpasses a Million Signatures

Nov 09, 2026

Calls from progressives demanding new leadership in Congress continue to grow. An online petition urging Democratic Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to remove himself from the running to become the next House speaker has surpassed 1 million signatures. Jeffries has faced mounting opposition over his pro-Israel interests and continued acceptance of corporate PAC money, including from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, AIPAC. Incoming Congressmembers-elect Chris Rabb, Melat Kiros and Darializa Avila Chevalier, all members of the Democratic Socialists of America, DSA, have already declined to pledge support for Jeffries if he’s up for House speaker.

Chuck Schumer is facing similar calls to step down as Senate Democratic leader. Senators-elect Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed, Juliana Stratton and Adam Hamilton have all said they won’t support Schumer.

30 People Killed in Yemen in Missile Attack

Nov 09, 2026

In Yemen, at least 30 people were killed and more than three dozen injured on Friday as a missile slammed into a market in the southwestern province of Taiz. Women and children are among the dead. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government blamed the attack on fighters with Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, while a Houthi-linked television channel reported the attack was carried out by Saudi warplanes. This follows the deadliest month of attacks on Yemen since 2017. According to the Yemen Data Project, Saudi-led attacks killed 426 civilians in October — almost a quarter of them children.

Meanwhile, a missile fired by Houthi fighters struck an administrative building run by the state oil giant Saudi Aramco in Riyadh on Sunday, shattering windows on several floors of one of the tallest buildings in the Saudi capital’s King Abdullah Financial District.

Israeli President Herzog Picks Opposition Leader Eisenkot to Form Next Government

Nov 09, 2026

In Israel, President Isaac Herzog has picked opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government, passing over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Sixty-seven lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, backed Eisenkot, while 46 backed Netanyahu. Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to build what he calls a “national emergency government,” but his bloc is divided over allying with Arab-led parties, which won a historic 19 seats in elections last month.

Israeli Forces Release Palestinian Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh

Nov 09, 2026

Israeli forces have released Palestinian journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh without charge, five days after armed police and Shin Bet agents raided his Jaffa home. Police accused the +972 Magazine contributor of “contacting a foreign agent” after he interviewed exiled former lawmaker Azmi Bishara in Qatar ahead of Israel’s election last month. Adalah, a legal group that supports Palestinian citizens of Israel, said, “The message to Palestinian citizens is unmistakable: a public conversation with a political figure can land you in a cell. This is political persecution carried out through criminal law.”

Storm Triggers Mass Flooding in Gaza, Killing 5 Palestinians, as Israel Bars Imports of Shelter

Nov 09, 2026

In Gaza, health authorities say heavy rains collapsed a sandbank onto tents in Deir al-Balah, killing at least five people, including four children. Gaza’s Government Media Office says the storm flooded at least 70,000 tents, and the U.N. says about 950,000 displaced Palestinians live in areas exposed to flooding. Ahmad Alhendawi of Save the Children said, “This is not simply the result of bad weather. Tents, shelter kits and fuel are waiting at Gaza’s borders while children sleep in floodwater, because the Israeli authorities are blocking their entry. This is a choice, and children are paying the price.” This is a displaced Palestinian woman.

Olfat Magdoub: “This is the first day of rain, and of course we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first day, and we’re already overwhelmed. Two weeks ago, when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet, so we sleep on the ground.”

Hundreds of Thousands March in Amsterdam Demanding Action to Stop Gaza Genocide

Nov 09, 2026

In the Netherlands, more than 200,000 protesters marched through Amsterdam on Sunday demanding the Dutch government take action to halt Israel’s attacks on Gaza. Protesters wore red, many of them carrying signs reading “Stop the Genocide.” They’re demanding a halt to all direct and indirect arms trade with Israel, an expanded import ban on products from illegal Israeli settlements and for Dutch leaders to exert more political and diplomatic pressure on Israel to end its illegal occupations.

Protesters Take Direct Action to “Stop Dirty Data Centers” in Europe

Nov 09, 2026

In more news from the Netherlands, over 100 protesters broke into a construction site of a Microsoft data center in the ​outskirts ​of Amsterdam on Friday. It was the first of many direct action protests held across Europe in 16 countries over the weekend by the “Stop Dirty Data Centers” coalition. Protesters are calling for a large-scale pause on new data center construction.

bq. Protester: “There’s for sure a lot of opposition. I think it would be good for governments to do more research into what the people actually want. There’s very much opposition against Big Tech, against their surveillance, against the power that they have over democracies. And they should not be able to get away with that, especially since the people don’t agree.”

Nvidia Share Prices Plummet as CEO Jensen Huang Admits to Affair with Alleged Chinese Spy

Nov 09, 2026

The billionaire tech CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an extramarital relationship with a business executive who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy. On Sunday, the chip maker Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into Huang after he apologized to his colleagues, his wife and their children. The New York Times reports Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation that sought to convince him to lobby U.S. officials to allow the export of advanced computer chips to China. According to the New York Times, President Trump eased some of those limits on the sale of advanced chips to China after Huang’s lobbying. Jensen Huang is a close ally of President Trump, and Nvidia is currently one of the world’s two largest publicly traded corporations, along with Apple. Nvidia’s stock tumbled on the news, wiping hundreds of billions of dollars from its nearly $5 trillion valuation.

U.S. Is Absent as United Nations Climate Talks Open in Antalya, Turkey

Nov 09, 2026

In Turkey, world leaders, delegates and climate activists are convening in Antalya today to mark the start of another round of U.N. climate talks. Heads of governments and officials from more than 190 countries are expected to attend — with the glaring absence of the United States, after President Trump last year withdrew the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement for the second time.

Nations in the Global South are again expected to pressure richer countries responsible for the climate crisis to commit to more financing of a loss and damage fund that was established at the U.N. climate summit in Egypt four years ago to cope with climate-related disasters. Though Turkey is hosting the U.N. talks, Australia is presiding over the negotiations.

Disgraced Paraguayan Ex-President Charged with Corruption over Bank Collapse

Nov 09, 2026

In Paraguay, former president and Trump ally Santiago Peña has been impeached and charged over his alleged role in the collapse of the major digital lender Ueno Bank. Pedro Alliana has been sworn in as interim president of Paraguay as Peña remains under house arrest. Alliana served as vice president under Peña. The collapse of Ueno Bank left at least 3 million people — nearly half of Paraguay’s population — without access to their money and froze hundreds of millions of dollars in public funds, including state pension money.

Cinthia Vargas: “I had my entire life savings in Ueno Bank. I’d been saving there for five years, and overnight I lost everything. I was left with nothing. Five years of savings, five years of honest work. I never stole from anyone, never bothered anyone. What for? So that Santiago Peña and his whole gang of criminals could come and rob us?”

Read more news aquí en Havana Times.

World.title: Learning the Trade of Nets, Fish, & the Sea in Mariel, Cuba
World.content:
Photos: Idania Cardenas

Photo Feature by Idania Cardenas

HAVANA TIMES – At a maritime and fisheries training center, education goes far beyond the classroom. Amid nets being cast, fish being transferred from ponds to laboratories, and boats setting out at dawn, students learn the trades that will connect them to the sea and its resources.

In Mariel, vocational training comes with the smell of salt air, hands learning new skills, and workdays that begin before sunrise. Located in the municipality of Mariel, in western Cuba’s Artemisa Province, the center is Cuba’s only institution dedicated to training mid-level technicians in maritime and fisheries professions. It has approximately 90 students enrolled in three specialties: fishing vessel captain, marine engine mechanic, and fisheries biology.

A visit to the institute reveals that much of the learning takes place outside the classroom. Practical training plays an essential role in preparing these young people, who must become familiar with equipment, marine organisms, vessels, and the real-world conditions in which they will practice their future professions.

This photo series captures three aspects of their training: a demonstration of fishing gear, a laboratory exercise with live fish, and a practical session on personal survival techniques at sea, one of the fundamental skills required in international maritime training. Three different scenes from the same educational experience: learning by doing.

1. Among Nets and Traps: Knowledge Gained Through Practice

A demonstration by students training to become fishing vessel captains reveals skills developed through practice and knowledge of fishing techniques. Nets and traps are put into action. The students demonstrate how to prepare, operate, and retrieve this fishing equipment, with each movement revealing a skill that cannot be mastered overnight.

What might appear to visitors as a simple demonstration is actually part of a much broader training process. Future fishing vessel captains must understand the characteristics of each type of gear, identify the species that can be caught with it, and know when and how to use it. Training begins in the early years of study through various intensive practical sessions and reaches a decisive stage in the fourth year, when students undertake internships at fishing enterprises.

Coastal and small-scale fishing demand more than strength and dexterity. They require observation, knowledge of the environment, and sound judgment in making decisions. That is why behind every net cast and retrieved lie hours of training and accumulated knowledge that gradually become professional experience.

2. From the Pond to the Laboratory: Learning About Marine Life

Working with live fish taken from the center’s ponds, fisheries biology students develop essential skills for their future professional careers.

In the laboratory, teaching takes on another dimension. The instructor removes live fish directly from the institute’s pond and places them in the students’ hands. Gathered around him, the young people carefully observe, examine, and handle the specimens. Studying external characteristics, identifying anatomical structures, measuring specimens, and recording data are fundamental activities for understanding aquatic organisms.

The fisheries biology specialty has a unique distinction: it is the only program of its kind at the mid-level technical education level in Cuba. Its graduates can work in fishing companies, aquaculture facilities, and research support centers, where direct contact with living organisms is part of the job.

Training does not end in the laboratory. Near the institute are genetics and aquaculture facilities that complement the students’ practical education. However, many essential skills begin to develop through that direct interaction among the pond, the instructor, and the students.

Each fish thus becomes an opportunity to learn how to observe, identify, and understand aquatic life from a scientific perspective.

3. Learning to Survive at Sea: A Lesson That Can Save Lives

Wearing life jackets in rough seas, students participate in survival training designed to prepare them to respond to emergencies aboard vessels.

The sea does not always offer favorable conditions. For those preparing to work aboard boats and ships, knowing how to swim is not enough. They must also learn how to react in an emergency, remain calm, and coordinate their actions with others.

In the waters near the Mariel training center, a group of students performs personal survival exercises. Equipped with life jackets, they stay afloat and form groups while coping with the movement of the waves.

The exercise is part of essential training for seafarers, helping them acquire skills that could prove decisive if they must abandon ship or face an emergency. Every movement has a purpose. Staying afloat, maintaining group formation, moving through the water while wearing a life jacket, and learning to act together are skills that go far beyond a classroom exercise.

For those hoping to pursue careers aboard passenger vessels, including cruise ships, these skills are part of a safety culture that must accompany every working day.

Each specialty involves its own learning process, but all share the same fundamental principles: respect for the sea, an understanding of its challenges, and the responsibility that comes with working on it.

Because in Mariel, students do more than learn about the sea; they learn how to live and work on it, and how to be prepared to face its challenges.

See more photo features here at Havana Times.

World.title: Protesters in Santiago de Cuba Demand Freedom for Activist Who Feeds Those Most in Need
World.content:
An officer attempts to dissuade protesters outside the El Cobre police station, where they are demanding the release of Yoel Perez Serrano. / Social media

Dozens of residents, marched to the police station following the arrest of community activist Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Dozens of residents of El Cobre, in Santiago de Cuba, took to the streets on Saturday to demand the release of Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano, a young activist known for his community work who had been arrested hours earlier by State Security during an operation involving armed agents.

Videos shared on social media show mothers, children, and other local residents marching with signs and banging pots and pans while chanting, “The people united will never be defeated!” The slogan, widely used by the Cuban government, has also been heard at other recent anti-government protests. Later, the crowd chants in unison, “Freedom for Yoel, freedom, freedom!” as they advance toward the police station.

Another video shows protesters confronting police officers outside the station’s doors as the officers attempt to discourage the demonstration. Meanwhile, an elderly woman near the camera comments, “They can’t beat them… we’re not living in Batista’s time!”

Opposition leader Jose Daniel Ferrer García, founder of the Patriotic Union of Cuba (Unpacu), was the first to report the young activist’s arrest, during a livestream from Miami. According to information he was receiving directly at the time, Ferrer said agents arrived at Perez Serrano’s home in Guamuta at around six in the morning, carrying assault rifles, and blocked access to the neighborhood, preventing anyone from entering or leaving.

“They stormed in with the Black Berets, armed to the teeth… They turned the house upside down, took the phones, took whatever food they found, took the cooking pots, jewelry, everything they came across,” Ferrer said. He added that officers told people attempting to pass through that “worms were not allowed through,” using the regime’s derogatory term for its opponents.

Perez Serrano, a resident of the rural community of Guamuta, in the Santiago de Cuba municipality of El Cobre, is known locally for promoting the humanitarian project “Save Cuba.” With support from Unpacu and the Cuban Resistance Assembly, the initiative provided at least one daily meal, Monday through Friday, to elderly people, malnourished children, the sick, and vulnerable families. The young man was also promoting the construction of a community medical clinic and a dining facility, which is why some residents call him “the mayor of Guamuta.”

Ferrer also said the activist devoted between 12 and 14 hours a day to his community work. “The dictatorship uses its military forces to repress a peaceful man, a noble, generous, deeply humane man who is sacrificing himself to help the people,” he stated.

Last July, Perez Serrano staged a public protest: he went out into the street barefoot and wearing only underwear, carrying a white sheet bearing the words “Freedom,” “Democracy,” “Justice,” and “Dignity.” Shortly afterward, he was summoned by the police.

Cuban authorities have not publicly disclosed Perez Serrano’s whereabouts or the formal charges against him. Social media users expressing solidarity with the young activist are demanding clarification about where he is being held, the conditions of his detention, and the justification for his arrest.

Perez Serrano’s arrest comes amid a growing wave of repression, with recent harassment and arrests of activists, opposition figures, independent journalists, and other dissident voices. In recent days, several people have been surrounded and confined to their homes, including independent journalists Yoani Sánchez, director of this newspaper, after being detained for nine hours by the political police; Adelth Bonne Gamboa, who was also detained; Camila Acosta, Yunia Figueredo, Marthadela Tamayo, and Osvaldo Navarro, as well as activist Yamilka Lafita (Lara Crofs).

Karel Daniel Hernandez, a member of the independent project Fuera de la Caja Cuba (Outside the Cuba Box), was also arrested. Meanwhile, evangelical pastor Rolando Fidel Perez Lora, known as “Pregonero de Cristo” (Herald of Christ), who is being held at Villa Marista, will be forcibly deported from Havana to Las Tunas.

The protest in El Cobre comes amid a year of intense social unrest in eastern Cuba. In Santiago de Cuba, power outages last more than 24 hours on average, and pot-banging protests have multiplied across neighborhoods. In October, Cubalex recorded 48 public protests throughout Cuba, 11 of which took place in this eastern province, the second-highest number in the country after Havana’s 15.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Controversy Over Aid to Cuba’s Political Prisoners
World.content:
In their September report Prisoners Defenders documents 1,351 political prisoners in Cuba.

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – This week, the confrontation between influencers Yusmani Companioni Vila and Eliecer Avila over assistance to Cuba’s political prisoners went viral.

It is a thorny issue, and personally, I believe that those who call for insubordination in Cuba do far less than they should. It is very easy, sitting comfortably in a chair in Miami, to ask those of us who live in this country to take to the streets and risk spending several years in prison.

Obviously, the income anyone legitimately earns in the United States or any other country is not meant to solve Cuba’s problems. But just as no one demands anything from them, I don’t understand why they demand personal sacrifices from others. If you ask others to give, you must be willing to give yourself. None of them has thought of creating a fund to help the families of political prisoners.

According to the nongovernmental organization Prisoners Defenders, Cuba had 1,339 political prisoners at the end of August 2026, including 155 women (a record number) and 38 people who were detained when they were minors.

The cases include people imprisoned for protesting shortages of water and electricity, filming government agents, or denouncing abuses, actions that lead to imprisonment, threats, and punishments affecting entire families.

According to the organization’s records, 463 of those still imprisoned suffer from serious medical conditions, while 54 have severe mental health disorders resulting from beatings, forced labor, involuntary psychiatric confinement, and lack of medical care.

This is an extremely high number considering the reasons these people are serving sentences, but economically speaking, it would not be so complicated to ensure that they receive the assistance they deserve for their sacrifices. Mind you, everything they have done has been without asking for anything in return, so this is not about payment, but rather an expression of gratitude and, more importantly, a message to those who are afraid to take to the streets: if they do, they will not be left without support.

I know of people who were imprisoned following July 11, 2021, and spent three years behind bars without their families receiving a single dollar from abroad. That does not seem right to me when it comes to those who continue calling for sacrifices. Those who make so much noise from the comfort of their armchairs should be the first to reach into their pockets to help those who had the courage to express their opposition to the island’s regime.

Instead, many were left to fend for themselves, and only the best-known prisoners have received any kind of assistance, and even that has been sporadic because it depends on individual efforts.

We are not naive. We know that providing assistance also involves many complications, because anyone who approaches these people, considered “untouchables” by the regime, can face consequences such as losing the right to travel to Cuba. But there are many ways to help their families. For example, a bank account can receive money without revealing where it came from.

For years, dissidents living abroad have used these difficulties as an excuse to abandon those who need help the most, including people who have no stable source of employment because the dictatorship denies them that opportunity.

It is legitimate for them to argue that those who should first bear these costs are the Castro regime’s ruling clique, owners of hotels, luxury residences, yachts, and countless other assets, as US representative Mike Waltz denounced last week at the United Nations itself.

We are fully aware that those primarily responsible for alleviating the misery they themselves have created are the dictatorship’s chosen leaders. But then don’t ask others to make sacrifices if you are unwilling to help those who will subsequently face the wrath of the Cuban government. And not just the famous ones, but anyone.

Now Companioni says he wants to create a foundation to serve the Cuban people, according to his announcement, although not specifically to help the families of political prisoners.

The confrontation ended with Companioni asking Ávila to donate $200 to a child with health problems in the central province of Sancti Spíritus. Avila countered by proposing that two children of political prisoners also receive assistance, with all those involved identified by their full names.

The political implications here are considerable, but according to Companioni, he can reach everyone. We will see whether he can actually do so and, above all, whether he is allowed to.

Helping a political prisoner does not always mean performing some grand gesture. Often, it consists of delivering a letter, obtaining medication, accompanying a family to court, keeping a copy of a document, or repeating someone’s name so that it is not erased.

It is also necessary to stand by those left outside, because prison does not confine just one person: its bars extend into the home, to the dinner table, to the bed where someone lies waiting.

Families can lose income, housing, access to medication, or educational opportunities. Sometimes they need money, food, transportation, or simply someone’s presence to remind them that they have not been abandoned. Sitting beside a mother in a waiting room, helping care for her children, listening without demanding that she be strong: these gestures carry a quiet dignity.

But helping also requires thinking about safety, because for years the dictatorship has taken advantage of the recklessness of those who want to do good too quickly.

From outside the country, people can send letters to the authorities, support amnesty campaigns, contact international organizations, share reports from the independent press, and demand that governments, universities, labor unions, and associations keep public attention focused on those behind bars.

But putting food on the table is essential, and providing transportation so that relatives can visit prisoners is indispensable, because international pressure cannot replace the struggle of those who resist from within.

No one can sustain a cause if they are silently breaking down. Dictatorships want terror to isolate us, to make each person believe they are alone, because sometimes simply knowing that they have not been abandoned is enough to make it through the night.

Lee más desde Cuba aquí en Havana Times.

World.title: The first Islander aircraft built entirely in the UK arrives in the Falklands
World.content:
The first Islander aircraft built entirely in the UK arrives in the Falklands

9th Monday, November 2026 - 15:59 UTC Full article

The Falkland Islands Government Air Service (FIGAS) is welcoming a new Islander aircraft on Monday, VP-FTS, the first of the type to be assembled entirely in the United Kingdom, which arrives in Stanley from Punta Arenas, Chile, after a delivery flight of almost three weeks.

It is due to land at around 2.30 p.m., after a celebratory run down Stanley Harbour and a flypast of the aerodrome.

The aircraft was built from detail component level at Britten-Norman's Bembridge facility on the Isle of Wight, marking the return of full civil Islander manufacturing to the United Kingdom, according to the Falkland Islands Government.

It made its first flight on September 3 and was handed over to FIGAS Chief Pilot Troyd Bowles on October 8. It left the UK on October 20, fitted with ferry tanks, and flew via Iceland, Greenland, the United States and the length of South America before reaching the islands.

“Islanders remain the most suitable aircraft for FIGAS operations. They're well suited to our short runways, offer a practical payload, and are familiar to our crews and engineers,” said FIGAS General Manager Duane Stewart. MLA Roger Spink, portfolio holder for Commercial Services, said the fleet provides “a vital link for our Camp community”.

FIGAS has operated Islanders for more than four decades, flying from short grass and gravel strips on passenger, freight and mail services between settlements, as well as medical flights, environmental monitoring and charter work.

World.title: Hidden armoured vault found in a Peña home built with Ueno Bank loans
World.content:
Hidden armoured vault found in a Peña home built with Ueno Bank loans

9th Monday, November 2026 - 10:57 UTC Full article

The search is part of the case in which Peña was charged on Saturday with alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator

Paraguayan prosecutors and police on Sunday searched a residence of former President Santiago Peña in Ciervo Cuá, in the San Bernardino district, about 50 kilometres from Asunción, built with loans from Ueno Bank. According to the newspapers ABC Color and Última Hora, they found an armoured vault behind a false wall that they were unable to open. The Prosecutor’s Office confirmed the search, although its statement did not mention the vault, whose contents are unknown.

According to ABC, the team found a concealed door in one of the rooms leading, through a corridor, to an armoured vault with a level 7 security system requiring several keys to open: facial or iris recognition, a fingerprint, a PIN code and security keys. Despite Peña’s removal from office, members of the Presidential Escort Regiment were still guarding the property, his summer residence, on Sunday.

The house cost about 7.7 billion guaraníes, roughly US$1.3 million, to build. According to the indictment, on May 13, 2024, already as president, Peña received two simultaneous loans from Ueno Bank totalling 3.548 billion guaraníes, about US$600,000, with monthly instalments of some 239 million guaraníes, almost six times his salary. Prosecutors estimate the total damage in the case at US$809.5 million.

The search is part of the case in which Peña was charged on Saturday with alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator. Judge Humberto Otazú ordered his pre-trial detention the same day, which he is serving at the Presidential Escort Regiment barracks, citing a flight risk. Prosecutors allege that during his term Ueno received large deposits from public bodies while granting irregular loans to companies linked to its owners, the Vázquez Group. Peña, who was a shareholder in the bank’s controlling group until 2025, says he is innocent. Eight of the bank’s executives are in custody.

The new president, Pedro Alliana, ordered on Sunday that those affected by the bank’s closure should not pay fines, late-payment surcharges or interest arising from the crisis, and said nearly 1.2 million savers have already recovered their deposits, totalling about US$158 million. Repayments will continue throughout the week.

World.title: 1982 veterans parade in London as the Falklands honour the fallen on Remembrance Sunday
World.content:
1982 veterans parade in London as the Falklands honour the fallen on Remembrance Sunday

9th Monday, November 2026 - 10:45 UTC Full article

In Stanley, at the service held at the Cross of Sacrifice, a roll of honour was read out, a two-minute silence was observed and wreaths were laid by the Governor. Photo: Judy White

The Falkland Islands community paid tribute on Sunday in Stanley to those who lost their lives in conflict at the Remembrance Sunday service, while in London many British veterans of the 1982 war paraded at the main commemorations.

In Stanley, at the service held at the Cross of Sacrifice, a roll of honour was read out, a two-minute silence was observed and wreaths were laid by the Governor, the Commander of British Forces in the islands, MLA Lewis Clifton on behalf of the community, and representatives of military and veterans’ organisations, according to local broadcaster FITV.

In London, the Falkland Islands Government Office in the UK welcomed the presence of many 1982 veterans at the parade. “We remain hugely grateful to all Falklands veterans for their service and sacrifice during the liberation of our Islands in 1982,” it wrote on social media. Last week, the Falkland Islands Government Representative to the UK and Europe, Richard Hyslop, placed a commemorative cross in the House of Commons Garden of Remembrance.

In the north of England, the leader of Burnley Council, Afrasiab Anwar, withdrew on the eve of the commemoration a motion, tabled in September, backing the islanders’ right to self-determination and paying tribute to the British service personnel who fought in 1982, including some from the town. The initiative had been criticised by Reform UK, which accused Anwar of grandstanding. “It’s not appropriate for us to cause any issues with the Remembrance service, and in respect of our veterans, I am withdrawing this motion,” Anwar said, adding that he had received thanks from a former member of the islands’ government.

Remembrance Sunday, held on the second Sunday of November, honours British and Commonwealth service personnel who have died in conflicts since the First World War. The 1982 war left 255 British servicemen, three islanders and 649 Argentine servicemen dead.

World.title: Lost savings and broken trust: life for those hit by Ueno Bank’s closure
World.content:
Lost savings and broken trust: life for those hit by Ueno Bank’s closure

9th Monday, November 2026 - 03:07 UTC Full article

Marlyn López, a 43-year-old university lecturer, lives in Piribebuy, about 75 kilometres from Asunción

For nearly three million Paraguayans, November 3 began with a message on their phone screens: “We cannot display your balance.” Early that morning, Paraguay’s Central Bank took over Ueno Bank over a critical solvency problem and froze its deposits. A week later, with President Santiago Peña removed from office and in pre-trial detention, many of those affected still have no access to their money and say they have also lost faith in the country’s institutions.

Marlyn López, a 43-year-old university lecturer, lives in Piribebuy, about 75 kilometres from Asunción. That morning she was about to buy fuel using the bank’s app, where she kept her newly paid salary and some savings, about 24 million guaraníes, or roughly US$3,800. She had only 30,000 guaraníes in cash, about US$5. “I was left with nothing, like nearly three million people,” she told El País. She has survived thanks to colleagues who transferred money to her without being asked. The authorities say they have paid an advance to half of the depositors, but she has yet to receive any notice. “I have not only lost money. I have also lost faith in the authorities, in the state institutions that should have supervised the financial system. I believed them when they said everything was fine,” she said.

Peña had repeatedly defended the soundness of the bank, in which he was once a shareholder, and blamed allegations of irregularities on campaigns by some media outlets. Prosecutors are investigating an alleged scheme of unsecured loans to companies of the Vázquez Group, the bank’s owner, which held some US$850 million in public deposits.

Rubén Causarano, 48, is a blacksmith, mechanic and beekeeper who sells food from a cart on an Asunción street corner. He had about 5 million guaraníes, roughly US$800, in Ueno, and that Tuesday he needed to send money to his daughter so she could travel to her studies. Since he always paid by card or transfer, he had no cash: he broke open the piggy bank where his daughters saved coins so he could buy fuel and drive her to the bus. He then worked for hours repairing vehicles to get paid in cash. “I’m left with the fear that they’ll screw us again. We’ll have to go back to our grandmothers’ old tradition of keeping our money under the mattress,” he said.

“These politicians are crooks; it can’t be that out of greed they have left half the country without money for daily life, without food, without medicine,” added Causarano, who has also yet to be told when he will be repaid. “Now the president has been kicked out, several of them are in jail, but those who take their place are just as crooked. How can we believe them?”

The new president, Pedro Alliana, has promised that everyone affected will recover their savings. Customers with small balances have begun to be repaid, and repayments will be extended to an initial maximum of 40 minimum wages, about US$19,300.

World.title: Leo XIV, before Milei: “The economy must serve the person”
World.content:
Leo XIV, before Milei: “The economy must serve the person”

9th Monday, November 2026 - 03:00 UTC Full article

Leo XIV referred to “families who carry the burden of uncertainty”, those looking for work, the elderly and those who, even while working, struggle to meet their household needs

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Buenos Aires on Sunday, the first papal visit to Argentina in 39 years, and in his first address to the authorities, with President Javier Milei at his side, said that “the economy must be at the service of the person, and not the person at the service of the economy”, urged those in authority to “recognise the limits of power” and called for “special attention” to the sick and people with disabilities.

The pontiff arrived from Montevideo and was greeted at the foot of the plane by Milei, with whom he held a 30-minute private meeting at the Casa Rosada. At dusk, at the Palacio Libertad, before national and provincial authorities, religious representatives and diplomats, the Pope championed a democracy strengthened “by a willingness to listen, care in the use of words, the patient search for agreements and the ability to recognise in those who think differently a compatriot with whom one shares a common destiny”. “Those who exercise authority also have a duty to act prudently, recognise the limits of the power entrusted to them and direct their decisions towards the good of the whole community,” he added.

Leo XIV referred to “families who carry the burden of uncertainty”, those looking for work, the elderly and those who, even while working, struggle to meet their household needs. “A nation must ask itself seriously where it has failed when its young people must leave their land to fulfil their dreams,” he said, calling for “particular strengthening of education, vocational training, universities and research”. Reiterating his opposition to abortion, legal in Argentina since 2020, he also called for “special attention in illness, dependency and disability”.

The Pope did not mention Milei or the government, but several passages were read by the Argentine press as allusions to criticism of the president over his cuts to education, disability and pensions and the tone of his attacks on opponents. Argentina’s Catholic hierarchy has been one of the most critical voices against the government’s austerity policies.

Milei, who spoke before the Pope, gave a restrained speech, far from his usual tone. “I am pleased to see the entire political spectrum here, showing that there are reasons and occasions that go beyond our differences,” he said, and described Pope Francis, whom he had harshly criticised in the past, as “the most important Argentine in history”. Francis, who died last year, never returned to his country during his pontificate.

Authorities expect some seven million people to take part in the Pope’s events in Argentina, supported by more than 25,000 volunteers. On Monday, a national holiday, Leo XIV will visit the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione, a home for people with disabilities in Claypole, celebrate Mass at the Monument of the Spaniards in Palermo, and meet trade unionists, business leaders and social movements at the Catholic University of Argentina.

World.title: Leo XIV leaves Uruguay urging Catholics to reach out to “those who have drifted away”
World.content:
Leo XIV leaves Uruguay urging Catholics to reach out to “those who have drifted away”

8th Sunday, November 2026 - 20:16 UTC Full article

Leo XIV’s was the first papal visit to Uruguay in 38 years, since John Paul II’s in 1988

Pope Leo XIV ended his visit to Uruguay on Sunday with a Mass before some 30,000 faithful in the city of Florida, where he urged Catholics to reach out to those who have drifted away from the Church in South America’s most secular country, before flying to Buenos Aires, the second stop on his regional tour.

“We cannot always wait for those who have drifted away to return on their own. Uruguay, we must set out! We must enter homes again, draw close to people, listen to their questions and bring them to Christ!” the pontiff said at the most forceful moment of his homily, celebrated before the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, the country’s patron saint, on her feast day. “Do not be afraid to say you are Christians,” he added, in a message that also focused on the role of mothers and grandmothers in passing on the faith.

Leo XIV’s was the first papal visit to Uruguay in 38 years, since John Paul II’s in 1988. In just over two days, the pontiff championed humanism and warned about the risks of technology, but also questioned Uruguay’s abortion and euthanasia laws in his speech to the authorities in Montevideo. On Saturday he celebrated Mass before some 30,000 faithful in Paysandú, where he praised mate as a symbol of unity and the bridge linking the city with Argentina as a call to dialogue; he visited the Casavalle neighbourhood and the Catholic University, and led a vigil before some 60,000 people at the Centenario Stadium.

The visit made the faith of some political leaders visible. “We must take care of the body but also of the soul,” said Fernando Pereira, president of the ruling Broad Front. Juan Martín Fernández, president of the Christian Democratic Party, said the Pope “has stood up to leaders like Donald Trump and has questioned Israel over Gaza” and has endorsed “the option for the poor”. “Uruguay is the most secular country, but we have his presence at the traditional pilgrimage of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, and it is something that happens very rarely,” said Florida’s mayor, Carlos Enciso.

In Buenos Aires, the Pope is due to pay tribute to General José de San Martín, meet President Javier Milei at the Casa Rosada and address the authorities at the Palacio Libertad. It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since 1987.

World.title: Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse
World.content:
Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse

8th Sunday, November 2026 - 01:53 UTC Full article

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator

Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday charged former President Santiago Peña, removed from office by the Senate on Friday, and requested his pre-trial detention in the case over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which froze the savings of nearly three million customers. A judge must rule on the request. Prosecutors also charged former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, who is in custody.

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator. Carvallo, who had been Ueno’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration. According to prosecutors, between 2023 and 2026 the bank received large deposits from public bodies and the pension system while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies linked to its owners, the Vázquez Group. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The former president, who had been placed under house arrest after his removal, was moved overnight to the barracks of the Presidential Escort Regiment, responsible for presidential security, after protesters threw stones at police and tore down fences near his residence in Asunción. Police dispersed the protest. Dictator Alfredo Stroessner took refuge in the same barracks in 1989 during the military coup that toppled him.

The new president, Pedro Alliana, began his term with cabinet changes. He appointed Ariel Martínez as interior minister, a post he held under former President Horacio Cartes (2013-2018), and Juan Carlos Baruja, also close to Cartes, head of the ruling Colorado Party, as public works minister. Alliana said he would suspend foreign travel to focus on the crisis and promised that all those affected would recover their savings.

Customers with balances of up to about US$1,500 have begun recovering their money, and payouts will later be extended to an initial maximum of 40 minimum wages, about 121 million guaraníes or US$19,300. Banks will open exceptionally on Sunday so that those affected can open accounts and complete the necessary procedures.

Tension remains high. Protesters and the opposition accuse Alliana of failing to act in time to prevent the bank’s collapse and are also demanding his removal and early elections in early 2027.

World.title: Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing
World.content:
Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:55 UTC Full article

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment

Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, will visit the Falklands and South Georgia from Monday, November 9, the day before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on Argentina’s case against the Sea Lion oil project, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment. The Princess, who will travel with her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, will begin with a series of engagements in the Falklands: she will meet members of the community, visit Cape Pembroke Lighthouse, Tussac House and the newly completed Falkland Islands National Sports Complex, and attend a reception at Government House in Stanley.

In South Georgia, a territory with no permanent civilian population, she will see the Trust’s work, meet British Antarctic Survey staff and members of the territory’s government, and commemorate the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton (1874-1922), who sailed some 1,500 kilometres in a lifeboat to the island to seek help for his crew, trapped by ice in Antarctica.

The palace presents the trip as a heritage and commemorative visit. Its timing, however, coincides with a key week in the dispute over the islands: the Hamburg tribunal will hear Argentina and the United Kingdom on November 10 and 11, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies plans to debate the sovereignty defence bill on November 12, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

World.title: Sargassum season is officially over, a month later than last year and with nearly double the seaweed
World.content:
Sargassum season in the Mexican Caribbean has officially ended.

The conclusion date came a month later than in 2025, but finally, autumn’s cold fronts are bringing a drop in sea temperature and a consequent reduction in seaweed arrivals.

Figures from Quintana Roo’s state Ministry of Ecology and Environment (SEMA) indicate a record collection of 156,631 tonnes of seaweed throughout the year — nearly double the 85,000 tonnes reported in 2025. The Mexican Navy was responsible for the removal of 72,000 metric tonnes of that amount, representing a fourfold increase in its sargassum missions over last year.

The navy used drones and satellite images to anticipate sargassum’s movement at sea. Still, it’s estimated that only about 16.4% (25,751 tonnes) was collected from the open ocean.

According to local media, approximately 4.3 billion pesos (US $231 million) was allocated to clean-up, a combined effort by hoteliers and all three levels of government.

Sargassum levels at the source in Northwest Africa — of which 1-5% reaches Mexico — rose by 10% to 15% compared with 2025 (from about 900,000 tonnes to 1 million), according to Esteban Amaro, director of the Sargassum Monitoring Center in Quintana Roo.

Agencies predict that 2027 could bring even more sargassum to the region, depending on several factors. The “Super El Niño,” one of the strongest climate events of its kind in modern records, as well as changes in the Atlantic Ocean’s hydrodynamics, could determine when the next season begins and how much seaweed the tides will bring.

The Quintana Roo state government is aiming to install a large ocean barrier, known as GO 60 by 60, between Cozumel Island and Tulum to reduce the quantity of seaweed reaching the region’s main tourist destinations.

The structure would be placed 60 km offshore at a 60-degree northeast orientation, where it can take advantage of ocean currents to divert the seaweed.

The project is expected to comprise six 10 km sections, arranged in a staggered pattern, allowing ships to traverse the waters if approved. However, the extremely strong currents in the Cozumel Channel, between the island and the beach town of Playa del Carmen, pose a significant technical challenge for construction.

In addition, concerns about the structure’s potential impact on marine life mean that further analysis must be conducted before it can proceed.

With reports from La Jornada and N+

World.title: Authorities rescue Río Bravo mayor in Coahuila a day after armed highway abduction
World.content:
The mayor of the northern border municipality of Río Bravo, Tamaulipas, was found safe and sound in the state of Coahuila on Sunday, one day after armed men allegedly stole his vehicle and abducted him on a highway that links the states of Zacatecas and San Luis Potosí.

Miguel Ángel Almaraz Maldonado, mayor of Río Bravo since 2024, was “rescued” at a state police checkpoint near Coahuila’s border with Zacatecas, according to the government of Coahuila.

*BAJO RESGUARDO DE AUTORIDADES DE COAHUILA, ALCALDE DE RÍO BRAVO.* • Fue rescatado en un filtro de la Policía Estatal en los límites con Zacatecas. Saltillo, Coahuila de Zaragoza; 8 de noviembre de 2026.— El Gobierno del Estado de Coahuila y la Fiscalía General del Estado https://t.co/nRyonPUGH0 — Gobierno de Coahuila (@GobDeCoahuila) November 8, 2026

Almaraz told reporters that he escaped from his captors after being held in a field for an unspecified period of time.

“[I was held] in a field but suddenly they left,” he said, referring to his captors.

“We jumped the fence, ran an hour without stopping and then wandered the whole night, 80 kilometers, until we arrived here,” Almaraz said, referring to the police checkpoint in Coahuila.

While he spoke in the first-person plural, the mayor didn’t say who was with him during his escape, according to the newspaper El Universal. At some stage, the mayor and an unidentified companion boarded a bus that took them to the police checkpoint in Coahuila.

Almaraz described his ordeal as a “bad experience” and said he suffered a “terrible fright.”

However, he said he felt “well,” telling reporters that he wasn’t beaten and didn’t sustain any injuries.

Almaraz didn’t specify the location of the field where he said he was held, and didn’t provide detailed information about the men who allegedly kidnapped him.

Federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that Almaraz had been located just before noon on Sunday.

“He was located by the Security Cabinet of the government of Mexico in coordination with the authorities of the governments of Zacatecas, Coahuila, San Luis Potosí and Tamaulipas,” he wrote on X.

García Harfuch noted that Almaraz had been missing, but didn’t make any reference to the mayor’s alleged kidnapping.

The abduction

Almaraz, a National Action Party (PAN) mayor, was traveling to Real de Catorce, a pueblo mágico (magical town) in San Luis Potosí, when armed men allegedly intercepted his vehicle on the highway between San Tirbucio, a small town in Zacatecas, and Vanegas, a town in San Luis Potosí. The mayor was traveling with at least one colleague and members of his family when his car was allegedly intercepted on Saturday night. Alleged criminals hijacked other vehicles near the border between San Luis Potosí and Zacatecas on Saturday, according to the Zacatecas Attorney General’s Office.

According to the Tamaulipas Attorney General’s Office, Almaraz and his travel companions were abducted. However, the alleged kidnappers later released their victims, with the exception of the mayor. Those released were left on the side of the highway and subsequently sought assistance from authorities in the town of Cedral, San Luis Potosí, according to state authorities, who cited the testimony of an unidentified victim.

The motive for the alleged abduction of the mayor was unclear.

With reports from El Universal, El Financiero, La Jornada and El País

World.title: Mexico’s inflation rate rises for third straight month, hitting 3.75%
World.content:
Inflation is showing no sign of letting up and, led by green tomatoes, consumer prices rose more than expected in October, marking three consecutive months of increases.

According to data released on Monday by the national statistics agency INEGI, the annual inflation rate reached 3.75%, up from 3.57% in October 2025.

October’s Consumer Price Index (CPI) exceeded the 23 estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists, which yielded a median prediction of 3.65% and was 0.65% more than the 3.45% recorded in September of this year.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, accelerated to 3.80% year-on-year and rose 0.34% month-on-month, while non-core inflation reached 3.59% year-on-year.

Within the core inflation index, goods increased by 0.22% and services by 0.44%.

On a monthly basis, the non-core price index rose 1.75%, with fruit and vegetable prices climbing 2.35%. Energy and government-regulated prices rose 2.13%, which was largely due to the end of the summer electricity tariff subsidy in 18 cities

The six products that increased the most were:

Green tomatoes: 35.58%.

Air transport: 26.36%.

Pumpkins: 23.22%.

Electricity: 18.51%.

Professional services: 9.88%.

Red tomatoes: 9.68%

The six products that decreased the most were:

Limes: -16.53%.

Serrano chilis: -8.98%.

Oranges: -8.90.

Avocados: -7.20%.

Potatoes and other tubers: -6.29%.

Bananas: -4.83%.

Just last week, the central bank cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25%, a decision that reignited debate over whether policymakers are easing the economy too quickly before inflation has sustainably returned to the bank’s target of 3%.

The bank also revised its forward guidance, indicating that the new rate is likely to remain unchanged for an extended period. In a statement, it argued that keeping borrowing costs at current levels would help inflation converge toward the target, while acknowledging that risks to the outlook remain tilted to the upside.

And even as economic activity continues to rebound — GDP expanded by 3.2% year-on-year in the third quarter — the bank maintains that the economy is still operating below its potential, limiting demand-driven inflation.

However, if the economy demonstrates sustained growth, the bank’s position might be difficult to sustain.

With reports from El Financiero, El Economista and LopezDoriga.com

World.title: Belgian artist Carsten Höller unveils towering ‘Mexico City Slides’ at Polanco-area mall
World.content:
Four giant, intertwining spiral slides — the tallest reaching 38.5 meters, or about 126 feet — have been installed at Mexico City’s upscale Antara shopping center by Carsten Höller, a Belgian-born sculptor known for his interactive works.

Touted as a permanent feature, “Mexico City Slides” is part of a big expansion at the 20-year-old Polanco-adjacent shopping center located in Colonia Granada.

Made of steel and polycarbonate, the slides range from about 12 to 38.5 meters tall, with slide lengths of about 32 to 91 meters.

Each slide carries an individual rider, allowing four people to descend simultaneously from different starting points before reaching a common landing area.

According to ARTnews, riders will enter the slides from a restaurant area, Google’s offices, the future Rosewood hotel and a new exhibition space for Arte Abierto. Rosewood lists 2028 for the hotel’s planned opening in the tower of Antara’s expansion.

Right now, the slides are available to view, but Arte Abierto — a contemporary art nonprofit with sites in Cabo San Lucas and elsewhere — has not specified on its website when visitors can begin riding them. It advises checking Instagram for updates.

Arte Abierto and developer SOMA commissioned the installation in collaboration with the architecture firm Sordo Madaleno, according to the online magazine Designboom. The firm also designed the recently opened St. Regis Costa Mujeres resort in Quintana Roo.

The slides accompany an expansion of Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site. The open-air mall’s current lineup includes stores such as Carolina Herrera, Hugo Boss, Apple and Zara.

Höller, born in Brussels to German parents, trained as a scientist before becoming a full-time artist in 1993. He earned a doctorate in agricultural science at the University of Kiel in 1988 and worked as an insect researcher, according to a biography by the international art gallery Gagosian.

He began his slide series at the 1998 Berlin Biennale. Later installations included five slides inside London’s Tate Modern in 2006 and projects in New York, Florence and Copenhagen.

Arte Abierto calls the Mexico City version Höller’s largest slide installation to date.

“Sliding is a way of thinking through the body,” Höller, 64, says on Instagram. “It is a controlled fall that opens a space between fear and pleasure, where the mind momentarily reorganizes itself.”

With reports from Designboom, Radio Fórmula, ARTnews.com and Lado.mx

World.title: CJNG operator ‘R2’ and 19 others arrested following shootout with Mexican Navy in Guadalajara
World.content:
Listen to this article

The alleged leader of a criminal cell linked to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) and 19 other people were detained in Guadalajara on Sunday after a shootout with members of the special operations unit of the Mexican Navy.

Rafael Álvarez Ayala — a man known as “R2” who federal authorities say is the leader of the “Los Rs” cell of the CJNG and linked to the 2025 assassination of Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo — was shot before he was arrested and taken to a hospital in Guadalajara. He reportedly underwent surgery after being shot in his abdomen, leg and arm.

The clash between the alleged criminals and navy personnel occurred at the Sabea restaurant and hookah lounge, where Álvarez reportedly arrived 20 hours before he was shot and arrested on Sunday afternoon. Authorities said that his arrest occurred at a restaurant in Zapopan, but Sabea is actually in Guadalajara’s Vallarta Norte neighborhood, near the state capital’s municipal boundary with Zapopan.

According to the navy and the federal Security Ministry (SSPC), the alleged criminals began shooting first and navy personnel returned fire.

A member of the navy was also shot during the gun battle, but the injury doesn’t pose a risk to his life, according to the SSPC.

R2 is the brother of R1, the alleged mastermind of Carlos Manzo’s assassination

Rafael Álvarez Ayala is the brother of Ramón Ángel Álvarez Ayala, identified as the mastermind behind the Nov. 1, 2025, assassination of Carlos Manzo. Ramón Ángel, a “Los Rs” leader known as R1, was arrested in Jalisco in July. Both he and his brother were previously arrested in 2012 and spent a decade in prison before their release in 2022.

The Navy Ministry (SEMAR) and federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported the arrest of R2 and 19 other people in social media posts on Sunday afternoon. In a statement, the SSPC described the 19 additional suspects as “alleged lawbreakers” and said they were turned over to the “appropriate authorities.”

García Harfuch said that authorities located Álvarez thanks to intelligence work carried out by the National Intelligence Center (CNI) and information shared by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). The Michoacán Attorney General’s Office also provided information, according to the SSPC.

García Harfuch said that a judge in Michoacán had issued an arrest warrant for R2 on a homicide charge. García Harfuch also said that Álvarez was subject to an arrest warrant for the purpose of extradition to the United States.

In his social media post, the security minister also wrote that “Los Rs” are “mainly” involved in “extortion, drug trafficking, homicide, unlawful deprivation of liberty, kidnapping and attacks against authorities.”

The criminal cell’s “extortion victims” include business owners and avocado producers, he added.

The SSPC called Álvarez “one of the main generators of violence in the region.” The ministry was referring to Jalisco and the neighboring state of Michoacán.

R1, R2 and another brother, Jesús Santiago, known as “R3,” used to take direct orders from former CJNG leader Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera Cervantes, according to a Reforma newspaper report that cited information from Mexico’s Defense Ministry. Oseguera was fatally wounded in a Mexican military operation in Jalisco in February.

DEA commends Mexican authorities for arrest of R2

The DEA acknowledged the arrest of R2 in a social media post. The agency called Álvarez “a senior leader of the CJNG terrorist organization responsible for drug trafficking, extortion, kidnapping, and deadly violence across Mexico.”

Mexican authorities have arrested Rafael Álvarez Ayala, alias “R2,” a senior leader of the CJNG terrorist organization responsible for drug trafficking, extortion, kidnapping, and deadly violence across Mexico. Intelligence shared by DEA helped Mexican authorities locate R2, who is also wanted in the United States on federal drug trafficking and firearms charges.
