World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra at Degollado Theater, a vermouth festival and airport updates
World.content:
As Guadalajara eases into the year-end holiday season, the events calendar is heating up. This week, we preview the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra’s upcoming performances at Degollado Theater and the second annual Guadalajara Vermouth Festival.

But first, we have some news regarding expanding international air service at Guadalajara’s Miguel Hidalgo Airport and an update on road work happening on the Chapala Highway.

Guadalajara gains another nonstop connection to Seattle this winter

Those plotting an escape from Seattle’s notoriously gray and rainy winter months will soon have another option to consider.

According to Simple Flying, Alaska Airlines is set to begin nonstop service from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport to Guadalajara on March 18, 2027. The airline expects to fly the route year-round, up to three times weekly, using Boeing 737-800 aircraft. While the exact days and times have not yet been announced, the planned flight would give Seattle travelers their third nonstop route to Guadalajara.

Mexican carriers Volaris and Aeroméxico are already offering nonstop flights between Seattle and Guadalajara. Volaris began offering the route 10 years ago, while Aeroméxico launched its service between the two cities last year.

According to the Port of Seattle, outbound travel from SEA to Mexico in 2024 was double its 2019 levels.

New project on the Chapala Highway is slowing traffic and fraying nerves

Municipal workers kicked off paving work on the southbound lanes of the Chapala Highway on Nov. 1. The project is causing new headaches for motorists headed to and from the airport and those traveling between the city and Lake Chapala.

Workers are reportedly occupying the center lanes in both directions, so motorists are being diverted to outer lanes, which is causing bottlenecks about 700 meters from the entrance to Guadalajara International Airport.

On top of the congestion, motorists complained that signage didn’t make it clear which lanes pass by the airport and which ones lead to it.

As one female driver told El Informador, “It’s a mess … they don’t warn you. I was going to take the horseshoe to avoid taking the road to Chapala … but it turns out it’s closed and they diverted me to the airport.”

The current project is part of the comprehensive renovation of the Chapala Highway that began last year. The latest phase aims to modernize the road surface and prevent structural damage from the thousands of heavy trucks that ply the highway daily.

While local officials have not announced a target completion date for the paving work, it’s likely to run through most of November. For anyone planning to fly out of Guadalajara airport in the coming weeks or during the Thanksgiving holiday, it’s best to build extra time into your schedule.

When construction work wraps up, traffic flows, road safety and access to the airport should all materially improve.

The Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra performs at Degollado Theater this month

The Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra (known locally as Orquesta Filarmónica de Jalisco, or OFJ) returns for its final season of 2026 with a handful of concerts at the venerable Degollado Theater throughout the month.

The season’s performances will bring together works by Beethoven, Mahler, Stravinsky, Sibelius, Tchaikovsky, Dvořák and several Mexican composers. It will also feature the world premiere of a work commissioned by the OFJ itself.

The concerts will be led by artistic director José Luis Castillo, along with guest conductors and soloists such as David Cohen, Rodolfo Ritter, Dieter Hennings and Cristian Coliver.

Looking ahead to the upcoming performances on Nov. 12 and 15 to be conducted by José María Moreno, the program features works by Florence Price, Carlos Chávez, Mozart Camargo Guarnieri and Joaquín Turina.

Later in the month, Rodrigo Sierra Moncayo takes the helm as guest conductor, accompanied by Carlos Gutiérrez on piano, with a program that includes Ludwig van Beethoven’s Violin Concerto (piano version) and Johannes Brahms’ Symphony No. 3.

Wrapping up the series on Nov. 23 and 29 are two special concerts featuring the world premiere of “Ruiseñor de la sombra” (“Nightingale of the Shadow”), a work commissioned by the OFJ from the Guadalajara-born composer Ricardo Zohn-Muldoon.

The concerts are performed each Thursday evening at 8:30 p.m., as well as on Sundays at 12:30 p.m. To view the full schedule and buy tickets, visit the Jalisco Philharmonic Orchestra website or the Teatro Degollado box office in person.

The Guadalajara Vermouth Festival returns to Colonia Americana mid-month

In just its second edition, the Guadalajara Vermouth Festival returns to the city on Nov. 14.

Long a popular apéritif in Southern Europe, vermouth is beginning to find a receptive audience here in Mexico. Made from a base of neutral wine, the drink is fortified with a distilled spirit and infused with a wide variety of botanicals (herbs, spices and florals). Vermouth can be dry or sweet, white or red.

Guests at this year’s event will have the opportunity to learn about how this drink is made and sample a wide variety of vermouths made in Europe and Mexico. For those interested in taking things a step further, there will also be hands-on vermouth-making workshops where participants can craft their own recipe.

Live music and bar snacks are also in the works, to keep the buena onda flowing.

Tickets to the festival are available online and from a handful of Guadalajara bars partnering with the event, including Metódico Café, Lito Aperitivo Social, Ocio en Plural and Vermutería Don Ajenjo.

Each ticket grants the holder a commemorative glass and one complimentary tasting. For more details, check out the festival website.

Date: Nov. 14 from 6 p.m. to midnight

Nov. 14 from 6 p.m. to midnight Location: Patio Paraíso at Loba Cervecería, Gregorio Dávila 86 in Colonia Americana

Patio Paraíso at Loba Cervecería, Gregorio Dávila 86 in Colonia Americana Cost: 350 pesos, not including fees

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Mexico’s National Energy Commission approves 6 solar energy permits worth US $750M
World.content:
Mexico’s National Energy Commission has approved six photovoltaic power generation permits with investments totaling US $750 million that will add 649 megawatts (MW) of net capacity to the National Power System (SEN), through projects that will begin operations in 2028 and 2029.

The commission (CNE) granted the six permits, dated Nov. 5, to subsidiaries of Cox, Invex Controladora and Viva El Sol for private projects with an estimated investment of US $750 million.

According to information reported by Bloomberg Línea, Green Park Energy, a subsidiary of Cox, obtained three permits; Invex Controladora’s Ammper Generación received two, while Viva El Sol obtained one.

In a statement announcing the approval, the CNE said the permits are part of the Second Call for Proposals (Privados II) for priority processing of generation and interconnection permit applications to the SEN, in accordance with the binding planning issued by the Energy Ministry.

The Second Call received 57 applications, of which 31 met the basic requirements to obtain an electricity generation permit. However, only the six approved projects met all the criteria established.

The permits granted will operate under the Wholesale Electricity Market generation model and will provide greater operational flexibility while also strengthening the stability and reliability of Mexico’s grid.

Although the six projects represent a net capacity of 649 MW, they represent a combined installed capacity of 751 MW alternating current (MWac) and an estimated annual generation of 1,881 gigawatt-hours (GWh).

They also feature battery storage systems for 204 MW and approximately 628 MWh, which will serve to strengthen the stability and reliability of the electrical grid.

More than one-third of the capacity will become operational in 2028 and the remaining 63% in 2029.

Cox’s plants will be built in the states of Aguascalientes, Jalisco and Guanajuato, while the Invex subsidiary Ammper will locate its two in Tlaxcala and Morelos, and Viva El Sol’s project will be located in Coahuila.

Strategic Energy published details of the six projects, reporting that Ammper Generación’s Antares project to be built in Tlaxcala will be the largest single power plant among the six authorized, and is the development with the highest planned production within Privados II.

As such, the Western Region will add 350 MW, the Eastern Region 289 MW and the Northeastern Region 10 MW.

With reports from El Financiero and Bloomberg Línea

World.title: Tourism to Mexico City projected to hit nearly 66M visitors in 2026
World.content:
Mexico City authorities expect to close 2026 with a total of 65.9 million tourist arrivals — approximately double the arrivals 10 years ago — driven primarily by a packed schedule of concerts, sporting events and cultural activities that have bolstered the capital’s appeal as a travel destination.

The city’s Tourism Minister Alejandra Frausto Guerrero presented the projection during her appearance before the local Congress, as part of Mayor Clara Brugada’s second annual government report.

According to Frausto, the capital received 61.2 million tourists and visitors in 2025, compared to the 58 million recorded in late 2024 at the start of the current administration.

If the projection for this year is met, cumulative growth would have reached 13.6% between 2024 and 2026.

“Mexico City is experiencing one of its best periods for tourism,” Frausto said, which has greatly benefited the local economy.

Between January and September, tourists staying in hotels spent nearly 120 billion pesos (US $6.44 billion) — up 6% compared to the same period in 2025. Furthermore, revenue from the state lodging tax (ISH) reached 840 million pesos (US $45.1 million), an increase of 15.9%.

Entertainment events are drawing massive influxes of tourism and income

Musical performances and cultural events have become a significant driver of tourism activity in the capital, attracting both domestic and international visitors who also make use of lodging, dining and transport services.

According to Ticketmaster data cited by the newspaper El Sol de México, the musical artist The Weeknd drew an audience from 74 countries across three concerts in Mexico City, while AC/DC attracted attendees from 56 countries, also throughout three performances. Meanwhile, 43% and 41% of their respective audiences traveled from other parts of Mexico.

Frausto also highlighted the overlap of the Formula 1 Grand Prix and Day of the Dead celebrations in the capital, which boosted hotel occupancy to 92% between Oct. 30 and Nov. 1.

Finally, the tourism minister noted that the administration’s goal is to expand the positive impact of tourism across the capital’s 16 boroughs by promoting different neighborhoods, markets and original Indigenous communities, along with their cultural and culinary offerings.

With reports from El Sol de México

World.title: Exxon Signs Preliminary Venezuela Oil Pact
World.content:
File photo: an oil pumpjack in Zulia state, western Venezuela.

The top US oil producer is edging back into the country that once seized its oil fields. ExxonMobil said on Monday that it signed a preliminary agreement with Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), the state oil company, to look at oil projects there, a preliminary step toward a return after nearly two decades. The paper is a non-binding memorandum of understanding, a preliminary agreement, with PDVSA, which runs the country’s oil industry.

It comes as Venezuela US tensions give way to a scramble among US companies for access to some of the world’s largest crude reserves.

In plain English A memorandum of understanding is a signed statement of intent, not a contract. Exxon has agreed to study Venezuela’s oil fields but has not promised to spend money.

What Exxon Actually Signed

Exxon said the memorandum covers potential “upstream” opportunities, the industry word for finding and pumping oil. The company called it “a meaningful first step.”

Why Exxon Is Cautious

Exxon left Venezuela nearly two decades ago, after the government of the late socialist President Hugo Chávez expropriated its assets there. Few oil companies have more reason to read the fine print.

Exxon chief executive Darren Woods has kept expectations low. On the company’s late-October earnings call, its quarterly briefing for investors, he said operating in Venezuela would require substantial changes to how business has historically been done, and added: “We’re not in a rush.”

A Crowded Field Is Forming

Exxon is not the first US major back. On 2 September, US rival Chevron announced plans to invest more than US$7 billion over five years and to roughly double its Venezuelan output to about 600,000 barrels a day, under new agreements that it said improve fiscal and legal terms.

Washington has pushed hard for this. President Donald Trump’s administration wants US companies at the front of rebuilding Venezuela’s energy sector, after US forces captured then-President Nicolás Maduro in January.

The prize is large. The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the oil producers’ group, counts roughly 300 billion barrels of reserves in Venezuela, the most of any member.

Years of neglect have left production far below that potential, and analysts say a revival will take years.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, the memorandum is a signal rather than a number. It adds no barrels today and no spending to Exxon’s budget, but it shows the top US producer now sees enough political change to start talking.

Chevron is the early winner, already pumping and expanding. Exxon and others risk losing the best acreage if they wait, while the risk of another seizure keeps them from rushing.

What Is Not Known

Exxon has not named projects or areas, and the text of the memorandum has not been published. Some accounts say the Venezuelan government is also a signatory, while Exxon’s statement names PDVSA; we found no response from either side.

The exact time of the announcement is not confirmed. The next signal to watch is whether Exxon moves from a memorandum to a joint-venture or production-sharing contract, and on what terms.

Does Exxon now have to invest in Venezuela?

No. The memorandum is non-binding. A joint venture or production-sharing contract would still be needed before Exxon commits money.

Why did Exxon leave Venezuela?

The government of then-President Hugo Chávez expropriated Exxon’s assets, and the company left nearly two decades ago.

03 Why it moved

First cause, and the heaviest: the dollar. The dollar index fell 0.61% to 101.68, and gold, which pays no interest, tends to rise when the dollar softens.

Second, fear faded. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, fell 22.31% to 19.92 while the S&P 500 gained 2.35% to 7,550, which usually reduces demand for safe havens, so the metals’ gains came despite the calm.

The conflicting signal is oil. The oil-tracking fund USO fell 3.87%, so the metals did not rise on a broad commodity bid. Our best reading, with medium confidence, is that the weaker dollar and bargain-hunting after the October slide did the work.

The RT economic calendar, our database of scheduled data releases, listed the October consumer inflation expectation at 16:00 UTC, with a forecast of 3.8% against 3.9% before; the actual figure was not available in our calendar when we published. China’s factory-gate prices, a sign of industrial demand that matters for silver, rose 5.7% year on year in October against 5.3% expected.

04 The trend behind it

GLD hit US$495.90 on 29 January and is 23.5% below it. It has fallen 5.47% over 60 sessions and 0.69% over 20, and sits 6.7% above its 12-month low of US$355.78, set on 30 October.

SLV’s journey is wilder: from US$105.60 on 28 January to US$44.60 at its 12-month low on 30 October, and it is now 54.4% below the peak. It has lost 11.43% over 20 sessions and 17.68% over 60.

This looks like a continuation of the post-January slide, with a rebound inside it. A new uptrend would need the funds to hold above their recent lows while the dollar stops climbing.

05 What it means for Latin America

Mexico was the world’s top silver producer in 2025, with about 172.9 million ounces, roughly a fifth of global supply, according to the 2026 World Silver Survey, which the consultancy Metals Focus prepared for the Silver Institute, the industry body. Its output fell 5%, the third annual decline in a row, so Mexican miners are leaning on price rather than volume.

Peru ranked second with about 130.6 million ounces, up 7%, and China third with about 112.8 million. The top three together mine about half of the world’s silver.

Behind the price sits a real shortage: the 2025 market deficit, where demand outran supply, was 40.3 million ounces, the fifth in a row. Metals Focus expects 46.3 million ounces for 2026, which is why silver’s long-term story is better than its recent chart.

For importers there was a second tailwind: the oil-tracking fund USO fell 3.87% on the day, easing fuel costs across the region.

06 The names to watch

Fresnillo, Mexico’s largest primary silver miner, and Buenaventura, a Peruvian miner of silver and gold, are the most direct listed plays on silver’s direction. Buenaventura rose 3.25% on Monday to US$28.90 in New York.

The US dollar index is the other name to follow. It decides whether metals that pay no interest can keep their rebound.

07 What would end it

The nearest support is the 30 October low for both funds: US$355.78 for GLD and US$44.60 for SLV, with the round numbers of US$360 and US$45 just above them. A close below either low would reopen the January slide.

The next test is the US consumer price report on Tuesday, 10 November at 13:30 UTC, with a forecast of 3.9% year on year against 3.7% before, according to the RT economic calendar. Softer inflation and a weaker dollar would end the pressure; hotter data would extend it.

08 What to watch

US inflation data: The consumer price report on Tuesday decides whether the dollar and yields keep falling.

The consumer price report on Tuesday decides whether the dollar and yields keep falling. The dollar index: A move back above 102 would ease the rebound in both metals.

A move back above 102 would ease the rebound in both metals. GLD at US$355.78: The 30 October low is the line that separates a rebound from a fresh slide.

The 30 October low is the line that separates a rebound from a fresh slide. Mexico and Peru output: Mexico’s third straight annual decline versus Peru’s 7% gain shows who is winning on volume.

Polymarket, where users bet real money, lists a market on where gold, priced in US dollars an ounce, will trade in November, with US$110,024 traded as of 8:21 p.m. ET on 9 November 2026. It prices a touch of US$4,200 an ounce at 73.5%, US$4,300 at 46.0% and US$4,400 at 24.5%, and a fall to US$4,000 at 58.0%.

A second market on silver, with US$89,658 traded, prices a touch of US$54 an ounce at 89.7%, US$56 at 60.5% and US$58 at 36.5%, and a fall to US$50 at 48.0%. These prices are bets, not polls, and some price levels in these markets were already reached earlier in the month.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why did gold rise on Monday, 9 November 2026?

A weaker US dollar and a Wall Street rally helped: the dollar index fell 0.61% to 101.68, and the gold-tracking fund GLD rose 1.88% to US$379.53.

Why is silver so far below its January high?

The silver-tracking fund SLV is 54.4% below its 28 January high of US$105.60, as a strong dollar and fading haven demand since January hit it harder than gold.

Which countries mine the most silver?

Mexico leads with about 172.9 million ounces in 2025, followed by Peru with about 130.6 million and China with about 112.8 million.

Are GLD and SLV the same as the metal price?

No. They are US-listed funds that hold gold and silver, so their prices follow the metals closely but are not the price of an ounce.

World.content:
Key Facts Wheat is the story: the wheat-tracking fund WEAT closed Monday, 9 November 2026, at its lowest in at least six months, 22.7% below its 28 August high of 28.00 and down for a third session running.

the wheat-tracking fund WEAT closed Monday, 9 November 2026, at its lowest in at least six months, 22.7% below its 28 August high of 28.00 and down for a third session running. Soybeans and corn slipped too: SOYB, the soybean-tracking fund, moved −0.40% and CORN, the corn-tracking fund, moved -0.17%, extending a month of steady losses.

SOYB, the soybean-tracking fund, moved −0.40% and CORN, the corn-tracking fund, moved -0.17%, extending a month of steady losses. The main cause is supply: traders pointed to a large US harvest, with 74% of the corn crop in by 1 November, and cautious export demand.

the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) publishes its monthly supply and demand report (WASDE) on Tuesday, 10 November. History is mildly kind to soybeans: after earlier falls this large, soybeans were higher 20 sessions later in 65% of cases, wheat in only 38%.

Today’s Focus Wheat had a miserable Monday. The wheat-tracking fund WEAT closed at US$21.65 after a move of −0.37%, its third straight fall and its lowest close in at least six months. Soybeans and corn drifted lower in sympathy, with SOYB at US$25.22 and CORN at US$17.16. The common cause is plentiful supply: a big US harvest is reaching market while buyers hold back. For Latin America the pressure is double-edged. Brazil and Argentina sell grain to the world, so lower prices trim their export earnings, while Brazil’s own record soybean crop is adding to the glut. Grains ended Monday, 9 November 2026, lower across the board. Wheat led the retreat, closing at its weakest in at least six months.

Think of the market as a warehouse filling faster than customers are collecting. Farmers in the northern hemisphere have nearly finished harvesting, and buyers see no need to rush.

03 Why it moved

Cause one, with high confidence, is harvest supply. Wire reports from earlier this month say wheat, corn and soybeans all fell on a large US harvest, and 74% of the US corn crop was gathered by 1 November.

Cause two, with medium confidence, is soft export demand. Traders were cautious about buying, especially from markets outside China, although CME Group noted in September that Chinese import demand continues to underpin prices.

Cause three, with medium confidence, is positioning before today’s USDA report. Analysts expected it to lift the US wheat ending-stocks forecast by 4 million bushels to 744 million, and traders tend to sell ahead of bearish news.

The usual outside drivers were mixed and explain little. The US dollar index eased 0.61% to 101.68, which normally helps US grain sales abroad, yet prices still fell; the 10-year Treasury yield rose 3 basis points to 4.89%; and the S&P 500 jumped 2.35% as the VIX fear gauge dropped 22.31%.

Oil, tracked by the USO fund, fell 3.87%, which lowers costs for farmers and for ethanol makers who buy corn. Gold, tracked by GLD, rose 1.88%, so money was not fleeing risk; it simply did not want grain.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a new phase. Soybeans are 8.19% lower over 20 sessions and 10.4% below their 10 September high of 28.14, though still 16.2% above the January low of 21.71.

Corn has lost 7.04% in 20 sessions and sits 15.4% below its 1 September high of 20.29, only 4.2% above its 29 June low of 16.47. Wheat has fallen 11.49% in 20 sessions and 13.3% in 60.

The turn came in late summer. CME Group reported soybean futures at a three-year high on 1 and 2 September on strong export demand, and every grain has drifted lower since.

Our own archive adds a measure of perspective. After earlier falls as large as soybeans’ 8.19%, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 15 of 23 cases (65%), with a median of +1.1% and a worst case of -6.0%.

Corn is a coin toss: after 50 earlier falls like this one, it was higher in 24 cases (48%), median -0.7%, worst -12.5%. Wheat is the weak link, higher in only 8 of 21 cases (38%) with a worst case of -25.3%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is both seller and cause. CONAB expects a record 181.64 million tonnes of soybeans in 2026/27 from 49.3 million hectares, and the private forecaster AgRural sees 182.7 million tonnes, so supply is rising just as prices sag.

Lower prices squeeze the export earnings and farm incomes of Brazil and Argentina, which feed the real and peso economies through dollar receipts. The Brazilian exporters’ association ANEC expects 6.02 million tonnes of corn shipments in November, so volume holds up even as the price per tonne softens.

Importers gain. Wheat-buying countries across the region, including Mexico, Peru and Colombia, benefit from cheaper cargoes and lower bread and feed costs.

CONAB flags El Niño, a Pacific weather pattern, as a risk to yields, which it expects to fall about 0.8%. That is the main Latin American wildcard for prices.

06 The names to watch

The three trackers are the cleanest gauges: WEAT for wheat, SOYB for soybeans, CORN for corn. Wheat is closest to a breakdown, with its 22.7% drop from the August high the largest of the three.

Beyond them, watch the Brazilian crop agency CONAB, the exporters’ association ANEC, the private forecaster AgRural and the USDA. Their numbers set the tone for supply.

07 What would end it

The nearest hurdle for soybeans is the 21.71 January low, and for corn the 16.47 June low, now only 4.2% below the market. For wheat, the high of 28.00 is distant, so the next test is simply whether the six-month low holds.

The next dated event is the USDA WASDE report on Tuesday, 10 November. A cut to crop or stock estimates would calm the slide; a rise, as analysts expected for wheat, would deepen it.

Beyond that, Brazilian planting weather and Chinese buying decide the winter. The honest answer is that the slide may pause on a bullish report, but a lasting reversal needs demand to pick up.

08 What to watch

USDA report: The WASDE release on 10 November, especially US wheat ending stocks against the expected 744 million bushels.

The WASDE release on 10 November, especially US wheat ending stocks against the expected 744 million bushels. Brazil crop: CONAB updates and El Niño weather for the record 181.64 million tonne soybean forecast.

CONAB updates and El Niño weather for the record 181.64 million tonne soybean forecast. China demand: Whether Chinese buyers book US and Brazilian cargoes or leave the market quiet.

Whether Chinese buyers book US and Brazilian cargoes or leave the market quiet. Corn floor: Whether CORN holds above its 16.47 June low, now 4.2% away.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did grain prices fall on Monday?

A large US harvest, cautious export demand and positioning before the USDA report weighed on all three grains, with wheat at a six-month low.

Does cheaper grain hurt Brazil?

Yes for farm incomes and export earnings, though Brazil’s record soybean crop of 181.64 million tonnes is forecast, so volumes stay large.

Is SOYB the soybean price?

No. SOYB is a fund that tracks soybean futures, so it is a proxy and not the commodity’s own price.

Will the fall continue?

History offers no promise: soybeans rose after earlier similar falls in 65% of cases, wheat in only 38%.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest, falling fear: with shares surging and the VIX down 22.31%, traders sold the war premium. Confidence is medium, because we have no single confirmed trigger for the move.

Second, a softer dollar and a stock-market rally made holding oil as a hedge less attractive. Confidence is medium.

The usual drivers were mixed. The dollar index eased 0.61% to 101.68 and the S&P 500 jumped 2.35% to 7,550, while the VIX fear gauge dropped 22.31% to 19.92, all of which show calmer nerves.

The 10-year US Treasury yield rose 3 basis points to 4.89% and gold’s fund gained 1.88% to 379.53, so the picture was not one of simple risk-on buying. Our best reading is that falling fear, not weaker demand, pulled oil lower.

04 The trend behind it

Oil is cooling from a spike. The fund is 9.06% lower over five sessions and 5.54% lower over 20, yet still up 12.7% over 60 sessions.

This looks like a pullback inside a high-price phase, not a new bear market. Monday’s fall extends a slide that has now lasted five sessions.

Our own history since 2007 adds context. After 106 earlier cases with a 20-session fall this size, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 56 of them (53%), with a median of +0.4% and a worst case of -54.6%; history is not a forecast.

Petrobras tells a darker story: down 27.81% in 20 sessions and 13.28% in five. Of 17 earlier falls that large it rebounded in 8 (47%), with a median of -6.4% and a worst case of -45.2%.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil feels it most through Petrobras, whose shares are 59.0% above their January low but far below October’s peak. Its pre-salt fields, deep offshore deposits beneath a layer of salt, pay well only when crude stays high.

Argentina’s YPF, which leans on the Vaca Muerta shale basin, gave up 1.47% in a day. Colombia’s Ecopetrol, whose shares are 14.5% below their 15 September high, held up better.

Importers such as Chile and Peru gain from cheaper crude, while budgets built on high prices in Mexico, with its state firm Pemex, and in Venezuela and Guyana lose some cushion.

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is the stock to watch. Six straight losses mean sellers are in charge, and traders will look for a stable close above US$18.

YPF and Ecopetrol show how local factors matter: Ecopetrol rose while its peers fell. Guyana’s offshore boom and Venezuela’s output are worth watching, since a sanctions-bound barrel returning would add supply.

07 What would end it

The fall ends if tensions around Iran flare again, because the war premium would rebuild quickly. It continues if the calm holds and shipping near Hormuz stays safe.

On the chart, the fund’s nearest resistance is the 169.53 high from 23 October, and the round 150 level sits below it. Support is the 140 round number, and then the 12-month low of 66.17 from 16 December 2025.

For Petrobras, the 26.16 October high is far overhead, so round-number support near US$18 matters first. There is no scheduled date that settles this, so the next headline from Iran or Hormuz is the event.

Iran and Hormuz: Any new attack on shipping decides whether the war premium shrinks further or rebuilds.

Calmer nerves and a stock-market rally led traders to sell the extra price paid for war risk. The USO fund, tracking WTI, lost 3.87%.

No. It is a US-listed fund that tracks WTI crude, so its US$142.66 close is the fund’s price and not the barrel’s.

Today’s Focus Steel shares across Latin America rose on Monday, 9 November 2026, but the gains owed more to a strong day for markets in general than to any news about steel itself. 03 Why it moved

The first and heaviest cause was the market-wide rally, with high confidence. The dollar index eased 0.61% and the VIX collapsed, which usually helps companies tied to factories and building sites. The one conflicting signal was the 10-year US Treasury yield, which rose 3 basis points to 4.89%, normally a drag on such shares, so the move looks like a relief rally rather than a rethink of steel.

The second cause was Ternium’s company-specific strength, with medium-to-high confidence. Its third-quarter profit was US$368 million, against a loss of US$270 million a year earlier, and its Mexican shipments grew 18% year on year to a record 2.18 million tonnes. The chief executive attributed most of that growth to winning market share from imports, and the company expects strong domestic sales and pricing through the first half of 2027.

The third cause, with medium confidence, is trade protection. Brazil imposed five-year antidumping duties on Chinese steel earlier this year, which analysts expected to help CSN, yet importers simply moved to other Asian suppliers. That explains why Brazilian names rally less convincingly than Mexican ones, and why CSN could fall on a day when everything else rose.

China’s annual inflation rate was 0.7% in October, below the 0.8% forecast and the 0.9% of September, according to the RT economic calendar. Factory-gate prices rose 5.7% year on year against 5.3% expected and 5.0% before. China is the world’s largest steelmaker, so its price data shapes the import pressure Latin American mills face.

04 The trend behind it

Monday’s gain was a bounce inside a downtrend. The SLX fund is 12.3% below its 12-month high of 113.57 but 31.4% above its November 2025 low of 75.82, and it has lost 7.7% over 60 sessions.

Gerdau is 12.6% below its 20 October high of 5.24, though 40.5% above its March low of 3.26. CSN has been the most violent: it rose 13.27% over five sessions from a low of 0.71 on 3 November, then gave some back, so this looks like a continuation of a weak phase with sharp rallies, not a new one.

05 What it means for Latin America

For Brazil, steel is a story of fairness and survival. Gerdau’s chief executive has called competition from Chinese steel ‘not isonomic, it’s not fair’, and has warned that investment could move abroad without protection. Imports reportedly take about 30% of local steel sales, so every duty matters to the jobs and shares of Gerdau, Usiminas and CSN.

For Mexico, the picture is brighter. Ternium has taken market share from imports, and Mexican prices follow the US market while staying well below it, even with US tariffs on steel at 50%. A Mexico City investor holds the stronger of the two stories.

For a traveller or ordinary saver, the point is practical: steel tracks building and car production, so these shares are a bet on regional growth. They are volatile, and a day like Monday does not change that.

06 The names to watch

Gerdau is the bellwether. It fell 10.89% in 20 sessions, and our own history since 2007 offers a sobering note: in the 88 earlier cases with a fall at least that large, the shares were higher 20 sessions later in 45 cases, or 51%, with a median change of +0.6% and a worst case of -56.6%. History is not a forecast.

CSN is the riskier case. In 14 earlier comparable falls, it was higher 20 sessions later in 6 cases, or 43%, with a median of -2.1% and a worst case of -45.5%.

Usiminas, a petitioner in Brazil’s case against Chinese hot-rolled steel, is worth following for the outcome of that investigation, which we could not confirm. Ternium guides fourth-quarter operating profit broadly in line with the third.

07 What would end it

On the chart, the SLX fund meets resistance at US$100, a round number just above Monday’s close, and then at its 113.57 high; its support is the 75.82 low. Gerdau faces 5.24 above and 3.26 below, and CSN has support at 0.71 and the round US$1 above.

The rally ends if the VIX climbs back or the Treasury yield keeps rising. The bigger test is trade policy: no date is set for a US-Mexico deal or for the review of the USMCA trade pact, and either could reshape Ternium’s outlook. Does the weakness stop? Not until Brazil’s duties start to reduce imports from the new Asian suppliers.

08 What to watch

Brazilian antidumping: Whether importers keep shifting to Vietnam, South Korea and Egypt, and whether Brazil widens its duties.

Whether importers keep shifting to Vietnam, South Korea and Egypt, and whether Brazil widens its duties. US-Mexico trade: Any date for a deal or the USMCA review, which would affect Ternium’s pricing.

Any date for a deal or the USMCA review, which would affect Ternium’s pricing. SLX at US$100: A close above this level for several sessions would signal the rally has legs.

A close above this level for several sessions would signal the rally has legs. CSN debt: Its New York shares need to hold above 0.71 to avoid fresh selling.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did CSN fall when other steel shares rose?

CSN carries heavy debt and has been more exposed to Chinese import pressure, so its shares fell 3.80% even on a strong market day.

Why is Ternium doing better than the Brazilian producers?

Mexican shipments hit a record 2.18 million tonnes as local steel replaced imports, and the company expects strong sales and pricing into the first half of 2027.

What are antidumping duties?

They are extra taxes on imports sold below fair prices, and Brazil applied them to Chinese steel for five years.

Does a one-day rally mean the downturn is over?

No. The SLX fund is still down 3.37% over 20 sessions, and the sector remains well below its June high.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest, a broad appetite for risk. The S&P 500 rose 2.35% and the VIX fell 22.31%, so investors who had been hiding returned to cyclical stocks such as miners; confidence in this cause is high.

Second, a softer dollar. The dollar index slipped 0.61%, and metals priced in dollars become cheaper for buyers in euros, yuan or reais; the 10-year US Treasury yield rose 3 basis points to 4.89%, which is a small counterweight rather than a reversal.

Third, a metals-wide mood. Gold’s tracking fund gained 1.88% and market reports described copper bouncing after its worst week since March amid a scramble for metal in China. Oil’s tracking fund fell 3.87%, which eased inflation worries and supported the rally.

Underneath sits a tighter ore market. Treatment charges, the fees miners pay smelters, have repeatedly set record lows in 2026, which means smelters are fighting for scarce concentrate. Our confidence that this matters for the share moves is medium, because it is a slow-moving background force rather than a Monday trigger.

China’s annual inflation rate was 0.7% in October, below the 0.8% forecast and the 0.9% of September, according to the RT economic calendar. Factory-gate prices rose 5.7% year on year against 5.3% expected and 5.0% before. China is the world’s largest zinc consumer, so its factory prices matter for miners such as Nexa and Buenaventura.

04 The trend behind it

The bounce sits in a weak picture. Nexa has gained 5.34% over five sessions but lost 15.1% over 60, and it sits 28.0% below its 12-month high of 16.72 reached on 6 May 2026, though it is 129.3% above its low of 5.25 on 7 November 2025.

Buenaventura has risen 7.64% over five sessions but lost 14.3% over 60. It sits 33.8% below its 12-month high of 43.67 from 27 February 2026 and 29.2% above its low of 22.37 on 7 November 2025.

This looks like a continuation of a correction after a big run, with a short rebound on top. Nexa has now had two up sessions in a row, Buenaventura one.

Our own price history offers a sober check. After Nexa’s 20-session fall of 6.52%, there were 60 earlier cases of a move that large; the share was higher 20 sessions later in 29 of them (48%), with a median change of -0.5% and a worst case of -40.9%.

For Buenaventura, after a 20-session fall of 10.53%, there were 83 earlier cases; it was higher 20 sessions later in 41 (49%), with a median of -0.4% and a worst case of -35.0%. History is not a forecast, but it says such dips are roughly a coin toss.

05 What it means for Latin America

Peru, Bolivia and Mexico are among the world’s main zinc producers, so higher prices feed straight into export earnings, mining royalties and provincial budgets. Peru is the most exposed, with Buenaventura and Nexa’s Peruvian mines at the centre of that trade.

For Brazil, Nexa’s smelters in Minas Gerais and São Paulo state turn concentrate into refined metal, so tight ore supply squeezes their margins even when the zinc price is firm. Nexa’s Brazilian units were behind US$118m of its latest write-down.

Weaker oil helps importers across the region, from Chile to Central America, by lowering fuel bills. A softer dollar also tends to help the Brazilian real, the Mexican peso and the Peruvian sol, which cushions local costs for miners that earn in dollars.

06 The names to watch

Nexa Resources reported a third-quarter net loss of US$47m on 29 October, after a US$124m non-cash write-down, in which a company takes a lower value for assets it holds. Yet adjusted EBITDA, a measure of operating profit, was US$301m and free cash flow US$73m.

Mined zinc reached 85,000 tonnes, up 7% on the second quarter, and Nexa raised its capital spending guidance by 10% to US$420m. That is a miner investing for growth, not retreating.

Boliden’s planned purchase of Votorantim’s controlling stake should close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to approvals. A Nordic mining group taking control would change the company’s ownership and strategy.

Buenaventura offers a different bet, because its gold and silver exposure matters as much as its zinc. With gold’s fund up 1.88% on Monday, that helped its shares as well.

07 What would end it

The rebound fails if the dollar turns higher again or if US inflation data, due in the coming days, pushes bond yields up. Another broad sell-off in equities would hit miners harder than the metals they dig.

The levels to watch are the recent 60-session slide for confirmation of a floor, then the 12-month highs of 16.72 for Nexa and 43.67 for Buenaventura as distant resistance. On the downside, the November 2025 lows of 5.25 and 22.37 mark the extreme floors.

The honest answer is that the bounce can continue for days if the dollar stays soft, but a durable turn needs evidence from steel and construction demand, especially in China. Until then, treat Monday as relief.

08 What to watch

US dollar: The dollar index at 101.68 is the quickest gauge for metals; a rebound would pressure miners.

The dollar index at 101.68 is the quickest gauge for metals; a rebound would pressure miners. US inflation data: The next US inflation report will steer bond yields, which at 4.89% weigh on mining stocks.

The next US inflation report will steer bond yields, which at 4.89% weigh on mining stocks. Treatment charges: Record-low smelter fees show how tight ore supply is; any recovery would signal easing.

Record-low smelter fees show how tight ore supply is; any recovery would signal easing. Nexa ownership: Regulatory approvals for Boliden’s purchase of Votorantim’s stake, due to close in the first quarter of 2027.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does zinc matter to ordinary people?

Zinc coats steel to stop rust, so it sits inside cars, bridges, roofs and appliances. Its demand follows construction and manufacturing.

Are Nexa and Buenaventura the zinc price?

No. They are company shares that tend to move with zinc and the wider market, but each also depends on its own costs, debts and other metals.

Which Latin American countries gain from zinc?

Peru, Bolivia and Mexico are major producers, so export income and mining taxes rise and fall with the metal. Brazil benefits through Nexa’s smelting.

Is this the start of a recovery?

Not yet. Both shares remain well below their 12-month highs, and our history shows a dip like this has been followed by gains only about half the time.

03 Why it moved

The first and heaviest cause was a broad return of appetite for risk. The S&P 500 rose 2.35%, the VIX fell 22.31% to 19.92, and when fear drains out of markets, cyclical stocks such as miners tend to lead the recovery. Confidence in this reading: high.

The second cause was a softer dollar. The US dollar index fell 0.61% to 101.68, which makes ore priced in dollars cheaper for buyers using yuan, euros or reais. Confidence: medium, because the US 10-year Treasury yield edged up three basis points to 4.89%, a signal that normally works against commodities.

The third cause is China, and here the evidence is thinner. Chinese futures climbed to a four-week high in early November and the margin on importing ore turned positive, which means mills could profit from buying overseas cargoes. A broader metals bounce, with copper recovering after its worst week since March amid a scramble for metal in China, supports that story, but we have no hard October steel figures to confirm it. Confidence: medium to low.

Oil told a different tale: the oil fund fell 3.87% and gold’s fund rose 1.88%, as lower crude eased inflation worries ahead of the next US inflation report. That mix suggests investors are betting on easier policy, which is friendly to mining shares even without a Chinese revival.

China’s annual inflation rate was 0.7% in October, below the 0.8% forecast and the 0.9% of September, according to the RT economic calendar. Factory-gate prices rose 5.7% year on year against 5.3% expected and 5.0% before. China’s steel mills buy most of the world’s seaborne iron ore, so their input costs are a key signal for Vale and its peers.

04 The trend behind it

The wider picture is still grim. Vale’s shares are 32.8% below their 12-month high of 17.82, set on 20 April, and are down 11.46% over 20 sessions and 12.2% over 60.

In mid-October the ore price touched a two-year low as weak Chinese demand met rising supply from big miners. The latest rise is a continuation of a bruised market catching its breath rather than a new upward phase.

Our own archive, which runs back to 2007, offers a sober note. After 78 earlier falls as large as Vale’s recent one, the shares were higher 20 sessions later in 39 cases, or 50%, with a median change of -0.6%, a worst case of -32.8% and a best of +37.6%. History is not a forecast, but it says a deep fall does not guarantee a quick rebound.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is the region’s iron ore power. Vale’s fortunes feed into Brazilian export earnings, state tax receipts in Minas Gerais and Pará, and the weight of mining stocks on São Paulo’s Ibovespa index.

CSN Mineração, which sells ore from Minas Gerais, is 28.0% below its September high of 6.99 yet 23.3% above its May low of 4.08. That shows how violently small producers swing with the price.

A firmer ore market also supports the Brazilian real, because ore is one of the country’s largest dollar earners. Peru, Chile and Mexico are more tied to copper and silver, but they gain when the same Chinese demand story improves.

06 The names to watch

Vale is the bellwether: a close above this week’s highs would suggest the rebound has legs. Rio Tinto, still 22.9% below its 12-month high of 112.04 yet 25.6% above its November 2025 low of 68.78, shows how much of the sector’s damage has been repaired.

CSN Mineração carries more risk because it has a single product and a smaller balance sheet. Its 5.96% gain on the day was smaller than its sharp five-session run, so it may be the first to give back gains if the mood sours.

07 What would end it

The nearest support is the November low of 10.98 for Vale’s shares, and the first test above is the area around 12, with the April peak of 17.82 far overhead. A close below the November low would signal that the autumn slide had resumed.

The next catalysts are China’s monthly steel and trade data and the coming US inflation report, which will shape the dollar and the mood for risk. Honest answer: the bounce can continue while fear stays low, but it will fade unless Chinese mills show real appetite for imported ore.

08 What to watch

China steel demand: Monthly output and import figures will show whether mills are truly restocking or merely trading a rebound.

Monthly output and import figures will show whether mills are truly restocking or merely trading a rebound. US inflation report: A hot reading could lift the dollar and yields, which would cool the commodity bounce.

A close below the November low would signal that the autumn fall has resumed. Supply growth: Rising output from the biggest miners was a major driver of October’s two-year low and could cap any recovery.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Vale’s shares used for iron ore?

Iron ore’s own price is not on our feed, and Vale is among the world’s two largest exporters, so its New York shares move closely with the commodity, though they also reflect the mood of investors.

Why did iron ore rise on Monday, 9 November 2026?

The most likely cause was a broad rally in markets plus a weaker US dollar, with early signs of renewed Chinese buying as a supporting factor.

Is this the start of a recovery?

Not yet. Vale’s shares remain 32.8% below their April high, and Chinese steel demand has not clearly improved.

How does it affect Brazil?

Higher iron ore prices lift Vale and other miners, boost export earnings and tax revenue, and support the real.

03 Why it moved

The first and heaviest cause is the price of the metal itself. We could not verify a spot price for China’s battery-grade lithium carbonate for this session, so we leave it out; the lithium miners’ fund is our live gauge of the sector.

The second cause is Albemarle’s third-quarter report on 4 November. Earnings were US$2.58 a share against a forecast of US$2.53, and sales of battery materials were about US$1.1 billion, up 58% on a year earlier thanks to higher prices.

Revenue of about US$1.55 billion came in just under the US$1.57 billion forecast, and the company’s average realised price was US$20.02 per kilogram of lithium carbonate equivalent. That mix explains a rebound that stopped short of a rally.

The third cause was the wider market. The S&P 500 gained +2.35%, the VIX fear gauge fell -22.31%, the dollar index eased -0.61% to 101.68, and the US 10-year yield barely moved at 4.89%.

Oil fell -3.87% and gold rose +1.88%, so investors were rotating, not panicking. The usual drivers agree with the fund’s rise but not with the falls at Albemarle and SQM.

Our best reading, with medium confidence, is profit-taking in the two leaders after Albemarle’s quick run-up, while smaller miners caught the market’s good mood. Stocks of lithium in Chinese warehouses fell by 2,994 tonnes to 125,391 tonnes, which suggests buyers are using up stock, a modestly positive sign.

China’s annual inflation rate was 0.7% in October, below the 0.8% forecast and the 0.9% of September, according to the RT economic calendar. Factory-gate prices rose 5.7% year on year against 5.3% expected and 5.0% before. China is the main market for battery-grade lithium, so its factory prices matter for the metal’s outlook.

04 The trend behind it

The slump is long. The fund is 33.0% below its May high, 2.6% above its 30 October low of 59.81, and has risen for two sessions in a row.

Albemarle is 54.0% below its April high of 215.62, and SQM is 40.5% below its April high of 95.31 yet 16.1% above its low of 48.83 from November 2025.

This is a continuation of a bear phase with a possible basing attempt. A bounce of two days is not a new trend.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile is most exposed, because SQM is its flagship lithium company and its shares have lost 23.7% over 60 sessions. Lower prices shrink the profits that feed Chilean company taxes and royalties.

Argentina and Bolivia hold the other two corners of the Lithium Triangle, the salt flats that hold much of the world’s reserves. Both need high prices to justify new projects, and a market near multi-month lows delays them.

For a saver in Santiago, Buenos Aires or La Paz, the lesson is that mining wealth moves with a Chinese factory price, not with local politics alone.

06 The names to watch

Albemarle is the barometer for Western producers: its 3 November low of 90.19 is the line the bulls must defend, and the 100 mark is the nearest round number above.

SQM is the one to watch for Latin America. An earlier company executive forecast a 2026 price floor of US$15 to US$18 per kilogram, which is a forecast, not a market price, but it frames what management thinks is a bottom.

07 What would end it

For the fund, support is the 30 October low of 59.81, only 2.6% below Monday’s level, and resistance is far away at 91.62. A close under 60 would suggest the slide resumes.

For history, RT’s own record since 2010 shows 41 earlier falls of 10% or more in 20 sessions. In 23 of them, 56%, the fund was higher 20 sessions later, with a median of +0.9% and a worst case of -14.9%. History is not a forecast.

SQM tells a similar story: after 83 earlier falls of this size, it was higher 20 sessions later in 46 cases, or 55%, with a median of +0.7% and a worst case of -39.8%.

The decisive signal is China’s weekly carbonate price holding above the bottom of its 82,000 yuan range while warehouse stocks keep shrinking. Until then, expect rebounds to fade.

08 What to watch

China carbonate price: Weekly battery-grade price against the 82,000 to 105,000 yuan range.

Weekly battery-grade price against the 82,000 to 105,000 yuan range. Chinese stockpiles: Warehouse stocks at 125,391 tonnes: further falls would signal real demand.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is LIT the price of lithium?

No. LIT is a fund holding lithium-mining and battery-metal companies, so it reflects company shares, not the metal’s spot price.

Why did Albemarle and SQM fall while LIT rose?

Smaller miners rallied with a strong stock market, while the two leaders, after a sharp Albemarle rebound, saw profit-taking.

Who is hurt by cheap lithium?

Producers in Chile and Argentina and their tax authorities lose, while electric-car and battery makers gain from lower costs.

Is the slump over?

Not yet. The fund is 33.0% below its May high, and the Chinese spot price was still falling in the latest weekly reading.
