World.title: Costa Rica Paid $701 Million More for Fuel This Year as Diesel Soared
World.content:
Costa Rica paid about $701 million more for imported fuel in the first nine months of 2026 than in the same period last year, as higher international prices drove up the cost of every barrel, according to figures from the state fuel company, Recope. Fuel imports through September totaled $2,267 million, up 44.77% from $1,566 million a year earlier.

The volume imported grew only about 5.5%, from 18.81 million to 19.85 million barrels, so most of the increase came from higher prices. The average cost of a barrel rose 37.17%, from $83.27 to $114.22. Diesel was the largest single expense, at $961 million. Its average import price climbed from $90.79 to $135.82 per barrel, while jet fuel rose from $93.36 to $138.84. Karla Montero, Recope’s executive president, attributed the jump in diesel to attacks on Russian refineries.

The Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) projects in its Monetary Policy Report that the country’s oil bill will close 2026 at $3,086 million, compared with $1,976 million in 2025. Montero said higher import costs reach consumers gradually, through the monthly price adjustments approved by the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep). Diesel and regular gasoline currently sell for 808 colones per liter, about $1.80, or roughly $6.80 per gallon. Super gasoline sells for 806 colones per liter.

Diesel has historically been cheaper at the pump because it carries a lower single fuel tax, but international cost pressure has narrowed that gap. Diesel was up 17% in October’s inflation figures, as consumer prices rose for a second straight month. Alonso Alfaro, chief economist at the BCCR, said more expensive fuel adds inflationary pressure that could spread to other prices. He also said larger import payments increase demand for dollars and put pressure on the external deficit, although that demand has so far been met without instability.

The exchange rate has softened part of the blow. Recope said this year’s roughly 10% shift in the exchange rate has offset part of the increase in import costs, with the dollar now trading near 450 colones. Recope expects international prices to remain between $90 and $110 a barrel in the coming weeks. Pablo Guzmán, executive director of the Costa Rican Fuel Chamber, said Costa Rica is a price taker and that prices could ease or rise moderately in 2027.

Any relief next year depends on smoother oil shipments through the Middle East and a recovery in diesel supply. Recope said it has completed its annual tender for 2027 contracts, which fixes freight, insurance and supplier margins for the year.

World.title: Costa Rica Asks You to Cut Water Use as the El Niño Dry Season Begins
World.content:
Costa Rica’s national water utility is asking everyone to use less water as the dry season begins this week in Guanacaste and the Central Valley, with a strong El Niño expected to keep conditions drier and hotter than normal through January. The Costa Rican Institute of Aqueducts and Sewers (AyA) made the appeal on Monday. It is a request, not a restriction. AyA said it is not rationing water and has no plans to do so in the near future.

The reason is timing. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects the dry season to start this week in the North Pacific and Central Valley, during Nov. 16–22 in the Central Pacific and during Nov. 23–29 in the South Pacific. Once the rain stops, the sources that feed many water systems stop recharging. IMN director Bernard Stolz said in May that AyA is among the institutions hit hardest by El Niño because rain stops falling in the high parts of the mountains. Water saved now helps carry systems through the driest months of the year.

Here is what AyA is asking you to do at home.

Take shorter showers, and turn off the tap while you soap up or shampoo.

Fix leaks, and check faucets, pipes and toilets for water running when it shouldn’t be.

Don’t hose down sidewalks, patios or driveways.

Reuse water for household jobs that don’t need drinking water.

Collect rainwater for plants and outdoor cleaning, but don’t drink it.

Run the washing machine only with a full load.

One thing AyA does not want you to do is stockpile. Drinking water stored too far in advance can lose quality and become contaminated, so there is no need to fill containers unless your provider announces a cut. This year has already tested the supply. Water rationing reached dozens of Pacific communities, and in October authorities issued the country’s first red alert at sea.

The Central Valley is exposed too. A national El Niño contingency strategy drawn up by the National Emergency Commission (CNE) with AyA and other institutions projected lower output from the surface and underground sources that supply the Greater Metropolitan Area. That plan listed at least 120,579 AyA customers in San José districts, including Pavas, Tibás, Goicoechea, Moravia and La Uruca, as facing possible supply impacts. It also set out tanker-truck service for critical areas such as La Carpio.

If your water comes from a local ASADA rather than AyA, as it does in many Guanacaste beach towns and rural communities, that provider sets its own schedules. Check its notices or social media pages for any changes. AyA’s appeal did not single out specific regions or set a consumption target. If supply does tighten, service schedules would come from AyA or from local providers.

World.title: Spot an Injured Animal on Route 27? Don’t Touch It. Here’s Who to Call
World.content:
If you see an injured animal on Route 27, the toll highway between San José and the central Pacific coast, don’t pull over and try to pick it up. Slow down, keep your distance and call the highway’s 24-hour control center at 2588-4040. That is the advice from Route 27’s operator, Globalvia, and from specialists at Refugio Animal de Costa Rica, a wildlife refuge in Santa Ana. The highway has recorded 299 animal rescues since 2015, according to Globalvia.

The total includes 149 dogs, 58 cats and 92 wild animals. Among the wildlife were sloths, snakes, turtles, iguanas, birds, coatis and ocelots. An animal that has been hit by a car may be stunned, in shock or carrying a fracture you can’t see. Even one that looks calm can bite or lash out when you get close, and handling it the wrong way can make its injuries worse. Snakes and other potentially dangerous species add another layer of risk.

Stopping suddenly is a danger of its own on one of the country’s busiest highways. Brake gradually, don’t swerve, and give the drivers behind you time to react. Rodolfo Vargas, a biologist at the refuge, advises alerting other motorists without making sudden maneuvers. Don’t try to touch, capture or carry a wild animal yourself. Report it instead, so trained staff can deal with it safely.

The Route 27 control center answers 24 hours a day at 2588-4040. If the animal or the situation puts other drivers in immediate danger, call 911. For specialist advice on what to do, you can reach Refugio Animal de Costa Rica at 8828-0324. When you call, give your location as precisely as you can, ideally the nearest kilometer marker, along with your direction of travel. Say whether the animal looks injured and whether it is blocking a lane.

Route 27 recently trained 15 of its staff with specialists from the refuge. The course covered how to identify potentially dangerous species, how to recognize injuries and fractures, and how to handle animals safely. Montserrat Courrau, Route 27’s director of communications and corporate social responsibility, said every animal presents its own situation, which is why staff need to know how to handle each one correctly.

Globalvia says the highway has run its animal assistance and staff training program for more than a decade. The rescues are a small window onto a wider problem, as wildlife deaths on Costa Rica’s roads continue to mount and a new law requires wildlife crossings on public infrastructure.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Marchamo Amnesty Is Off for 2027, So Pay by Dec. 31
World.content:
If you’re behind on your marchamo and hoping lawmakers would wipe the debt this year, don’t wait. The amnesty proposed for 2027 failed, and a new version wouldn’t help anyone until 2028. Your 2027 marchamo is due by Dec. 31. Any older years you haven’t paid still carry their interest and fines.

The original plan was simple. Bill 25.630, filed on June 22 by Liberación Nacional deputy Mangell McLean, would have forgiven every unpaid marchamo from 2026 and earlier, including interest, fines and penalties. All you had to do was pay the 2027 marchamo before Jan. 1, 2027.

To take effect in time for this year’s payments, the bill needed a fast track. On Sept. 8, lawmakers voted 29 to 20 against that, with the ruling Pueblo Soberano caucus opposed. Without the fast track, the bill went into the regular queue and can’t move quickly enough to cover your 2027 payment.

McLean has now filed a new bill, number 25.886. It moves everything forward a year. You would have to pay the 2028 marchamo before Jan. 1, 2028, and anything unpaid from 2027 and earlier would be forgiven. The new version is narrower. It covers only cars and motorcycles with a fiscal value of 13,020,000 colones (about $28,700) or less, so newer and higher-value vehicles would not qualify.

It is a proposal, not a law. It still has to clear committee and two floor votes, and it would need support from a ruling party that has so far opposed it. The debt behind the push is large. According to Finance Ministry data cited by McLean, 10.6 million unpaid marchamos piled up between 2015 and 2026. That figure counts unpaid years, not vehicles, because a single car can owe several.

McLean argues that an amnesty would turn debt the state can’t collect into immediate revenue and help families get their vehicles back on the road legally. Opponents in the ruling party argue that forgiving the debt would reward people who didn’t pay. Costa Rica has done this before. In January 2022, lawmakers forgave old marchamos for nearly a million vehicles, but only 108,785 of the 992,598 eligible vehicles took advantage. A second amnesty passed in September 2023.

Here is what to do now. Look up your total by license plate on the INS marchamo website or by calling 800-MARCHAMO (800-6272-4266). The breakdown shows each item, including any older years you still owe. Expect the mandatory SOA insurance in your marchamo to cost a little more. For a private car, it rises 5.4% to 31,881 colones (about $70). The SOA covers medical care for people injured in a crash, up to 6 million colones per person.

This is also the first year of the new digital sticker, which is meant to last up to 10 years. It carries a separate charge of about 1,200 colones. Motorcycles keep the traditional sticker for now. Before you pay, check your total for an optional add-on insurance policy. If you don’t want it, you can uncheck it and the amount will adjust.

Regular collection of the 2027 marchamo runs through Dec. 31. More than 2 million marchamos were issued for collection this cycle.

World.title: Guanacaste Town Hall Took 29 Million Colones in Cash Its Bank Refused
World.content:
A Guanacaste municipality accepted 29.3 million colones (about $64,600) in cash for a property tax bill after its bank refused to deposit the money. The municipality held the cash until judicial agents seized it, according to internal audit documents. The Municipality of Nandayure, on the Nicoya Peninsula, received the payment on March 4. A man came to the counter to pay a corporation’s property taxes on two properties, covering 2023 through the first quarter of 2026.

He paid in bundles made up mostly of 10,000- and 20,000-colón bills. He also handed over copies of his identification, a sworn statement, the company’s legal registration, a trust agreement, a loan contract and a promissory note. Municipal staff tried to deposit the cash at Banco Nacional that same day and again on March 6 at the bank’s Jicaral branch. Each time the bank turned it away and asked for a withdrawal slip or other proof of where the money came from.

On the March 6 trip, the cash went by municipal vehicle with no police escort and no transit insurance, the documents show. The money stayed under municipal control until March 10, when agents of the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) seized it. The municipality’s Internal Audit has since sent its documentation to the OIJ, which is working to establish the origin of the funds.

According to the audit findings, municipal accountant Xinia María Cambronero and cashier Lilliam Artavia warned that the cash should not be accepted without proof of its origin. Artavia told auditors she asked Mayor Teddy Zúñiga Sánchez directly what to do. She said he told her to accept the money and issue a receipt, and assured her she would not face problems. She described the situation as unprecedented at the municipality.

Cambronero said she warned the mayor the bank would likely reject the cash. She said he told staff to accept it because municipal taxes must be honored. The documents also note that the municipality had no security cameras, no permanent security staff and no protocol for handling large cash payments.

Zúñiga denied giving a specific order to the finance department or the accountant. In a written response, he described the matter as an institutional consultation for the responsible department to resolve. In other official communications, the mayor said he had asked for more documents, including a withdrawal slip, and that the cash should have stayed in the municipal safe. He argued that the municipality acts as a tax collector, not a financial institution.

Zúñiga also said he does not know the people involved and was not part of the receiving process. He said the municipality is cooperating with the investigation and has annulled the 29.3-million-colón receipt, so the tax debt is pending again. The mayor said the judicial case is against an unidentified person and that, as far as he knows, no criminal investigation targets municipal officials. He said the taxpayer may have filed a constitutional appeal but that he had not confirmed it.

The Public Prosecutor’s Office said in April that the case was being investigated against an unidentified person and did not involve municipal employees at that stage. That same month, the Comptroller General’s Office closed a separate administrative complaint over the payment because a judicial authority was already handling the matter.

The cash payment is one of two matters at the Nandayure municipality now before judicial authorities. On Nov. 4, the OIJ and prosecutors raided the town hall in an unrelated case and detained two officials. One is an inspector surnamed Venegas. The other works in the Maritime-Terrestrial Zone Department, which handles beachfront concessions.

The two are suspected of concusión, a crime in which a public official uses the position to demand an improper payment. According to the court file, the inspector allegedly used WhatsApp to ask a resident for 4 million colones (about $8,800) to speed up a land concession process. He allegedly also offered privileged information about other lots in the area.

The resident wanted to buy a lot from a third party and did not know it was a concession inside the maritime zone. The events date to June 12, and the case began with the resident’s complaint. The court file points to possible involvement by other officials, who have not been named.

The municipality confirmed the detentions and the seizure of files related to the case. It said it is cooperating with judicial authorities, recently made changes in the Maritime-Terrestrial Zone Department, and that procedures for concession holders and applicants will continue as normal.

No connection between the two cases has been reported. No one has been charged in either matter. Under Costa Rica’s maritime zone law, the strip of land within 200 meters (656 feet) of the high-tide line is public. The first 50 meters (164 feet) cannot be privately held, and local governments grant concessions on the remaining 150 meters (492 feet). That makes municipal concession offices one of the most consequential public counters along the country’s coast.

World.title: Driving South This Week? Térraba Bridge Closures Run Through November 14
World.content:
If you’re driving the Interamericana Sur through Palmar Norte this week, check the clock before you leave. The bridge over the Térraba River, between Palmar Norte and Palmar Sur in Osa, has partial closures every day from Monday, November 9 through Saturday, November 14. Tonight it closes completely.

Both lanes close from 10 p.m. tonight until 5 a.m. Tuesday, according to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT). If you reach the bridge during those hours, you’ll have to wait until morning to cross. Today’s partial closures run from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. before the full overnight shutdown. From Tuesday through Friday, partial closures come in two blocks each day, from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. and again from 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. On Saturday, partial closures run from 7 a.m. to noon.

Outside those hours, both lanes stay open as usual, MOPT said. This bridge is the gateway to everything south of Palmar Norte. That includes Palmar Sur and its airport, Sierpe, where boats leave for Drake Bay, the turnoff to Puerto Jiménez, Golfito, and the Paso Canoas border crossing into Panama. The Costanera Sur coastal highway joins the Interamericana Sur at Palmar Norte, so drivers coming down from Dominical and Uvita who are heading farther south cross it too.

If you have a flight out of Palmar Sur or a boat to catch in Sierpe, leave extra time during the daytime closure hours. If you’re driving to the Panama border tonight, plan to cross the bridge before 10 p.m. or after 5 a.m. MOPT hasn’t announced an alternate route, so your best option is to time your trip around the schedule.

MOPT says the work will raise the bridge’s clearance and let heavy trucks cross safely. Repairs began in late January, and a second phase is reinforcing the structure from underneath. The ministry reported the project was 70 percent complete in late October, up from 40 percent in March.

The rehabilitation costs more than $10 million and is funded through the government’s emergency infrastructure reconstruction program, known as Proeri. The bridge is one of the most important structures on the southern Interamericana. It opened on February 26, 1961, and MOPT’s historical records describe close to 161 metric tons (about 177 US tons) of reinforced steel in its frame and supports.

This week’s closures won’t be the last. MOPT said closures like these will continue into early 2027 and that it will announce new dates as the work moves forward. Check the schedule before any trip through the southern zone in the coming months.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Dry Season Starts This Week in Guanacaste and the Central Valley
World.content:
If you live in or are visiting Guanacaste or the Central Valley, the rain is about to switch off. Costa Rica’s dry season settles over the North Pacific and the Central Valley this week, and the rest of the Pacific coast follows within three weeks. That is the outlook from the National Meteorological Institute (IMN), whose four-week forecast goes from Nov. 9 to Dec. 6 and describes the dry season taking hold across the Pacific slope and the Central Valley under a pattern of below-normal rainfall.

With that said, here is the timeline. The North Pacific, which is Guanacaste and the Central Valley, home to San José, Alajuela, Heredia and Cartago, enter the dry season this week. The Central Pacific, including Quepos and Manuel Antonio, follows the week after.

The South Pacific, from Dominical and Uvita down to the Osa Peninsula, joins the week of Nov. 23 to 29. By Nov. 30, the IMN expects very dry conditions across the North Pacific, the Central Pacific and the Central Valley. Keep in mind, dry does not mean zero rain, at least not yet. For this week, the forecast still allows weekly totals of 1 to 70 millimeters (up to 2.8 inches) in the North Pacific and 5 to 80 millimeters (0.2 to 3.1 inches) in the Central Valley, mostly as isolated afternoon showers in the mountains.

The Central Pacific could also see 10 to 80 millimeters (0.4 to 3.1 inches) this week, and the South Pacific 20 to 80 millimeters (0.8 to 3.1 inches). Today is the hand-off. The low-pressure system that soaked the Pacific over the weekend is drifting west, away from the coast. Expect some early rain on the Guanacaste coast this morning, isolated afternoon showers in the mountains and stronger trade winds from the afternoon on but tonight should be dry.

The weekend left its mark first. Nosara recorded 51 millimeters (2 inches) of rain on Sunday, and parts of the eastern Central Valley reached 60 to 65 millimeters (2.4 to 2.6 inches), according to the IMN. That followed a Saturday when five regions were on yellow alert. Those afternoon winds are the real signal. Trade winds are the signature of the dry season in the Central Valley and Guanacaste as they bring cool, clear mornings and blue skies, but they also dry out pastures and forest quickly.

If you are on the Caribbean coast or in the Northern Zone, nothing changes. Those regions have no defined dry season but even so, the IMN expects rainfall there to run about 30 percent below normal from November through January. This year’s switch comes in the middle of a very strong El Niño, which the IMN expects to hold at that intensity through January. The institute has warned that temperatures could run up to 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal and may break records, in line with a December El Niño peak forecast by the World Meteorological Organization.

IMN climatologist Daniel Poleo said in October that the transition could be drier than normal, after a month the institute projected would end 40 to 60 percent short of normal rainfall in much of the country. Back in September, forecasters were already saying El Niño could end the rainy season early.

A drier-than-usual start matters most for water availability. Guanacaste enters the dry months after a year in which water rationing reached dozens of Pacific communities and authorities issued the country’s first red alert at sea. One caveat before you put the umbrella away. The hurricane season runs until Nov. 30 in both the Atlantic and the Pacific, and storms during the transition can still bring short, intense downpours. On Sunday, the US National Hurricane Center gave the weekend’s low a 20 percent chance of becoming a tropical depression within 48 hours.

Having said all that, what does this mean for you? Pack a light layer for windy Central Valley mornings, carry more water than you think you need on Pacific beaches, and keep an eye on afternoon clouds in the mountains for the rest of November. For most of Costa Rica, the change means clearer skies, cooler highland nights and long stretches of sunshine through April. It also starts the five-month stretch when every liter of water on the Pacific side counts.

World.title: Diesel Up 17% as Costa Rica Prices Rise for a Second Straight Month
World.content:
Costa Rica’s cost of living is climbing again. Consumer prices rose 0.39% in October, and the year-on-year rate reached 0.55%, the second straight month above zero after 16 months of annual declines, according to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC).

That October jump compares with 0.11% in September and 0.19% in October 2025. The interannual rate also climbed from 0.34% a month earlier. Transport drove most of the increase. INEC reported that the transport division rose 1.71% in a single month and accounted for 0.30 percentage points of the overall index, with diesel up 17.39%, gasoline up 3.10%, taxi fares up 5.73% and bus fares up 2.02%.

Nelson Castillo Mendoza, coordinator of the INEC price index unit, said the main upward pressure came from fuel and public transport fares. He noted that those prices are set by the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep) and moved in line with international fuel prices during the month.

The rise follows September’s warnings of higher fuel prices as oil climbed back above $100 a barrel. Regulated goods and services rose 1.99% in October, according to INEC data, while unregulated items rose just 0.16%. Energy prices as a group rose 2.75%. Entertainment also cost more. The recreation, sport and culture division rose 0.96%, which INEC attributed mainly to higher ticket prices for events. Eggs rose 4.09%.

Some grocery staples moved the other way. Onions fell 10.73%, potatoes 3.50%, ground beef 2.44% and chicken breast 1.73%, and food and non-alcoholic beverages as a whole rose only 0.09%. Of the 293 goods and services in the basket, 45% rose, 33% fell and 22% were unchanged, with 10 of 13 spending divisions moving higher.

The longer view still shows Costa Rica with unusually low inflation. Cumulative inflation from January through October was -0.01%, essentially flat, compared with a 1.77% decline over the same period of 2025. Full-year 2025 inflation was -1.23%.

That keeps Costa Rica well below the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) target of 3%, with a tolerance band of one percentage point in either direction. The October reading sits 1.45 points below the bottom of that range, and inflation has now been below target for 42 consecutive months. The last time it was inside the band was April 2023.

The BCCR expects that gap to close. In its October Monetary Policy Report, the bank projected headline inflation near 2.7% in the second half of 2027, higher than its July forecast, and tied the revision to expected higher hydrocarbon prices. It kept its monetary policy rate at 3% and said it would adjust its stance if conditions or risks change.

The central bank listed extreme weather, including El Niño, geopolitical conflict and higher oil and grain prices among the risks that could push inflation up faster. A stronger colón and weaker global growth were among the factors that could hold it down. For households, the October figures arrive alongside other pressures. Earlier this month, INEC data showed unemployment climbing to 6.5%, while the exchange rate has left dollar earners with fewer colones than in January.

Rents have also been outpacing general inflation for months. The return of rising prices ends a long stretch of falling prices in Costa Rica. Whether the shift becomes a steady climb back toward target or a short fuel-driven spike will depend largely on oil markets and on the next round of regulated price adjustments, which anyone who fills a tank, rides a bus or takes a taxi in Costa Rica will feel first.

World.title: San Felipe man charged with two counts of attempted murder after machete attacks on tortilla man and hammock man
World.content:
San Felipe man charged with two counts of attempted murder after machete attacks on tortilla man and hammock man

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged 26-year-old Dwight Hernandez of San Felipe Village, Orange Walk District, with two counts of attempted murder following a pair of machete attacks that left two men injured on Friday, November 6.

According to police, the incidents occurred shortly before 6:00 p.m. when Hernandez allegedly confronted 51-year-old Cesar Bolaños, a tortilla factory owner, on an unnamed road in San Felipe Village and inflicted several chop wounds before fleeing.

Investigators say Hernandez then travelled approximately three blocks away, where he allegedly attacked a second man, identified as 50-year-old Jorge Moo, who was lying in a hammock. Moo also sustained chop wounds during the attack.

Police subsequently launched an operation to locate Hernandez, with assistance from residents of the community. He was eventually apprehended and taken into custody.

Both victims were reported to be in stable condition as of Monday’s police briefing.

Investigators also disclosed that Hernandez and Bolaños had reportedly been involved in a previous altercation. Police further indicated that they are examining information concerning the suspect’s alleged substance use and behaviour, although the precise motive for the attacks has not been established.

The incident had previously sparked alarm in San Felipe Village, where residents reportedly assisted in searching for the alleged attacker. Reports from Friday night indicated that villagers beat Hernandez to subdue him.

Hernandez has now been charged with two counts of attempted murder as investigations continue.

World.title: Migrant caravan sets off in southern Mexico after Trump’s midterm losses, and Belize is watching
World.content:
Migrant caravan sets off in southern Mexico after Trump’s midterm losses, and Belize is watching

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Hundreds of migrants, most of them from Honduras, have set off on foot in a caravan through southern Mexico, saying they believe US President Donald Trump’s tough immigration policies will soften after his party’s losses in last week’s midterm elections.

According to Reuters, the group left the Mexican border town of Metapa de Dominguez and walked to the city of Tapachula in Chiapas state, near the border with Guatemala.

Migrants told Reuters they expect Trump’s anti migrant measures to weaken now that Democrats control the US Senate. Some said they were happy to see the President’s party suffer losses.

“I think we’re all people who want to work,” one migrant said.

The caravan’s journey is a reminder of how closely Belize is tied to migration in the region. Belize borders both Mexico and Guatemala, and many Central Americans pass through or settle in Belize while searching for work and safety. Communities across Belize are home to large numbers of Honduran, Guatemalan and Salvadoran families.

Thousands of Belizeans also live in the United States, and many households here rely on the money they send home. Any change in how Washington treats migrants could affect those families directly.

Democrats flipped six Republican held Senate seats on November 3. However, immigration enforcement remains largely in the hands of the White House, and it is not yet clear whether the vote will lead to real change.

World.title: Shiloh Coleman found murdered near Mile 8 on George Price Highway after being reported missing
World.content:
Shiloh Coleman found murdered near Mile 8 on George Price Highway after being reported missing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating the murder of 19-year-old Shiloh Coleman of Belize City, whose decomposing body was discovered shortly before midday on Monday, November 9, approximately one and a half miles into the Western Paradise community near Mile 8 on the George Price Highway.

According to police, Coleman’s body was already showing signs of decomposition and had apparent gunshot wounds when investigators arrived at the scene.

Coleman had been reported missing by his mother at approximately 5:30 p.m. on Sunday, November 8. She told investigators that she last communicated with her son shortly before 9:00 p.m. on Saturday, November 7, after noticing that his vehicle was not parked at home.

She reportedly sent him a message asking about his whereabouts, and he responded that he would return home. However, when she received no further communication from him the following day, she contacted police.

During Monday’s press briefing, police confirmed that investigators are pursuing two possible motives for the killing but declined to disclose either, citing the ongoing investigation.

Authorities also confirmed that Coleman’s vehicle had not yet been recovered, although investigators have received information about its possible whereabouts and are following leads with assistance from the Crime Fusion Centre and surveillance camera operators.

Police have not disclosed whether any suspects have been identified or whether the killing is connected to the recent wave of gang-related violence in Belize City.

The investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: GI3 officer Michael Anthony Wagner remanded to prison over gun-in-mouth incident in San Pedro, disciplinary proceedings underway
World.content:
GI3 officer Michael Anthony Wagner remanded to prison over gun-in-mouth incident in San Pedro, disciplinary proceedings underway

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police Constable Michael Anthony Wagner, 30, has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being formally charged with aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a disturbing incident in San Pedro Town in which he allegedly placed his service weapon into a man’s mouth. Police have also confirmed that disciplinary proceedings are underway against the officer.

Wagner, a resident of Orange Walk Town who was attached to the GI3 police unit operating in San Pedro, appeared in Court #5 at the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday afternoon, November 9, before a Magistrate in the presence of his attorney, Arthur Saldivar.

The charge alleges that on Thursday, November 5, Wagner committed an aggravated assault upon Azzaine Guerra with the use of a firearm.

The incident attracted widespread public attention after video footage circulated on social media showing a police officer confronting a man lying on his back. The officer was allegedly seen placing a firearm against or inside the man’s mouth during the encounter.

As previously reported by Breaking Belize News, Wagner was suspended from duty following the incident while police launched criminal and disciplinary investigations.

During Monday’s police press briefing, Assistant Superintendent of Police Stacy Smith confirmed that Wagner had been formally arrested and charged following a complaint made by a San Pedro resident.

Smith also confirmed that disciplinary proceedings were underway and addressed questions surrounding the officer’s presence at the location where the incident occurred.

She explained that several operational police units were conducting activities in San Pedro, including GI3, to which Wagner was attached. However, she said she had not been informed of the specific purpose of Wagner’s presence on that particular street.

Smith indicated that investigators would seek to establish those circumstances as part of the ongoing investigation. When questioned further about the officer’s actions, she declined to discuss details of the criminal case, noting that the matter was now before the court.

Meanwhile, at Wagner’s arraignment later that afternoon, his attorney challenged the application of the Crime Control and Criminal Justice Act (CCCJA), under which the aggravated assault charge carries restrictions on bail at the Magistrate’s Court.

Saldivar argued that the legislation was specifically intended to address criminal gangs and persons involved in organized criminal activities rather than police officers carrying out their lawful duties.

He submitted that Wagner was on duty at the time of the alleged offence and was legally authorized to carry a firearm while patrolling the community.

According to Saldivar, the law was designed to address the misuse of firearms by civilians and criminal gangs, and his client should not automatically fall within those provisions simply because he was charged with aggravated assault involving a firearm.

However, the police prosecutor opposed the application for bail, maintaining that Wagner had been charged with aggravated assault with a firearm under the CCCJA and that the legislation prevented the Magistrate from granting bail.

The sitting Magistrate agreed with the prosecution’s interpretation and denied bail, ordering Wagner’s remand to the Belize Central Prison.

Wagner is scheduled to return to court on December 29, 2026, before the San Pedro Magistrate’s Court, when he is expected to receive disclosure in the case.

The criminal proceedings and the police department’s internal disciplinary process remain ongoing.

Wagner is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in a court of law.

Jamaica’s beaches are more than just beautiful places to visit. They sustain livelihoods, bring families together, and let visitors experience the best of our island. But what happens when the very spaces we depend on become dumping grounds?

World.title: Warning!
World.content:
PASCOE...find something more productive, even going into farming yourself, it will be in your best interest (Photo: JIS News)

SENIOR Superintendent of Police (SSP) Oral Pascoe is urging agricultural thieves to abandon their criminal activities and find legitimate employment, warning that the police intend to intensify their crackdown on offenders amid an increase in large-scale livestock theft across Jamaica.



His warning comes as the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Agricultural Protection Branch (APB) is reporting 1,424 arrests for agriculture-related offences islandwide so far this year, a more than 600 per cent increase from the approximately 200 arrests during the corresponding period in 2025.

“My warning to the thieves is that they need to change the profession of stealing agriculture produce for a living, because we are sharpened and we are determined to ensure that the farmer benefits from what they do,” Pascoe declared on Sunday in an interview with the Jamaica Observer.

“We have zero tolerance, and we’re going to ensure that once we identify you as a larcenist, and you prey on farmers, we’re going to put you on our monitoring list, and we’re going to target you for snap raids and other operational activities to ensure that you do not carry out those offences,” he charged.

Pascoe, head of the APB, disclosed that the increase is consistent with a seasonal trend in which the demand for meat rises ahead of the Christmas period, with some farmers losing dozens of animals in a single incident.

“Traditionally in Jamaica, in the Yuletide, meaning from about September, accelerating in October to December, there’s a spike in the demand for meat and, of course, our local goat and beef is preferred,” he explained.

He said that, while thieves would usually target one or two animals at a time, the police are now encountering cases involving significantly larger numbers.

“We have about three or four instances where they stole about 40 goats, 30 goats, [animals] in large numbers. Normally, they steal one or two during the year, but…the value of what they steal in terms of livestock is a lot larger,” he noted.

Pascoe further disclosed that the police have received approximately 230 reports of praedial larceny up to the end of September, with that figure climbing to just over 250 following an increase in incidents during October.

He identified Manchester, Clarendon, St Elizabeth, St Mary, St Catherine, and St Thomas among the parishes most affected, noting that the highlighted areas account for approximately 70 to 80 per cent of reports islandwide.

The senior officer said that some of the thefts were not necessarily being committed by individuals acting alone, but by organised criminal groups.

He pointed to incidents in Colbeck, St Catherine, where several animals were reportedly being stolen nightly, forcing the police to intensify their presence.

“They were just going on, and four, five, six animals per night — cows, herds of cattle — were being stolen, until we had to set up foot patrol in the area…and do some serious investigation,” he told the Observer.

The SSP explained that some criminals slaughter animals in remote areas, a practice commonly referred to as bush slaughter, while others attempt to pass stolen livestock off as legitimately owned animals.

“Sometimes those animals end up in another farmer’s [herd], especially if they’re untagged…and they launder them, and they use their legitimate receipt book from RADA [Rural Agricultural Development Authority] and sell them on as if they are legitimate livestock, [as if] they are the owners,” he explained.

“So that is one of the practices that we’re stamping out. We have increased patrols in the vulnerable areas, and the sensitisation with the farmers have increased significantly,” the SSP added.

Pascoe also expressed concern that some farmers are failing to report incidents of theft, making it more difficult for the police to respond effectively.

“Some farmers are not reporting the situation to us, so we can’t respond. So, once we get a report, immediately, we have an operational response, an internal mechanism, to try to recover, arrest, detain, and arrest suspects, and try to control so that it doesn’t escalate,” he said.

The senior lawman encouraged farmers to report suspicious activities and the public, generally, to remain vigilant, while maintaining that the police will continue their operations to disrupt livestock theft networks.

“So just change your lifestyle, find something more productive, even going into farming yourself. It will be in your best interest,” Pascoe warned.

World.title: Return of Spanish right risks reigniting Catalan separatist flame
World.content:
“We know that they are certain to cut back our self-governing powers and intervene in Catalan society in a very heavy way,” Francesc-Marc Álvaro, a candidate for the Senate in the upcoming election for the Catalan Republican Left (ERC), said. “This would amount to throwing gasoline on Catalan society.”

Lawmaker Míriam Nogueras from the pro-independence Junts party said Catalonia had “never been respected by any Spanish regime or government,” and the next would be no exception. “Whatever its political color, the next Spanish government will be exactly the same as the previous one on one fundamental issue: Catalonia,” she said, adding that “the independence movement will regain momentum, and it will do so with renewed strength, because Catalonia’s dependence on Spain makes everyone poorer.”

For Madrid, the stakes are economic as well as political. Catalonia is Spain’s second-biggest autonomous region after Andalusia, representing about 19% of the national economy and 16.5% of the population.

End of Sánchez era

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez took office shortly after a failed independence drive in 2017 saw several nationalist politicians flee abroad and nine others jailed.

In contrast to the PP’s uncompromising approach to Catalonia, Sánchez negotiated with pro-independence parties, making concessions in exchange for their parliamentary support.

An amnesty benefiting Catalans involved in the secession attempt angered the Spanish right but helped calm the political atmosphere in the region, eliminating a major nationalist grievance.

World.title: Why the Democrats’ midterm blowout is making Burnham’s Labour nervous
World.content:
A Labour MP, granted anonymity like others in this article to speak frankly, said their own engagement with Democratic New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s team had hammered home “the politics of trying.”

“If people think you’re not even trying, which obviously is what they thought about Trump, then you’re just going to get blown away,” they said. By making small adjustments, the MP argued, Burnham has begun to “develop a coherent argument — which is actually voters have to see you trying on the cost of living.”

Yet beyond this apparent vindication of the PM’s basic strategy, members of his party see clear warning signs for the incumbent British government in the U.S. political shift. An administration only just coming out of a dire stretch in public opinion polls, they worry, could take the wrong lessons from the Dems’ triumph across the pond if they don’t heed the deep anti-incumbent sentiment that drove it.

Reasons to be fearful

Burnham has badged his fledgling administration as a “cost of living government” since he replaced Keir Starmer at the top of Labour earlier this year.

Yet he has faced criticism from some quarters that a government-wide budget unveiled last month lacked real ambition — and now the pressure is on to deliver before a general election, due by 2029.

Claire Ainsley, a former adviser to Starmer who works for the Progressive Policy Institute think tank on both sides of the Atlantic, told POLITICO that, despite arguments about the future direction of the Democratic Party, “what they’ve all had in common is a real focus on affordability.”

World.title: Europe needs Nvidia. It’ll take more than a spy scandal to change that.
World.content:
A German government spokesperson said Monday in response to a barrage of questions on the upheaval at Nvidia that it "does not comment on the media reports," and that "we always adhere to the highest standards, including when agreements are being reached." A European Commission spokesperson also had no comment on the matter.

In both Silicon Valley and Washington, investigators are already busy. Nvidia has opened an internal investigation into whether its CEO was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation, after Huang developed an intimate relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of trying to funnel intel on U.S. chips to Beijing. Huang has admitted publicly to having an affair.

The U.S. Congress, particularly its factions wary of China, is also set to take action. “The U.S. should immediately pause the shipment of advanced AI chips to China until we can get to the bottom of this incident and ensure our national security is not being undermined,” Rep. Michael McCaul, a Republican from Texas, and former chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said on X.

In Brussels, the blow to the Silicon Valley giant might appear to be good news for those who warn of U.S. tech dominance in the AI race. But as with the recent results of the midterm elections, the woes at Nvidia don't change Europe's reality because the bloc is so reliant on the company's AI chips.

"We don't have any alternative, the design [of chips] is almost entirely U.S.," said Dutch European Parliament lawmaker Bart Groothuis, one of the negotiators of the bloc's latest chipmaking plan.

Groothuis decried Nvidia's "bizarre monopoly position."

World.title: EU offers cash for Black Sea attack response
World.content:
She also announced an additional €10 million in EU cash for Romania’s search-and-rescue operations. The sums are tiny compared to the €16.7 billion Romania is getting under the EU's SAFE arms loans program.

The hub, announced last year, is a joint control center to be run by Romania and Bulgaria and is expected to be fully operational by the end of the year.

It aims to monitor maritime activity in real time and safeguard vital infrastructure such as undersea power and communication cables. It would offer both countries a unified view of the sea and sky, helping them detect threats before they strike.

Monday's announcement follows weeks of mounting violence on the Black Sea. Since early October, at least nine ships have been struck in the exclusive economic zones of NATO and EU members Romania and Bulgaria; four were sunk, and 34 sailors are dead or missing.

Other ships have been hit off Russia's shores.

Both Romania and Bulgaria raised the issue at last month's meeting of EU leaders and are pressing for more security support. However, while Romania has blamed Russia, Bulgaria has stopped short. Von der Leyen is set to visit Varna, on Bulgaria’s coast, on Tuesday.

World.title: Pourquoi la COP31 pourrait être la dernière chance pour l’UE de peser sur les négociations climatiques
World.content:
Des députés européens d’extrême droite et de droite originaires de Pologne, d’Allemagne et d’Autriche se sont aussi fait l’écho de ces prises de position. Dans leurs pays respectifs, ces partis font campagne, à la fois, pour tailler dans les mesures nationales et européennes permettant de diminuer les émissions, et pour réduire l’aide au développement, dont la partie destinée à la lutte contre le changement climatique à l’étranger. Or, de telles décisions saperaient l’influence de l’UE lors des COP, alors même qu’elle cherche à consolider son leadership.

Les responsables politiques centristes sont conscients du risque, mais ils n’ont pas perdu espoir.

“Nous avons vu les Etats-Unis tourner le dos à la lutte contre le changement climatique ainsi qu’à la science du climat, et je crains que d’autres pays, y compris au sein de l’Union européenne, ne s’engagent dans la même voie”, a confié la ministre danoise du Climat, Samira Nawa, à POLITICO. Mais la victoire de nombreux démocrates favorables à la lutte contre le changement climatique lors des élections de mi-mandat aux Etats-Unis pourrait marquer un tournant, a-t-elle ajouté. “Espérons que nous puissions observer la même évolution en Europe.”

Changement stratégique

Les gouvernements européens se sont engagés à intensifier leurs efforts diplomatiques après s’être retrouvés isolés lors de la COP30 qui s’est tenue l’année dernière au Brésil. Les ministres concernés se sont réunis à plusieurs reprises cette année pour discuter de la manière dont l’UE pourrait mieux se préparer à cette conférence, et mieux travailler son message.

“Beaucoup de travail a été fait au cours de l’année écoulée, tant sous la présidence chypriote [du Conseil de l’UE] qu’actuellement sous la présidence irlandaise, afin de veiller à ce que nous soyons encore mieux préparés”, a retracé Mattias Frumerie, ambassadeur suédois pour le climat.

Résultat, les Européens ont acté une position de négociation plus ferme. Ils ont aussi décidé de regrouper tous les pavillons nationaux présents dans l’espace dédié à la conférence au sein d’un “village européen” unique afin de donner l’impression d’avoir plus de poids. Et ils ont défini une stratégie de communication commune inédite pour la COP31, visant à parler d’une seule voix.

World.title: La France accuse l’Iran d’être à l’origine des cyberattaques visant les supermarchés
World.content:
PARIS — Le ministre français des Affaires étrangères, Jean-Noël Barrot, a déclaré que l'Iran était à l'origine de la récente série de cyberattaques "sans précédent" visant les réfrigérateurs de plusieurs grandes chaînes de supermarchés du pays le mois dernier.

"Grâce à l’excellent travail des services gouvernementaux, je suis en mesure de confirmer que la responsabilité de cette attaque incombe aux Gardiens de la Révolution iranienne", a déclaré le ministre aux journalistes lundi, lors d’une réunion du G7 à Paris. "Nous allons imposer des sanctions au niveau européen à l’encontre des responsables", a-t-ajouté.

Jean-Noël Barrot a déclaré que 700 points de distribution alimentaire en France avaient été touchés par cette cyberattaque. Peu après, le parquet français a annoncé l'ouverture d'une enquête.

Bien que Jean-Noël Barrot ne fasse référence qu’aux incidents signalés en France, des supermarchés dans toute l’Europe, et même des banques de sang françaises, ont été pris pour cible par des pirates informatiques ces derniers jours. Des experts en cybersécurité avaient déjà fait part de leurs inquiétudes quant au fait que ces attaques pourraient s’inscrire dans le cadre de la guerre hybride que mène actuellement la Russie contre l’Europe, bien que le Kremlin ait nié toute implication.

World.title: Who’s who for Europe at the Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
World.content:
The European contingent includes national security advisers from France, the U.K., Germany and Italy, in addition to senior officials from NATO as well as the European Commission and the European Council. The inclusion of EU figures as well as an Italian representative follows a push by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who warned of fragmentation in a letter to European Council President António Costa last week.

Despite their presence in Abu Dhabi, though, the European team is not expected to be inside the room during the main negotiations, according to two senior officials aware of the format. A German official told POLITICO that the format of talks would be “determined as the discussions progress.” The Kremlin has voiced opposition to Europeans directly participating in the talks, according to the same senior officials.

Here’s a quick look at the key players from Europe in Abu Dhabi.

Günter Sautter (Germany)

Sautter is German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s foreign and security policy adviser and a senior career diplomat who has become a major figure in Europe’s efforts to end Russia’s war — and secure a European seat at the negotiating table.

Besides representing Germany in the E3 format, Sautter is also coordinating the German-led “Berlin Format” — a German-led coalition to bring together Ukraine, the E3 and other European nations such as Italy, Poland or the Scandinavian countries as well as NATO, EU and others including Canada — that seeks to steer Ukraine’s peace talks and coordinate support for Kyiv.

At a press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week, Merz remarked that Sautter “is now devoting a significant portion of his workforce to diplomatic efforts to end this war.”

World.title: Spain’s conservatives promise to relax climate rules if they win election
World.content:
Spain under Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been one of the bloc's most influential cheerleaders for ambitious climate goals, advocating to protect key EU policies like the Emissions Trading System, pollution reduction targets and the phase-out of gasoline cars.

But the PP's manifesto shows that would change if the EU's fourth-largest economy votes for a conservative government led by PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo.

Polls point to a clear majority for a coalition between the PP and Vox, a far-right party which is highly hostile to climate policies and is rising in the polls — potentially giving it significant weight in the next cabinet.

Feijóo’s team advocates assessing and relaxing Spain's climate policy sector by sector, considering three factors: “What is happening in the rest of the world, the technology that is available at the moment, and changes in demand.”

“We will not impose unnecessary obligations and will remove those that harm competitiveness, industry, or employment,” the document adds.

The PP has taken a more skeptical approach to EU climate policy than many of its fellow conservatives in other countries. In November 2025, for example, it voted against the 2040 climate goal in the European Parliament, breaking ranks with most of the EU's center-right umbrella group, the European People’s Party.

World.title: M John Harrison becomes oldest ever winner of the Booker prize for his satirical novel 'The End of Everything'
World.content:
At a ceremony in London the winner of the most prestigious literary award in Britain was announced by the classicist Mary Beard, the chair of the judging panel which also included pop musician Jarvis Cocker.

 

The End of Everything is set on England’s Channel coast in the near future, after an unspecified calamity has shattered society and brought an influx of enigmatic alien entities to Britain. It centers on a beachcomber who lives with his gun-toting aunt and discovers a puzzling, shapeshifting artifact on the shore.

Mary Beard said the book is “the politics of now seen through the lens of the future,” and about a society “undergoing a catastrophe that they don’t really understand.”

Harrison said before he won that he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic. Why shouldn’t a well-written (work of science fiction) be considered to be literary fiction?”

This year’s shortlist – 6 novels whittled down from a longlist of 163 - was a typically mixed bag of fiction. It included two former winners, Marlon James from Jamaica and Scot Douglas Stewart. A win by either one would have made that author the fifth double Booker winner, after J.M. Coetzee, Peter Carey, Hilary Mantel and Margaret Atwood.

Pulitzer Prize winner Elizabeth Strout was also on the shortlist, as were Luke Kennard’s satirical campus novel Black Bag; and Rebecca Perry’s Medieval-to-modern tale May We Feed the King.

Founded in 1969, the Booker Prize is open to novels written in English from any country published in the U.K. and Ireland. It has a reputation for transforming writers’ careers.

Its winners have included Salman Rushdie, Ian McEwan, Bernardine Evaristo and Arundhati Roy. Last year’s prize went to “Flesh” by Hungarian-British writer David Szalay.

World.title: Turkey: Steel plant explosion kills 17 in Izmir province
World.content:
The blast occurred at 11:46am local time on Monday 9 November, triggering a fire and sending thick smoke above the industrial complex. Aerial footage showed emergency vehicles surrounding the site as ambulances transported casualties to nearby hospitals.

 

İzmir governor Süleyman Elban said an overhead crane had collapsed into an electric arc furnace during maintenance work, damaging a gas line and causing the explosion.

One worker told AFP that a snapped crane cable had sent around 120 tonnes of molten steel crashing onto the furnace, triggering a violent reaction.

Around 200 employees were in the affected area at the time, fewer than usual because production had been suspended for maintenance.

Five people have been detained and four prosecutors assigned to investigate the circumstances of the disaster, while rescue teams continue searching the wreckage.

World.title: Poland: Tusk and Nawrocki honour six victims of Kraków shooting
World.content:
The two political rivals arrived together at the memorial, where Tusk held a candle as a uniformed officer played a horn nearby. They then placed candles among those left in memory of the victims before kneeling side by side in a moment of remembrance. Nawrocki repeatedly made the sign of the cross as the two leaders paid their respects. Footage shows rows of flickering candles, mourners gathered at the site and a Polish flag, reflecting the grief following Saturday's attack, which also left 15 people injured.

 

The rare public appearance together comes amid a bitter political dispute between Tusk and Nawrocki over reforms to Poland's Constitutional Tribunal. Despite their disagreements, both leaders took part in the ceremony honouring those killed in the 7 November shooting.

The attack in the heart of Kraków, one of Poland's best-known historic cities, had triggered scenes of panic as people fled the gunfire. In the days since, residents have returned to the area to light candles and pay their respects, while bullet marks remain visible on nearby café windows. Monday's vigil brought the country's two most prominent political figures together in a shared tribute to the victims, offering a moment of unity despite their continuing political differences.

World.title: Turkey: Delegates arrive in Antalya as COP31 climate talks begin
World.content:
Delegates arrived at the conference venue beneath rows of national flags and prominent COP31 signs, while buses and vehicles lined the surrounding roads. Running until 20 November, the summit focuses on cutting emissions, expanding electrification, reducing methane and building more resilient cities.

 

Talks are taking place amid turmoil in global energy markets, with the war in Iran effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz and driving up fuel and fertiliser prices. The disruption has renewed debate over energy security and investment in renewables.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell warned that progress remained “nowhere near far enough or fair enough”, urging governments to deliver on existing promises.

Climate finance for developing countries and the role of natural gas are expected to dominate negotiations. More than 90,000 participants are anticipated, with world leaders due to meet on 11 and 12 November.

World.title: Polish president and PM join Krakow Silent March for victims of market shooting
World.content:
The march began promptly at 20:00 to the sound of the St Mary's bugle call, at the junction of the Main Market Square and Sławkowska Street, the place where the first shots were fired during Saturday's attack. The participants then walked towards St Mary's Basilica. The march ended near the Town Hall Tower.

 

Those taking part, at the invitation of the mayor of Kraków, Łukasz Gibała, included the President of Poland, Karol Nawrocki, Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the Archbishop of Kraków, Cardinal Grzegorz Ryś, the governor of the Małopolska region, Krzysztof Klęczar and the marshal of the region, Łukasz Smółka.

Even before the ceremony began, the mayor of Kraków had encouraged residents to commemorate the victims together.

"In this difficult time, let us show solidarity and show that Kraków will always be a proud city, but also hospitable and open" wrote Łukasz Gibała on social media. Prime minister Donald Tusk also encouraged people to take part in the event.

"This evening in Kraków thousands of Poles have gathered to pay tribute to the victims of the attack of 7 November. May they rest in peace" wrote Prime Minister Donald Tusk on X.

As the mayor had previously announced, no speeches were planned during the march. No addresses were scheduled after it either.

An important element of the ceremony was the commemoration of the places where the tragic events took place. Candles were lit at each of the three locations where victims of the attack were killed.

At the end of the event, the bugler played "The Sound of Silence" on the trumpet, and the Archbishop of Kraków, Cardinal Grzegorz Ryś, said a short prayer for the dead.

The March of Silence was held on the last day of national mourning, declared by President Karol Nawrocki for 8 and 9 November. The authorities of Kraków have, however, decided on a longer period of remembrance. In the city the period of mourning will last until the end of Wednesday, 11 November.

During this time the flags on public buildings will remain at half-mast or draped in black crepe. Signs of mourning have also appeared on public transport - flags with black ribbons have been placed on Kraków's buses and trams.

Residents who want to express their sympathy to the families of the victims can also write in a book of condolence.

The traditional book has been made available in the lobby of Kraków City Hall on Wszystkich Świętych Square. It can be signed until Wednesday 11 November, between 9:00 and 19:00.

The city has also opened an online condolence book which will remain available until 11 November at 19:00.

Injured police officers decorated by the president

Even before the March of Silence began, information emerged that two officers who had been seriously wounded while intervening against the attacker were to be honoured.

The head of the National Security Bureau, Bartosz Grodecki, announced on social media that President Karol Nawrocki had decided to award Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur Morański the Officer's Cross of the Order of Polonia Restituta.

The decorations were awarded for special services in actions for public safety and order, as well as for courage and dedication in the performance of their duties.

"The heroic conduct of the officers, who at the risk of their own lives stopped the attacker, inspires admiration and deserves the highest recognition. I thank both officers for their decisive intervention and their readiness to defend others. I wish them a swift recovery" said Bartosz Grodecki, conveying the president's position.

Both injured police officers received the decorations from the President of Poland, Karol Nawrocki in person.

First words of one of the injured police officers after waking from coma

27-year-old Senior Constable Artur Morański and 24-year-old Senior Constable Jakub Kulik were the first to intervene directly against the armed attacker who opened fire in the centre of Kraków on Saturday.

During the operation they neutralised the attacker, but were themselves shot by him and taken to hospital in a critical condition. Morański and Kulik were then placed in a medically induced coma.

On Sunday doctors began the process of waking both officers. A day later further information appeared on the condition of the 27-year-old.

The mayor of Kraków, Łukasz Gibała, reported that the officer had been extubated and his condition had started to improve.

As the mayor of Muszyna, Jan Golba, said on social media, Morański first words after waking up were: Is Kuba [Jakub] alive? ("A Kuba żyje?").

Bloodbath in tourist hotspot

On Saturday a 24-year-old man, Michał Oksiński, drove a car onto the main market square in Kraków and opened fire with an automatic weapon, apparently at random.

Six people were killed and 16 were injured, including two police officers and the attacker, who died in hospital early on Monday morning.

Those killed in Krakow's mains square and tourism hotspot were four Polish citizens, a British man and an Austrian woman. Among the 15 wounded are people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

In Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, in the attacker's family flat, police also found the bodies of his parents and sister, believed to have been killed hours before the attack in the centre of Krakow.

World.title: A huge explosion at a steel factory in Western Turkey has left at least 17 people dead and 13 injured
World.content:
The blast happened at midday local time, when a crane lifting a replacement boiler collapsed and fell into a furnace used during the liquid steel casting process.

 

The fire at the HABAS plant in Aliaga, Izmir province, claimed at least 17 people's lives and also injured 13 people, two of them critically, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said in a televised address following a scheduled Cabinet meeting.

"The circumstances surrounding this tragic incident, which has deeply saddened our nation, including how and why it happened, whether there was any negligence and who bears responsibility, will be established," Erdogan said on television.

According to eye witnesses, the explosion "felt like an earthquake".

Izmir mayor Cemil Tugay said on X that rescue teams were "continuing their work to remove the collapsed platform" and that those affected were factory workers.

EU president Ursula van der Leyen has expressed her condolences

HABAS is a privately owned group and one of Turkey's top steel producers. The plant was established in 1987 and can produce 4.5 million tons of steel annually, according to the company’s website.

Workers' groups said there was a long record of safety issues at HABAS.

World.title: China's robots, AI agents and Nvidia probe: Web Summit 2026 Opens in Lisbon
World.content:
Dancing robots from the company Aigibot opened the Web Summit 2026 technology conference in Lisbon on Monday, putting China's artificial intelligence technology firmly on stage.

 

"The superstars of the future are not coming from California; they're coming from China," Web Summit CEO and founder Paddy Cosgrave told an audience of up to 12,000 people.

"Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else," he added, referring to the open source technology.

The United States and China are in an artificial intelligence race to build out the technology, as Washington has tried to restrict exports of the most high-powered chips to China.

The US and China are locked in an escalating tech race, with artificial intelligence at the forefront, and Washington has sought to restrict exports of the most high-powered chips to the country.

Meanwhile, US chip giant Nvidia US tech giant Nvidia is opening a probe into its CEO, Jensen Huang, after reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort” in his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked about the news of Huang, Cloudflare's cofounder and CEO Matthew Prince said on stage, "it's very salacious" but that in the long term it remains to be seen if he would be "a hero or villain," referring to the impact on the industry, adding that "Jensen did a lot to cement the AI ecosystem."

AI agents were also featured on the Web Summit stage. The technology is designed to take autonomous actions to assist humans and does not require a human to tell it what to do.

Manus AI, originally founded in China, showed off an impressive 30-second AI-generated video with its new 2.0 video technology that required just a 13-word prompt.

Tao Zhang, co-founder and CPO of Manus, said AI was changing how he hires his own team of engineers.

"We found the people we are looking for; it's not just a good attitude. We don't need more people; we need people who can work with AI," he said.

Web Summit expects to receive close to 70,000 attendees, including 900 speakers, and more than two thousand startups.

Cosgrave said it was the most international edition of Web Summit Lisbon with every European country present.

World.title: How could the Jensen Huang 'spy' scandal affect Nvidia's future?
World.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing scrutiny over alleged links to Chinese intelligence involving a businesswoman with whom he had an intimate relationship.

 

The company's board has launched an independent investigation into the matter. Nvidia says it has no reason to believe its trade secrets or US national security have been compromised.

The controversy has raised questions about the potential impact on the company and its investors. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives & Co, says Huang has been central to Nvidia's success, particularly its shift towards artificial intelligence.

"Jensen's almost been a superhero for Nvidia's shareholders," Ives says, adding that many investors have come to view him differently from other corporate leaders.

Nvidia shares fell around 5% in premarket trading on Monday following news of the investigation.

World.title: Turkey courts Egypt to tip the scales in eastern Mediterranean power game
World.content:
This week’s joint naval exercises between Turkey and Egypt in the eastern Mediterranean are the latest move in a burgeoning partnership, as Ankara intensifies its efforts to draw Cairo closer and loosen its bonds with Turkish rivals Greece, Cyprus and Israel.

Advertising

The "Sea of Friendship 2026" naval drills, held from 4-9 November off the coast of Alexandria, follow five years of rapprochement after nearly a decade of mistrust sparked by the 2013 ouster of Mohamed Morsi, a close ally of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, by Egypt's President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi.

It is the second year in a row that Turkey and Egypt have held the joint drills, after a 13-year break.

“I think it's already a sign that the two countries are getting closer,” said Africa expert Elem Tepecikoglu of Ankara’s Social Sciences University. In her view, the naval exercises are part of an evolving partnership.

“This normalisation process started five years ago in the diplomatic realm,” she explained. “And then we see cooperation in the security domain as well. So this is why I say I'm optimistic that Egypt might come closer to the Turkish side.”

The strengthening alliance between Turkey and Egypt is stirring unease in Israel, at a time when Israeli-Turkish relations are already frayed by the war in Gaza and Ankara’s support for Hamas.

“Obviously, Israel does not see this as necessarily positive, because of the heightened tensions between Israel and Turkey,” warned Turkey analyst Gallia Lindenstrauss of the Institute for National Security Studies at Tel Aviv University.

She noted that Israel is growing ever more wary of Turkey’s expanding reach in the eastern Mediterranean. “There is concern that Turkey and Egypt can cooperate in ways that will squeeze Israel’s room to manoeuver, politically but also militarily.”

Lindenstrauss said she does not see this as a likely scenario, affirming that the 1979 peace agreement between Israel and Egypt is “still very much in place, despite many geopolitical turnovers”.

“But there was always a fear that the other countries surrounding it would unite and act against Israel,” the analyst added.

Lindenstrauss believes Egypt’s strong ties with Turkey’s rivals, Greece and Cyprus, allay fears of Israeli encirclement. “It is very important that this relationship keeps going ahead because it is a source of stability in the eastern Mediterranean,” she said.

Houthi war risks dragging Israel and Turkey into Horn of Africa standoff

Turkish leverage

Egypt, Greece, Cyprus and Israel are bound by a tightly knit strategic energy alliance centred on the Eastern Mediterranean Gas Forum, a regional organisation formed in 2020 that has its headquarters in Cairo.

Just last month, they stood united in condemning the Libyan parliament's ratification of a maritime deal with Turkey that encroached on Greek and Egyptian waters.

Still, Jalel Harchaoui, a regional expert at the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies, a London-based think tank, observes that Turkey and Egypt are forging ever-closer collaboration on issues ranging from Libya to the Sudanese civil war to the Horn of Africa. Harchaoui suggests this growing cooperation is steadily boosting Ankara’s leverage over Cairo.

“I think observers should ask, can Egypt afford to do without Turkey? And the answer is probably no, and Turkey probably is aware of it,” he said.

Even so, Harchaoui doubts Cairo is ready to pivot fully toward Ankara. “If [Egypt] switches 180 degrees, it would be a disaster for the other side. I'm talking about Greece and Cyprus and Israel. So you could also ask yourself, can Egypt afford to anger its traditional friends?”

Libya-Turkey maritime deal stokes tensions in eastern Mediterranean

Egypt's balancing act

Ankara is stepping up its diplomatic courtship of Cairo, hoping to lure Egypt away from its longstanding partners.

But Turkish ambitions stumbled when Egypt declined to join the Mecca Defence Alliance with Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August. Analyst Lindenstrauss sees this as a clear sign of the boundaries in Turkish-Egyptian ties.

“Egypt has already moved closer to Turkey than was imaginable a few years ago,” she said. “However, at the end of the day, there are limits to how much it can accept greater Turkish influence. I think Turkey pretty much reached where Egypt is willing to agree to, and it will not give Turkey concessions in the eastern Mediterranean that will endanger its relationship with Greece and Cyprus, or its peace agreement with Israel.”

Lindenstrauss believes that despite diplomatic tensions with Israel over the war in Gaza, it still remains in Egypt’s interests to maintain ties with all sides. “Because of Egypt's importance in the region, I think it can definitely go ahead with this balancing act. It gives it all the gains and the risk is relatively low compared to having Egypt choose sides,” she added.

Ankara stands ready to ramp up its campaign to win over Cairo as the battle for influence in the eastern Mediterranean intensifies. In the unfolding rivalry between between Turkey on one hand and Greece, Cyprus and Israel on the other, Egypt is emerging as the pivotal player.
