El accidente ferroviario de Urda, nueve meses después del de Adamuz, con la suma de 115 fallecidos y centenares de heridos, entra dentro de la reivindicación imprescindible de levantar el sector ferroviario, la seguridad y las infraestructuras. Los partidos de izquierda, desde el primer momento Frente Amplio y Podemos, se unieron a la convocatoria de huelga por el deterioro evidente del Estado de bienestar, en la misma línea que los sindicatos. Todo empezó por la vivienda, pero los salarios forman parte indisociable de la dificultad de acceder a un piso por su alto coste, ya sea en régimen de alquiler o de compra. Los incrementos de todos los productos entierran las mejoras salariales que los sindicatos consiguen en la negociación con los empresarios. Las organizaciones sindicales han encontrado poco a poco la razón para justificar una convocatoria de huelga general que en un primer momento les desconcertó.

La defensa de lo público ha sido el banderín de enganche de los partidos de izquierda para alinear la huelga con la campaña electoral del 29 de noviembre. Este miércoles debiera ser una jornada de movilización que haga sentir concernidos a los votantes potenciales de izquierdas en el voto del 29 de noviembre, reconocen interlocutores de esos partidos; también del PSOE. No hay una declaración oficial a favor de la huelga, sino menciones esporádicas de distintas federaciones. El presidente del Gobierno no mencionó ayer este paro en un mitin en Bilbao, pero sí hace cinco días en Valencia para proclamar que esta huelga “no va contra nadie”, sino que nació por el desahucio de Maricarmen y requiere “el apoyo de todas las instituciones”. Sánchez sí habló de la involución de España en todos los terrenos, desde el gasto militar hasta las políticas sociales, con un gobierno de las derechas. “La única frontera entre el avance y la involución se llama voto”, señaló este domingo en un mitin en Bilbao.

En este terreno es en el que se mueven los distintos actores que quieren llevar el espíritu movilizador de la huelga hasta las elecciones. La Plataforma de Intervención Democrática, coordinada por Nicolás Sartorius, vicepresidente de la Fundación Alternativas, y Manuel de la Rocha, presidente de la ONG Movimiento por la Paz, han elaborado un manifiesto para conectar la huelga con las elecciones, en el que alertan sobre la importancia máxima de estas elecciones por el avance de la ultraderecha en España en un contexto internacional con esa tendencia. El PSOE y Pedro Sánchez colocan la movilización en la base de su campaña. “Votar en masa”, pidió ayer en Bilbao a todos los progresistas. Las encuestas manejan un nivel de apoyo fuerte para el PSOE y un desplome muy importante de los partidos de la izquierda: Frente Amplio y Podemos. No así, ERC, Bildu, BNG y otros partidos nacionalistas de izquierda.

Los estudios demoscópicos después del accidente ferroviario continúan con oscilaciones que los expertos acogen con cautela para no establecer conclusiones asentadas sobre su impacto en el voto. La movilización de la derecha se mantiene muy alta, así como cierto trasvase de la izquierda al PSOE.

La primera movilización buscada por los sindicatos y las izquierdas es la jornada de huelga. La magnitud del paro en los centros de trabajo no se prevé extraordinaria, pero sí se pone el foco en las concentraciones y manifestaciones en la calle, en las que cuentan con los jóvenes y estudiantes, como broche de la huelga. Los partidos tienen información demoscópica de que la posición ciudadana ante la huelga va en línea con la polarización política. No se detecta transversalidad social. Los votantes del PP están en desacuerdo con la convocatoria; los de izquierda se muestran a favor.

World.title: Nanomáquinas, pegamentos contra la psoriasis y ecuaciones para entender el cerebro: tres ideas ganadoras de científicos españoles
World.content:
Por buscar coincidencias, podría decirse que estos tres científicos crecieron lejos de Madrid y que pertenecen a la generación millenial. Pero también que los tres forman parte de los 59 seleccionados por la Fundación BBVA para las Becas Leonardo 2026, dotadas con 50.000 euros por proyecto. Desde la química supramolecular, la biología química y la matemática aplicada, Jesús Mosquera, Cristina Mayor-Ruiz y David Poyato dedican sus esfuerzos a ensanchar los cimientos del conocimiento científico, ese edificio abstracto sobre el que se sostienen las sociedades modernas.

La ciencia es “lenta y trabajosa”, como dice Mosquera, quien desde su laboratorio en A Coruña busca desarrollar unas nanomáquinas que puedan replicar la función de las proteínas que podrían aplicarse en el ámbito de la medicina o la energía. Mayor-Ruiz, por su parte, investiga una nueva clase de tratamientos contra las enfermedades inflamatorias de la piel, y Poyato estudia el cerebro humano y cómo se alteran sus dinámicas. Los tres son conscientes de que los resultados aplicables de los proyectos en los que trabajan todavía necesitan de tiempo y de financiación. En la ciencia, cada minuto cuenta, y cada centavo también. Estos son los trabajos a los que dedican todos sus esfuerzos:

Las “máquinas” de la vida

Desde el laboratorio de la Universidad de A Coruña que dirige, Jesús Mosquera estudia las proteínas. No es que Mosquera (Arzúa, Galicia, 42 años) haya traicionado a su yo más pequeño que quería convertirse en astronauta, sino que es una consecuencia natural de ser alguien interesado en “explorar las fronteras del conocimiento”, como recuerda en una videollamada con EL PAÍS. Y eso es lo que intenta hacer junto al equipo de más de 20 personas que lidera. Busca desvelar cómo las proteínas se organizan y, así, dar los primeros pasos hacia la construcción de nanomáquinas sintéticas capaces de replicar sus funciones.

Las proteínas son esenciales porque son como “las máquinas” que permiten la vida, sostiene este químico gallego. Sin proteínas no podríamos alimentarnos, protegernos contra enfermedades, ni transportar el oxígeno a la sangre. Pero son elementos complejos, por lo que replicarlos en un laboratorio es muy difícil. Mientras en la naturaleza las proteínas se sintetizan con una precisión subnanométrica, las que usa Mosquera en sus ensayos todavía están “en una escala 1.000 veces por debajo”. Esto es crucial porque, para sintetizarse, las proteínas deben adoptar formas únicas mediante un complejo plegamiento. Y solo si encajan correctamente —con la geometría adecuada y la precisión necesaria— pueden cumplir su función.

Pese a estas dificultades, los modelos sintéticos tienen una ventaja frente a sus contrapartes naturales. Fuera del laboratorio, las proteínas biológicas tienen una vida útil muy limitada y deben estar “continuamente reciclándose” para cumplir con sus tareas con rapidez, explica Mosquera. Este doctor en Química Supramolecular confía en aprovechar las ventajas de imitar estas estructuras mediante materiales simplificados para descubrir nuevos usos. Y las posibilidades son enormes. En un horizonte de unos cinco a seis años, podría tener implicaciones reales en la medicina o en la obtención de energía.

Pegamentos para curar

Cristina Mayor-Ruiz (Soria, 37 años) recuerda con claridad el momento en el que quiso dedicarse a la ciencia. Fue durante una clase del instituto, cuando quedó fascinada con el funcionamiento de las células: “A lo que pasa dentro, a pensar que las enfermedades surgen porque se desregulan esos mecanismos moleculares”, rememora en una conversación con este diario. Esa fascinación la ha llevado a dirigir uno de los laboratorios encargados de descubrir nuevos fármacos en el Instituto de Investigación Biomédica (IRB), en Barcelona. Allí lidera un proyecto que plantea desarrollar una nueva clase de tratamientos contra las enfermedades inflamatorias de la piel, como el lupus cutáneo o la psoriasis.

El gran inconveniente de estas enfermedades que estudia Mayor-Ruiz es que, al tratarse de trastornos autoinmunes, son todo un desafío científico. “Es luchar contra tu propio cuerpo”, explica esta biotecnóloga. De ahí la importancia de la investigación que desarrolla junto a un equipo de 14 personas, en la que busca sentar las bases para elaborar un nuevo tipo de fármaco pegamento molecular, que permita luchar con más eficiencia contra este tipo de dolencias. Unos problemas cuyos tratamientos disponibles en la actualidad —como los corticosteroides e inmunosupresores— se quedan a menudo cortos y conllevan importantes efectos secundarios.

Para explicar la diferencia entre lo que buscan desarrollar en el laboratorio (pegamento molecular) y lo que está disponible (fármacos inhibidores), Mayor-Ruiz emplea metáforas de cerrajería: “Un fármaco inhibidor de una proteína funciona como una especie de llave que encaja en una cerradura. La cerradura es la proteína y el inhibidor la bloquea”. En cambio, continúa, con los pegamentos moleculares, “en lugar de inhibir una función de la proteína, se engaña a los mecanismos desarrollados en las células para que destruyan esas proteínas”. Es una forma más directa de lidiar con el problema: en vez de limitarse a bloquearla, se busca eliminar la proteína causante de la inflamación.

Ecuaciones y neuronas

Los profesores del colegio de David Poyato supieron encaminarlo bien. Lo motivaron a estudiar Matemáticas. Desde entonces, este jienense ha dedicado buena parte de sus 35 años a resolver ecuaciones y a estar inmerso en los números. A través de una videollamada con este periódico, Poyato relata los principales retos del proyecto por el que fue reconocido por la Fundación BBVA. Investiga cómo se comportan los sistemas formados por un sinnúmero de individuos que se relacionan entre sí, con especial énfasis en el reto que implica estudiar el cerebro humano, con los más de 86.000 millones de neuronas que lo constituyen.

Describir matemáticamente estas dinámicas requiere entender en detalle cómo funciona el cerebro. En este sentido, Poyato explica que un cerebro sano funciona de manera “modular”. Es decir, a través de pequeños grupos de neuronas que se coordinan para realizar tareas concretas. Si este patrón se rompe, entonces surgen patologías. En un extremo, cuando los módulos se sincronizan al unísono de forma anómala, se produce lo que se conoce como “hipersincronización”, un fenómeno asociado a las crisis epilépticas o a trastornos como el párkinson. En el extremo opuesto, en cambio, la falta de sincronía se vincula con dolencias como el alzhéimer.

Para este profesor de la Universidad de Granada, y para el grupo de físicos y matemáticos con los que trabaja, el reto consiste en entender “cómo manejar de manera teórica y computacionalmente menos costosa estos sistemas formados por un gran número de partículas”. Poyato elabora que no hay ningún sistema de simulación numérica disponible que soporte la complejidad de analizar una ecuación para cada una de las 86.000 millones de neuronas del cerebro humano. Además, a nivel teórico, tampoco es una descripción manejable para entender su comportamiento. Por lo que su equipo intenta deducir ecuaciones que describan a las neuronas en promedio, pero sin borrar la heterogeneidad y las diferencias individuales entre cada una de ellas. Y así, en un eventual escenario, poder predecir cómo y por qué se alteran las dinámicas del cerebro.

World.title: Jetten says it is “not his place” to join Gaza demonstration
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has defended his decision to stay away from last weekend’s mass demonstration in Amsterdam against Israel’s war in Gaza.

Organisers claimed around 200,000 people joined the Red Line rally, the fourth to be held since Israel began its bombing campaign and ground offensive in response to the attacks by Hamas in October 2023.

Jetten took part in a similar demonstration in Amsterdam in October last year as leader of the D66 party, which was then in opposition, but said it was “not his place” to attend as prime minister. He also declined to describe Israel’s offensive as a genocide, as he did a year ago.

“Hundreds of thousands of people in the Netherlands took to the streets because they are concerned about the terrible humanitarian situation of many Palestinians,” he said.

“That’s why the cabinet has pledged from the outset to offer more help and put pressure on Israel.”

But he added: “I don’t think it’s my place at all to be at a demonstration like this. People have shown how moved they are by the situation of millions of Palestinians and at the same time they have urged the cabinet to act.”

VVD blockade

The prime minister has come under pressure from human rights organisations to speak out against Israel, but his coalition includes the right-wing liberal VVD party, whose leadership is staunchly pro-Israeli.

Jetten insisted at his weekly press conference on Friday that the Dutch government had made clear during bilateral talks with Israel that “the situation in Gaza, the West Bank, but also in Jordan and Syria is unacceptable”.

But he ruled out taking stronger measures such as an arms embargo or declaring that Israel was committing “genocide and ethnic cleansing against Palestinians”, as the protest organisers demanded.

Senior politicians including Amsterdam’s former Labour party (PvdA) mayor Job Cohen have also criticised Jetten’s leadership on the issue.

Cohen and former VVD foreign affairs minister, Jozias van Aartsen, who are both Jewish, said in an interview with the Volkskrant at the weekend that they were joining the demonstration to protest against Israel’s actions.

Humanitarian values

Cohen told TV talks show Pauw, De Wit and Moggré: “I have had doubts in the past, specifically about the term genocide, because I found it so incredibly difficult to apply it not to Israel, but to this Israeli government.

“I think it’s extremely important that Israel exists as a place of refuge where Jews can go, but I think this government is appalling. My feeling is that it’s almost impossible to deny anymore that what is happening, to an increasing degree, has elements of genocide.”

Van Aartsen was critical of his own party for refusing to push for sanctions against Israel. “It would be fitting for a party that claims to be liberal to defend basic values such as humanity and international law, but they are standing by and watching,” he said.

World.title: Tilburg arms manufacturer buys rights to Israeli weapon designs
World.content:
Tilburg-based defence company AIA is buying technological data from Israeli arms manufacturer IWI, best known for the Uzi machine gun, and which is the main supplier of small arms for the Israeli military and police forces, broadcaster NOS reported.

AIA is specifically buying design information for two guns, noted for their ability to shoot down drones, the Arad 5 rifle and the Negev UX light machine gun.

AIA’s director Gerard Zondervan told NOS that “Europe is calling”, that the bloc needs to produce its own weapons, and that he would not discuss politically contentious issues regarding Israel such as the war on Gaza.

In January, MPs adopted a motion calling on the government to reduce the Netherlands’ reliance on Israeli weapons, citing concerns about war crimes. The motion says the Netherlands has bought €2 billion worth of equipment from Israeli defence firms in recent years.

The Netherlands has also blocked exports of F-35 fighter jet parts to Israel since an appeals court ruling in February 2024, and kept the ban in place after the Supreme Court overturned that ruling in October 2025.

Zondervan said AIA had had no contact with the Dutch government regarding the deal, and that production will begin in Tilburg and then move into an expanded facility in Overijssel.

The announcement comes shortly after the defence ministry launched the National Institute for Defence technology (NIDT), to speed up development and cooperation for the arms industry.

NIDT will get €350 million a year from 2028 onwards, intended to strengthen defences in the North Sea amid escalating conflict with Russia.

World.title: Parents spending more on private lessons to boost exam chances
World.content:
Parents are booking extra home school lessons in the last years of primary school to boost their children’s performance in tests and improve their chances of being accepted for the top tier of secondary schools.

Official government figures show that the amount households spent on help with homework, out-of-school lessons and exam training more than tripled in the 10 years from €151 million to €472 million.

Support for primary school children accounted for €44 million of the total, but education specialist told the Volkskrant that the strongest growth was in help for children in groups 6, 7 and 8 of primary school.

Dutch children are streamed when they enter secondary school, from vwo level, which prepares children for university, down to vmbo and praktijkonderwijs, which focus on practical skills.

Sezgin Cihangir, director of the Mathematisch Instituut in Amstelveen, said many parents were paying for extra lessons to compensate for the poor quality of school education.

His institution, which charges €1,790 for a 12-week course of extra maths tuition, claims on its website to have improved the Cito test scores for 92% of children who take part.

“For us it’s about improving children’s basic skills so that they can go through school with more self-reliance and self-confidence,” he said. “What we do isn’t extra tuition, it’s damage limitation.”

Inequality

Louise Elffers, professor of equality in education at the University of Amsterdam, said the growth of out-of-school tuition favoured families who could afford to pay for the lessons.

“Research has shown that the educational level of parents is a bigger factor in choosing to send children for extra lessons than their income, but well-educated people often earn more as well,” she said.

“Parents want their child to achieve the best possible diploma so they can get further up the hierarchy. Well-educated parents are especially conscious of this and investing more in their children’s school careers.”

But Cihangir said parents on all income levels were prepared to pay extra to improve their children’s chances.

“I’ve had people here who live on welfare,” he said. “If parents see that their child needs it, they make sure they can find a way to afford it.”

World.title: Dutch state collecting too much data on activists, report says
World.content:
The Dutch institute for human rights says it is concerned about how much information the government is collecting on political activists, and fears an expansion in technological and legal powers by state forces could suppress protests in the future.

In its annual report, the institute looked at the different ways local authorities collect information on protestors. Legally, it says, people only need to notify that demonstration will take place – not get permission. And they can do that anonymously, the report says.

But several local authorities ask for personal information from people when they register a protest notification. Institute chair Rick Lawson told broadcaster NOS that organisers are asked for their name, where they live, whether they have social media accounts, who they expect to attend and what message they want to put across.

That information can help councils and police make sure a protest runs smoothly and assess the risk of counter-protests or disorder, Lawson said. “That is understandable, but it leads to distrust.”

A specialist unit in the Dutch police called TOOI researches people through social media and other sources before a protest goes ahead to prevent potential threats. Police also gather information from citizen informants and officers on the street. The institute wants these powers limited to what can be legally justified in every case.

The use of cameras at demonstrations is a case in point. They can be used for facial recognition at protests under strict circumstances but never in real-time. What data is collected and how long it actually stored in reality is a threat that could deter lawful protesting, the institute says.

Three new bills seeking to expand data collection powers are currently in the works, which the institute stresses are not necessary. It says 97% of protests go ahead without incidents, and only 0.03% ever record more than 10 incidents.

The institute is calling on the government to be cautious about implementing new powers, to collect as little personal data as possible on notification forms and make clear that organisers can notify anonymously, and to tell people what information is held on them and what rights they have.

The report follows a year of frequent protesting, often over the influx of asylum seekers. Mass protests against the war on Gaza have also been held four times this year and last.

World.title: Housing minister plans new village at Netherlands’ lowest point
World.content:
The government is pressing ahead with plans to build a new village of 6,000 homes at the lowest point in the Netherlands, more than six metres below sea level.

The construction of Cortelande, in the Zuidplaspolder near Gouda, is one of five projects named by housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan in the latest stage of her national plan to build more than 400,000 new homes by 2040.

The €132 million project, originally announced by O’Sullivan’s predecessor Mona Keijzer, led to a legal row between the local council and the local water board, but the latter withdrew its appeal in July after talks to safeguard the water supplies.

Experts have warned that building the village, which lies 6.78m below NAP, the baseline used to determine elevation in the Netherlands, will be especially challenging.

“We’re pushing the boundaries,” researcher Floris Boogaard of hydraulic engineering research specialist Delatres told NOS. “The ground might rise here, but you’re building on soft ground, especially when it’s so deep. We’ve never built so deep before on such a large scale.”

The other four projects named by Boekholt-O’Sullivan are in Assen, Drenthe, where up to 6,000 homes will be built in three suburbs, another 3,500 houses in Best, Noord-Brabant, up to 6,000 homes in Roosendaal, a key rail hub on the Belgian border, and 5,000 homes in the Zeeland towns of Middleburg, Vlissingen and Veere.

World.title: Dutch home workers reluctant to spend more time in the office
World.content:
More than half of people who work from home would struggle to return to the office full-time because their home and working lives have become so intertwined, according to a survey for the FNV union and current affairs show Nieuwsuur.

The most common reasons for the 3,000 workers not to increase their office hours were concerns about declining productivity, more time spent commuting and a negative impact on their health and well-being.

Businesses have tried to encourage their staff to spend more time in the office since the end of the coronavirus pandemic, but none of the Netherlands’ 25 largest companies said they require their employees to leave the house five days a week.

Jelle Kajim, who works for HR support company Remote, told Nieuwsuur he valued the flexibility of working from home.

“We have 2,000 people, but we don’t have any offices,” he said. “In 10 years I’ve never worked in an office and sometimes I’m curious about it.

“I recently had to go to Paris for work, but I don’t see myself sitting in a metro train every day.”

Booking.com case

Travel website Booking.com won a court case last month against its works council, which objected to the company’s plans to compel staff to spend 40% of their contracted hours at its head office in Amsterdam.

The judge in the case remarked that it was “very normal” for people to travel to work two days a week, but only around a quarter of the company’s staff currently do so.

Other major employers said they had embraced the concept of homeworking in recent years. Just 14% of new collective bargaining agreements in 2019 made arrangements for working from home, but last year the proportion rose to 38%.

A spokesman for insurer Nationale Nederlanden said it promoted a balanced approach, with staff encouraged to spend two days a week in the office.

“The strength of working in the office lies mainly in co-operation, innovation, development and social conections. The strength of home working lies in flexibility, concentration and a good balance between work and private life,” a spokesman said.

Rabobank, which does not have a minimum office-time requirement, said: “We see no reason to set a target for presenteeism. Our experiences with hybrid working are positive.”

World.title: Foreign workers often left in the dark over EU pension rights
World.content:
People in the Netherlands who have worked in multiple EU countries have no way of knowing how much pension they’ve built up, and the country is not yet part of a European system to fix the problem, according to broadcaster NOS.

There is no single body covering all EU member states, so if you lived and worked in other countries for some time you have to remember to contact each one before retiring.

“It is incredibly complicated,” Lisa Bruggen, director of pension research institute Netspar, told NOS. You can’t simply add up the amounts you see on, for example, the Dutch and German pension portals, because they’re calculated differently.

Around 700,000 people receiving the Dutch state pension (AOW) currently get a reduced amount because they lived abroad, according to social insurance bank SVB.

Foreign workers in lower-paid sectors such as construction, hospitality and transport are most at risk of pension poverty, NOS said.

One pension fund told the broadcaster it has some 18,000 retired members who have not claimed their pension, but that privacy rules prevent it from tracing them.

An EU-backed platform, Find Your Pension, aims to show people where they have pension savings, how much they are worth, and how to claim them. The Dutch pension law must be changed before the Netherlands can join, the social affairs ministry told NOS, saying that the cabinet is working on it.

The organisation behind the platform does not expect the Netherlands to join before 2028. Even after more than a decade of work, the platform can so far retrieve personal pension information only from Belgium and France, and users say that does not always work.

World.title: Work exhaustion rising, especially among women and young people
World.content:
Exhaustion from work has been on the rise in the Netherlands for the past decade, with 21% of people saying they feel mentally fatigued at least a few times per month, according to new research by national statistics office CBS and research institute TNO. In 2015, the figure was 13%.

The findings are drawn from an annual national survey of around 57,000 people aged 15 to 74, excluding self employed. Mental fatigue was defined as feeling mentally exhausted several times per month at least, for example feeling emotionally drained or empty at the end of the day.

Women are more affected than men, the survey showed. In 2025, 24% of female employees reported fatigue, up from 14% a decade earlier. Among men, the figure rose from 13% to 18%.

Younger people are the most affected, with the 25-34 year-old age group showing the biggest rise. In 2015, 15% reported fatigue and in 2025 the number had risen to 28%. In 2023, TNO found that one in four workers aged 18 to 34 had burnout complaints.

The more complex the job, the higher the chance of mental fatigue. People in the most complex jobs, which involve highly specialised tasks and usually require a higher level of education, had a fatigue rate of 23%, compared with 18% in the least complex jobs.

Psychologists and sociologists reported the highest rate of fatigue, at 37%. The least exhausted were those working in agriculture, at only 12%.

Psychological complaints, stress and burnout were the reason for 9% of employees’ most recent sick leave, second only to flu and colds (55%). They also kept people off work the longest, at an average of 67 days, compared with 15 days for sick leave overall.

Burnout was also the most commonly reported occupational illness, with 1.9% of workers saying a doctor had diagnosed them with burnout or work-related stress. In July 2025, psychiatrists and occupational health experts called for a rethink of burnout diagnosis in the Netherlands, after Sweden dropped the term.

Two months later, the government’s health advisory council RVS warned of a “hypernervous society”, estimating the cost of mental health problems at €18 billion a year.

World.title: Coalition of the Willing military exercises begin in Poland to prepare support for postwar Ukraine
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Thousands of soldiers from 11 countries began military exercises in Poland today. They are the first organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, with the aim of preparing for a role in supporting Ukraine following a potential future peace deal with Russia. The manoeuvres, which are being jointly led by France and the UK, are taking place in Nowa Dęba, around 100 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, and will last until 22 November. The development has been condemned by Russia, which says it shows that Western countries are ignoring Moscow’s “legitimate security concerns” and “fueling the spiral of escalation”.​ 🇫🇷🇬🇧 KOALICJA: The MNF-U is training to ensure a solid and lasting peace in Ukraine The Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U), formed from the Coalition of the Willing and under 🇫🇷🇬🇧command, is launching its first major exercise: KOALICJA 📅 November 9–22, 2026 📍In Poland,… pic.twitter.com/Ikcl1uY8N2 — The 🇫🇷 Joint Staff – Military operations (@FrenchForces) November 7, 2026 The plans were first announced in July by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk following a summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Paris. The exercises, taking place on land, in the air, and at sea, are being conducted by the Multinational Force Ukraine (MNF-U), which serves as the military component of the coalition. “This exercise will show that the Multinational Force-Ukraine is a real, capable, readily deployable force that represents a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine’s long-term stability and security,” said Tom Bateman, the British lieutenant-general commanding MNF-U. The British Ministry of Defence says that the exercise, which has been named “Koalicja” (meaning “Coalition” in Polish), “will test Allies’ readiness to support Ukraine and rebuild their Armed Forces once the conflict ends”. France’s armed forces ministry, meanwhile, says that the aim is to ensure that MNF-U is “ready to deploy at the request of the Ukrainian government” in order to help “guarantee a robust and lasting peace in Ukraine”. Around 2,800 troops are being deployed for the manoeuvres, with AFP reporting that this includes 1,100 from France alone. The British defence ministry says it has sent 300 personnel, as well as Typhoon and Voyager aircraft. In addition, just under 2,000 Polish troops will take part, bringing the total to almost 5,000 personnel, reports Polska Zbrojna, a publication linked to the Polish defence ministry. Other countries taking part are Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and Turkey. Poland’s defence ministry says the exercises will “demonstrate how quickly participating nations can mobilise and establish forces capable of supporting Ukraine after the end of the war”. However, although Poland is hosting the manoeuvres, the defence ministry reiterated the country’s position that “it would not send its own soldiers to Ukrainian territory” as part of any postwar settlement. Poland has made clear it intends instead to help provide logistical support. Nederland doet met enkele honderden militairen mee aan oefening Koalicja in Polen. De Coalition of the Willing traint er met 11 landen op snelle verplaatsing, commandovoering en bevoorrading ter voorbereiding op mogelijke steun aan Oekraïne na beëindiging van de oorlog. pic.twitter.com/JLE6W91HnZ — Ministerie van Defensie (@Defensie) November 9, 2026 France says that the deployment of forces to Ukraine would include sending instructors to help the country rebuild and strengthen its armed forces, while air missions would enable civlian aircraft to resume flying in Ukrainian airspace. At sea, MNF-U forces could help clear mines from shipping routes in the Black Sea. The maritime component of the current exercises is being led by Turkey through a simulated operational exercise, without deploying troops to Poland itself. France, the UK and Poland have emphasised, however, that the MNF-U forces would only be deployed once fighting in Ukraine has ceased and would not carry out peacekeeping or ceasefire-monitoring duties. Poland will host military exercises later this year with France and the UK to prepare for providing future security guarantees to Ukraine, says PM @donaldtusk. He also declared Poland's willingness to permanently host more troops from its European allies https://t.co/couian4FrP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 14, 2026 On Saturday, the spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, Maria Zakharova, condemned the exercises, saying that they make “absolutely clear that the West remains unwilling to take Russia’s legitimate security concerns into account and continues to fuel the spiral of escalation”. She described the deployment of any foreign armed forces to Ukraine as “absolutely unacceptable” and said they would “create additional threats to Russia’s security”. “Any military units in Ukraine will be regarded by the Russian armed forces as legitimate targets, with all the risks and consequences that entails,” warned Zakharova. Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova’s answer to a media question in connection with the first military exercises of the so-called Multinational Force – Ukraine under the Coalition of the Willinghttps://t.co/GiouEAmT6J — Jeff Franzius (@jk55044) November 9, 2026 The exercises come as Ukraine and Russia meet the United States and others for peace talks in Abu Dhabi this week. Ukraine has repeatedly insisted that European security guarantees would be necessary for any peace agreement. British defence secretary Wes Streeting suggested the exercises forecast precisely such a scenario: “This isn’t a hypothetical plan, it’s a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops.” Zakharova, however, says that the exercises are “yet another confirmation that the Europeans have no place at the negotiating table”. World.title: Polish government ministers suggest tighter gun controls after deadly terrorist shooting
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In the wake of Saturday’s deadly terrorist shooting in Kraków, a deputy defence minister has called for debate on limiting the number and types of weapons people can own. Meanwhile, a deputy interior minister says the tragedy provides an “incentive” to revisit proposals to better register certain guns. Poland has among the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe, though the number of firearms licences being issued has risen in recent years and some politicians have called for expanded access to guns. Saturday’s attack was carried out by a man who legally owned firearms. On Saturday, 24-year-old Michał Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, which was packed with tourists and locals, firing at random from his car. He killed six people and injured over a dozen more. Later in the day, the bodies of the perpetrator’s parents and sister were found in his home, where they had been shot dead. Oksiński’s rampage was brought to an end in a shootout with two police officers, which left all three with serious injuries. On Monday morning, the police announced that Oksiński had died in hospital. One of the police officers remains in what is described as “serious but stable” condition. The man who carried out Saturday’s deadly terrorist attack in the Polish city of Kraków has died in hospital from the injuries he sustained during a shootout with police. One of the two officers who stopped him remains in serious but stable condition https://t.co/rT1YBXhkp7 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 9, 2026 The incident has caused shock in Poland, a country that has never previously experienced this type of mass public shooting. Speaking to Polsat News on Sunday, deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said that the tragedy “is the best illustration that it makes no sense to talk about expanding access to firearms”. She added that “it’s already relatively easy” to obtain a gun licence, which can be granted to anyone aged 21 or over who has passed the relevant tests and declared that the firearm is for sporting purposes. Both Oksiński and his father had such licences and legally owned 11 firearms. “I would like to start a discussion about whether access to such a large number of weapons should actually be so easy,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “This is also a question of whether someone who uses weapons for sporting purposes should have so many different types of weapons stored at home.” Also speaking to Polsat on Sunday, Czesław Mroczek, a deputy interior minister, said that “weapons are certainly a challenge for us”. He noted that “in Poland we have had many cases of killings using black powder weapons, for which there is not even a register, let alone a permit procedure”. Such weapons use traditional black powder rather than modern smokeless powder and include firearms manufactured before 1885 and their modern replicas. According to a recent study by researchers from the Jagiellonian University in Kraków, they make up a considerable proportion of firearm-related fatalities in the country. While noting that the issue is not directly related to the Kraków attacks, Mroczek said that plans to include these weapons in a register had already been drawn up and “this event [in Kraków] is an incentive for us to reexamine the matter”. 🇵🇱 Poland's interior ministry says black-powder guns, currently exempt from registration, will be entered into the register. The Krakow attack is described as an impulse to review the whole permit system.https://t.co/Nh7dr46MJ7 — Олег Рощин (@oleg_roshchin) November 9, 2026 On Monday morning, the spokesman for the National Prosecutor’s Office, Przemysław Nowak, held a press conference at which he provided further details on their findings so far. He revealed that Oksiński had been found with two AR-15 rifles and two handguns on his person and in his car, as well as around 500 rounds of ammunition. He had earlier fired “several dozen, possibly several hundred, shots”. A further seven guns had been found at Oksiński’s home. The total of 11 firearms matched the number of weapons there were permits for, noted Nowak, quoted by news website Wirtualna Polska. “The entire matter related to the weapons and the firearms permits will be reviewed,” added the spokesman. “We know that, since March of this year, he [Oksiński] has held firearms permits for one rifle and one pistol.” Prosecutors have launched a terror investigation into Saturday’s shooting in Kraków, which left six dead. Three more bodies were later found in the suspect's home. Further details have also emerged about the heroic actions of police and medical personnel https://t.co/icBJWLRK7c — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 8, 2026 Although gun ownership in Poland is relatively low, it has been rising steadily in recent years, particularly since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with the total number of registered firearms owned by Poles surpassing 1 million, up from around 380,000 in 2014. Last year, a record 50,709 new gun licences were issued in the country in 2025, up 10.6% compared to a year earlier. Under Polish law, civilians can apply for licences for sporting, hunting, collecting and personal protection purposes. To obtain one, applicants must undergo medical examinations, pass a test, and join a relevant association, such as the Polish Sports Shooting Association, the Polish Hunting Association, or a collectors’ group. Licences for sports and collection purposes are the most popular types of permits, together making up 76% of last year’s permits. But the number of licences issued for “personal protection” has grown from just 81 in 2021 to 7,254 last year. A record 50,709 gun licences were issued in Poland last year and the total number of registered firearms has now surpassed 1 million. Gun ownership in Poland has risen particularly rapidly since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 https://t.co/axt2YS044Z — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 11, 2026 Access to firearms widened in 2023 under the former government, when parliament passed a law removing “unnecessary administrative and legal barriers.” That allowed members of uniformed services to apply for personal protection permits, a change lawmakers said was intended to “strengthen Poland’s defence potential”. However, some politicians, especially on the right, have pushed for ownership rules to be further loosened. In September, speaking at the opening of a shooting range, President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, called for “public discussion about responsible access to weapons”. “Even in the European Union, Poland remains at the bottom of the list in terms of access to firearms,” he said, quoted by Polsat. “Only about 1% of Polish citizens have access to weapons and are skilled at using them. Fortunately, I’m in that 1%.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Fugitive Polish opposition politician attends gala at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Fugitive Polish opposition politician Zbigniew Ziobro, who fled to the United States rather than face criminal charges in his homeland, has been pictured attending a gala at Donald Trump’s luxury Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida. The US president himself spoke at the event. The Polish justice minister has responded by saying that he hopes the US will show “true friendship” by cooperating with Poland’s request to extradite Ziobro, just as Poland would do if an American fugitive was on its territory. Ziobro na przyjęciu w rezydencji Trumpa. Wiadomo, co podano na eleganckiej kolacji w Mar-a-Lago [ZDJĘCIA] https://t.co/geANxBTn0J — Andrzej Holinka 🇵🇱 #Nawrocki2030 🇵🇱 ✌️ (@HolinkaPis) November 7, 2026 On Saturday, Blask Online, a news website linked to conservative broadcaster TV Republika, published images of Ziobro at Mar-a-Lago alongside senior Republika figures. They were attending a “retreat and gala” hosted by CPAC, which also organises a major annual conservative political conference and has close ties to Trump. The cheapest tickets to attend the gala cost $2,500, ranging up to $7,500 for VIP access. Blask Online’s photos show Ziobro eating dinner at the event and speaking to former British Prime Minister Liz Truss. Trump himself addressed the guests, saying that he “wants to congratulate everybody here”. Nikodem Rachoń, an advisor to Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who is aligned with the opposition and is a close Trump ally – also attended the CPAC event, where he was listed as a speaker. Ziobro is a deputy leader of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, which is aligned with Trump and his Republican Party. From 2015 to 2023, Ziobro served as justice minister in a PiS-led government, overseeing judicial reforms that are widely seen as having undermined the rule of law. After a new, more liberal ruling coalition led by the current prime minister, Donald Tusk, took power in December 2023, it launched a number of investigations into the actions of senior PiS officials. That led, last year, to prosecutors announcing that they want to charge Ziobro with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware, which was used to surveil some of PiS’s political opponents. However, although parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution, he had by then already travelled to Hungary, which was at the time ruled by conservative PiS ally Viktor Orbán. In December 2025, the Hungarian government granted Ziobro political asylum. At this year’s Hungarian parliamentary elections in April, Orbán’s Fidesz party was removed from power and his successor, Péter Magyar, pledged to extradite Ziobro to Poland. But, just as Magyar was being sworn in in May, Ziobro left Hungary and flew to the United States, reportedly with the help of a senior US State Department official. In July, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office announced that it was sending a request to the US authorities to detain and extradite Ziobro. In late October, the National Prosecutor’s Office told newspaper Fakt that “we have so far not received any response from the US”. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. He denies wrongdoing and calls the case political revengehttps://t.co/BXdQgWm61q — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 On Saturday, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, was asked by Fakt about the newly published images showing Ziobro attending the gala at Mar-a-Lago. “I’d like Polish-American friendship to be a true friendship,” replied Żurek. “If a fugitive from the US was being prosecuted by the US justice system for embezzling hundreds of millions, we would cooperate with the US [if that fugitive was in Poland].” “But when I see that, the day after the US elections, which should be a reflection for Republicans, the president [Donald Trump] is focusing on building a ballroom, nothing will surprise me anymore,” he added. “We’re doing our job and we’ll see this matter through to the end.” Ziobro na przyjęciu w rezydencji Trumpa. Reaguje Żurek ⬇️ https://t.co/JT8o7d2X1w — DoRzeczy (@DoRzeczy_pl) November 7, 2026 Last week, before the CPAC event at Mar-a-Lago, Żurek had joked that “Ziobro brings bad luck”, noting that Orbán had lost elections after sheltering him and that now so had Trump’s Republicans. Żurek added that he hoped the shifting balance of power in the US might weaken the “protective political umbrella” Ziobro had so far enjoyed there and make the American “administration more willing to cooperate with the Polish justice system”, reports news website Onet. Ziobro himself has denied any wrongdoing and claims that the prosecution against him is an act of “political revenge” by the current government. He says he is willing to face justice in Poland, but only “when the rule of law is restored”. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Perpetrator of Kraków terrorist attack dies of injuries in hospital
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. This is a breaking news story and will be updated as further information becomes available. The man who carried out Saturday’s deadly terrorist attack in the Polish city of Kraków – and who can now be named as 24-year-old Michał Oksiński – has died in hospital. Oksiński suffered serious injuries in a firefight with two police officers, who heroically brought his rampage to an end. On Sunday, Krzysztof Klęczar, the governor of the Małopolska province in which Kraków is located, revealed that Oksiński remained in critical condition. On Monday morning, provincial police announced that “the perpetrator of the tragic events [in Kraków] died this morning in hospital”. “There was a constant struggle to save this man’s life, despite the evil he had committed,” Klęczar told broadcaster TVN after the death was confirmed. “He underwent at least three surgeries.” Informujemy, że sprawca tragicznych wydarzeń zmarł dzisiaj nad ranem w szpitalu. — Małopolska Policja (@kwpkrakow) November 9, 2026 The two police officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who engaged Oksiński also suffered serious injuries, with Kulik’s condition the more critical of the two. The situation would have been much worse were it not for the fact that two leading local surgeons had, by pure chance, been eating a meal with their families in a restaurant near where the shootout took place, and provided emergency aid to the officers. There was also a huge public response to appeals for people to donate blood for Kulik, who underwent a series of surgeries. On Sunday, it was announced that both Kulik and Morański had come out of the comas they had previously been placed in. Kulik’s condition was described as “serious but stable” by Karolina Gałecka, spokeswoman for the interior ministry. CCTV footage shows the moment two police officers confront the Krakow shooter. pic.twitter.com/vcQ0Xvi1nX — WarMonitor🇺🇦🇬🇧 (@WarMonitor3) November 7, 2026 Just after 3 p.m. local time on Saturday afternoon, Oksiński drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, including its famous market square, which was packed with tourists and locals. He fired at random from the car, killing six people. Four of those victims have been identified as Polish women, aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man in his 50s. The other two were foreign nationals: a 32-year-old British man and a 51-year-old Austrian woman. A further 16 people were injured in the attack, 11 of them Polish. The interior ministry has said that, among the dead and injured are citizens of the UK, Austria, Germany, Russia and Portugal. On Saturday evening, it was announced that a search of the perpetrator’s home in the small town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski in southeast Poland, around 160 km from Krakow, had revealed three further dead bodies. They were later confirmed to belong to Oksiński’s parents, aged 53 and 52, and 21-year-old sister. Prosecutors believe Oksiński murdered them before launching his rampage in Kraków. Oksiński’s motive remains unknown. On Saturday evening, in the wake of the attacks, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced at a press conference that the information obtained so far indicated that the suspect had “very, very radical views” and “may have been fascinated by far-right ideologies”. However, when pressed on this claim during an interview with TVN on Sunday evening, Kierwiński refused to provide evidence, said that his remarks had referred to “initial hypotheses”, and confirmed that the potential motive was still being investigated. Poland's interior minister refuses to reveal on what basis he said the Kraków terrorist had "very radical views" and was "fascinated by the far right". "In cases like this, there are always first hypotheses, first clues. That's why I made this statement" pic.twitter.com/Wpud1FrAYM — Daniel Tilles (@danieltilles1) November 8, 2026 The incident has caused shock in Poland, where gun crime is exceedingly rare. The country has one of the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe and has never previously suffered a mass public shooting of this kind. In response to the tragedy, a period of two days of official public mourning has been declared, with a decree to that effect signed by President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk. On Monday evening, a silent march will be held in Kraków at 8 p.m. to pay tribute to the victims. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prosecutors launch terror investigation as Poland reels from fatal shootings
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Polish prosecutors have announced the opening of a terrorism investigation following Saturday’s attack in the city of Kraków, where a man opened fire from his vehicle, killing six people. Later, three further bodies – believed to be the perpetrator’s parents and sister – were found in his home. Further details have also emerged regarding the victims of the attack, the heroic actions of police and medical personnel, as well as the attacker himself – though the motive for his actions remains unknown. On Saturday, the suspected attacker, who has been named only as 24-year-old Michał O. under Polish privacy law, drove through the historic city centre of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, including its famous market square, which was packed with tourists and locals. He fired at random from the car, killing six people. Three of those victims have been identified as Polish women, aged 47, 53 and 61. Another was a 32-year-old British man. The final two victims were a foreign woman aged 51, whose nationality has not yet been announced, and a Polish man in his 50s. A further 16 people were injured in the attack, 11 of them Polish. The interior ministry has said that, among the dead and injured are citizens of the UK, Austria, Germany, Russia and Portugal. Two of the injured are police officers who pursued the attacker and engaged in a firefight with him. They and Michał O. were hospitalised with what have been described as critical injuries. Due to his ongoing medical treatment, law enforcement authorities have not yet been able to formally take the suspect into detention. CCTV footage shows the moment two police officers confront the Krakow shooter. pic.twitter.com/vcQ0Xvi1nX — WarMonitor🇺🇦🇬🇧 (@WarMonitor3) November 7, 2026 However, on Sunday morning, the National Prosecutor’s Office announced that it has launched a formal investigation into the killing of six people in Kraków and the attempted murder of numerous others. The actions are being treated as a terrorist offence. Meanwhile, they are also investigating the killing by gunshot of three people in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, also on Saturday. That is Michał O.’s hometown, and on Saturday evening Prime Minister Donald Tusk revealed that three bodies had been found at the address where he lived. Prosecutors say that “the evidence indicates that the same person committed the acts” in both Kraków and Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Previously, on Saturday evening, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced that initial findings indicate the suspect had “very radical far-right views”. However, he cautioned that investigators were still seeking to confirm this, as well as to understand the possible motive behind the attack. Minister @MKierwinski na konferencji w Krakowie: 💬 Sprawca mógł być zafascynowany ideologiami skrajnie prawicowymi. Ten wątek będzie jednak szczegółowo weryfikowany. Czynności prowadzą funkcjonariusze @PolskaPolicja, jak i @ABW_GOV_PL – na miejscu zdarzenia oraz w domu rodzinnym… pic.twitter.com/PppmMPmWYW — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) November 7, 2026 Gun crime is exceedingly rare in Poland, which has one of the lowest levels of gun ownership in Europe. Saturday was the first time that the country has experienced a mass public shooting of this type. In response, a period of two days of official public mourning has been declared, with a decree to that effect signed by President Karol Nawrocki and Tusk. Meanwhile, political leaders have praised the heroic actions of police, especially the two officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who were critically injured while bringing Michał O’s rampage to an end. “They are heroes,” said Krzysztof Klęczar, governor of the Małopolska province in which Kraków is located. “Considering how many weapons were still in the perpetrator’s car, if it weren’t for the effective and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher.” It has also emerged that the police officers were treated by two leading surgeons who, by complete chance, had been eating dinner with their families at a restaurant near where the final shootout took place. One of them, Michał Pędziwiatr, a professor of surgery at the Jagiellonian University, told the media that he and fellow surgeon Mateusz Wierdak had seen the police subduing the attacker. While their families took shelter, the two doctors rushed to the scene once the shooting had finished. “Mateusz’s dedication in stopping the bleeding of the most injured police officer [Kulik] undoubtedly saved his life,” Pędziwiatr told the Fakt newspaper. Pędziwiatr himself called a local hospital that he knew would be best equipped to treat the officer so that they could prepare for his arrival. ⚫️"Tato, strzelają do ludzi!". Lekarz ujawnia kulisy zamachu Prof. Michał Pędziwiatr i dr Mateusz Wierdak byli w pobliskiej restauracji, gdy doszło do strzelaniny. Zanim przyjechały karetki, lekarze udzielili pomocy rannym. – Wyszliśmy na zewnątrz. Już się żegnaliśmy. Nagle mój… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) November 8, 2026 Public authorities in Poland, including the police and military, launched a drive for blood donations to help in the treatment of Kulik, who remains in critical condition. They said they had been overwhelmed by the number of people coming forward. The defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, also revealed that Kulik is a former soldier from the elite 6th Airborne Brigade, which is headquartered in Kraków. “The entire military community is proud of Jakub. We will support him and his loved ones,” wrote Kosiniak-Kamysz. A public fundraiser launched by Krzysztof Stanowski, a prominent media personality, has, at the time of writing, raised over 3.5 million zloty (€777,000) to support the police officers and their families. On Sunday morning, Klęczar also confirmed that Michał O. had “undergone several surgeries during the night” and “remained in critical condition”. ❗Kiedyś żołnierz 6 Brygady Powietrznodesantowej, dziś policjant i bohater- starszy posterunkowy Jakub Kulik, który wczoraj został ranny w zamachu w Krakowie potrzebuje naszego wsparcia. Ranny policjant przebywa w szpitalu. Potrzebna jest krew grupy AB Rh+. Krew można oddać… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 8, 2026 The authorities have confirmed that Michał O. holds a firearms licence. During the incident on Saturday, he appears to have used an AR-15-style rifle, but police also found a number of other firearms in his vehicle. On Sunday morning, a shooting club in the town of Starachowice that media reports suggested had been used by Michał O. and his father issued a statement saying that the suspect “has never been trained in dynamic, tactical or combat shooting in our club”. They added that the club is fully cooperating with the authorities to provide any necessary and relevant information for the investigation. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Police have apprehended the perpetrator. The interior minister says that the incident is being treated as a terrorist attack, and that preliminary indications suggest the perpetrator had “very radical far-right” views. Police later discovered three further dead bodies in the suspect’s home, who are believed to be his parents and sister. 📌Premier przekazał, że policja, służby specjalne, prokuratura zrobią wszystko, żeby jak najszybciej przekazać informacje opinii publicznej o powodach (strzelaniny – PAP) – powiedział w sobotę na briefingu premier Donald Tusk. 📌- Prawdopodobnie w domu zamachowca są nieżywi… pic.twitter.com/gnV7c1TALa — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) November 7, 2026 At around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday, a man who had driven onto Kraków’s market square – a large public space filled with tourists and locals – “began firing at random people from his car”, said police. World.title: Rating agency S&P shifts Poland’s credit outlook to negative and lowers currency rating
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Credit rating agency S&P has revised Poland’s outlook to negative, saying that the country has seen “one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally” and that “political polarisation hinders fiscal consolidation”. It also lowered the country’s long- and short-term local currency ratings. S&P’s decision follows similar ones by the other members of the big three rating agencies. Fitch has had Poland on negative outlook since last year, while Moody’s cut the country’s credit rating in September this year to its lowest level since 2002. In a statement issued on Friday evening, S&P said that its “negative outlook reflects the risk that elevated budgetary deficits and rising government debt could constrain policy flexibility in the face of future shocks”. “This could expose Poland to shifts in investor sentiment or necessitate a sharp fiscal adjustment that would weigh on economic growth,” they added. 🚨Bardzo źle to wygląda! S&P o finansach Polski: „Takie pogorszenie sytuacji budżetowej należy do najpoważniejszych na świecie”. Dług netto ma wzrosnąć o ponad 20 pkt proc. PKB w 5 lat i przekroczyć 70% PKB w 2029 r. S&P obniżyła rating długu w PLN i perspektywę do negatywnej. — Piotr Nowak (@PiotrNowak_PL) November 7, 2026 Poland has struggled with ballooning budget deficits in recent years, driven by a rapidly expanding defence budget in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and longer-term increases in social spending. Last year’s deficit, at 7.3% of GDP, was the second-highest in the European Union. This year it is forecast to drop slightly, to 6.7%, according to recent finance ministry projections. But next year’s budget foresees a deficit of 7.1%. Those figures are much higher than those the government pledged to reach when, in 2024, Poland was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. For example, the deficit was supposed to fall to 3.7% of GDP in 2027. Moody’s, one of the big three global credit rating agencies, has cut Poland’s rating from A2 to A3. The last time the agency had Poland at such a low level was 2002. It is also the first time any of the big three agencies has downgraded Poland since 2016 https://t.co/qUAEouqhlx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 19, 2026 S&P says that it projects Poland’s net debt exceeding 70% of GDP by 2029. That rise of “more than 20 percentage points over five years marks one of the most significant fiscal deteriorations globally”. The agency notes that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in 2027, making any “meaningful consolidation unlikely” before then. Moreover, the veto power of opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki means the government “faces constraints in advancing its legislative and fiscal consolidation agenda”. Pointing to the ongoing crisis around the constitutional court, S&P also warns that “renewed institutional tensions could weigh on policy predictability”. However, the agency notes that Poland’s economy remains “resilient”, with real GDP growth projected to average around 3% between 2027 and 2029. It also points to the fact that the country has seen a peak in EU-funded investment this year, while exports have picked up. As well as shifting Poland’s overall outlook to negative, S&P downgraded its local currency ratings – meaning its assessment of the country’s willingness and ability to service debt denominated in domestic currency – from A/A-1 to A-/A-2, the same level as its foreign currency ratings. “Our fiscal projections are now weaker than previously envisaged, and we note a track record of recent fiscal slippages amid a challenging policy environment, which underpin our assessment of Poland’s reduced fiscal flexibility,” wrote the agency. Finance minister Andrzej Domański acknowledged S&P’s decision to lower Poland’s outlook to negative in a social media post. However, he pointed to the section of the agency’s report in which it said that the government is constrained by presidential vetoes. Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year, including several fiscal measures. “Despite the presidential vetoes, we will continue taking steps to strengthen the country’s finances,” wrote Domański. 🇵🇱 Agencja S&P utrzymała rating Polski na poziomie A-, obniżając jednak jego perspektywę do negatywnej. W uzasadnieniu decyzji czytamy wprost: „Rząd premiera Donalda Tuska napotyka ograniczenia w realizacji swoich planów legislacyjnych i konsolidacji finansów publicznych ze… — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) November 6, 2026 However, Nawrocki notes that the ballooning budget deficits preceded his coming to power, and has blamed the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk for overseeing budgetary “chaos” and causing “a deep crisis of credibility”. In response to S&P’s announcement, Marcin Ociepa, deputy head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, accused the government of “trying to shift responsibility for Poland’s credit rating downgrade [sic] onto the president”. “Any family that managed its finances the way Donald Tusk manages our country’s finances would drown in debt and go bankrupt,” wrote Ociepa. “That is exactly what awaits Poland if this government remains in power.” ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: 2,000-year-old Vandal artefacts anonymously handed to Polish museum
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A collection of artefacts associated with the Vandals and dating back almost 2,000 years has been handed anonymously to a museum in eastern Poland. The collection includes a sword, spear and javelin heads, shield components and spurs. Museum staff do not know who originally discovered the burial or exactly where it was located, leaving the circumstances of the find largely a mystery. The Father Stanisław Staszic Museum in Hrubieszów announced in a Facebook post that the objects had been passed to them anonymously through an intermediary. The items are in poor condition and will undergo urgent conservation, with the iron components of the weapons particularly vulnerable after centuries in the ground. They were also exposed to high temperatures during a burial practice in which the deceased was burned along with their personal belongings. The museum says that the nature of the objects indicates that their owner held a high social position. The most notable object is a sword preserved in three pieces, reflecting the Vandal practice of deliberately breaking or bending weapons and other grave artefacts as part of funeral rituals. The collection also contains two spearheads, both broken. Other items include a shield boss with a spike, a shield grip, a fragment of a knife, a belt buckle and two spurs. Fragments of a bone comb and a bronze fibula, used to fasten a cloak, were also recovered. The circumstances surrounding the discovery and recovery of the objects remain unknown, but the museum says that, according to the information it has received, the burial site was discovered in an agricultural field several years ago in the municipality of Werbkowice. “We intend to verify the exact location through archaeological excavations, most likely next summer,” they added. “Based on the information we have gathered, there are strong indications that there may be more similar burials in the area that have been disturbed by agricultural work.” The opportunity to recover the objects and transfer them to an appropriate institution arose only recently. The museum said that a local metal detectorist played a key role in arranging the transfer, acting as an intermediary in securing the artefacts. The recovery of the artefacts follows another recent archaeological discovery in the same region. In August, the museum announced that a metal boss from a warrior’s shield dating to the second century was found at a scrap metal yard near Hrubieszów. The Vandals were an ancient Germanic people believed to have reached the territories of present-day Poland around the 3rd or 2nd century BC. They lived in the region for several centuries and are generally associated by researchers with the Przeworsk culture, which flourished across parts of present-day Poland during the Iron Age and Roman period. Around the turn of the 4th and 5th centuries AD, amid the expansion of the Huns, they left Central Europe and moved westwards into the declining Roman Empire. As the Vandals left Central Europe, the Slavic population gradually moved into the region over the following centuries. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Three Days of Chocolate and Sweet Treats Await in Prague
World.content:
Chocolate lovers in Prague will have a sweet reason to head to Novo Plaza this weekend as ČokoFest arrives at the shopping centre for the first time.

The three-day chocolate festival will take place from Friday, November 13, to Sunday, November 15, offering visitors free entry and a programme filled with tastings, handmade sweets and activities for children.



Visitors can expect a selection of handmade chocolates, pralines, cakes and other sweet specialties, with plenty of opportunities to sample different products throughout the weekend.

Families with children will also find a range of activities, including chocolate workshops designed for young visitors. Meanwhile, Thermomix will host live demonstrations and chocolate tastings during the event.

ČokoFest will also offer the chance to win several prizes. One of the main giveaways is a weekend drive in a Chery Tiggo 7, provided by Mach Motors. Visitors can also enter to win a ČokoBox and other sweet prizes.
