With Christmas just around the corner, the festival could also be a good place to find original gifts for chocolate lovers.

ČokoFest takes place at Novo Plaza Shopping Centre in Prague 4, and admission is free throughout all three days.

World.title: Micro Praha Festival Returns With 93 Watch Brands From 27 Countries
World.content:
The fourth edition of the international watch festival will take place at Fantova budova on November 28–29. Admission is free with online registration.

The Micro Praha Festival will return to Prague on November 28–29, bringing together 93 independent watch brands from 27 countries.



The fourth edition of the event will take place at Fantův sál inside the historic Fantova budova, near Prague’s Main Railway Station. Visitors will be able to discover new collections, try on watches and meet the people behind the brands.

Organisers say this year’s edition will be the largest so far, with microbrands and established independent watchmakers exhibiting alongside each other for the first time.

Brands from countries including Switzerland, Germany, the United States, Canada, France, the Netherlands, Japan, Taiwan and the Czech Republic will take part. Several exhibitors will be appearing in Prague and Central Europe for the first time.

Among the newcomers are New York-based Brew, known for watches inspired by coffee culture; MING, which focuses on experimental designs and engineering; Atelier Wen, specialising in watches with hand-crafted guilloché dials; and Lorier, a brand recognised for its vintage-inspired designs.

Chrono24 Joins as Main Festival Sponsor

The 2026 edition will also see Chrono24, the international online marketplace for luxury watches, join the festival as its primary sponsor and partner.

Representatives from the company will be present throughout the weekend to discuss the watch market, industry trends and the platform’s latest features. KB Bank is also listed among this year’s primary sponsors.

The festival was founded in 2023 by Bhanu Chopra and Ondrej Vislocký, two watch enthusiasts who wanted to create a platform for smaller independent brands in Central Europe.

Chopra is a watch journalist who previously served as editor-in-chief of Revolution USA, while Vislocký is a Prague-based photographer whose work has appeared in international watch publications and brand catalogues.

The two also co-own INFINTY Watches, a specialist retailer of microbrand and independent watches in central Prague.

World.title: Record Number of Stores to Join Czechia’s National Food Collection
World.content:
On Saturday, November 14, more than 3,500 retail stores across the Czech Republic will take part in the national food collection, a major increase from last year’s 2,250.

The event, organized by the Czech Federation of Food Banks and the Czech Trade and Tourism Association, will run from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.



Donations will include non-perishable food and personal hygiene items, which will later be distributed to families and individuals in need. Starting Tuesday, people can also contribute through six online retailers, where the food collection will continue for two weeks.

Organizers say the number of participating outlets has been steadily growing, showing greater public involvement each year. When the initiative began in 2013, donations could be made at 750 stores.

During last year’s autumn round, 702 tons of food and hygiene products were gathered—34 tons less than the previous year. According to organizers, the lower figure may have resulted from earlier donations made in September, when the public responded to flood relief efforts.

The food collection takes place twice a year, in spring and autumn.

Aleš Slavíček, Chairman of the Czech Federation of Food Banks, noted that the two annual collections together provide about 10% of the non-perishable food needed each year by Czech food banks. “Many people in our society still struggle to put food on the table,” Slavíček said at a press conference in Prague. “The food collection is a simple way for anyone to help those who are facing difficult times.”

The federation recommends donating canned food, baby food, soups, powdered milk, butter, rice, legumes, pasta, and personal care products.

A large portion of the donations goes to single mothers, who are among the most frequent recipients of food bank assistance.

World.title: Prague Welcomed 2.3 Million Visitors This Summer, Up 3% Year-on-Year
World.content:
Prague welcomed nearly 2.32 million visitors between July and September 2026, a 3 percent increase compared with the same period last year.

The number of Czech visitors rose faster than international arrivals, although foreign tourists continued to account for more than 80 percent of all guests.



Visitors recorded a total of 5.51 million overnight stays in the capital, up 3.8 percent year-on-year, according to figures released Monday by the Czech Statistical Office (CZSO).

Accommodation establishments across Prague registered 402,021 domestic guests during the third quarter, a 9.4 percent increase from a year earlier. The number of international visitors reached more than 1.91 million, representing growth of 1.7 percent.

Foreign tourists accounted for approximately 4.79 million overnight stays, compared with 725,167 by Czech visitors. The average stay was 2.4 nights. International guests spent an average of 2.5 nights in Prague, while domestic visitors stayed for 1.8 nights.

Germany remained the largest source of international visitors, with 274,885 guests. The United States ranked second with 172,126 visitors, followed by Poland with 128,076.

Arrivals from Taiwan increased by 27 percent year-on-year, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

Hotel occupancy in Prague has also continued to recover. According to PCT, the average occupancy rate reached 78 percent this year, approximately 12 percent higher than in 2023. In September, occupancy at luxury hotels stood at 83 percent.

PCT has increasingly focused its marketing campaigns on visitors over the age of 30 with an interest in culture, history and architecture. The strategy aims to strengthen Prague’s position as a cultural destination rather than a place primarily associated with cheap drinking and party tourism.

Across the Czech Republic, collective accommodation establishments recorded 8.17 million guests during the third quarter of 2026.

World.title: Prague Ice Rinks Guide This Winter: Opening Dates, Prices and Locations
World.content:
As temperatures fall, public ice rinks are beginning to reopen across Prague for the 2026–27 winter season.

Several districts have already confirmed opening dates, while others are still finalising their winter programmes. From free skating in Smíchov to rinks beneath the Žižkov Television Tower and on the Letná Plain, residents and visitors will have plenty of options in the coming months.

Here is what has been announced so far.



Prague 1

The Na Františku ice rink is scheduled to open on November 13. Public skating will begin at 8 a.m., with closing times varying between 6:30 p.m. and 8:30 p.m., depending on the day. Skate rentals, refreshments and a heated tent will be available.

A second rink is expected to open on Wenceslas Square on November 28. It will operate daily in four sessions between 9 a.m. and 10 p.m.

A two-hour ticket will cost 200 CZK for adults and 100 CZK for children under 15. Visitors will be able to rent skates and helmets, while skating aids for children, skate sharpening and storage facilities will also be available.

It remains unclear whether the rinks at Ovocný trh and Čapadlo will return this winter.

Prague 2

Three outdoor ice rinks are planned in Prague 2.

The rinks at Havlíčkovy sady, also known as Grébovka, and Svatopluk Čech Park are scheduled to open on November 20. A third rink, located in Folimanka Park beneath the Nusle Bridge, is expected to follow on December 1.

All three venues are expected to operate daily from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. On weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m., the ice will be reserved for kindergartens and primary schools in Prague 2. Public skating will take place in the afternoons and throughout weekends.

On December 24 and December 31, the rinks will close at 3 p.m.

Prague 3

Prague 3 will again operate two public ice rinks.

Both are scheduled to open on November 14. One will be located in Mahlerovy sady, beneath the Žižkov Television Tower. A two-hour ticket will cost 150 CZK for adults and 50 CZK for children.

The second rink will return to the Pražačka sports complex. It will be open from 1 p.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. on weekends. All-day admission will cost 120 CZK for adults and 80 CZK for children.

Skate rentals and refreshments will be available at both locations.

Prague 4

So far, one public ice rink has been confirmed in Prague 4.

The rink near the Prague Congress Centre, close to Vyšehrad metro station, is scheduled to open on November 13. It will operate from 1 p.m. to 9 p.m. on weekdays and from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. during weekends.

Admission will cost 120 CZK per hour for adults and 80 CZK for children. Skate rentals and refreshments will also be available.

The opening date for the public rink in Podolí has not yet been announced.

Prague 5

Residents will once again be able to skate for free at the Aréna sportu on Hořejší nábřeží in Smíchov.

The rink is scheduled to open on November 13, with the official launch of the winter programme planned for the afternoon of November 20.

The venue will also host several themed events during the season, including St. Nicholas on Ice, a superhero-themed skating event and a Valentine’s Day programme.

Prague 6

Two Prague 6 locations are expected to offer outdoor skating this winter.

The rink in Ořechovka is provisionally scheduled to open around November 20, although the final date has yet to be confirmed.

At Vypich, a trial operation is expected to begin on November 27. The official opening is planned two days later and will coincide with the lighting of the local Christmas tree.

Prague 7

The ice rink on the Letná Plain is scheduled to open on November 14 and remain in operation until March 7, 2027.

It will be open daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. A two-hour ticket will cost 150 CZK for adults and 120 CZK for children under 15.

Children under 15 who live in Prague 7 or attend school in the district will be able to skate free of charge.

Prague 8

Three outdoor ice rinks are planned in Prague 8.

On November 17, rinks are scheduled to open in Libeňské podzámčí and near the Krakov Cultural Centre in Bohnice. A third location near the Ládví swimming pool is expected to open on November 20.

Further information on admission and operating hours is expected to be announced by the district.

Prague 9

The rink in Park Přátelství in Střížkov has already opened for the season.

It has been operating since November 5 and is open daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Morning hours are reserved for schools, while skate rentals are available to visitors.

Another rink will open in Zahrádky Park on December 5. It will also operate daily from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.

On weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m., schools will be able to reserve the ice. Visitors will have access to skate rentals and refreshments from Café Park Zahrádky.

Prague 10

Prague 10 will again open a public ice rink in Heroldovy sady in Vršovice.

The rink is scheduled to open on November 29, 2026, and is expected to remain in operation until February. The final closing date will depend on weather conditions.

With opening dates spread throughout November and early December, Prague’s winter skating season is now gradually getting underway. Several districts are still expected to release further details, and visitors should check local announcements before heading to the rink.

World.title: St. Martin’s Day 2026 in Prague: Where to Enjoy Traditional Goose
World.content:
St. Martin’s Day, which Czechs celebrate on November 11, is a holiday of good food and drink. Autumn slowly alternates with winter, and it begins to snow.

In the past, the economic year was ending at this time, and the landowners were preparing a feast for their people as a form of thanks, when they were also paid out their wages.

St. Martin’s Day in restaurants

You can be sure that almost every restaurant around mid-November will be offering its visitors a special St. Martin’s Day menu. What does it feature?

According to a tradition that has lasted for several centuries, geese were always roasted in the autumn, fresh cabbage was processed, and wine or beer was drunk. And today’s restaurants and pubs remain faithful to these basic ingredients.

Typically, you will be served liver pâté as an appetizer, followed by a strong broth with liver dumplings and noodles, which the chefs usually leave to simmer overnight, with the main course being roast goose with red or white cabbage and dumplings.

Where to taste St. Martin’s menu?

Restaurant Salabka (November 6 – 14): Choose from 3 to 5 courses featuring seasonal autumn ingredients and contemporary gastronomy. Available from November 6, alongside the regular autumn tasting menu.

More info here.

Restaurant Obecní dům: (November 7–11): Enjoy a festive menu combining traditional roast goose with creative starters, including smoked duck and goose prosciutto carpaccio. A special St. Martin’s brunch takes place on November 8, while the restaurant’s beer hall joins the celebrations from November 9 to 15.

More info here.

Restaurant Masaryčka: Here the highlight is a tender goose leg confit with caraway, served with braised red cabbage, plums and assorted dumplings (499 CZK). Alternatively, guests can enjoy homemade potato lokše filled with pulled goose meat, onion cabbage and apples (359 CZK). To finish on a sweet note, the menu offers apple strudel with vanilla sauce, walnuts, honey and cinnamon crumble (149 CZK).

More info here

Restaurant Deer: a special four-course menu by chef Lubomír Dolejš, available until November 11. The menu features goose breast, traditional goose soup (kaldoun), confit goose leg with cabbage and bread dumplings, followed by miniature St. Martin’s pastries. The full menu costs 1,295 CZK per person, with individual dishes also available.

More info here

Le Petit Beefbar at the W Hotel: the “Made the List – Holiday 2026 Edition” program features everything from St. Martin’s goose and Advent brunches with oysters and champagne to Christmas dinners at Le Petit Beefbar au Grand Café, culminating in a New Year’s Eve celebration. Starting November 11, the restaurant will host “St. Martin’s Week,” serving slow-roasted goose with all the traditional sides during dinner service.

World.title: Prague Welcomes Tea Experts and Producers from Around the World
World.content:
Prague will welcome tea producers, experts and enthusiasts from around the world next weekend as Euro Tea Expo returns to the Czech capital for its second edition.

The two-day event, taking place on November 14 and 15, will bring together 37 exhibitors and focus on tea traditions from different parts of the world.



This year’s theme is “Chinese White Tea – The Heritage of Fuding.”

One of the main guests will be Master Lin Zhenchuan, a recognised inheritor of the traditional Fuding white tea-making techniques and founder of PINPINTEA.

Fuding white tea production is listed as part of China’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage.

With more than 30 years of experience, Master Lin will introduce visitors to the craftsmanship and history behind Fuding white tea through presentations and guided tastings. Guests will also be able to compare fresh and aged white teas and learn more about the ageing process.

The programme will feature demonstrations and presentations covering several tea traditions, including a traditional Shē ethnic group white tea performance, Sichuan gaiwan tea culture and long-spout teapot demonstrations.

Visitors can also learn about Kenyan tea, Japanese hojicha, ancient tea trees in Guangxi and the connection between tea and wellbeing. Beyond tea, the programme includes Taiji sessions, a tea and Taiji performance, and a Japanese Nerikiri confectionery workshop.

Organisers say this year’s edition will also expand beyond tea. Five European vegan brands will present plant-based products and sustainable lifestyle concepts as part of the event.

The first Euro Tea Expo was held in Prague in 2025 and brought together 33 exhibitors from 15 countries, attracting around 960 visitors. The organisers say the event aims to further strengthen connections between tea producers, professionals and consumers across Europe.

Event information

Dates: November 14–15, 2026

Opening hours: 10:00–18:00

Venue: U Slavie 1540/2a, Prague 10 – Vršovice

Theme: Chinese White Tea – The Heritage of Fuding

Exhibitors: 37

World.title: Canva Closes Prague Office as More Than 1,200 Jobs Are Cut Worldwide
World.content:
Canva is shutting down its Prague office, leaving only six employees from a workforce of around 50 as part of a company-wide restructuring affecting more than 1,200 people.

According to a former employee familiar with the situation, staff first received a company-wide email from Canva CEO Melanie Perkins outlining major changes.

Around 20 minutes later, employees whose positions were being eliminated received individual notifications.



Those affected were reportedly given about a week to collect their belongings. Access to most internal work systems was cut immediately, with employees retaining access only to services such as Slack and email.

The Prague closure comes during what has been described as the largest restructuring in Canva’s history and the company’s first major round of mass layoffs.

The changes are expected to affect 1,271 employees, equivalent to roughly 22 percent of the company’s workforce.

Prague Staff Point to Structure and AI Costs

A former member of the Prague office said two factors appear to have contributed to the decision.

The first is the company’s organizational structure. Responsibilities were divided across several layers, making communication and decision-making more difficult. The problem was further complicated by the ten- to eleven-hour time difference between Central Europe and Sydney.

The second issue, according to the former employee, involves the cost of artificial intelligence.

Canva has invested heavily in AI tools and technology, initially facing significant costs associated with computing power. Over the past month, the company has begun introducing its own models, although it remains unclear how much this could reduce the cost of processing graphics and other AI-related tasks.

The company has integrated tools and services linked to platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude. At the same time, users are increasingly able to generate images, designs and other visual content directly through competing AI systems without relying on Canva’s traditional platform.

World.title: VIDEOS: Áron Orbán arrested in case involving more than 100 Vietnamese nationals smuggled through Hungary
World.content:
Áron Orbán, the younger brother of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, was among four people arrested in a suspected human-smuggling and corruption case involving more than 100 Vietnamese nationals. Photographs published by HVG on Monday evening showed him arriving at the Gyorskocsi Street detention facility in Budapest in a police car.

The National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) and the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) carried out a coordinated operation on Monday morning in Budapest, Fót and Dunakeszi. Police confirmed that three men and one woman were detained. Two arrests were carried out by the Counter Terrorism Centre (TEK), as investigators had reason to believe that firearms might be present at the properties.

HVG reported that its photojournalist photographed Áron Orbán outside the detention facility on Monday evening. Footage released by the police earlier in the day also showed the suspects being taken away in handcuffs, with Orbán identifiable among them.

Check out the photos here.

More than 100 Vietnamese nationals allegedly involved

According to investigators, the four suspects helped Vietnamese nationals obtain visas through Hungarian diplomatic missions over several months in 2024. They allegedly charged each person a so-called recruitment fee and divided the proceeds among themselves. Authorities believe they may have assisted more than 100 people.

The Vietnamese applicants reportedly stated that they intended to stay in Hungary temporarily to attend short training courses. However, investigators say most did not attend the courses listed in their applications. Even those who did take part allegedly failed to leave Hungary before their visas expired.

According to the police, the applicants’ actual intention was to use Hungary as a route to Western Europe, where they hoped to find better living conditions.

Orbán also suspected of influence peddling

The NNI suspects all four individuals of human smuggling committed as part of a criminal organisation for financial gain. The NVVH has additionally questioned one of the men on suspicion of influence peddling as an instigator.

In a separate statement, the NVVH said the person brought in had allegedly invoked political connections and influence to request an unlawful advantage through an intermediary from the head of a labour recruitment company. In return, he allegedly promised to arrange the company’s reinstatement on the register of priority employers. The authority did not identify the person by name, but the description matches the case involving Áron Orbán.

During searches at four locations lasting several hours, investigators seized documents, electronic data and other potential evidence. The NNI suspects all four individuals of human smuggling committed as part of a criminal organisation for financial gain. The NVVH has additionally questioned one of them on suspicion of influence peddling as an instigator.

The investigation is ongoing, and authorities are planning to seek measures restricting the suspects’ freedom. Europol also supported the coordinated operation.

Earlier reports linked Orbán to visa arrangements

Áron Orbán’s business connections and alleged involvement in visa arrangements had previously been investigated by Telex. The news site published an extensive investigation into the matter in 2025, following the leak of a recording in which Orbán discussed visa applications with a government official.

On Monday, Prime Minister Péter Magyar initially said, citing press reports, that Viktor Orbán’s brother had been detained on suspicion of human smuggling. Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán subsequently described the case as a political attack, writing that he was the real target and that his brother was merely being used as a tool.

World.title: Orbán government allegedly discussed a EUR 5 billion loan from China weeks before parliamentary elections
World.content:
Hungary’s Orbán government reportedly held discussions with China over a financing framework worth up to EUR 5 billion in the weeks before the country’s parliamentary elections, according to investigative outlet Átlátszó, which obtained a draft agreement between the Hungarian Ministry of National Economy and China’s state-owned Export-Import Bank (CEXIM).

Orbán government apparently wanted an even bigger loan from China

The document, prepared in spring 2026, outlines a possible expansion of financial cooperation between Budapest and Beijing. The proposed framework could have supported infrastructure, transport and energy projects across Hungary, including railway developments, geothermal energy, the battery industry and small modular nuclear reactors.

The EUR 5 billion figure, currently equivalent to approximately HUF 1.8 trillion, would have been five times the size of the EUR 1 billion Chinese loan Hungary drew down in 2024, widely described at the time as a major Chinese financing deal.

However, the draft does not represent a signed agreement or a confirmed loan. It contains no final interest rates, repayment periods or specific allocations for individual projects. Átlátszó claimed the inclusion of proposed amendments nevertheless indicated that substantive negotiations may have taken place.

Financing could have included yuan-denominated bonds

The draft reportedly envisaged several potential funding mechanisms, including project-specific loans, investment financing instruments and capital market transactions. It also mentioned the possibility of issuing so-called panda bonds and dim sum bonds, which would allow Hungary to raise funds in Chinese yuan on international markets.

Financing could have been denominated in euros, US dollars or yuan. The document did not establish whether the proposed framework would have resulted in a single borrowing arrangement or several separate transactions.

The Ministry of National Economy’s successor, the Ministry of Economy and Energy, and the Hungarian Government Debt Management Agency (ÁKK) were approached for comment by Átlátszó. The outlet said it had not received responses to its questions at the time of publication. It also remains unclear whether the negotiations led to any subsequent agreement or borrowing.

China’s expanding financial role in Hungary

CEXIM has already played a significant role in Hungary’s infrastructure financing. The bank provided funding for the Hungarian section of the Budapest–Belgrade railway, a project whose financial terms and costs have attracted sustained scrutiny.

In 2024, Hungary also drew down a EUR 1 billion loan from three Chinese financial institutions, including CEXIM, the China Development Bank and the Hungarian branch of Bank of China. The transaction was not publicly announced by the Orbán government at the time and was identified through debt management data.

Chinese financing has been a key component of the Orbán government’s ‘Eastern Opening’ policy, which sought to strengthen economic ties with Asian countries. Chinese companies have also expanded their presence in Hungary through major industrial investments, particularly in the battery and electric vehicle sectors.

The proposed EUR 5 billion framework could have extended this cooperation into additional areas, including geothermal energy and small modular nuclear reactors. The draft, however, did not identify specific projects or establish the conditions under which Chinese financing might have been provided.

Long-term costs and transparency concerns

The potential expansion of Chinese lending raises questions about Hungary’s future debt obligations and the transparency of financing arrangements. Foreign-currency borrowing can expose governments to exchange-rate risks, while the economic benefits of funded projects must be weighed against repayment costs.

The draft agreement does not establish that Hungary borrowed EUR 5 billion or that CEXIM committed to providing the funds. It does, however, suggest that the Orbán government was considering a substantial expansion of its financial cooperation with China shortly before the election.

World.title: Tragedy: Worker dies in fatal accident at industrial gas plant in Hungary
World.content:

Fatal accident at gas plant

The company, a leading supplier of industrial, medical and speciality gases, also said it was working closely with the relevant authorities. It expressed its condolences to the deceased employee’s family and colleagues.

Police investigating the circumstances of the accident

World.title: Austrian woman kidnapped and tied up in van for three days by Hungarian man
World.content:
A 62-year-old Austrian woman was allegedly kidnapped, tied up and held captive in a modified van for three days during a short trip to Hungary with a 41-year-old Hungarian acquaintance.

Woman reportedly lured across the border by Hungarian acquaintance

The woman, from the Innviertel region of Upper Austria, reported the incident to police in Braunau on Saturday, claiming she had been assaulted, threatened with a firearm and detained in appalling conditions. The case was reported by Austrian media outlet Krone.

According to investigators, the pensioner had recently received a substantial sum of cash following the sale of a property. Her Hungarian acquaintance allegedly became aware of the money and persuaded her to travel to Hungary for a brief holiday.

Victim allegedly confined in van and threatened

The woman was reportedly taken to Győrújbarát, around 400 kilometres from her home, where the suspect allegedly knocked her down, restrained her and locked her in the cargo compartment of a specially prepared van in a wooded area.

She is said to have been held between 4 and 6 November, during which time the man allegedly demanded money and repeatedly threatened her with a firearm. The victim reportedly sustained significant injuries, including severe bruising, bleeding and marks from the restraints, and later required hospital treatment.

As the woman’s family repeatedly attempted to contact her, and amid increasing intimidation, the suspect allegedly abandoned his plan and drove her back to Austria. Before releasing her, he reportedly threatened to seriously harm her family if she reported the incident to police.

Hungarian suspect arrested in Austria

Following the woman’s report, Austrian police launched an investigation and established the identity and whereabouts of the suspect through cross-border inquiries. The Ried Public Prosecutor’s Office ordered his arrest, which was carried out by the Cobra special operations unit at a residential property in Maria Schmolln, Upper Austria.

During questioning, the 41-year-old Hungarian reportedly made a comprehensive confession. Prosecutors confirmed that the woman had been held captive from 4 to 6 November. The modified van allegedly used in the incident was recovered in Hungary. The suspect was subsequently transferred to Ried Prison.

He is being investigated on suspicion of unlawful deprivation of liberty, aggravated coercion and grievous bodily harm. Austrian authorities said he had not previously been known to the police in the country.

World.title: Hungarian bank OTP arbitrarily closes refugees’ accounts while asking for non-existent documents
World.content:
Hungary’s largest bank, OTP, is facing an investigation by the country’s ombudsman following allegations that it discriminated against officially recognised refugees by unilaterally closing their existing bank accounts.

Russian psychologist loses access to six-year-old account

The proceedings were initiated after the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, a human rights organisation, filed a complaint claiming that the bank had refused to accept documents confirming refugees’ legal status and had demanded residence permits they were not required to possess.

The Committee has highlighted the case of Aleksandr, a Russian psychologist who was forced to leave his home country and has lived in Hungary since 2019. He was officially recognised as a refugee last year, but subsequently lost access to his six-year-old OTP account.

OTP didn’t accept official documents

During a routine customer identification procedure aimed at preventing money laundering, Aleksandr sought to update his documents. According to the Helsinki Committee, OTP refused to accept his refugee status papers, including an official certificate issued by the immigration authority. The bank reportedly told him he could either close the account voluntarily or have it terminated by the institution, potentially losing access to his money.

He eventually transferred his savings to an account he had previously opened at another bank. The organisation says the case is not isolated. Other refugees, including Russian and Palestinian nationals, have allegedly faced similar treatment, with some having their funds frozen and bank cards blocked.

A separate case involved a Russian refugee student and his mother, whose accounts were terminated after the bank had previously apologised for requesting a residence permit on what it acknowledged was an incorrect legal basis.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Refugees allegedly asked to provide documents they cannot obtain

The Helsinki Committee argues that the bank’s requirement is impossible to meet. Unlike other foreign nationals, officially recognised refugees and people granted subsidiary protection do not hold residence permits. Their legal status is closer to that of Hungarian citizens, who identify themselves using personal identity cards and address cards.

The organisation says no Hungarian law requires refugees to provide residence permits to access banking services. It alleges that OTP has nevertheless continued to rely on its internal rules and interpretation of legislation.

The bank has maintained its position in its response to the ombudsman, according to the Helsinki Committee. The organisation contends that internal policies or a mistaken interpretation of the law cannot override statutory requirements.

Investigation could have wider implications

The ombudsman’s investigation follows the Committee’s action as a public interest claimant. The outcome could have implications beyond OTP, with the human rights organisation hoping the proceedings will also provide guidance to other financial institutions.

The allegations have raised concerns about refugees’ access to essential financial services, including receiving wages and paying everyday bills. OTP has not been independently established to have acted unlawfully; the matter is now subject to the ombudsman’s proceedings.

World.title: Man sexually assaults 15-year-old girl then chases her with running chainsaw in Hungary
World.content:
Prosecutors in northeastern Hungary have brought charges against a repeat offender accused of sexually assaulting a 15-year-old girl at his home before chasing her and her boyfriend down the street with a running chainsaw. The prosecution is seeking a prison sentence, a ban on holding public office and no possibility of parole.

According to the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Chief Prosecutor’s Office, the incident took place in January last year, when the accused invited several guests to his family home in Borsod County. Among them were a male acquaintance and another man who attended with his 15-year-old girlfriend. The group consumed alcohol during the evening.

The accused allegedly approached the girl on the veranda and made a sexual proposition. When she refused, he restrained her hands and sexually assaulted her, according to prosecutors.

She managed to escape by biting his arm.

Couple fled as man followed with chainsaw

The girl ran to her boyfriend and asked him to leave the house with her. The accused allegedly tried to prevent them from leaving, leading to a physical confrontation with the boyfriend, whom he struck once.

The couple eventually managed to escape when another guest arrived at the property.

However, the accused then allegedly followed them into the street carrying a running chainsaw, waving it around and threatening them. The girl sought police assistance from a public telephone box before taking refuge in a nearby house.

Prosecutors seek prison sentence without parole

The Sátoraljaújhely District Prosecutor’s Office has charged the man with aggravated sexual assault and other offences, the Hungarian news agency MTI reported on Monday, citing Zsolt Jogg, deputy press spokesperson for the county chief prosecutor’s office.

The accused has a criminal record and is classified as a repeat offender. Prosecutors are seeking a prison sentence and a ban on holding public office, and have also proposed that he should not be eligible for conditional release.

The case will now proceed through the courts. The allegations have not yet been established by a final court judgment.

World.title: Airbnb says short-term rentals play small role in Hungary’s housing crisis – But bring millions to economy
World.content:
Airbnb says short-term rentals account for only a tiny share of Hungary’s housing stock, while making a significant contribution to tourism and the wider economy. According to the platform’s latest analysis, Hungarian hosts welcomed 1.4 million guests in 2025, with Airbnb-related activity contributing an estimated €351 million to the country’s GDP and supporting around 13,600 jobs.

The company argues that Hungary’s housing affordability problems are rooted primarily in insufficient new construction, rising property prices and the large number of vacant homes, rather than short-term holiday rentals. According to Portfolio, its findings come amid continuing debate over restrictions on Airbnb-style accommodation, particularly in Budapest.

How many homes are actually rented out?

Airbnb estimates that entire properties rented out for at least 120 nights in 2025 accounted for just 0.12% of Hungary’s approximately 4.6 million homes. The company describes the 120-night threshold as a strict illustrative measure, while acknowledging that it does not necessarily mean these properties would otherwise have been available for long-term tenants.

By comparison, the company cites Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) figures showing around 564,000 vacant residential properties nationwide, equivalent to nearly 12% of the housing stock.

Airbnb also points to the scale of property price increases: between 2015 and the fourth quarter of 2025, Hungarian house prices rose by 290%, according to Eurostat data cited in its analysis. Rents increased by 105% over the same period.

What Airbnb guests bring to local businesses

The platform estimates that guests staying in Hungarian Airbnb accommodation spent more than €438.9 million in the country in 2025. Beyond accommodation, 38% of their spending went to restaurants and other hospitality businesses, while 20% was spent on entertainment and cultural activities.

Retail accounted for 18% of additional spending, groceries for 14% and local transport for 10%.

The company also says that around 80% of Hungarian hosts rented out just one entire property last year. Their average annual hosting income was approximately €4,600. In Airbnb’s own survey, 70% of respondents said they used the extra income to cover rising living costs.

Would tighter restrictions make accommodation more affordable?

Airbnb argues that restrictions alone do not necessarily improve housing affordability. Citing its analysis of Amsterdam and Barcelona, the company says the number of Airbnb listings fell by 54% and 24% respectively following tighter rules, while long-term rents continued to rise by 34% and 37%.

These comparisons reflect Airbnb’s interpretation of the data and do not establish that short-term rentals have no effect on housing availability in particular neighbourhoods.

The company is calling for proportionate, data-based regulation that takes local conditions into account. For travellers, the debate matters because changes to short-term rental rules could affect the availability of alternatives to hotels, particularly in popular urban destinations such as Budapest.

World.title: PM Magyar: Viktor Orbán’s brother has been detained on human-smuggling suspicion
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has said that former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s brother, Áron Orbán, was detained on suspicion of human smuggling, citing press reports. However, authorities have not yet confirmed his alleged detention or the specific grounds for it.

The announcement came on Monday, after the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) and the National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) carried out a joint operation in Budapest and two locations in Pest County. According to the authorities, several people were detained, and searches were conducted at multiple properties as part of two parallel criminal investigations. Further details were expected later in the day.

Magyar made the claim in a Facebook post, but did not provide further information. The Kontroll news site reported that Áron Orbán could be among those affected by the operation. The NVVH’s president, Anna Róza Unger, declined to confirm or deny reports that counter-terrorism officers had visited a property in Fótliget linked to one of Áron Orbán’s companies. She told Telex that the office had carried out further investigative measures in the case involving him and would provide more information later.

The investigation into alleged visa dealings

Áron Orbán’s name had previously emerged in an investigation into suspected abuses involving work-related residence permits for foreign nationals. According to earlier reporting by Telex, business interests linked to him may have helped Vietnamese applicants travel to Hungary. His company, Multi Shoot Zrt., reportedly enrolled Vietnamese applicants in a two-day life-saving course at the University of Pécs, which could have helped them obtain Schengen visas. The report also said that Áron Orbán had approached a government commissioner to help speed up certain visa applications.

In September, the NVVH announced that it had taken over the investigation. According to the office’s account of the suspicion, a group closely connected to senior political figures allegedly offered to secure work-related residence permits for clients in exchange for payment. The office said the case concerned suspected influence peddling and other offences.

In April, the Central Investigative Prosecutor’s Office reported that four people had been questioned as suspects in a related case involving the recruitment and employment of foreign workers. Two were taken into custody, with a court subsequently ordering their pre-trial detention for one month. Prosecutors said the suspects had allegedly invoked trusted connections with influential public officials while promising to arrange residence permits smoothly. They were accused of dividing €17,000 received in advance from a business owner.

The NVVH’s September announcement described the wider investigation as examining whether people with political connections had used their relationships to obtain preferential treatment in official procedures.

World.title: EU Offers Black Sea Countries Support to Counter Security Threats
World.content:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Romanian President Nicusor Dan at Cotroceni Presidential Palace in Bucharest, 9 November 2026. Photo: EPA/ROBERT GHEMENT.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday announced a new support package worth around 60 million euros for EU countries bordering the Black Sea, as the region faces growing security challenges linked to Russia’s war against Ukraine, including drone incursions and attacks on commercial shipping.

Around 10 million euros will be allocated to maritime surveillance and search-and-rescue operations, while a further 50 million euros will go towards establishing a planned Security Hub, von der Leyen said in Bucharest, where she met Romanian President Nicusor Dan.

The proposed hub – including Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey – is intended to strengthen regional cooperation and improve the ability of countries in the area to monitor and respond to security threats, including incidents affecting maritime infrastructure and commercial navigation.

The Commission president said the EU needed to step up its response to escalating threats and ensure the safety of shipping routes across the Black Sea, which have become increasingly vulnerable since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Von der Leyen wrote on X before the visit that “security threats are escalating, attacks are increasing, and innocent lives have been lost” in the Black Sea region.

Von der Leyen reiterated the EU’s support for a ceasefire in Ukraine covering attacks on energy and food infrastructure, stressing the importance of protecting civilian facilities and ensuring the continued flow of essential goods.

Drone attacks reportedly damaged at least seven commercial vessels in the Black Sea last month, claiming the lives of two sailors and leaving at least 25 others unaccounted for. The incidents have heightened concerns over the spread of the conflict beyond Ukraine’s borders and its growing proximity to NATO territory.

While Romanian authorities have pointed the finger at Russia, Bulgaria has avoided naming the suspected perpetrator, saying only that the drones came from “an eastern direction”.

On Tuesday, von der Leyen is due to travel to Bulgaria, where she will meet Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Varna and visit the Naval Academy, before attending the COP 31 climate summit in Turkey.

World.title: Greece Retrieves 21 Dead Migrants off Crete Island
World.content:
Photo illustration: Greek Coast Guard.

Twenty-one people have been found dead in the sea area of Kaloi Limenes, a port village in the Heraklion regional unit of southern Crete, trying to reach Greek shores, authorities said.

A rescue operation took place overnight from Saturday to Sunday after a boat carrying migrants in distress was spotted. The Greek tugboat Pyrros rescued 28 people from Sudan and recovered the dead body of one man.

“It is reported that there may have been additional bodies on the migrants’ vessel; however, towing the boat or attempting further recoveries proved entirely impossible and extremely dangerous due to severe weather conditions, specifically, gale-force northerly winds reaching 6–7 on the Beaufort scale. Consequently, the vessel had to be left at the scene,” the coast guard said on Monday.

According to the survivors, on the afternoon of November 6, two passengers fell into the sea in an unknown location and are missing. Throughout the night, vessels in the area were alerted due to the drifting boat, and an aircraft from the EU border agency Frontex conducted search operations in the broader area.

In a separate incident, the coast guard rescue vessel located seven dead bodies on Monday in the sea area 10 nautical miles west-southwest of Kaloi Limenes.

The survivors told the coast guard they left on November 3 or 4, each paying 12,000–16,000 Libyan dinars, equal to 1,668.51–2,224.79 euros, for transport to Greece.

The Port of Heraklion in Crete, which is conducting the preliminary investigation, arrested two foreign nationals from Sudan, aged 28 and 16, on charges of “illegal entry into the country,” “facilitation [of illegal entry],” “formation of a criminal group,” and “endangerment resulting in death,” as the others identified them as their smugglers.

Hours later, a Moroccan-flagged container ship sailing in the area spotted a small boat carrying 18 foreign nationals 15 nautical miles off Kali Limenes. The coast guard rushed to the scene, where the 18 people were transferred to a coast guard vessel, while 13 dead bodies were recovered from the small boat.

Finally, a Frontex unmanned aerial vehicle located 40 foreign nationals on board a small boat 31 nautical miles southeast of Kali Limenes, as well as 100 foreign nationals 47 nautical miles southeast of Kali Limenes.

Greek islands have long been a point of arrival for migrants seeking to reach Europe by sea. UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, reported 41,695 sea arrivals in Greece in 2025 and 7,075 land arrivals, while the number of dead or missing was put at 107. Crete has seen a significant increase in arrivals from Libya.

Greece has toughened up its measures to deter irregular migration and has supported stricter EU legislation on issues such as ‘return hubs’, detention and deportation centres sited outside the European bloc.

World.title: Montenegro Registers 14 Citizens Fighting in Foreign Wars Since 2022
World.content:
A building hit by a Russian strike in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine, September 2026. Photo: EPA/MARIA SENOVILLA.

Montenegrin authorities said on Monday that 14 Montenegrin citizens have travelled to foreign conflict zones since 2022, adding that their recruitment took place mainly through the internet and digital communication platforms.

Montenegro’s National Operational Team for Combating Violent Extremism, Terrorism, Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, NOT, said the country’s security agencies are monitoring citizens heading to foreign battlefields and their potential return, while exchanging information with international partners.

“According to the available data, 14 Montenegrin citizens have been recorded as travelling to foreign conflict zones since 2022. Current findings indicate that recruitment takes place predominantly through the internet and digital communication platforms, involving cross-border contacts and transit through third countries,” NOT said.

Under Montenegrin law, participation in foreign armed formations is a crime punishable by six months to five years in prison. Organising trips to war zones and recruiting fighters carry prison sentences ranging from two to ten years.

Montenegro has issued two final convictions for participation in foreign armed formations. In 2017, Marko Banovic was sentenced to six months in prison for fighting alongside pro-Russian forces in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region. In 2018, Hamid Beharovic received the same sentence for joining Islamic State, IS, in Syria. Both received the minimum prison sentence prescribed by law.

In February 2025, Montenegro’s Higher Prosecution accused Danko Savic from Danilovgrad of fighting in Ukraine’s Luhansk region and of acquiring substantial financial assets as a result, including 1.5 million euros held in a bank account.

Savic was arrested last November, and police also searched 11 other people’s residences, seizing 24 firearms, more than 1,000 rounds of ammunition, bladed weapons, insignia of foreign armed formations and foreign documents.

A BIRN investigation found that Savic had been linked to pro-Russian Cossack organisations. Analysis of publicly available sources showed that he had attended numerous public events in Montenegro, the region and Russia wearing a Cossack uniform.

During his trial at Podgorica Higher Court, Savic claimed he has been a Russian citizen since 2023.

World.title: Polish Mass Shooter Dies of Injuries; Motive Remains Unclear
World.content:
A gunman who killed six people in Krakow and injured many more has died of his injuries in hospital, Polish police said on Monday, as prosecutors continue investigating Saturday’s mass shooting in Krakow in an attempt to establish what motivated the 24-year-old.

The shooter, identified in the foreign press as Michal Oksinski, killed six people in the southern Polish city and is believed to have murdered three family members earlier that day. Investigators said on Sunday they had found no letter or other document explaining the Polish man’s actions, either on him or in his car.

“We’ll see what the examination of his phone and electronic devices seized from his family home reveals,” prosecutor Eryk Stasielak said. Justice Minister and Prosecutor General Waldemar Zurek added that investigators had obtained “certain symbols associated with the suspect” and “some evidence that sheds more light on this whole tragedy”, but declined to elaborate, citing ongoing investigation.

At an evening press conference on Saturday, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that, according to preliminary findings, the gunmen had acted alone, held “very, very radical views” and was “fascinated by far-right ideologies”. Prosecutors, however, said on Sunday that searches had uncovered no evidence of active political or extremist involvement. Kierwinski’s remarks drew criticism from right-wing lawmakers, and on Sunday he clarified that the motive was still under investigation.

The attack, Poland’s deadliest mass shooting since World War II, took place shortly after 15:00 on Saturday, when the gunman drove onto Krakow’s historic Main Market Square, normally closed to traffic, and opened fire on pedestrians from his car. Wearing a bulletproof vest, military-style helmet and tactical equipment, he sent people fleeing into nearby restaurants, cafés and building entrances.

The six fatalities were: three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, a Polish man of about 50, a 32-year-old British citizen and a 51-year-old Austrian woman. Fifteen others were wounded, including five foreign nationals from Austria, Portugal, Germany, Britain and Russia.

Police responded within minutes. The first emergency call came at 15:00, with municipal guards arriving within two minutes and police firing their first shots at the attacker by 15:03. Officers exchanged fire with the shooter before disabling him. Two policemen were wounded in the exchange, and one remained in serious condition on Sunday, although officials said his health had improved. Both are being hailed in Poland as heroes.

“In the face of the tragedy in Krakow, we saw the best in people: the courage of police officers, the dedication of paramedics and the selfless help of ordinary people who rushed to save others,” Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on X.

Family killings and firearms

Following the attack, police discovered three bodies at the shooter’s family home in Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski: his parents and 21-year-old sister Magdalena, who studied painting at Krakow’s Academy of Fine Arts and had returned home for the weekend. Investigators believe he killed them before driving more than 160 kilometres to Krakow in his father’s car. Two family cats were also shot dead.

The gunman worked as a turner at a local refractory materials plant, had no criminal record and was not known to the police. He held a valid firearms license and used a civilian version of an AR-15 rifle in the Krakow attack.

His father, a sport-shooting enthusiast, was also a licensed gun owner. Between them, father and son held permits for 11 firearms. Investigators are examining which weapons were used in the attacks. Authorities believe the gunman acted alone.

Mass shootings are exceptionally rare in Poland, and Saturday’s killings were unprecedented in scale in the country’s postwar history. Other recent attacks were of political background and include the 2010 shooting at a Law and Justice party office in Lodz, which left one person dead, and the fatal stabbing of Gdansk mayor Pawel Adamowicz at a charity event in 2019.

The Krakow attack follows three unrelated stabbing incidents at schools across Poland, which took place within the space of one week in October. It also comes amid growing civilian gun ownership, with registered firearms more than doubling over the past decade to exceed 400,000 in 2025. A report published in May by Poland’s Supreme Audit Office (NIK) warned of serious gaps in firearms oversight, including the absence of mandatory periodic medical and psychological assessments for people holding sporting, hunting and collecting licences, which are generally issued indefinitely.

Poland declared two days of national mourning on Sunday and Monday. In Krakow, the hejnal – the trumpet call played every hour from the tower of St Mary’s Basilica at the Main Square, which is one of the symbols of the city – fell silent for the first time in 87 years.

World.title: Bye-Bye Serbia’s SPS, the Socialists Who Weren’t
World.content:
There are two untrue things one might have said about the Socialist Party of Serbia: that it was socialist, and that it was a party.

The founding of the SPS was auspicious: it inherited from the League of Communists of Serbia a large membership, considerable property, and formal and informal control of nearly every institution in the state.

Born as a party of power, it held nearly absolute power until it was removed in 2000, and acted like a party of [secondary] power afterwards.

If we want to talk about the SPS’s ideas, it never had many; the party was happy to parrot some slogans from the state socialist period to satisfy a part of its electoral base, and [like other parties in Serbia], to borrow most of its programme from Vojislav Seselj’s Serbian Radical Party, SRS, to [de]mobilise the rest.

What it had instead was a structure that became the foundation for how power would be exercised in Serbia in the coming decades: privatise public property to your wealthier supporters and hire the rest; marginalise alternatives while promoting fear; and maintain control over the media, the police and intelligence services, and the grey economy.

World.title: Kosovo Fortress Faces Uncertain Future After Flawed UNESCO Restoration
World.content:
A herd of unattended goats grazes freely beneath the walls of the fortress of Novoberde/Novo Brdo. One of Kosovo’s best-known cultural heritage sites, the fortress has been closed to visitors for more than eight years after its walls began to collapse less than two years after a major UNESCO-led renovation project.

Last month, shortly after approving a conservation project for the fortress, Kosovo’s Ministry of Culture took “emergency measures” to secure the medieval fortress and prevent further collapse.

Novoberde/Novo Brdo, 35 kilometres southeast of Pristina, was established near silver and gold mines in the medieval period. Mining and trade connected it to other regions, transforming it into an economic and commercial hub that drew Saxon miners and spurred the construction of the significant fortress.

World.title: ‘We Could Have Waited’: Caesareans the Norm for Pregnant Women in Greece
World.content:
Ioanna Vasilaki, an independent midwife and president of the Association of Independent Midwives of Greece, EAMME, said doctors will sometimes suggest inducing labour so the baby can be delivered during his or her shift. Often this ends in a C-section.

A third of respondents said their labour was induced; a quarter of these women said they were not told why.

Half who underwent C-sections said it was conducted as an emergency procedure.

Gourounti said it was “quite strange that when you go to give birth, one in two women ends up having some kind of difficulty or medical issue that arises during labour, necessitating an emergency C-section”.

According to Giorgos Daskalakis, professor of obstetrics and gynaecology at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and director of the first obstetrics and gynaecology clinic at the public Alexandra Hospital, some doctors in public hospitals outside Greece’s main urban centres work too many shifts, “so it is extremely difficult for them to spend too much time performing normal deliveries on women”.

Midwives say that often epidurals are not provided to women giving birth vaginally because there aren’t enough anaesthesiologists in Greece.

According to a report in the Greek newspaper Kathimerini in 2024, there are roughly 1,000 anaesthesiologists in Greece. The Hellenic Society of Anaesthesiology puts the figure at 750, in a country of some 10.5 million people. That’s far fewer than global healthcare bodies recommend.

“If you pay,” said Kentrifylli, “if you find a hospital doctor and they see you privately in their office and take you to the emergency room without it being time for you to give birth and put you in a labour induction position, then you will have the option of an epidural.”

Daskalakis said that issues with the legal framework in the event of alleged malpractice are also driving doctors to err on the side of caution by recommending C-sections.

“Consequently, every time a complication arises, the simple question asked is: ‘If a C-section had been performed, would things have turned out differently? Would it have been better?’ And the inevitable answer is that a caesarean section would obviously have led to a better obstetric outcome. Terrified of legal repercussions, doctors are highly susceptible to performing a C-section just to get through the process easily.”

In mid-2024, a law was passed allowing for the creation of Natural Birth Centres within public hospitals and independent institutions, where midwives would oversee deliveries. Amid what midwives say is resistance from obstetricians, no such centre has been opened in the public health system. One private centre was opened, but it closed in January this year, citing financial constraints.

Daskalakis is not enthusiastic about such birth centres. Instead, to encourage natural childbirth, he says staffing should be approved, uniform protocols introduced, and public awareness raised.

Financial incentives?

Daskalakis also argues for bonuses for hospitals that cut their own rate of C-sections.

“The money won’t go into someone’s pocket,” he said. “It will go to the hospital, which will automatically have an incentive to monitor the process because it will receive a bonus.”

Mouzalas, however, said the way a birth is handled should have nothing to do with “economic or ideological” considerations. “It should be related exclusively to scientific reasons”.

In 2017, the WHO proposed the use of the Robson classification as the global standard for assessing and comparing C-section rates across healthcare facilities.

The Robson classification was applied for the first time in 2019 by scientists in Greece to identify trends in caesarean births by examining 8,572 women in a private health facility. Just under 61 per cent of births were caesareans, 34.6 per cent were induced, and 30.7 per cent were births after a previous C-section.

However, in Greece, there is a complete absence of any oversight mechanism for C-sections.

“There is no system in place to require every hospital and every physician to provide a substantiated explanation as to why they deemed a C-section necessary,” said Gourounti, who expressed doubts regarding the widespread application of the Robson classification system in Greece.

“Each hospital and each doctor must provide a substantiated explanation as to why they deemed the choice of a caesarean section necessary,” she said.

Professor Athanasiadis told BIRN that the Robson classification is used in all Obstetrics and Gynaecology departments of the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, as well as at the Aretaieion and Alexandra public hospitals in Athens, though he stressed he cannot speak for all Ob-Gyn departments across Greece.

According to him, the Robson classification serves as an “internal audit” tool that helps refine clinical practice and reduce unnecessary C-sections. He also underlined that the Robson system can be implemented in public hospitals, but not in private ones, which do not have a departmental structure but instead rely on collaborating private physicians.

The role of the midwife

World.title: Bulgaria’s Foreign Ministry warns of public sector strike in Ireland planned for November 12
World.content:
A strike by public sector trade unions is planned for Ireland on November 12, Bulgaria’s Foreign Ministry said.

Local authorities are warning of protest marches and rallies in the time range of noon to 2pm, which will cover the entire country.

Marches and rallies are reportedly planned for the capital Dublin, they will pass through O’Connell Street and are expected to head towards government buildings; and the cities of Cork, Limerick, Galway, Waterford, Sligo, Tullamore and Letterkenny will also be affected by the protest marches.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs recommends that Bulgarian citizens located or residing in Ireland inform themselves and monitor current developments, including possible restrictions on certain public services, the ministry said.

(Photo: Gareth Jones, via Wikimedia Commons)

World.title: EU extends EU Military Assistance Mission supporting Ukraine for further two years
World.content:
European Union ministers adopted a decision on November 9 extending the mandate of the European Union Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM Ukraine) for a further two years, until November 15 2028, with a budget allocation of nearly 300 million euro for this period, a statement by the Council of the EU said.

The decision follows the recent strategic review of EUMAM.

In this context, the Council also decided to establish a presence in Ukraine to ensure direct and effective coordination with the Ukrainian military authorities, the UAF and like-minded international partners, thus ensuring that the EU training continues to evolve in line with the UAF’s needs.

The mission’s mandate is also enriched so as to focus on lessons learned from the battlefield and on strengthening military training in support of Ukraine’s defence agenda.

EUMAM Ukraine will continue to coordinate closely with other like-minded international partners such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Norway.

It will also cooperate with the Coalition of the Willing, as well as with Nato within the framework of the Nato Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine (NSATU) command.

EUMAM Ukraine is a key tool for the EU’s military support to Ukraine, with its core objective of contributing to enhancing the military capacity of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, the statement said.

The mission has trained more than 100 000 soldiers since it was established in October 2022 at Ukraine’s request.

World.title: German Christmas Market in Sofia’s City Garden to open on November 14
World.content:
Sofia’s now-traditional German Christmas Market in the City Garden opens in 2026 on November 14 and continues until December 21.

Bulgaria’s capital city’s oldest German Christmas Market (Deutscher Weihnachtsmarkt ) was first held in 2011, in its location in Alexander Battenberg Square near the Ivan Vazov National Theatre.

It features food and drink including mulled wine, crafts on sale, and fun for the children.

(Photo via the event’s Facebook page)

World.title: Anglican Church in Sofia holding Christmas Carol service on December 15
World.content:
The Anglican Church in Sofia is starting off its Christmas celebrations with a carol service on December 15 at 10am, the church said on its Facebook page.

“We will welcome our guest choir to support us as we join together to sing some familiar carols. Afterwards we will have seasonal refreshments including cakes and mulled wine,” the church said.

The doors are usually open by 9.30am, and you can enjoy some refreshments before the service, it said.

The church’s services are held in the chapel at 5 Oborishte Street, Sofia.

More information via Facebook.

World.title: Bulgaria’s consumer watchdog fines retailer Kaufland 75.7 M euro
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Consumer Protection Commission (CPC) said on November 9 that it fined supermarket chain Kaufland Bulgaria 75.7 million euro, citing “unfair trade practices towards Bulgarian food producers.”

CPC said that it launched an investigation against Kaufland Bulgaria in May, following an analysis of competition in the retail trade of agricultural and fast-moving food products.

The regulator said that it found Kaufland breached competition rules by seeking discounts from suppliers, taking advantage of its stronger negotiating position; applying further supplier price reductions by subtracting the cost of services rendered to suppliers; and by creating “unjustified barriers” for suppliers who sought a price increase for their goods.

CPC said that it imposed separate fines for those violations, which combined for 75.7 million euro. This is one of the largest amounts imposed as a fine by the regulator on a single entity.

In a statement, Kaufland Bulgaria said that it rejected in full both the accusations and the fines imposed on the company. It questioned the size of the fines, arguing that CPC’s decision disregarded European proportionality standards.

The company said that it intended to fight the fines in court (the fines can be appealed within 14 days of being handed down) and said that it would be “forced to review in full future investment in the country, including 200 million euro planned for the next three years ago.”

The statement further said that Kaufland would recommend that its parent, Schwarz Group, review its planned investments in Bulgaria. The group owns retailer Lidl, which also operates in the country.
