“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape,” Mr. Trump said at a White House briefing.

The sudden emergence of Mr. Huang's infidelity has rocked the political class and America's tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence.

Mr. Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Mr. Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes.

“I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Mr. Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

Mr. Huang -- a singular figure in the technology landscape and one of the world's wealthiest people -- has acknowledged that he had an affair, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia's website. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing.

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security,” Mr. Huang said in his letter.

Nvidia announced Sunday (November 8, 2026) it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Mr. Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The episode is also attracting congressional scrutiny, with top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries saying on Monday (November 9, 2026) that they are interested in investigating it further. Jeffries said the Nvidia issue came up during a closed-door session with the CIA director and the Director of National Intelligence that was primarily about Iran.

“We're going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened,” he said, “and what the implications are in terms of America's national security.”

China has denied plot to ensnare Nvidia chief

Mr. Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Mr. Xi.

“No, I don't think so,” Mr. Trump said. “I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honourable man.”

FBI counterintelligence investigations often examine efforts by foreign powers to spy on the United States, whether by surreptitiously stealing technology designed by American companies, covertly waging foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping public opinion or cultivating relationships with powerful political and industry figures. Such investigations can take years and do not necessarily culminate in criminal charges. China has been regarded across presidential administrations of both political parties as a persistent counterintelligence threat.

China denied on Monday (November 9, 2026) that it had engaged in an attempt to ensnare Mr. Huang. “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Mr. Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.

Huang has had Trump's ear on AI regulation

Mr. Huang and Nvidia play a critical role in the artificial intelligence industry, as many of the world's leading AI developers rely on the company's specialised chips to power their systems. Mr. Huang has also helped persuade Mr. Trump to take a lighter touch on regulating AI, arguing that existing laws could cover any security issues stemming from the technology and that individual companies should behave responsibly with the products they develop and release.

Mr. Huang has also lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Mr. Trump's approval to sell its H200 chips this year. It's unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.

The H200 chips are not Nvidia's most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to allow Nvidia to sell its less advanced H20 chips, designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.

In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press in June, Mr. Huang said: “National security should always be the top concern of all technologies. But having said that, you know, you have to be very specific about the risk that you're concerned about, before setting up policies for export controls.”

Nvidia shares dropped more than 4% in trading on Monday (November 9, 2026). Nvidia stock has shed roughly 11% of its value since last Wednesday (November 4, 2026).

Attention turns to data centre company in Singapore

The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data centre company whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia.

Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday (November 9, 2026) for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology.

“The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.

“Those questions require evidence rather than speculation,” he added in a text message to reporters.

Chinese media have largely focused on Mr. Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilising U.S.-China relations.

“Whenever China-U.S. relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows,” the state-owned Global Times said.

World.title: Prashant Kishor’s Brahminical criticism of BJP’s Hindutva
World.content:
Secularism is a modern, constitutional principle. In real-world politics, the manifestation of this principle is tested against a rather narrow yardstick: the fair representation of religious minorities, particularly Muslims. Generally speaking, the English-speaking secularists are unaware of the caste dynamics that come into play in the field operation of representative politics, and they are also resistant to the idea of discussing caste as a determinant.

The intersection of caste representation and religious representation can be framed as an intersection of social justice and secularism in electoral politics. The caste dynamics of politics are often manifested as critiques by non-Brahmins against Brahminism. A Brahmin perspective on these dynamics is rare, and that is the reason why Jan Suraaj Party founder Prashant Kishor’s address to fellow Brahmins in Bihar’s Mithila region is an extremely valuable opportunity to peer into the emerging thinking within the community. He said BJP’s Hindu communalism, which excludes Muslims from electoral calculations, has cost the Brahmins heavily and asked them to rethink their position.

World.title: Popular cinematographer Shaji Kumar passes away
World.content:
Noted cinematographer Shaji Kumar, 57, who cranked the camera for popular movies including Thudarum and Pulimurugan, died in Kochi on early Tuesday (November 10, 2026) morning.

The death occurred around 12.36 a.m. following cardiac failure, according to private hospital authorities in Kochi.

Representatives of the Film Employees Federation of Kerala (FEFKA) Directors’ Union said that he experienced uneasiness at his place of stay in Alappuzha after returning from the location of a new movie featuring actor Dileep on Saturday night (November 7, 2026). He was rushed to a nearby hospital and later shifted to Kochi. His condition worsened around Monday midnight (November 8, 2026). A native of Thiruvananthapuram, he has been staying in Perumbavoor, Ernakulam for a long time. He is survived by his wife, Smitha, and children, Aryan and Sooryan, they said.

Popular among filmmakers for his excellence in capturing mass action scenes, he had worked in nearly 50 movies in a career spanning over two decades. He had worked with leading movie directors.

The slick action scenes in movies like Pulimurugan, Naran, Odiyan, to name a few, had won the appreciation of the movie buffs. He was a much sought-after technician among the senior and new crop of filmmakers for his discipline and swift execution of even tough scenes.

The year 2025 was special for him after his collaboration with director Tharun Moorthy in Thudarum wove magic on screen and at the box office. The blockbuster movie raised his graph again, and the young filmmaker had no second choice but to fill the seat of cinematographer for his latest venture, Athimanoharam, featuring actor Mohanlal in the lead role. He was behind the camera for the forthcoming movie Ottakomban, featuring actor Suresh Gopi in lead role.

Some of his popular movies included Uthaman (2001), Valkannadi, Pakalpooram (2002), Ammakilikoodu, Pattanathil Sundaran (2003), Sathyam, Vesham (2004), Athbhuthadweep (2005), Mahasamudhram (2006), Nasrani (2007), Robinhood, Red Chillies (2009), Pokkiriraja (2010), Seniors, Ponnar Shankar (2011), The King and the Commissioner, Mallu Singh (2012), Ramaleela (2017), Madhura Raja (2019), Pathonpatham Nootandu (2022), Once Upon a Time in Kochi (2024).

World.title: Opposition demands ‘return to talks’ in AJK
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Calling for immediate talks with the Joint Awami Action Committee, the main opposition alliance claimed on Monday that a delegation of the Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayin-i-Pakistan (TTAP) was stopped from travelling to Azad Jammu and Kashmir.

The delegation was travelling to AJK to meet protesters, express solidarity, and assess the situation, but was stopped at Kahuta and not permitted to proceed further, TTAP spokesperson Hussein Ahmed Yousafzai said.

There is no justification for stopping a peaceful political delegation from accessing protesters, and the government ought to have provided an explanation for this action, he said.

The opposition alliance called for meaningful talks with protesters and sought practical progress on their demands, and sought an impartial inquiry into allegations of the unnecessary use of force.

The injured must be provided immediate and best medical facilities, and arrested individuals be granted access to justice in accordance with legal requirements, according to the alliance.

It also demanded that political and social representatives, including their delegation, be granted unhindered access to AJK.

Assuring that the Kashmiri people were not alone in their struggle, the opposition alliance said that it would raise a voice on every constitutional and legal forum for the protection of their constitutional, democratic, and fundamental human rights.

Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

World.title: Another Chaudhry slams Maryam over ‘development bias’
World.content:
• Hussain Elahi seemingly backs cousin Salik’s allegations against Punjab CM

• Azma Bokhari says CM’s hard work causing ‘considerable discomfort to certain political elements’

• Moonis’ jibe against Chaudhry Shujaat and Chaudhry Wajahat dispels impression ‘family reunion’ is in the offing

GUJRAT: What began as a tiff between a federal minister and a provincial chief minister has apparently re-ignited the political family feud among the Chaudhrys of Gujrat, whose various members have been drawn into the latest war of words between the two coalition partners, PML-N and PML-Q.

The latest salvo was fired by PML-Q MNA Chaudhry Hussain Elahi, who echoed his cousin Chaudhry Salik Hussain’s criticism of Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz over alleged corruption and a discriminatory approach in the allocation of development funds for various constituencies.

Speaking at a recent public gathering at Qila Islam Nagar near Tanda, Hussain Elahi accused the incumbent chief minister of blocking uplift funds for schemes launched during the tenure of former CM Chaudhry Parvez Elahi in 2022.

He claimed that the provincial government had spent Rs11 billion on a plane for the chief minister, but could not release Rs3bn earmarked for the completion of ongoing development schemes in his constituency.

He questioned whether the purchase of a plane was more important than the completion of public welfare schemes, alleging that only Lahore’s development seemed to be the rulers’ priority, while the rest of the province was being ignored.

The tiff between the Punjab chief minister and the federal minister for overseas Pakistanis was sparked by remarks the latter made during a television appearance earlier this month, when he lavished praise on former CM Parvez Elahi and took a swipe at the incumbent provincial chief executive.

In response, CM Maryam had challenged Chaudhry Salik Hussain to prove his claims and sent him a legal notice.

“If you have evidence, bring it forth — otherwise I will drag you to court,” she said. She also asked him why he remained a minister in a government that he considered corrupt.

At the time, she maintained that the PML-Q leader’s actual grouse was neither a matter of corruption nor progress. The issue, she said, was that she changed the deputy commissioner (DC) of Gujrat a few days ago whereas Salik had wanted a DC of his choice to be appointed.

Gujrat’s problems

Recalling CM Maryam’s legal threats, Chaudhry Hussain Elahi said: “Let me tell her that I will drag the whole Punjab government into court, the people of Gujrat are never scared of going to court.”

He said the CM claimed to have spent Rs12bn for Gujrat city, but the people knew very well what the situation in the city was, despite these claims. A number of crucial roads in his constituency had remained dilapidated or incomplete for the last four years, he maintained.

He alleged the whole province knew about corruption in the Suthra Punjab and Model Village projects, adding that the rulers would have to account for their misdeeds.

Speaking on the occasion, his father Chaudhry Wajahat Hussain — the younger brother of PML-Q chief Chaudhry Shujaat — also praised the tenure of Parvez Elahi, recalling the public welfare schemes launched under his stewardship.

Responding to these latest remarks, Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari said that the development initiatives being undertaken by CM Maryam’s administration across Punjab were causing “considerable discomfort to certain political elements”. Sharing a clip of Hussain’s speech on X, Ms Bokhari said that those who had failed to change the conditions of Gujrat despite holding high public office for years, were now criticising Lahore “without any shame”.

Family ties

The political allegiances of the Chaudhrys of Gujrat are currently split between different camps. Even though they belong to the same party, PML-Q MNA Chaudhry Wajahat Hussain and his sons Hussain and Musa Elahi are not on very good terms with the sons of party elder Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain — Salik and Shafay — both of whom have been members of the federal and provincial cabinet, respectively, for two-and-a-half years.

Moreover, the PTI-aligned Parvez Elahi camp is also annoyed with Wajahat et al, as Musa secured the Punjab Assembly seat from Kunjah – the same seat Parvez Elahi had won at least eight times since 1985.

In recent speeches, however, Wajahat and his sons have seemingly gone soft on their rivals, creating the impression that some sort of reconciliation was on the cards.

However, Parvez’s son Moonis has dispelled the impression of a possible ‘family reunion’, saying that his camp would continue their “policy of social distancing” with the scions of Shujaat.

Taking to X on Monday, Moonis directly named the Chaudhry Wajahat camp, saying that his children were “making all this noise” because his brother Chaudhry Shujaat’s children had “kept everything for themselves”, leaving them without any ministerial portfolios. “Had the PML-N also made them ministers, they too would have been sitting happily today,” he tweeted.

Zulqernain Tahir in Lahore also contributed to this report

Published in Dawn, November 10th, 2026

World.title: ‘From terrorism to tourism’: Kundi presents vision for KP as South Air launches Peshawar-Lahore flight
World.content:
Governor Faisal Karim Kundi on Monday expressed his determination to take Khyber Pakhtunkhwa “from terrorism to tourism” as carrier South Air launched another route from Peshawar to Lahore.

He made the remarks while speaking at the inaugural ceremony of South Air’s flight route between Peshawar’s Bacha Khan International Airport and Lahore’s Allama Iqbal International Airport, providing the public another domestic air option between the two cities.

The ceremony took place at the Peshawar airport, from where the inaugural flight — with Kundi on board — departed at 1:56pm.

Addressing the ceremony, Kundi announced that his administration “has begun working on T-to-T: from terrorism to tourism”.

KP has been under governor’s rule and emergency since Oct 11, when the federal government took the measures citing the PTI-led KP government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the counterterrorism fight.

“We have begun a journey to build an evolving, bright and strong Khyber Pakhtunkhwa,” Kundi said, adding that South Air would provide support in this objective.

“We will end terrorism and promote tourism,” Kundi affirmed, reiterating his pledge to eliminate terrorism in the province, which has been facing security challenges.

“This (T-to-T) can also mean from terrorism to trade; trade is very important,” he added.

The governor contended that the additional flight option will boost both trade and tourism as it reduces a 10-hour road trip to a one-hour journey.

“This is why we want connectivity in different cities, like Lahore, Quetta; in the future we will have connectivity with Chitral in the future as well,” Kundi said, adding that South Air had the KP government’s support.

The event was attended by South Air’s Chief Executive Officer Nishat Fatima, the joint secretary from the Ministry of Defence, KP MPAs, senior government and airport officials, and representatives of the business community.

“The commencement of the new service adds another air connectivity option to the domestic networks of PAA’s (Pakistan Airports Authority) airports, facilitating passengers travelling between Peshawar and Lahore,” read a handout by South Air.

It added that upon the plane’s landing in Lahore, Kundi was received by Punjab Senior Minister Marriyum Aurangzeb, Provincial Minister for Specialised Healthcare Khawaja Salman Rafique and MPA Ramesh Kumar.

In a meeting on Sunday, Kundi and Gilgit-Baltistan Chief Minister Amjad Hussain had agreed to initiate negotiations to settle boundary disputes between the two regions and improve air connectivity.

The discussions focused on air links between Gilgit and Islamabad, where passengers have long faced difficulties because of limited flight operations and frequent cancellations.

During the meeting, representatives of South Air also held discussions with the GB chief minister regarding the introduction of additional air services.

In July, South Air launched services from Karachi to Quetta, via Turbat, and to Islamabad, via Bahawalpur, with inaugural flights departing from Jinnah International Airport.

World.title: 8 Pakistanis among global recipients of 2026 Diana Award recognising their social work
World.content:
Eight Pakistanis have been recognised this year by The Diana Award for their inspirational initiatives surrounding education, health and climate action.

They are among the 198 recipients from around the world of the award, a “global honour celebrating young social activists driving positive change in their communities and beyond”.

“Rooted in the legacy of Diana, Princess of Wales, the award celebrates young people who are working tirelessly to change the world — particularly those championing change for individuals from socio-economic [sic] disadvantaged backgrounds,” reads the charity’s website.

Each year, up to 200 exceptional young people are honoured with the Diana Award, which recognises youth-led projects and initiatives that align with four key Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): quality education, good health and wellbeing, reducing inequality, and climate action.

The Pakistani recipients are Ali Ahmed Manj, who wants to improve healthcare access; Areeba Suleman, founder of SheRise Pakistan; Mariam Rehman, heading The Pro-Justice Project; Muhammad Ibrahim, who used digital mapping to help flood-affected people; Noor Abdul Ghani, who encourages girls in science and technology; Reya Yassir Khawaja, who creates awareness on menstrual hygiene; Sara Ali, who supports polio campaigns; and Vishal Parkash, who works on improving financial access for marginalised communities.

They received letters from Kensington Palace, the office of Prince William and his wife Kate, as well as Prince Harry, for the awards announced on Nov 4.

In the letter to Suleman, seen by Dawn and seemingly identical for all honourees, Prince William praised her resilience, courage, compassion and belief in kindness.

“The impact you are having on your community and the lives of those around you is remarkable,” the letter read.

“The world we live in today can feel challenging and uncertain, and creating change is not easy. Yet, in the face of these challenges, you have shown extraordinary resilience, courage and a belief in the power of kindness to make things better.”

The Prince of Wales added: “My mother, in whose memory you receive The Diana Award today, would be so proud of your achievements and the deep care you show for others.”

In his letter, Prince Harry wrote, “This award is deeply personal to me, not only because it carries my mother’s name, but because it champions her belief that young people have the power to change the world.”

Noting that the recipient made it their mission to solve challenges in their communities, he stated: You are already leading with purpose and the rest of us have a responsibility to listen, invest in you and give you real opportunities to take that work further.”

8 Pakistanis awarded this year

“This year’s Diana Award recipients represent some of the most inspirational young people from across the UK and around the world,” the charity noted.

The award’s website also provided details of each recipient’s work for which they were recognised, as of their nominations in October 2025. Here is what the young Pakistani honourees have done to bring a positive change in their surroundings:

Ali Azan Ahmed Manj

Manj has made dedicated efforts to improve access to healthcare for underserved communities across Karachi and rural Sindh.

“Over five years with Humanity Initiative, he has helped lead student-led medical camps and collaborations with NGOs, providing longitudinal healthcare to communities with limited resources,” the website read.

It noted that Ali was helping to make healthcare “more accessible and equitable”, as his Humanity Initiative has served over 10,000 patients.

Areeba Suleman

Founder of SheRise Pakistan, Dera Ghazi Khan’s first student-led youth organisation, Suleman has built a “growing network of young women advancing educational equity across south Punjab”.

She has directly impacted more than 6,000 students, and her work has expanded access to leadership opportunities for young women, empowering them to become active participants in shaping their communities, the website noted.

Mariam Rehman

A Law and Finance graduate, Rehman was studying at university when she founded The Pro-Justice Project, a pro bono initiative supported by a network of more than 250 volunteer lawyers.

“Together, they have supported over 1,000 cases across Pakistan. Mariam has also provided free debate coaching to more than 200 girls, helping them develop confidence, critical thinking and public-speaking skills.”

The Diana Award noted she was creating opportunities for people to understand and exercise their rights through legal advocacy, community engagement and youth leadership.

Muhammad Ibrahim

Ibrahim decided to use technology to help those affected by natural disasters after noticing how floods could destroy homes, livelihoods and access to essential services.

He collaborated with the Punjab government on GIS-based damage assessments and field surveys across high-risk areas, combining digital mapping with on-the-ground verification to support fairer compensation planning for nearly 300,000 families, The Diana Award highlighted.

Ibrahim had also mobilised communities through the Murree Rainwater Harvesting Project, which provided free rooftop systems to around 4,000 families.

“By combining technology with community action, he is helping people recover from disasters while addressing water scarcity and reducing the daily burden of collecting water on women and girls.”

Noor Abdul Ghani

Aiming to close the gender gap in science and technology, Ghani founded WinSci Pakistan to encourage more girls and women to see themselves represented in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM).

A machine learning engineer and Master’s student in Artificial Intelligence, Ghani helps students through STEM sessions, school outreach and scholarship guidance.

“Under her leadership, WinSci has delivered programmes in underprivileged schools across Pakistan and received the Science Outreach Award from Springer Nature and Estée Lauder Companies. Noor is helping create a future where more young women have the opportunity to participate and succeed in STEM.”

Reya Khawaja

A student at Nord Anglia International School Dubai, Khawaja founded SAFE — Sanitation and Female Empowerment — in collaboration with the KCS Foundation to challenge the stigma surrounding menstrual health.

Through the initiative, she has distributed menstrual hygiene packs and organised educational awareness sessions that encourage open conversations about periods.

“Her work focuses on ensuring that girls in underserved communities have access to essential resources as well as the knowledge and confidence to discuss their health openly,” The Diana Award notes.

Sara Ali

Witnessing gaps in health awareness, Ali founded the Pakistan Polio Project to “strengthen vaccine confidence, combat misinformation, support frontline health workers and protect zero-dose children”.

Through community outreach, she has inspired more than 100 volunteers to educate families, promote immunisation awareness and support progress towards a polio-free Pakistan.

“Her work brings young people into the heart of public health advocacy, showing how youth leadership and community education can help build greater understanding and protect children from preventable illness,” the website reads.

Vishal Parkash

Growing up as a Hindu in Pakistan, Parkash became passionate about creating greater financial and legal access for excluded communities, The Diana Award noted.

He founded RUBAN, connecting more than 200 women artisans across Karachi, Lahore and Sindh with formal markets and generating over Rs5 million in revenue for its artisans, according to the website.

Parkash also founded Emprende, providing financial and legal literacy training to refugees and migrants around the world.

“Alongside this, he co-leads Rem & Company, a global student-run consulting network with more than 30 chapters, and founded Konnect to advance disability advocacy. From Karachi to Berlin, Lusaka and Cape Town, Vishal continues turning financial exclusion into entrepreneurial opportunity.”

World.title: Trump's 'Board of Peace' says Israel too slow as floods ravage Gaza
World.content:
United States President Donald Trump’s “Board of Peace” said on Monday that Israel needed to act immediately to help war-battered Gaza cope with impending winter, saying measures ahead of deadly floods had been insufficient.

“The situation no longer represents simply a threat posed by the approaching winter, but an immediate humanitarian emergency,” the Board of Peace said in a statement.

Heavy rain over the past two days has swept away tens of thousands of tents in the territory, where virtually the entire population has been displaced at least once, and killed at least five people, according to authorities in Gaza.

The Board of Peace, tasked with implementation of an October 2025 US-brokered ceasefire announced between Israel and Hamas, said it had been warning Israel, which controls all entry into the territory, of the need to prepare both for the winter and seasonal flooding.

Moments before the statement came out, the Israeli military claimed it had allowed more than 8,200 trucks to enter the Gaza Strip with supplies including 91,000 tents.

The Board of Peace acknowledged steps Israel said it took but noted that they remain “insufficient”.

“We call on the leadership of the current Government of Israel to act immediately to authorise and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterisation and humanitarian supplies,” it said.

Israel has taken a biting tone against Hamas over the floods, saying the group should have invested in infrastructure instead of weaponry.

“Hamas doesn’t get to escape responsibility every time it rains,” the Israeli foreign ministry posted on Sunday on X.

The Board of Peace also called on Hamas to abide by commitments under the ceasefire.

Despite the truce, Israel has kept up nearly daily strikes in Gaza.

Israel’s relentless campaign prior to the so-called ceasefire killed over 74,000 Palestinians and has left it increasingly isolated on the world stage, with Amnesty International , Human Rights Watch and experts declaring its actions in Gaza as a “genocide”, which Tel Aviv rejects.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political survival following tight elections last month, has vowed to kill anyone involved in Hamas’s Oct 7, 2023 attack, the deadliest day ever for Israel.

World.title: Punjab CM says those who 'raise their hand against a helpless woman' will suffer the same fate
World.content:
Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz said on Monday that those who dared to “raise their hand against a helpless woman” would suffer the same fate.

“Dare to raise your hand against a helpless woman who leaves her home every day to earn an honest living, and be prepared to face the same humiliation. She will have the right and the opportunity to slap you back,” she said in a post on the social media platform X.

Her comments came in response to a video of a man physically assaulting a salesgirl. According to a statement from Faisalabad police on Monday, the incident took place at Kohinoor Plaza. It said the salesgirl had informed the man that the shop was exclusively meant for women; CCTV footage shared by police on X showed that it was a lingerie shop.

Police said the “enraged” man then physically assaulted the girl, with CCTV footage showing him yanking her from behind the counter and eventually throwing her to the ground. The statement added that the suspect had been arrested and legal proceedings had been initiated against him.

According to the information shared in a visual post by the Punjab chief minister, the incident took place on Nov 8. It added that the shop owner had come to the store to collect rent, when the girl asked him to leave as it was a lingerie shop and contact the business owner.

“No one, no matter how wealthy, influential, or powerful, can now intimidate, exploit or harm an ordinary citizen with impunity. The state will stand firmly with the vulnerable and respond decisively to those who misuse their power,” CM Maryam asserted on X, also sharing a video of the alleged victim hitting the suspect in question.

“The days of the powerful getting away with abusing the powerless are over. The state will hit back!” she said.

A first information report (FIR), available with Dawn, was filed on the woman’s complaint at the Madina Town police station on Monday.

It invoked Sections 354 (assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty) and 509 (word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC).

In the FIR, the woman said she was working as an employee as usual at a lingerie shop on Nov 8, when the shop’s owner came to receive the rent. The woman explained that the rent was paid in instalments on various dates, so she paid him Rs5,000 and asked him to seek the rest later.

She alleged that the man escalated the matter and “started arguing about taxes”, at which point she told him that as a mere employee, she did not have the authority to decide on tax-related matters and urged him to speak to the business owner.

The woman said the man “adopted extremely unethical and insulting behaviour” with her and threatened to slap her. Despite her repeatedly telling him to take up the matter with the owner, the man began physically assaulting her and kicked her, the FIR said.

Last month, CM Maryam also took notice of a man who physically assaulted a woman riding a scooty on Mozang Ring Road in Lahore.

At the time, she said he had spoken to the victim and told her “she should slap the man as many times as he had slapped her”.

“But she said that, for her, it was enough that the government had made her feel protected, cared for, and assured that justice was on her side,” CM Maryam said. She had later also expressed displeasure at the suspect being granted bail.

In a similar incident last month, a man was accused of assaulting a petrol pump employee in Lahore. CM Maryam then shared a video of the employee slapping the arrested suspect while a cop attempted to stop him.

“This is a tight slap in the face of those entitled, spoiled brats who look down upon the poor as if they were lesser human beings,” CM Maryam said.

“They arrogantly believe that money and power put them above the law, allowing them to exploit, intimidate, and act with impunity,” she added.

The chief minister declared that she stood “firmly with the oppressed, regardless of how powerful their oppressors may be”.

World.title: Turkiye steel factory blast kills 16; probe launched
World.content:
An explosion ripped through a steel plant in western Turkiye on Monday, killing 16 people and injuring 13, President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said, announcing investigations into the tragedy.

Eight workers were trapped at the HABAS steel factory about 60 kilometres north of the port city of Izmir, where the blast struck around midday (2pm PKT), governor Suleyman Elban said.

Footage posted online showed a huge cloud of thick smoke pouring into the sky as flames appeared to engulf a tall structure within the HABAS Demir Celik plant in Aliaga.

“The circumstances surrounding this tragic incident, which has deeply saddened our nation, including how and why it happened, whether there was any negligence and who bears responsibility, will be established,” Erdogan said on television, adding that two of the injured were in serious condition.

HABAS is a privately owned group and one of Turkiye’s top steel producers.

Crane collapse

According to Izmir’s governor, the blast was caused by an overhead crane that collapsed into a large industrial furnace used during the liquid steel casting process.

“While a boiler replacement operation was being carried out at the HABAS iron and steel factory, the overhead crane fell and landed in the arc furnace, causing an explosion in the steel mill behind it,” Elban told reporters, referring to a large electric-powered steelmaking furnace.

Workers walk after an explosion at an iron and steel manufacturing plant in the Aliaga district of Turkiye’s coastal Izmir province on November 9, 2026. — Reuters

An eyewitness, Deniz Ulker, said it felt like an “earthquake”.

“When I looked at the factory across the street, thick black smoke was coming out. A fire broke out where the chimney was,” Ulker told Anadolu news agency.

“It was like a bomb going off,” said Turan Ilbay, who works as a truck driver at the factory and also spoke to Anadolu.

Izmir mayor Cemil Tugay said on X that rescue teams were “continuing their work to remove the collapsed platform” and that those affected were factory workers.

Safety issues

Workers’ groups said there was a long record of safety issues at HABAS. Contacted by an AFP journalist, HABAS declined to answer questions.

Before Monday’s explosion, the Evrensel daily said at least 11 workers had died over the past decade while working there.

Turkiye’s Labour Party, a small Marxist faction, said on X it was the third time in three weeks that workers had lost their lives at HABAS.

It said one man died after falling eight metres from a ladder on Oct 21, while another died when a tyre he was inflating on a construction machine exploded.

Outside the hospital where the injured were taken, two representatives of the leftist Aegean Workers’ Collective were arrested while trying to make a statement about workplace safety issues, a group spokesman said.

“The HABAS management’s blind greed for profit has resulted in a major disaster today,” their spokesman Oktay Turk told AFP.

“Those responsible for this massacre must be brought to justice,” he said, calling for the immediate release of his colleagues.

The pro-Kurdish DEM party, in a statement, called the disaster “unacceptable”.

“The causes of the explosion, any possible negligence and lack of oversight must be revealed transparently, and no one responsible must go unpunished.”

World.title: Water surges into nearby work areas after rock mass collapse at Tarbela Dam
World.content:
SWABI: A rock mass collapsed at the Tarbela Dam 5th Extension Project (T-5) construction site on Monday, causing a surge of water to enter nearby work areas, said the Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda).

An emergency was declared following the collapse; construction work was suspended and workers were directed to move to safer areas. However, no loss of life was reported in the incident.

In a statement, Wapda said that water entered the under-construction power house area and a tunnel of the T-5 project after a weak rock mass collapsed during excavation work, prompting the evacuation of workers.

The authority said the incident occurred during excavation of the 2nd Bench Connecting Tunnel, when the collapse allowed water from the Intake Pit to enter the tunnel and power house area.

“All workers were immediately evacuated safely,” the statement said, adding that the water from the Intake Pit had been completely drained and no further water was entering the downstream work sites.

Wapda said dewatering work at the under-construction power house had also started.

Authorities were assessing whether the tunnel, power house and other structures in the working area had sustained any damage, Deputy Commissioner Haripur Waseem Ahmed said, quoting officials of the T-5 project.

Senior Wapda officers, the project engineer and the contractor were assessing the situation to address any challenges to the T-5 project, the statement added.

The authority also dismissed reports circulating about the collapse of the T-5 tunnel, saying the main tunnel, under-construction power house, tailrace culvert and switchyard had not been damaged.

It further said there had been no injuries or loss of life among the workforce.

There is no threat of flooding or inundation in areas downstream of Tarbela at present, a senior district administration official said.

Meanwhile, Swabi Deputy Commissioner Nasarullah Khan said that additional water had been released from Tarbela Dam due to “unavoidable” reasons and was expected to increase the flow and level of water in the Indus River.

“All citizens are requested to take precautionary measures and completely avoid bathing, swimming and boating in the Indus River to prevent any untoward incident,” he said.

The deputy commissioner also urged the public to ensure their own safety and that of their families and follow public safety notices.

“Citizens should not pay heed to rumours and should visit our official page for authentic information,” Khan added.

Earlier in July, a government-constituted inquiry committee held all three key stakeholders — the contractor, consultant and employer (Wapda) — responsible for the cofferdam collapse at the 1,530MW T-5 Project, citing post-contract unauthorised design changes as one of the main reasons for the incident.

The collapse contributed to at least a two-year delay and more than 285 per cent cost escalation in the project, whose cost has risen from Rs82 billion to Rs317bn.

The project was scheduled for completion by the end of June 2028, instead of 2026, before Monday’s incident.

The fifth extension project has an installed capacity of 1,530MW. The World Bank and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank are providing $390 million and $300m respectively for its construction. Once completed, Tarbela’s total installed capacity will rise from 4,888MW to 6,418MW.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
