World.title: Russell Brand's ex Jemima Goldsmith accuses him of 'violence and abuse'
World.content:
Jemima Goldsmith, a former partner of Russell Brand, has accused him of committing "violence, coercive control and abuse" against her.

Brand, 51, was sentenced in the United Kingdom on Monday, local time, to 10 years and six months in jail for the rape and sexual assault of four women between 2004 and 2009.

He was also acquitted of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Jemima Goldsmith says she experienced violence and abuse while in a relationship with the actor. (AP: Supplied/Evan Agostini/Invision)

In a statement posted online hours after Brand's sentencing, Ms Goldsmith said she felt she needed to share her own experience with the convicted rapist.

"Firstly, and most importantly, I am and have always been strongly and unequivocally on the side of all of Brand's victims," she said. "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse. "I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident. "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children. "I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. "Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact. "Over several years, I assisted the journalists who finally exposed him; Ros Urwin, Louisa Compton and Dorothy Byrne. "I also undertook to testify in court to his abusiveness, if the newspaper that published the victims' accounts were ever to be sued. "I am glad and relieved that Russell Brand has finally faced justice."

Ms Goldsmith, who was once married to former Pakistani cricketer and prime minister Imran Khan, dated Brand between 2013 and 2014.

He then married Laura Brand (née Gallacher), his current wife, in 2017.

Russell Brand jailed for more than 10 years Russell Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault relating to four women between 2004 and 2009.

Ms Brand testified during her husband's four-week trial, and said his promiscuity left her "heartbroken" years before their marriage.

The pair met in Edinburgh in August 2006, when Ms Brand was 19 years old.

She told the jury she "felt entirely cared for and looked after by Russell" during their sex life, and described him as "caring, he's kind, he's a wonderful father".

"I was aware that he liked women and I was aware towards the latter part of the year that he was engaging with other women," she told the court.

" It was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous. "

Brand's rape conviction relates to a fan who was 21 when he met her after one of his London shows in 2009. He later raped her at his home.

Russell Brand in Los Angeles in 2009. (Reuters: Danny Moloshok)

His sexual assault convictions relate to his abuse of a woman in a bar in 2004, another woman at a radio station and a third woman he worked with in 2009.

In sentencing, Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a serial predator.

"The whole episode reeks of casual disrespect and your belief that fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live," he said.

"Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no."

'He was a vile predator'

In addition to Ms Brand and Ms Goldsmith, the comedian dated and interacted with a string of other high-profile women through the early 2000s.

Russell Brand’s path to prison The disgraced British entertainer-turned-conspiracy theorist charted a course towards fame and notoriety before a criminal trial in London found him to be a sexual predator.

In 2006, Australian pop star Dannii Minogue told the UK's Mirror Brand had acted like a "vile predator" toward her and once followed her down a corridor.

"He is completely crazy and a bit of a vile predator. I certainly don't think he has cured his sex addiction, that's for sure. He wouldn't take no for an answer," she said.

"He always goes that step too far. Never quite far enough to slap his face, but usually too far."

Brand's relationships also included supermodel Kate Moss and Spice Girl Geri Horner (née Halliwell), but his most famous partner was singer Katy Perry between 2009 and 2010.

Perry and Brand first met in 2008 before marrying in 2010. They filed for divorce in 2011, citing irreconcilable differences.

Brand and his former partner, singer Katy Perry, at a film premiere in London in 2011. (Reuters: Paul Hackett)

She told the Los Angeles Times in 2013 that Brand told her he wanted a divorce via text message on New Year's Eve in 2011.

"At first when I met him, he wanted an equal, and I think a lot of times strong men do want an equal, but then they get that equal and they're like, I can't handle the equalness," she said.

"He didn't like the atmosphere of me being the boss on tour. So that was really hurtful, and it was very controlling, which was upsetting.

"I felt a lot of responsibility for it ending, but then I found out the real truth, which I can't necessarily disclose because I keep it locked in my safe for a rainy day.

"I let go and I was like: This isn't because of me; this is beyond me. So I have moved on from that."

Perry has not commented on the allegations made against Brand or his conviction.

Russell Brand will not be eligible for release from prison until he serves two-thirds of his sentence, or at least seven years. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

In court, the jury also heard from two former partners who spoke of Brand's character.

A dance teacher who dated him for three years from 1996 described him as "gentle, warm, kind and adventurous" with a "bad boy reputation".

She said their relationship ended because she felt she could no longer trust him to remain faithful.

Another woman who met Brand in London in 1999 said he was "undoubtedly promiscuous" but they never engaged in sexual activity without consent.

Following Brand's sentencing, Metropolitan Police Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said the women who shared their experiences had done so with "immense bravery, dignity and resilience".

World.title: Liquidators probe multi-million-dollar sale of collapsed Mundella assets
World.content:
The former director of West Australian dairy company, Mundella Foods, says he "literally has nothing" left and has denied any improper transactions following the company's collapse into liquidation.

Hayden Russell is facing scrutiny from liquidators over what they say could be more than $2 million in potentially unreasonable director-related and insolvent trading transactions.

Liquidators are also investigating whether the multi-million-dollar sale of Mundella and the Margaret River Dairy Company (MRDC) to dairy processor, Artisanal Market, constitutes an "uncommercial" deal.

Creditors are still owed $12.5 million following the collapse of Mundella Foods and associated companies.

In a statutory report filed to the corporate regulator, liquidators at Mackay Goodwin said they had uncovered $778,000 of potentially unreasonable director-related transactions, including "frequent cash withdrawals".

They noted that further investigations were required to determine whether those withdrawals were used in the company's operations or were unreasonable.

The liquidators also found Mundella may have traded insolvent from as early as July 1, 2024, with transactions totalling $1.3 million.

The report did not make final findings and noted that further investigations would require additional funding.

Former director Hayden Russell. (Supplied: Kira Price)

'I acted in good faith'

Mr Russell denied making any unreasonable transactions, telling the ABC he acted "in good faith" at all times.

He claims he used cash withdrawals to pay for operations and workers' wages and had spent a few hundred thousand dollars of personal savings on the business.

"I literally have nothing now, because I put every single penny I had into there to try keep it afloat," he said.

The liquidators' report shows workers, who are priority creditors, are still owed almost $940,000 in unpaid wages, superannuation and entitlements.

Secured and unsecured creditors are owed a further $3 million and $8.5 million respectively.

Liquidators told creditors it was unlikely Mr Russell had the financial capacity to meet any claims brought against him, and further investigations would not be possible without further funding from creditors.

"At this stage of the Liquidation, it is unlikely that there will be a dividend to any class of creditors," the report stated.

Liquidators say they have identified potentially unreasonable transactions from the previous owner of Mundella. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

The last-minute sale

Last month, Artisanal Market announced its subsidiary had purchased the Mundella and MRDC brands, properties and assets.

The liquidators' report states the sale was agreed to on July 17, just weeks before creditors voted to put the companies, albeit what little was left of them, into liquidation.

The seller was mortgagee and private lender, Bowral Capital.

Bowral and another secured lender, Bizcap, received $5.85 million and almost $1 million respectively from the final sale of the dairy companies' property and assets in October.

Liquidators said investigations into whether the property deal was uncommercial were ongoing.

An uncommercial transaction occurs when a company makes a deal that a reasonable person in its circumstances would not have agreed to.

"For the avoidance of any doubt, proceeds from the Sale remain insufficient to repay Bowral and Bizcap in full for the amount owed by the Company and MRDC," liquidators said.

" Accordingly, the Sale will not result in any recoveries for other creditors. "

Bowral has been approached for comment on the liquidators' investigation of the sale.

The former director of Mundella and Margaret River Dairy Company said his financial rescue plan would have worked if his primary lender had provided more money. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

Failed bid for funds

The dairy companies were put into liquidation in August following a failed financial rescue plan set out in a Deed of Company Arrangement (DOCA).

The liquidators' report confirmed the companies failed to meet several obligations to creditors under the agreement, including $40,000 of unpaid funds to the Deed Fund.

Bowral acquired the properties and assets during the ongoing DOCA period from original lender Oak Capital, which went into its own liquidation in May this year.

Separately, Oak Capital is being sued in the federal court by the corporate watchdog, ASIC, for alleged unconscionable conduct and predatory lending practices, which it denies.

Mr Russell claims the DOCA would have succeeded if the subsequent mortgagee Bowral had lent him more money.

In a statement, Bowral said the company was not a party to the DOCA, "nor did it impose any obligation on Bowral Capital to provide further funding".

"Bowral Capital's responsibility was to manage the fund and protect the interests of its investors," the company said.

World.title: Woolies plans facial recognition trial in two Canberra supermarkets
World.content:
Supermarket chain Woolworths is considering a trial of facial recognition technology in two stores in Canberra in an attempt to better protect staff members from violent offenders frequenting their stores.

Woolworths stores in Woden and Gungahlin are being considered for the trial, and if it goes ahead, the technology could be implemented by the end of the month.

Woolworths' head of violence prevention Sarah Faorlin told 666 ABC Radio Canberra these two stores were chosen because of the "high number of workplace protection orders (WPOs) in place".

"The ACT unfortunately does have high levels of violence and aggression," Ms Faorlin said.

" The proposed trial of this technology will target known repeat violent, abusive or threatening offenders, including those served by court-ordered WPOs in the ACT. "

The head of violence prevention at Woolworths says if the technology is implemented, all customer's faces will be scanned but their profiles will be deleted if they are not on a watch list. (ABC News: Shaun Kingma)

Workplace protection orders are legal orders used to prevent and reduce workplace violence, and the ACT was the first to introduce them in 2016.

Ms Faorlin said Woolworths had seen "great success" using WPOs in the territory, but "assessing the merits of facial recognition technology in-store is another way we can help protect team members and customers".

"The aim is to use facial recognition technology to actively monitor for repeat violent and aggressive offenders who frequent our stores to protect team safety," she said.

Ms Faorlin said Woolworths had seen a 460 per cent increase in "unacceptable incidents" in their stores nationally since 2020.

"It is appalling that our team members continue to face unprovoked violence and aggression when they're just trying to do their jobs," she said.

" Our team members are your daughters, sons, brothers, sisters, mums and your dads, and we'll exhaust every avenue to ensure our team members come home safe at the end of the day. "

How will it work?

Ms Faorlin said the facial technology would scan every customer as they entered either the Woden or Gungahlin stores, creating a temporary biometric profile.

Woolworths is considering a trial of facial recognition technology in two of its Canberra stores, in an attempt to tackle violence against staff. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"That profile will be looked up against a known watch list [of] our repeat violent and aggressive offenders," she said.

"If there is no detection made, so our genuine customers, their biometric profile will be deleted within one second.

"If there is a detection made [staff] may have police called and our team will be alerted to their presence in store."

NSW and ACT Secretary of the Shop Distributive and Allied Employees Association (SDA) Bernie Smith said it was his understanding that Woolworths would not "call the police every time their machine pings".

"They're going to call the police for somebody's breached the workplace protection order and that then becomes a matter for the police, because it's a criminal offence that has to be enforced by the police," he said.

Mr Smith said he was aware of the high levels of violence and aggression in the two stores Woolworths was considering.

"People might be thinking this is just about people getting angry at the checkouts," he said.

"To put this in context, next door to Woolworths Woden a couple of months ago, a member of ours was beaten up with a baseball bat."

The union representing grocery workers says it supports the implementation of facial recognition technology in two Canberra supermarkets, as long as it comes with strict guidelines. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He said that facial recognition technology could help combat violence "as long as it's done within very strict guidelines as part of a social licensing of it".

Ms Faorlin said Woolworths would be "really transparent" about the trial, and added that signage would be displayed outside the two supermarkets.

"We're currently in consultation with our store team to understand if this is something that they want to proceed with," she added.

If the consultation process is successful, the technology could be implemented by the end of this month.

World.title: Will Russell Brand’s wife stand by him?
World.content:
WorldEuropeCourts Will Russell Brand’s wife stand by him? Guy Kelly November 10, 2026 — 2:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nobody was quite sure whether Laura Brand, Russell Brand’s wife of more than nine years and the mother of his three children, would make the journey from their home in Florida to support him for his recent trial. Those who know her didn’t question her support for her husband, nor her faith in his innocence, but they also know her to be intensely publicity-shy. Yet there she was, at Brand’s side as he arrived for day one of his trial at Southwark Crown Court last month, wearing a chocolate brown trouser suit, sunglasses and trainers. Russell Brand and wife Laura Brand arrive at Southwark Crown Court in October. AP In his particular way, Brand told journalists he was feeling “blessed” that morning. Laura, in her way, said nothing, and she maintained her silence when she arrived at court with him on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays throughout the trial, before returning with him in the evening to their accommodation near Waterloo station, and broadcasting with him on their YouTube channel at weekends. If there was a message, it was that she intended to stand by her husband. A penny for Laura Brand’s thoughts today, then, as she heads home from Southwark Crown Court after witnessing her husband being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault. When he was found guilty on Thursday (UK time), Laura rocked towards her knees in despair. Today, she and Brand had a brief conversation before he was led away by officers. Earlier he’d mouthed “we’ll be OK” to her.



Related Article Opinion

Crime Russell Brand blamed Kylie Minogue for his MTV sacking. But he left out a key fact Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor Now 38, Laura wasn’t always so publicity-averse. Born Laura Gallacher, she is the youngest child of Bernard Gallacher, the Scottish golf legend and former Ryder Cup captain. Her older sister is Kirsty Gallacher, a sports broadcaster. They grew up on the Wentworth Estate in Surrey, UK, surrounded by golf, but also by nature. Laura and Kirsty are close, but the age gap – Kirsty is 12 years her senior – meant Laura spent a lot of her childhood alone. “My parents allowed me a lot of time outside to be creative, like making mud pies or petal perfumes. To me, that was a world of magic,” she told London’s The Telegraph in 2022. She was an 18-year-old art student when, in 2007, she was introduced to Brand, then 31, who shared an agent with Kirsty. The pair met in London after one of his live events, and started a brief relationship. Her father, it has been reported, “begged her to end it”. Loading



At that time, Brand was hurtling to fame – as a comedian, TV host and notorious tabloid lothario – before he moved to Hollywood and gained greater renown when he married Katy Perry in 2010. They divorced less than two years later. Brand then had dalliances with Geri Halliwell and Jemima Khan, presumably among others, before he re-met Laura – freshly single and working in hospitality – by chance in 2015. “My ex had literally moved out of our flat that day, and I was heartbroken, with mascara running down my face,” she told Grazia in 2020. “A friend dragged me out on a walk to the canal in east London, where I’d never been in my life, and as we came on to the footpath, Russell was standing there, like he’d organised it.” Related Article Crime The rise and fall of Russell Brand, shapeshifting sexual predator Brand, she told the Made by Mammas podcast the same year, was “so different. We both immediately knew it was going to be serious”. She later recalled to You magazine that Brand said: “‘I think I want a quiet life and a family.’ And it was exactly what I wanted. So then it was about seeing if we could build a foundation to make that happen.” They married two years later, in a ceremony near Henley-on-Thames attended by Noel Gallagher and Jonathan Ross, among other stars. The event came a few months after the birth of Mabel, now 10. Another daughter, Peggy, now eight, arrived the following year – their son, Herb, was born three years ago.



Laura took to motherhood. So much so, in fact, that it inspired a writing career. In 2020, she published The Joy Journal for Magical Everyday Play, aimed at children. She followed this with The Joy Journal For Grown-ups, aimed at adults, and then Slow Down and Be Here Now, aimed at just about anyone. Laura Brand leaves the court after her husband, Russell Brand, was jailed for a decade. Getty Promoting her books with a handful of interviews, the picture Laura painted of family life at their rural Oxfordshire home – where they had dogs, chickens and more than a dozen cats, as well as a narrowboat for weekend cruises – was idyllic, and full of fun and colour. “We really do have fun together,” she said in one. “Sometimes, it can look like I’m dealing with an adult toddler, but Russell’s really into doing the stuff I’m into.” One journalist who visited the house to meet Laura remembers her as “very warm, but even then – before any [allegations] came out – very guarded about Russell. I felt like she was quite lonely, shut away in this slightly remote house, wary of publicity and judgement, and quite young”. More than one person who spent time with the family when the children were young mentions a clear imbalance. Laura, who by all accounts is a very likeable figure, had a lot on her plate. Brand once said he’d never changed a nappy, nor spent 24 hours alone with his children because “Laura ... respects and cares for their safety too much”.



Related Article Graphic content

Courts Russell Brand jailed for 10 years and six months for rape, sexual assaults Laura was asked about that. “Russell’s always been completely hands on,” she told Grazia in 2020. “What he meant, I think, is that he calls me 100 per cent the boss, because it took me a long time to relax into motherhood and I found it hard to let others in ... I’m learning to be less controlling.” Kirsty, for her part, came to his defence over the nappy comment, too. “I think that was a flippant comment, Russell does loads. He’s very hands-on,” she told You magazine in 2019. “I’ve known Russell a long time. He’s amazing, and they lead a fabulous lifestyle. Those little girls are his life. He’s so wonderful with them.” Fully embracing the good life, the Brands briefly started working together as wellness gurus, even running a festival, “Community with Laura + Russell Brand”, in Hay-on-Wye in the summer of 2023. The three-day vegan, alcohol-free event included “holistic therapies”, a “practical life workshop”, canoeing and comedy. Loading



If that was to be the start of a new era as a mindfulness power couple, it was short-lived. Just two months later, a joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4 saw five women publicly accuse Brand of sexual assault, as well as sexual and emotional abuse. Brand, in response, posted a video in which he said he had been “very very promiscuous”, but that all of his relationships had been “absolutely, always consensual”. He always denied all of the allegations made against him. The reporting led to the Metropolitan Police opening an investigation, which saw Brand charged in April last year with two counts of rape, one count of indecent assault and two counts of sexual assault, in relation to alleged offences involving four women between 1999 and 2005. New charges were brought in December last year, alleging one count of rape and one of sexual assault against two women, said to have taken place in London in 2009. During his trial, the court heard that Brand was a “ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator” who bragged about wanting to sleep with 5000 women in his lifetime. As the investigations took place, the Brands escaped the press scrutiny in Britain by moving to Florida. Brand came back and forth, including to be baptised by Bear Grylls in the River Thames in 2024, yet before the family left, he’d already reinvented himself as a YouTuber who specialises in conspiracy theories. In Florida, where such displays of faith and anti-establishment views are less unusual, he’s been welcomed – especially by the MAGA crowd. Brand and wife Laura Brand outside court during the trial. Getty Images All the while, Kirsty continued to support him. After the initial allegations surfaced, she reposted a denial video Brand had posted, and added a love heart. As for Laura, she has maintained a strict omerta. There have been no more books or wellness events. Her social media pages, once full of craft ideas and nature photography, have been deactivated. Yet she does occasionally sit beside Brand in his videos.



Quite what Laura does now is anyone’s guess, but it seems unlikely she will stay in Florida, given Brand will be imprisoned in Britain, and her family remains here. That said, the couple’s children will have to deal with their father’s notoriety in his home country. On Monday (UK time), Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter KC, said Laura is “standing by” her husband, and told the court: “Words are completely inadequate […] to convey the total devastation she’s experiencing. They are wrestling with how to explain to a child, who’s just turned 10, what has just happened here and the consequences of this conduct to totally innocent people who have been caught up in it.” Related Article Opinion

Religion Accused rapist Russell Brand has found God. If only he knew how to find Bible verses on live TV Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor Earlier this year, Laura spoke in a Facebook broadcast titled, “This is what me and my wife are doing now”. Dressed down and sitting on the floor of a terrace balcony, the Brands appeared together at home, with a crucifix behind them and a coffee table covered in lit candles. Brand had a Bible on a reading stand. Both wore cross necklaces. All around them were trees. It was never entirely clear what the “this” of the title meant – the video featured a mix of prayer, Bible lessons and rambling discussion over matters of the soul. “I know you hate this world, the culture of creating content,” Brand told his wife, after reflecting on his recent podcast appearances, which included one in which he confessed to sleeping with 16-year-olds. Laura, he eventually said, had agreed to join him for his new faith-based venture. Later, she would explain that she is a Christian, but seldom joins her husband at church or in the public eye. “I don’t find it easy, and that’s why I don’t ever really want to be doing any of it,” she said of content creation. “I have so many questions about it, and the exposure it inevitably leads to does expose you to a sort of dark energy.”



That much is clearly true. Still, as they set off on their free-form program, Brand thanked her for being with him. Laura smiled meekly. “I must be crazy.” The Telegraph, London Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491 or Lifeline on 13 11 14. World.title: What happens when a country forgets how to make its own fuel
World.content:
The fire at the Geelong oil refinery heightened anxiety over fuel shortages.

In the name of efficiency and transition, Australia shuttered nearly all its refineries. A single fire exposed how thin the margin really is.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The great red-hooped tower has stood above Geelong for almost half a century. For generations of travellers approaching Victoria’s second city by car or train, the enormous chimney, once emblazoned with the letters SHELL, has been as familiar a landmark as the football stadium or waterfront. Beside it, a flame burns day and night, an industrial beacon visible around Corio Bay. Across the water, the Spirit of Tasmania ferry is docked at the port. It is a reminder of what this city was, what it’s lost and what it – against considerable odds – has managed to keep. Viva Energy’s smokestacks dominate the horizon. Craig Sillitoe The city has spent two decades reinventing itself after the departure of the great employers that once defined its economy. Ford stopped making cars. Alcoa closed its aluminium smelter. Factories that sustained generations of working families gave way to universities, hospitals, government departments and a growing services economy. But beyond the refinery gates at Corio, where pipes twist between towering steel columns and enormous storage tanks, another story has been unfolding. This is a factory – opened 72 years ago – that refused to close. Viva Energy’s Geelong refinery is one of just two remaining in Australia, a country that once operated eight. It produces petrol, diesel and aviation fuel, alongside industrial products that can no longer be manufactured anywhere else in the nation. It has survived changing owners, international competition, the pandemic and the slow disappearance of Australia’s heavy manufacturing base. Then, on April 15, a massive fire tore through its petrol-processing complex. It threatened not just the plant but the country’s already fragile fuel security.



Seven months later, the refinery is producing about 90 per cent of its pre-fire capacity. Workers are dismantling damaged machinery while executives negotiate with the Albanese government over arrangements that could secure its operation until 2040. A global energy crisis, sparked by war in the Middle East, has transformed those discussions. For the first time in years, Australia’s remaining refiners have something they previously struggled to command: Canberra’s undivided attention. “We’re now much more appreciated for the role we play in energy security,” says Viva Energy chief executive Scott Wyatt. “Not just in supply in the country, but also in what we do here at Geelong from a refining perspective and the value of having a diverse supply chain.” Viva buys crude oil from all over the world and turns it into petrol at the refinery in Geelong. Inside the sprawling two-kilometre complex, executive general manager Bill Patterson navigates roads winding through an industrial city within a city. Kilometres of pipes spit and hiss, dive under tarmac and wrap around processing towers; Patterson points to a single 21-metre high steel tank holding 90 million litres of crude. Further along stands the refinery’s flare. Its purpose is less romantic than its appearance: burning excess gas during processing disruptions to prevent dangerous pressure building inside equipment.



Then the car passes the scene of April’s fire. Scaffolding climbs through damaged machinery. Contractors are working through demolition and decontamination while engineers have rerouted gas systems to compensate for the destroyed equipment. At about 11.15pm on April 15, fire erupted in the refinery’s alkylation unit. Patterson was speaking to Wyatt about securing emergency fuel cargoes when his telephone rang. He arrived about half an hour later. Emergency crews had isolated the blaze, preventing it spreading through the highly flammable complex. “They really did an amazing job just containing it,” Patterson recalls. “It was bad, obviously, but it could have been much worse. “If it had spread, we might not be doing this tour today.” Nobody was injured. Most major processing units escaped damage, allowing production to be gradually restored. For the refinery’s workforce, its recovery has become another chapter in a much longer fight for survival. Seven months later, it has recovered to about 90 per cent of its pre-blaze production capacity. At 32, Rikki Van Gemert represents the fourth generation of a family connected to the site.



One grandfather spent his career here, rising to become a plant controller. Another, who emigrated from the Netherlands along with scores of other families, helped build its jetty. Her mother worked in the laboratory and neighbouring polymers business, while her uncle Terry still returns as a contractor. Yet Van Gemert – whose partner also works on site – took an unconventional route into the family workplace. After growing up in nearby Lara, she travelled to Bali, met people working in Western Australia’s mining industry and moved to Port Hedland. Three years later, she returned home and joined Viva at 22. Her grandfather had died before she could tell him she would be following his career. “I was in tears. I was so excited,” she recalls of receiving the job offer. Now she trains new operators, guiding recruits through programs lasting up to six months. Refinery operations Tom Delamore and Rikki Van Gemert both hope the Viva plant has a strong future. Jason South For a workplace historically dominated by men, cultural change has been considerable. Women now account for about a quarter of operational roles.



Van Gemert acknowledges the contradictions of working in fossil fuels during the energy transition, but believes Australians sometimes forget the importance of industrial jobs. “We all have our own opinions on the way the world should go and the way we can all contribute to having a better world and a greener world for future generations,” she says. “But we all need to drive our cars, and we all want the lights to turn on when we turn them on and all that sort of stuff. I think sometimes it’s a little bit lost that that is what this place provides for those people that they can get from A to B whenever they want to and however they want to.” Tom Delamore, 36, knows what happens when a refinery disappears. He spent almost eight years at New Zealand’s Marsden Point refinery before its owners converted the country’s last plant into an import terminal in 2022. When Geelong advertised for experienced operators, he relocated his family across the Tasman. “We hadn’t even known where Geelong was until we started looking at the job here,” he says.

World.title: Revealed: What’s really in Usman Khawaja’s book
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Revealed: What’s really in Usman Khawaja’s book Tom Decent Updated November 10, 2026 — 2:27pm ,first published 11:35am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Usman Khawaja’s highly anticipated autobiography has finally landed. Here are some of the allegations worth knowing from Sabr, particularly from chapter 17, titled “Sandpaper”, which revisits the infamous 2018 ball-tampering scandal. Loading Amid a series of disclosures in the book, which was released publicly on Tuesday, Khawaja suggested the entire Australian team knew about the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the third Test against South Africa eight years ago and the tactic had also been deployed in the previous Test, in Gqeberha. While Khawaja doesn’t explicitly say specific players knew of the plot to use sandpaper to tamper with the ball, he implies that everyone in the Australian dressing room knew what was going on.



Editor's pick Australian cricket ‘People have different views’: Cricket Australia refuses to re-open sandpaper scandal investigation Meanwhile, Khawaja alleges members of Australia’s coaching staff in 2016 had a “serious issue” with drinking and reveals his disappointment with teammate Travis Head over the “pain and stress” caused by him publicly declaring he had always wanted to open the batting after his match-winning century against England in last summer’s Ashes Test in Perth. Khawaja also details how he was racially abused in the Lord’s long room in 2023. On Sandpapergate Before the 2018 Test series against South Africa, Khawaja says a member of Australia’s coaching staff talked about wanting players to work on the ball to make it swing more, saying “I don’t care what you have to do”.



“I personally never tampered with a ball – in terms of scratching it or anything – but I knew everything that was going on and I wasn’t against it, which makes me complicit,” Khawaja wrote. “Everything you might have heard or read about what happened … in South Africa in the sandpaper controversy isn’t entirely true. The cricket team management and Cricket Australia board at the time had their own agendas and they tried their best at damage control and to cover up as much as they could. Usman Khawaja. Darrian Traynor/Getty Images “I won’t speak on behalf of any other players – that’s for them to talk about. Of course, I bloody knew what was happening with the sandpaper. “I always wanted to talk about it. I never said I didn’t know about the sandpaper issue – not to anyone or any news organisation. I would never blatantly lie like that.”



On the use of sandpaper by the team Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket ‘A nightmare for Pat Cummins’: Why Khawaja claims are set to dog Australia captain Khawaja goes into detail on how the sandpaper was actually used in the second Test in Port Elizabeth, one before the infamous match in Cape Town. “We all knew that the umpire would drop the ball on the boundary as we went out onto the field. At that point, there’d be no cameras on us and the umpires would be about 100 metres ahead. We could then do whatever we wanted. Straightaway, Bull [David Warner] said, ‘Well, I can’t do it – they’re all over me.’ I was never going to do it, nor did I think anyone else would. So I just laughed. Then, Cameron Bancroft, who was only six games into his Test career and maybe wanting to fit in, said, ‘I’ll do it.’ “When something becomes so prevalent – like doping was in the Tour de France for years – it’s hard not to join in. Compete, or be left behind. Not that it makes it right.”



On other bowlers knowing Khawaja alleges the ball was moving so dramatically at one point that some Australian players asked those responsible for tampering with it to leave it alone. “One of the bowlers said in the huddle after a wicket, ‘Guys, it’s going heaps now. Just don’t do anything else to it, because it’s silly how much it’s going.’ Most of us just laughed.” Usman Khawaja’s memoir, Sabr, is published by Penguin Random House and available from November 10. On the coach’s instruction



Khawaja says an unnamed coach told Bancroft: “Whatever you’re doing, we need more of it.” “Then I saw Bangers pick up a piece of sandpaper and put it in his pocket,” Khawaja wrote. “The coach gave both me and Cameron a wry smile of satisfaction and walked away. The push from this coach, though, obviously made him feel like he had to do it more often.” How the drama unfolded Captain Steve Smith told Bancroft to put the sandpaper away, while Khawaja encouraged the youngster to get off the field. Bancroft stuffs a piece of sandpaper down his trousers in the infamous Test eight years ago. Nine



“But Cameron was catatonic at this stage. He didn’t know what to do. Every one of the boys on the field then was shitting themselves. And Bangers was the worst. “Then on the big screen came the biggest shock. It showed Cameron taking the sandpaper and putting it in his undies. By this stage, we knew: we’d f---ed up and f---ed up hard.” “Kick in the guts” on being overlooked for Test captain Khawaja said he was upset Tim Paine was appointed interim captain after Smith was sent home from Cape Town. “I was a natural selection for interim captain, but was overlooked. I knew why. One reason was that I’d been a main protagonist during those pay disputes with CA and the board – and the board was who appointed the captain. On that basis alone, they probably weren’t going to give it to me.



“But the second – and, I believe, more important – reason was that they weren’t ready for a brown Australian cricket captain, even as an interim. You may be thinking, How do you know this? It’s because the chairman of selectors had told a journalist I know very well that ‘Uzzy doesn’t “have” what we want in a captain. He doesn’t display the right stuff.’ I was pretty sure I knew what that meant. I didn’t fit the old-school Aussie mode or have the right skin colour for the job. It’s cool, but at minimum I should have got the vice-captaincy. Instead, they’d given it to Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh. For one of the more mature players, who’d been captaining his own state for a few years, that was a kick in the guts.” On the aftermath Khawaja says he tried to get the team to take collective responsibility for what happened in South Africa, but “two guys” disagreed. “This was the most disappointing part for me. I knew who those two guys were, and it was ludicrous that, out of everyone, it was them. It showed me their true colours, though. When the going got tough, all they cared about was themselves. But I wasn’t going to stop fighting this cause. “CA did a pretty unthorough investigation after that. It was almost as if they didn’t want to find out the whole truth.”



On why he chose to speak out now Khawaja says he wanted to stand up for Warner, Smith and Bancroft by going public. Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were all banned over the scandal. AP “This has been the hardest chapter to write … I still don’t think it’s right that those three boys copped all of the brunt. Their lives were turned upside down, and the psychological impact will remain with them forever. Unless I speak up about it, they’ll continue to have to hold the burden. “It’s very clear I knew what was going on. I just want to say sorry to the three guys. We let you down. But mostly to the guy who copped the lion’s share of the blame, my good friend David. You shouldn’t have to carry this your whole life. Over the years, you’ve suffered more insults than anyone about this. You were not the architect. We were all the architects.”



On being racially abused at Lord’s during the 2023 Ashes After the controversial stumping of England’s Jonny Bairstow in 2023, the Lord’s crowd turned on Australia, resulting in an incident in the long room. Khawaja was in the thick of it and revealed he was racially vilified. Loading “They [England spectators] were in unison, swearing, calling us ‘F-ing this’, and ‘F-that’, ‘C-nts this’. I couldn’t believe what I was hearing. As we kept walking, I pulled up when someone shouted right into my ear – as there was only a rope and about 20 centimetres between us. ‘Don’t you dare scream in my ear again, you dickhead,’ I said to the first guy. Then as I walked on, and I heard someone else say, ‘Shut up, you Paki,’ I lost it. I don’t know who this was exactly. I told security, ‘Get this guy out of here!’ But the most bizarre thing – and David Warner will attest to this – was that, as we went to walk upstairs, one of the members was trying to trip us up. Yes, genuinely! Sticking his leg out, so we’d fall ... Davey told him off first, so I didn’t think the bloke would do it again. But as I went to walk upstairs, he tried to do it to me too! I just looked up at security and said, ‘Are you f—ing serious right now?’ The security guy grabbed the man and got him to get his member card out. I’d seen enough.” On his blow-up with Australian team manager Gavin Dovey over the ‘Homeworkgate’ issue in 2013



Another perspective Opinion

Test cricket Usman Khawaja remained silent for eight years. Why did he speak out now? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist Khawaja was one of four Australian cricketers suspended for the third Test against India in Mohali in March 2013 after failing to complete a homework assignment set by coach Mickey Arthur. He details his blow-up with team manager Gavin Dovey. “‘Uz, that is f—in shit,’ said Gavin. ‘That’s the shit we’re trying to get rid of in this team. Your attitude is an absolute joke, and to think you’re a part of the Australian cricket team, it’s –’. “I cut him off. I looked him dead in the eye and said, ‘Are you f—ing serious, Gavin? What the f--k are you even doing here? You’re a glorified team manager. This is between the guys who actually know about cricket. Now you’re coming here like you own the joint. Shut the f--k up.’ Gavin tried to reply, but Pup [Michael Clarke] spoke up, trying to defuse the situation. ‘Uz, Uz, calm down.’ Now Gavin hadn’t earned my respect, but Pup was Pup. He had all my respect, and I’d never go against the captain – particularly someone who’d achieved what he had. So I shut up.” On Travis Head wanting to open in the summer of 2025-26



Khawaja injured his back during the first Ashes Test against England in 2025, prompting Travis Head to make a match-winning hundred opening. But it was what Head said afterwards that upset Khawaja. Travis Head’s remarkable century in the first Ashes Test. AP “Travis Head was sent up to open and batted unbelievably. He scored a hundred and we chased down the target of 205 in no time. Although my back was in pieces. I was so glad for the team. I gave Heady a huge hug when the game finished, apologised and said thanks and well done. I didn’t think he’d go out to the media and say he always wanted to open – in turn pretty much stabbing me more in the back! (That statement is a bit full on, but I couldn’t resist the pun. He didn’t stab me in the back, but I wouldn’t have said the same thing if the roles were reversed.) He wouldn’t have even thought about that statement as him trying to push me out of the team. Not at all, but I couldn’t believe he said that. He also said he was quietly always lobbying behind the scenes to open. Which wasn’t true and I knew it – he was never lobbying. But that was all the media needed and the narrative was off and running. I don’t think Heady realised the pain and stress it caused me and my family during the next few weeks.” On Australia’s disastrous 5-0 ODI series defeat to South Africa in 2016 Khawaja suggests alcohol was an issue on a tour of South Africa a decade ago. “The tour was a shambles. There was a serious issue with drinking at the time, particularly amongst the coaching staff. They were in the bar and chugging them down every night. They’d been doing this since I’d come back into the team. One evening, between the fourth and fifth game, we had a ‘crisis team meeting’. We all huddled in the big conference room and hashed it out. Well, not really. Most people who were there probably wouldn’t actually remember what was said that evening. As far as I could tell, many of the coaches were drunk. With red mouths from bottles of wine, stumbling and slurring their words. I looked over at George Bailey, our captain, who wasn’t drunk, and said, ‘Are we serious right now? Most of the guys in the room – including players and staff – are intoxicated. They won’t remember any of this tomorrow.’ With his classic humour and that trademark smile, George Bailey, eating his pizza, just looked at me and said, ‘I don’t think that’s a bad thing.’”

World.title: Trump says Iran war is ‘militarily effectively over’ at snap news conference
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Trump says Iran war is ‘militarily effectively over’ at snap news conference Michael Koziol Updated November 10, 2026 — 2:13pm ,first published November 10, 2026 — 10:38am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: US President Donald Trump said the Iran war was “effectively over” in remarks that suggest a resumption of major combat operations is unlikely, despite rampant speculation about renewed bombing following the midterm elections. In a snap news conference where he was joined by Ultimate Fighting Championship boss Dana White, Trump defended the eight-month-old war and his embattled Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, who now faces an impeachment resolution in Congress. Loading “Iran, militarily, is effectively over,” Trump said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo. We’re doing that really at the behest of countries that are their neighbours.” He reiterated that Iran was suffering crippling inflation, was failing to pay its military, and that its navy and air forces had been destroyed.



“At the conclusion of the military engagement, the American people and the people of the world will be far safer and more secure than they’ve been in many, many years,” Trump said. “That war was started in 1979. We didn’t start the war, they did … I don’t guarantee anything. But if we do have to go back in, we are locked and loaded and ready to go.” President Donald Trump said the war in Iran was “militarily effectively over”. AP The president’s remarks came shortly after a meeting at the White House on Monday (US time) with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, a key US partner in the region. Trump has made similar statements in numerous interviews and news conferences. But Monday’s comments were more definitive and appeared to dispel the notion that a fresh wave of strikes – a “final blow”, as some have described it – is under serious consideration.



In an interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes on Sunday, Trump said the US could bomb Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain if it needed to, but there had been “very little activity there”. “It would be done in one hour, it would be taken care of,” he said. The mountain – and the three other Iranian nuclear sites bombed by the US last year – were under constant surveillance, he added. Ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas in Iran. AP Photo/Amirhosein Khorgooi Other than limited strikes in the Strait of Hormuz, there has been little kinetic action in the war for months. While shipments of oil through the strait have increased under US Navy protection, a long-term plan for safe, toll-free passage through the strait – without ships being fired upon by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps – remains elusive.



White’s appearance at Monday’s news conference came after Trump’s weekend joke that he offered the UFC president the job of White House press secretary – a gag which White initially played up to, before rejecting. “I’ve always wanted to do this,” White told reporters, before bellowing: “Who has the first question?” Later, he clarified that he had no interest in going into politics. “I am devastated to hear this,” Trump responded as they shook hands. US President Donald Trump gestures to UFC president Dana White as he speaks in the James Brady Press Briefing Room. AP In his 60 Minutes interview, Trump acknowledged the unpopular Iran war cost his Republican Party votes at last week’s midterm elections, where they lost control of both chambers of Congress. “They didn’t like that [the price of] gasoline went up,” he said. “There’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel ... You have that, you have the war itself, you have the gas prices.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Big Build royal commission LIVE updates: John Holland superintendent claims CFMEU told his company it would help with future projects if they gave in to union demands
World.content:
Amid a pacey end to the morning session, we had our first swear word! It was always going to happen given the space we’re covering.

Giving evidence about that crucial meeting held at the union headquarters on the afternoon of June 7, 2022, Steve Testolin says union organiser Joe Myles started the meeting with “a lot of small talk”.

Former CFMEU boss Joe Myles. 60 Minutes

Myles asked the company what they wanted, followed by a silence.

The silence was broken, in Testolin’s recollection, when he himself said: “How about you cut the bulls--t and tell us what you want?”

What they wanted (as seen in the video in the post below) was a paid health and safety representative on site, as well as the union’s favoured labour hire firm and traffic management company.

Testolin finished giving evidence just before the break so a new witness will give evidence when the afternoon session starts shortly.

World.title: Cameron Bruce wins the race to be Brisbane’s next senior AFL coach
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Cameron Bruce wins the race to be Brisbane’s next senior AFL coach Jake Niall Updated November 10, 2026 — 1:58pm ,first published November 9, 2026 — 7:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Brisbane Lions have gone internal and appointed experienced assistant coach Cameron Bruce as the club’s next senior coach to replace three-time flag winner Chris Fagan. In a decision officially announced on Tuesday, Bruce will step up as the newest AFL senior coach. Cameron Bruce has landed the coveted gig. Getty Bruce beat home a field of experienced candidates, including 2018 AFL grand final coaches Nathan Buckley and Adam Simpson, as well as Collingwood senior assistant coach Hayden Skipworth. Bruce was strongly endorsed for the role by his mentor triple premiership flag coach Fagan, who has since retired from senior coaching and moved to a director of coaching position at Carlton.



The Lions released a statement on Tuesday confirming the appointment and said Bruce would bring a fresh voice to the club. “To be appointed an AFL senior coach is an incredible privilege, and to have that opportunity at the Brisbane Lions makes it even more special,” Bruce said. Editor's pick AFL 2026 ‘I’ve never wanted to lose a hitout’: Meet teenage goliath and hot draft prospect Harry Van Hattum “I’ve learnt so much throughout my time as an assistant, particularly from Fages. He has been a tremendous mentor and supporter of mine, and I’m incredibly grateful for the trust he has placed in me and the lessons he has shared. “I’ll carry those experiences with me, but I’m also looking forward to putting my own stamp on the role and being my own senior coach.”



Bruce has been involved in six premierships as a development and assistant coach at the Lions, Carlton and Hawthorn since 2013, and the players hold him in high regard. He played 224 matches for Melbourne and 10 games at Hawthorn before retiring in 2012. He joined the Brisbane Lions in 2022, and was responsible for midfield and centre bounces at the Lions in 2026. He also had the advantage of virtual incumbency at a club that had experienced remarkable success and represented stability for the playing group. Bruce had strong backing from many players, who he’d built a rapport with since he crossed from Carlton four years ago. Bruce’s coaching background included time with AFL coaching great Alastair Clarkson at Hawthorn, having been an excellent player for the Demons in the Neale Daniher era. Cameron Bruce flies high for the Demons during his AFL playing career. Getty Images Brisbane’s hierarchy insisted on an open process rather than simply appointing Bruce, hence the much later appointment than usual for a senior coaching position.



The Lions’ selection panel included chair Andrew Wellington, CEO Sam Graham, football manager Danny Daly and coaching mentor Phil Smyth. Board member and four-time premiership coach Leigh Matthews acted in an advisory capacity and Simon Black and Matti Clements were consulted. Wellington congratulated Bruce on his appointment, describing the new senior coach as “the standout candidate”. “Following three consecutive premierships, we are in an incredibly fortunate position, but we also recognise the importance of continuing to evolve and challenge ourselves,” he said. “Cameron understands the standards and culture that have underpinned our success, while bringing his own ideas and a clear vision for the future.” With Peter Ryan and Hannah Kennelly

World.title: ‘Judge, jury and executioner’: Republican congressman files resolution to impeach Hegseth
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaUS politics ‘Judge, jury and executioner’: Republican congressman files resolution to impeach Hegseth Michael Koziol Updated November 10, 2026 — 1:53pm ,first published November 10, 2026 — 6:41am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: US President Donald Trump is standing by his embattled defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, who faces impeachment proceedings in Congress accused of violating war powers laws, conducting extrajudicial killings and suppressing free speech. Republican congressman Thomas Massie read the articles of impeachment in the House of Representatives on Monday (Washington time), hoping to attract enough Republican support to send the resolution to the US Senate. Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, speaks outside the Capitol about articles of impeachment he introduced against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. AP Photo/Allison Robbert Meanwhile, Trump told reporters the Iran war was “militarily effectively over” at a snap news conference after meeting with the Qatari prime minister, and said a return to major combat operations was “quite unlikely”. The president has made similar remarks many times, and a peace deal to formally end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remains elusive. But these remarks were seen by some analysts as more definitive, and came amid speculation about a fresh wave of post-election strikes.



Trump also defended Hegseth, crediting him with improving military recruitment and helping “win” the campaign in Iran, as well as the capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January. “We won two wars, and we’ve made the world a lot safer place,” Trump said, suggesting that politicians who orchestrated previous failed American wars should have been impeached instead. “Massie’s a loser,” he said. President Donald Trump defended Pete Hegseth at an impromptu news conference, saying he should be praised, not impeached. Alex Brandon Later, on Truth Social, the president called Hegseth “perhaps the most popular and successful military official in the country”, who should be praised, not impeached. “Congress, stand up for Pete!!!” he wrote. Over eight articles of impeachment, Massie accused Hegseth of violating multiple sections of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, ignoring laws that minimise civilian casualties, conducting extrajudicial killings of people on boats alleged to be carrying drugs, suppressing free speech and kidnapping a foreign leader.



Addressing the House, Massie alleged Hegseth had breached the War Powers Resolution because he “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation [Iran]” without authorisation by Congress. Hegseth continued to break the law by ignoring a congressional resolution directing the president to remove US forces from hostilities with Iran, Massie said. Loading Massie also accused Hegseth of ignoring laws that minimise civilian casualties, citing the death or injury of more than 200 civilians at the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, Iran on the first day of the war in February. Hegseth directed the Defence Department in a manner that “foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives”, he said.



Massie put on public record details of the incident, for which the Pentagon has not admitted responsibility. The school was hit by three BGM-109 Tomahawk cruise missiles fired from US Navy warships, he said. They struck between 10.23am and 10.45am on a Saturday morning, while students were at the school. “Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians and abused the trust of the men and women under his command by requiring them to conduct military operations within a targeting and legal-review system that he had deliberately degraded,” Massie told the House. Loading In other articles of impeachment, the Republican congressman accused Hegseth of the extrajudicial killings of 243 alleged drug traffickers on small boats in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean. By killing people who were merely suspected of criminal conduct – and without establishing a lawful basis for treating them as military targets – Hegseth “arrogated to himself and the executive branch the roles of judge, jury and executioner, and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die”, Massie said.





Hegseth scheduled a news conference about the impeachment for Tuesday morning (Washington time), but defended his record when he briefly spoke to reporters while travelling on Monday. “We’re not worried about that,” he said of the impeachment proceedings. “There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements – but their disagreements are with success. President Donald Trump has stuck by Pete Hegseth despite conjecture that the defence secretary could be dumped from cabinet. AP “Getting our European partners to step up is historic. Getting these countries in Central and South America to come together into a counter-cartel coalition and put the cartels on the run is historic. “The things that we’ve accomplished in [operations] Midnight Hammer and Absolute Resolve and Southern Spear and Epic Fury are things that will change the face of the globe for a generation.

World.title: Will Russell Brand’s wife stand by him?
World.content:
WorldEuropeCourts Will Russell Brand’s wife stand by him? Guy Kelly November 10, 2026 — 2:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nobody was quite sure whether Laura Brand, Russell Brand’s wife of more than nine years and the mother of his three children, would make the journey from their home in Florida to support him for his recent trial. Those who know her didn’t question her support for her husband, nor her faith in his innocence, but they also know her to be intensely publicity-shy. Yet there she was, at Brand’s side as he arrived for day one of his trial at Southwark Crown Court last month, wearing a chocolate brown trouser suit, sunglasses and trainers. Russell Brand and wife Laura Brand arrive at Southwark Crown Court in October. AP In his particular way, Brand told journalists he was feeling “blessed” that morning. Laura, in her way, said nothing, and she maintained her silence when she arrived at court with him on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays throughout the trial, before returning with him in the evening to their accommodation near Waterloo station, and broadcasting with him on their YouTube channel at weekends. If there was a message, it was that she intended to stand by her husband. A penny for Laura Brand’s thoughts today, then, as she heads home from Southwark Crown Court after witnessing her husband being sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison for rape and sexual assault. When he was found guilty on Thursday (UK time), Laura rocked towards her knees in despair. Today, she and Brand had a brief conversation before he was led away by officers. Earlier he’d mouthed “we’ll be OK” to her.



Related Article Opinion

Crime Russell Brand blamed Kylie Minogue for his MTV sacking. But he left out a key fact Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor Now 38, Laura wasn’t always so publicity-averse. Born Laura Gallacher, she is the youngest child of Bernard Gallacher, the Scottish golf legend and former Ryder Cup captain. Her older sister is Kirsty Gallacher, a sports broadcaster. They grew up on the Wentworth Estate in Surrey, UK, surrounded by golf, but also by nature. Laura and Kirsty are close, but the age gap – Kirsty is 12 years her senior – meant Laura spent a lot of her childhood alone. “My parents allowed me a lot of time outside to be creative, like making mud pies or petal perfumes. To me, that was a world of magic,” she told London’s The Telegraph in 2022. She was an 18-year-old art student when, in 2007, she was introduced to Brand, then 31, who shared an agent with Kirsty. The pair met in London after one of his live events, and started a brief relationship. Her father, it has been reported, “begged her to end it”. Loading



At that time, Brand was hurtling to fame – as a comedian, TV host and notorious tabloid lothario – before he moved to Hollywood and gained greater renown when he married Katy Perry in 2010. They divorced less than two years later. Brand then had dalliances with Geri Halliwell and Jemima Khan, presumably among others, before he re-met Laura – freshly single and working in hospitality – by chance in 2015. “My ex had literally moved out of our flat that day, and I was heartbroken, with mascara running down my face,” she told Grazia in 2020. “A friend dragged me out on a walk to the canal in east London, where I’d never been in my life, and as we came on to the footpath, Russell was standing there, like he’d organised it.” Related Article Crime The rise and fall of Russell Brand, shapeshifting sexual predator Brand, she told the Made by Mammas podcast the same year, was “so different. We both immediately knew it was going to be serious”. She later recalled to You magazine that Brand said: “‘I think I want a quiet life and a family.’ And it was exactly what I wanted. So then it was about seeing if we could build a foundation to make that happen.” They married two years later, in a ceremony near Henley-on-Thames attended by Noel Gallagher and Jonathan Ross, among other stars. The event came a few months after the birth of Mabel, now 10. Another daughter, Peggy, now eight, arrived the following year – their son, Herb, was born three years ago.



Laura took to motherhood. So much so, in fact, that it inspired a writing career. In 2020, she published The Joy Journal for Magical Everyday Play, aimed at children. She followed this with The Joy Journal For Grown-ups, aimed at adults, and then Slow Down and Be Here Now, aimed at just about anyone. Laura Brand leaves the court after her husband, Russell Brand, was jailed for a decade. Getty Promoting her books with a handful of interviews, the picture Laura painted of family life at their rural Oxfordshire home – where they had dogs, chickens and more than a dozen cats, as well as a narrowboat for weekend cruises – was idyllic, and full of fun and colour. “We really do have fun together,” she said in one. “Sometimes, it can look like I’m dealing with an adult toddler, but Russell’s really into doing the stuff I’m into.” One journalist who visited the house to meet Laura remembers her as “very warm, but even then – before any [allegations] came out – very guarded about Russell. I felt like she was quite lonely, shut away in this slightly remote house, wary of publicity and judgement, and quite young”. More than one person who spent time with the family when the children were young mentions a clear imbalance. Laura, who by all accounts is a very likeable figure, had a lot on her plate. Brand once said he’d never changed a nappy, nor spent 24 hours alone with his children because “Laura ... respects and cares for their safety too much”.



Related Article Graphic content

Courts Russell Brand jailed for 10 years and six months for rape, sexual assaults Laura was asked about that. “Russell’s always been completely hands on,” she told Grazia in 2020. “What he meant, I think, is that he calls me 100 per cent the boss, because it took me a long time to relax into motherhood and I found it hard to let others in ... I’m learning to be less controlling.” Kirsty, for her part, came to his defence over the nappy comment, too. “I think that was a flippant comment, Russell does loads. He’s very hands-on,” she told You magazine in 2019. “I’ve known Russell a long time. He’s amazing, and they lead a fabulous lifestyle. Those little girls are his life. He’s so wonderful with them.” Fully embracing the good life, the Brands briefly started working together as wellness gurus, even running a festival, “Community with Laura + Russell Brand”, in Hay-on-Wye in the summer of 2023. The three-day vegan, alcohol-free event included “holistic therapies”, a “practical life workshop”, canoeing and comedy. Loading



If that was to be the start of a new era as a mindfulness power couple, it was short-lived. Just two months later, a joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4 saw five women publicly accuse Brand of sexual assault, as well as sexual and emotional abuse. Brand, in response, posted a video in which he said he had been “very very promiscuous”, but that all of his relationships had been “absolutely, always consensual”. He always denied all of the allegations made against him. The reporting led to the Metropolitan Police opening an investigation, which saw Brand charged in April last year with two counts of rape, one count of indecent assault and two counts of sexual assault, in relation to alleged offences involving four women between 1999 and 2005. New charges were brought in December last year, alleging one count of rape and one of sexual assault against two women, said to have taken place in London in 2009. During his trial, the court heard that Brand was a “ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator” who bragged about wanting to sleep with 5000 women in his lifetime. As the investigations took place, the Brands escaped the press scrutiny in Britain by moving to Florida. Brand came back and forth, including to be baptised by Bear Grylls in the River Thames in 2024, yet before the family left, he’d already reinvented himself as a YouTuber who specialises in conspiracy theories. In Florida, where such displays of faith and anti-establishment views are less unusual, he’s been welcomed – especially by the MAGA crowd. Brand and wife Laura Brand outside court during the trial. Getty Images All the while, Kirsty continued to support him. After the initial allegations surfaced, she reposted a denial video Brand had posted, and added a love heart. As for Laura, she has maintained a strict omerta. There have been no more books or wellness events. Her social media pages, once full of craft ideas and nature photography, have been deactivated. Yet she does occasionally sit beside Brand in his videos.



Quite what Laura does now is anyone’s guess, but it seems unlikely she will stay in Florida, given Brand will be imprisoned in Britain, and her family remains here. That said, the couple’s children will have to deal with their father’s notoriety in his home country. On Monday (UK time), Brand’s lawyer, Ian Winter KC, said Laura is “standing by” her husband, and told the court: “Words are completely inadequate […] to convey the total devastation she’s experiencing. They are wrestling with how to explain to a child, who’s just turned 10, what has just happened here and the consequences of this conduct to totally innocent people who have been caught up in it.” Related Article Opinion

Religion Accused rapist Russell Brand has found God. If only he knew how to find Bible verses on live TV Katy Hall Age deputy state topic editor Earlier this year, Laura spoke in a Facebook broadcast titled, “This is what me and my wife are doing now”. Dressed down and sitting on the floor of a terrace balcony, the Brands appeared together at home, with a crucifix behind them and a coffee table covered in lit candles. Brand had a Bible on a reading stand. Both wore cross necklaces. All around them were trees. It was never entirely clear what the “this” of the title meant – the video featured a mix of prayer, Bible lessons and rambling discussion over matters of the soul. “I know you hate this world, the culture of creating content,” Brand told his wife, after reflecting on his recent podcast appearances, which included one in which he confessed to sleeping with 16-year-olds. Laura, he eventually said, had agreed to join him for his new faith-based venture. Later, she would explain that she is a Christian, but seldom joins her husband at church or in the public eye. “I don’t find it easy, and that’s why I don’t ever really want to be doing any of it,” she said of content creation. “I have so many questions about it, and the exposure it inevitably leads to does expose you to a sort of dark energy.”



That much is clearly true. Still, as they set off on their free-form program, Brand thanked her for being with him. Laura smiled meekly. “I must be crazy.” The Telegraph, London Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491 or Lifeline on 13 11 14.
