World.title: Lockdown ends at New Plymouth Boys' High School following threat
World.content:
A lockdown at New Plymouth Boys High School has ended.

The school went into a precautionary lockdown after a threat was made.

Police began packing away their weapons into vehicles and began pulling away from the school shortly after 1.30pm.

Vernon, a parent who had been waiting outside the school in the rain, said he was delighted with the outcome.

Similarly, Tess, a New Plymouth Girls High student who had been concerned about her boyfriend, was now looking forward to giving him a big hug.

Tess had been walking back from her Math NCEA level exam when she saw a lot of police cars making their way to the school.

The school said the lockdown had lifted by 1.40pm.

Police said the threat was made on Tuesday morning, first being alerted to it at 9.50am.

"A substantial Police effort was put in place following the threat and included the Armed Offenders Squad which was called in as a precaution," Area Commander Inspector Matenga Gray said.

"Police enquiries continue into the circumstances of the incident."

Armed police at the school. ROBIN MARTIN / RNZ

"Police are in the area working to determine the veracity of the threat, police said.

Earlier, a mum standing outside the school said she is concerned for her son who was inside.

Parents said they had been sent no communication from the school, with more than an hour past since the lockdown began.

"Absolutely I'm concerned, my heart is going like the clappers, but obviously there's nothing I can do.

"As soon as I saw there was an incident happening, I came."

World.title: Clive Palmer says dilapidated luxury resort will reopen after decade in mothballs
World.content:
Billionaire Clive Palmer has begun revamping his luxury resort on the Sunshine Coast, with a new pledge to reopen the rundown site after a decade in mothballs.

The Queensland businessman purchased the five-star Hyatt Regency resort in Coolum in 2011 before shutting it four years later.

Mr Palmer announced a $100 million redevelopment in 2021 that would include replicas of famous landmarks, such as Rome's Trevi Fountain.

Clive Palmer erected a large Tyrannosaurus rex called Jeff at his resort in 2012, before the dinosaur burnt down in 2015. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

The work was due for completion in 2022 but has faced repeated delays.

Several job vacancies at the resort have been advertised recently, including skilled labourers, painters, security guards, electricians and plumbers.

A spokesman for Mr Palmer confirmed to the ABC the resort would reopen mid-next year.

Workers can be seen on site and renovations are underway.

Workers were seen clearing gutters at the Palmer Coolum resort on Tuesday. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

In its prime, the precinct employed 700 people and featured more than 300 luxury rooms and villas, a day spa and a popular village green.

The site still features an active 18-hole golf course, which used to host the Australian PGA Championship for 11 years from 2002 until 2012.

Mr Palmer rebranded the resort in his own name following a legal dispute with Hyatt in 2012, before closing the facility in 2015.

In 2023, dozens of tradesmen were among 125 employees sacked amid accusations of theft and fraud, with the Fair Work Commission later finding some dismissals were unfair.

Greg Norman plays a shot on the 13th fairway during the Australian PGA Championship at the Hyatt Regency Coolum in 2011. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Residents hopeful but sceptical

Many Coolum residents have fond memories of the old resort and hope it can be restored to its former glory.

"It would be extraordinary … everyone would support it," Coolum Business and Tourism vice-president Casey O'Hare said.

"It was absolutely gorgeous in its day … it was such an amazing asset for the Sunshine Coast.

"If Clive Palmer could rebuild and get it back on the market as a hotel and resort, it would be such a boon for the coast."

But Ms O'Hare said locals were sceptical given the repeated broken promises to reopen the premises.

Clive Palmer's resort in Coolum has been shut since 2015 but work has now begun to revamp it. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

"I'll believe it when I see it, because of the fact that this has happened before where it's been mooted as reopening," she said.

Retired builder Mark Hatfull helped construct the original resort back in the 1980s and said the "world-class" facility transformed the region.

"It took it from a backwater to where we are today … It was an absolute godsend," he said.

Residents like Mark Hatfull are hopeful the resort can be restored to its former glory. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Jessica Ross)

"The gym and the spa was something to die for … It was like something out of a dream.

"Obviously, Clive has got his business and then he makes a decision and one day a place is open, the next day it's closed."

'Devil in the detail': councillor

Local councillor Taylor Bunnag said he grew up around the resort where his father was a greenkeeper.

He said it would be "a wonderful thing" if it reopened, but he understood the scepticism.

"If you actually look at the site … there's a lot of existing infrastructure that's quite run down," Cr Bunnag said.

"I think the devil is in the detail with all these sorts of proposals.

A swimming pool area in disarray at the Palmer Coolum Resort in December 2017. (Supplied: Maree Frecklington)

"We've been told that Palmer Resort was going to reopen at certain times and that hasn't eventuated."

Cr Bunnag said a renovated facility would be "extremely welcome" in fixing the region's accommodation shortage ahead of the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

"We need thousands of extra hotel rooms added to our region by 2032 to cater for the demand," he said.

"It's hard to speculate about what further approvals they'll need because I'm not sure what product they're delivering.

Cr Bunnag said he had not seen any formal proposals for Mr Palmer's original plan of building replicas of famous landmarks such as Rome's Trevi Fountain.

A tradesman working on a building at the Palmer Coolum Resort on Tuesday. (ABC Sunshine Coast: Owen Jacques)

"I'd only be speculating but my assumption is that they'll be renovating certain parts of the resort and some might open, some might not," he said.

A Sunshine Coast Council spokesperson said the site held existing approval for a resort and residential community facility.

"Provided the development continues to operate in accordance with the conditions of that approval, no further development approvals are required from council," they said.

World.title: 2027 Netball World Cup the 'next defining moment in women's sport'
World.content:
The 2015 Netball World Cup final was the stuff of legend.

A good old-fashioned trans-Tasman clash, it was decided by just three goals, 58-55.

The Australians managed to survive a desperate comeback by New Zealand and send retiring players Julie Corletto, Kim Green and Bec Bulley out on a high. Gutsy Corletto famously played through the game with a broken foot, needing painkillers injected at half-time.

Being there in person to witness it is something netball fans love to reminisce about.

A world-record crowd watched the Diamonds hold on against the Silver Ferns in 2015. (AAP: Paul Miller)

The contest was enthralling of course, but it's the atmosphere they remember most.

As the 16,752-strong crowd at Sydney SuperDome cheered an octave higher than at other major sporting events, they set a world record attendance for the sport that is yet to be broken.

Now, 12 years later, the 2027 tournament heads back to the same venue and organisers are hoping that nostalgia will help them break the record again.

Can they break the crowd record?

They have boldly set a target of 200,000 attendees across 64 matches from August 25 to September 5 and would love to fill the venue's 18,000-seat capacity for the finals.

The first batch of tickets goes on sale on today.

Chief executive Jane Fernandez said it would be the next defining moment in women's sport.

Netballers from Australia, Uganda, Jamaica and England pose with administrators at a Netball World Cup event. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

"There's a connection to place that is still front of mind," Fernandez told ABC Sport.

"For the netball community, this is a huge opportunity to be part of another World Cup on home soil, and I've met with a lot of people who talk so fondly of 2015.

"I think it's going to take netball into the next stratosphere."

The introduction of new silverware

The impact of that 2015 World Cup was undeniable.

Two years later, Super Netball was born. The modern era of the elite competition has revolutionised the game and offered players a professional wage for the first time.

It also allows unlimited imports, opening up full-time contracts in high-performance environments to players all over the globe. This has helped opposition nations grow stronger.

Australia has had a rough patch of form, recently losing the Constellation Cup 3-1. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

If the Diamonds found it hard to win back then, imagine the immense pressure on the current crop of players.

Following its lowest-ever finish at a Commonwealth Games, the Australian team conceded the Constellation Cup and is on the verge of losing its number one ranking.

Twenty-four internationals have been signed for the next Super Netball season and most of them will occupy starting positions across the eight teams, so it's only going to get tougher.

No matter what happens at this World Cup, the impact will be felt by generations to come and greater competition for the host team should help with ticket sales, according to Fernandez.

As will the introduction of a new piece of silverware.

Australia will be hoping to defend the 2023 Netball World Cup title it won in Cape Town. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

"It's going to be absolutely fierce," Fernandez said.

"It changes the energy of a tournament when you've got strong competition, so I do think it's great for the World Cup.

"This is anyone's to win and for the first time, teams can also play for the plate.

"After the first four days, the teams will be split and the top eight will continue to play for the World Cup trophy, while the bottom eight continue to play for the plate.

"All participating teams will have something to play for, which is a great opportunity for fans to keep cheering their side on until the very end."

Learning from other sports

The Matildas celebrate victory after a penalty shootout in their quarterfinal against France in 2023. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Fernandez is best known for leading Australia and New Zealand's 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup bid and eventual tournament, which captured the hearts and minds of the nation.

A key marketing strategy from that event was the storytelling of teams and players. They rebranded the Matildas and built the profiles of the athletes over several years.

Momentum built and it paid off with enormous crowds and TV ratings.

Crowds celebrate the Matildas' win over France in the 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup. (AAP Image)

"We already know they are unbelievable athletes, and we knew that with the Matildas," Fernandez said.

"Our job is to make sure everyone knows the players by the time we get to the tournament.

"I mean the moment Sam Kerr started backflipping, which was around the time we were bidding, we were like, 'This is awesome.'

"We saw with the FIFA tournament that FOMO kicked in, and everyone wanted to be part of it."

Jane Fernandez (far right) poses with key figures at a 2023 FIFA World Cup event. (Getty Images: FIFA)

For this World Cup, Fernandez was hired once Netball Australia had won the hosting rights.

With less time up her sleeve, the aim is to leverage off the back of the Super Netball season, which culminates 25 days before the World Cup, and generate hype around the international players already at their disposal in the domestic competition.

The Super Netball grand final will be held at Sydney SuperDome on July 31, cementing the stadium as the home of netball next year, after the NSW government bought the hosting rights.

Melissa King was the CEO of the successful 2022 FIBA Women's World Cup at the same venue. It recorded the highest attendance across the event in the tournament's history.

Lauren Jackson was chaired off after playing her final game for the Opals at the 2022 FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup in Sydney. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

King met with Netball Australia at the end of that year to share her lessons from the event.

One of basketball's main strategies was also to tap into the story behind the athlete.

Legend Lauren Jackson came out of retirement to play for the Opals, so they leaned hard into that narrative with clever marketing strategies.

King said it was just as integral for organisers to engage the multicultural community in Australia linked to the travelling teams.

The 2022 FIBA Women's World Cup captured the attention of the Chinese community. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

"The United States and China were in the final and we had former NBA player Yao Ming here watching with FIBA," King told ABC Sport.

"The Chinese community really got into it, so it's important to keep promoting and telling people about who's coming to Sydney.

"We had a situation where Lauren Jackson had a birthday during the tournament, so we created a ticket promotion around her birthday number.

"Of course, an Australian team being there on the final day creates a powerful connection too, but that's out of your control and just a bonus, not a strategy."

What are the challenges?

Although the entire event happening in one place is easier logistically, it does create challenges.

Loading Instagram content

It can make it harder to draw attention across the country. There is risk that activation outside the arena could start to feel stale for returning fans, and Homebush isn't the easiest place to get to in the city.

Aside from that, there could also be crossover in timing with the NRL and AFL finals.

Fernandez said transport would be included with each ticket and there would be a considerable uplift in bus and train services.

She is confident about their position in the sporting calendar, placing a higher value on international competition and its appeal to a different audience.

"You can't compare a World Cup to a week-in, week-out national sporting league," she said.

"Our promotion is focused on it being the pinnacle of netball and that's what sets us apart."

Three types of tickets will be available to subscribers at NWC2027.com from today.

Vouchers will be available for Christmas gifts in December, while single-match tickets will go on sale in February.

World.title: Aloisi sacked from Chinese club after losing final five games in title choke
World.content:
John Aloisi has paid the price for Chengdu Rongcheng's catastrophic title choke, with the Chinese club sacking the Socceroos great.

Chengdu had appeared a lock to win the Chinese Super League for weeks, on top all season and leading the competition by 14 points with five rounds remaining.

But they lost all five games and, after slipping to a 3-2 defeat to Shandong Taishan on the final day, handed the title to Dalian Yingbo, where former Western Sydney Wanderers coach Mark Rudan is an assistant.

While Chengdu had a superior goal difference, the Chinese Super League prioritises head-to-head records between teams, and Dalian had won both meetings between the sides.

Aloisi had been hoping to become the next Australian to guide a team in China's top league to a championship after Kevin Muscat led Shanghai Port to glory in 2024 and 2025.

Instead, the former Western United championship winner will have to continue his journey elsewhere after Chengdu parted ways with Aloisi and his staff on Tuesday.

"Mr John Aloisi will no longer serve as head coach of Chengdu Rongcheng Football Club. Members of his coaching staff will also depart," the Chinese club said in a statement.

Aloisi had apologised to Chengdu fans after the capitulation.

"We are indeed very disappointed not to have won the championship. We are in a very despairing state. There is nothing else to say," Aloisi told local media via a Chinese translator.

"I want to say sorry to everyone. We certainly know that our fans have travelled a long way to fight alongside us and support us.

"Right now, my only feeling is one of great dejection and disappointment, because we could see the trophy right in front of us, but could not get it."

Meanwhile, John's older brother Ross Aloisi departed Zhejiang FC after just one season when they finished ninth.

AAP

World.title: Cricket Australia will not have another Sandpapergate investigation
World.content:
Cricket Australia will not reopen an investigation into the infamous 2018 Sandpapergate controversy, according to chief executive Todd Greenberg, in the wake of Usman Khawaja's claims that the entire Australian Test team knew it was happening.

Khawaja's book, Sabr, was released on Tuesday, but previews in the past week revealed some of the former Australian batter's claims about the ball-tampering saga, which led to the suspensions of captain Steve Smith and openers David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

In his book, Khawaja says the team started using sandpaper on the ball in the Test prior to the match in Cape Town, where Bancroft was caught on camera tampering with the ball.

Sandpapergate continues to wound Usman Khawaja and David Warner's Sandpapergate revelations may have set the scene for civil war in Australian cricket as the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to captivate and damage.

Speaking on radio station SEN, Greenberg said he respected Khawaja's right to tell his side of the story, but said his claims contradict the recollections of others in that 2018 team and CA would not be launching another investigation.

“There are specific details in his book that contradict the versions that have been provided by others," Greenberg said.

“It's important to know that back at that time, players were urged to come forward, and they had the opportunity to do so over these past eight years, and that remains the case.

“We have said we're comfortable with the outcome of the investigation based on the information we've received.

“That includes what we've seen from Usman, and our position hasn't changed on that.

“We don't see any compelling reason to open the investigation or revisit this again. I don't think there's anything that can be gained from that.”

CA's 2018 investigation determined only Smith, Warner and Bancroft knew of the ball-tampering ploy, suspending the trio while clearing all others of wrong doing.

Warner, who was vice-captain at the time of Sandpapergate, on Monday backed-up Khawaja's version of events and said the 2018 investigation by CA was "botched".

"Uzzie, I throw my full support behind you. I thank you for everything you've done," he said in an Instagram statement.

Loading Instagram content

"It's 100 per cent accurate, what you've said.

"Now everyone knows the truth, it's out there. People wanted to know it, you've come out and said it, and now people are saying, 'Why eight years on?' talking about selling a book.

"This is Usman's story. This is what Usman believes. Uzzie wrote down every single thing from that day on. Uzzie, thank you."

Warner slammed Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident in the wake of the 2018 tour of South Africa. Khawaja was not interviewed as a part of the probe.

David Warner was suspended from all international and domestic cricket for 12 months following Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident. (AAP Image/Ben Rushton)

"Now, this whole interview process was rushed and botched," he said.

"Uzzie was sitting next to Cameron Bancroft [in the dressing room]. Uzzie was not interviewed. How that is a thorough investigation? It baffles me.

"We're not here to point fingers and we're not opening old wounds.

"It's about accountability, transparency ensuring that the truth is properly examined, and perhaps it's time people stop scrutinising the person asking for accountability, and asking those responsible for the investigation to provide it.

"There [were] a lot of statements and inaccuracies over the last eight years that were out in the media by people and there were a lot of people who stayed silent."

Warner is the first of the banned trio to speak publicly in the wake of Khawaja's comments being made public.

Khawaja has also claimed that ball-tampering was commonplace in Sheffield Shield during his career, specifically highlighting Victoria as the state that was best at the "dark arts".

World.title: Oscar Piastri splits with manager Mark Webber
World.content:
McLaren Formula 1 driver Oscar Piastri has parted ways with his management, fellow Australian Mark Webber and his wife Ann, by mutual agreement.

Nine-time Grand Prix winner Webber began working with Piastri in 2019 and helped Piastri join McLaren in 2023 to replace compatriot Daniel Ricciardo, rather than stay at Alpine.

Renault-owned Alpine had wanted to promote Piastri to a race seat after double world champion Fernando Alonso announced he was leaving for Aston Martin, but the Australian rejected the offer.

Norris suffers champagne mishap in Brazil Lando Norris was near perfect to claim victory in Brazil.

"We are proud to have played a pivotal role in the formative years of Oscar's career and to have placed him in F1 so that he could compete at the front so early in," Webber said in a statement on Monday.

"Following our reduced trackside involvement this season, we have collectively agreed that now is an appropriate time to bring our management agreement to a close.

"This will allow Oscar to build on his achievements under a new management structure and for us to embark on our new ventures."

Piastri, who won back-to-back titles in Formula 3 and Formula 2 in 2020 and 2021, thanked the pair for support and recognised their guidance had been invaluable.

The Australian has not won a race this season, after looking like he might win the championship last year before being overhauled by teammate Lando Norris and ending up third. He finished sixth in Brazil on Sunday.

The winner of nine grands prix has not been on the podium for 16 races and is seventh in this year's standings.

Reuters

World.title: Popovic refuses to blacklist Socceroos who pull out of Jordan friendly
World.content:
Australia coach Tony Popovic insists Socceroos players who are reluctant to play Jordan due to security concerns will not be blacklisted from the national team set-up if they elect to withdraw from his squad.

The Socceroos, currently in camp in Doha, face Qatar in a friendly on Saturday, before they are expected to make the trip to Amman to take on Jordan next Wednesday.

Players have privately questioned the value of the friendlies due to the postponement of January's Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia to December 2027, and because of the security risk posed by travelling to Jordan.

Socceroos wary of Jordan friendly due to security threats The Socceroos have named an under-strength squad for upcoming friendlies against Qatar and Jordan, with Football Australia to monitor security in Jordanian capital Amman.

"If players are available for selection moving forward in any camps, any decisions made [in November] will not affect their possibility or availability for selection," Popovic said.

While usually rated one of the safer countries in the Middle East, Jordan has been the subject of heightened security concerns after a stabbing in Amman and an attack on an orthodox church in the country's south.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan "due to the unpredictable security situation" and the "threat of terrorism".

"The plan is to play the games, unless something else changes," Popovic said. "The safety and the wellbeing of the players and staff is of paramount importance."

Indonesia cancelled a friendly in Jordan this month, while the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia, said the Socceroos players had "overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated".

Alex Robertson has withdrawn from the friendly against Jordan for personal reasons. (Getty Images: Steve Christo)

The Socceroos coach revealed on Monday that Cardiff midfielder Alex Robertson had withdrawn from selection due to personal reasons — not related to security concerns — while Nashville's Patrick Yazbek had pulled out with an undisclosed injury.

Jackson Irvine has been left out after becoming a father for the first time, while back-up goalkeeper Paul Izzo remains in Denmark as he awaits the arrival of his first child.

Mat Ryan has been left out of the national team set-up for the second successive international window, leaving questions over the veteran goalkeeper's long-term Socceroos future.

"I think with [Ryan] and some of the other players, the focus just shifted with the Asian Cup changing. I'd like to see some other goalkeepers," Popovic said.

Popovic has left out Mat Ryan (pictured) for the second consecutive international window. (Getty Images: Jay Barratt)

"With 12 months of planning coming up I wanted to give some boys a chance; we haven't seen Joe Gauci or Tom Glover for a while.

"We [Ryan and I] have had discussions and he understands the decision."

Meanwhile, Popovic is taking a relaxed approach to his contract situation.

His deal was signed to expire at the conclusion of the Asian Cup but the delay by 11 months has thrown his commitment up in the air.

At the same time, reports in England have named Popovic as a potential contender to take charge of Premier League side Crystal Palace.

The Palace role would be a major step up for a coach who hasn't managed in a top-five league.

"I think both parties are comfortable with the situation," Popovic said of his Socceroos contract. "We've got no issues with how this is progressing."

AAP

World.title: Sandpapergate continues to wound Australia eight years on
World.content:
It's possible to forget now, obscured by the fog of the past eight years, just how extreme the national fury was in the wake of Cape Town, 2018.

This was a sporting scandal that broke containment lines. From your barista to your bus driver to the prime minister, everyone had something to say.

Sandpapergate touched something sensitive in the national psyche. It busted precisely the wrong myth, bruised just the wrong bit of our collective ego.

Khawaja's explosive Sandpapergate claim Usman Khawaja claims all staff and players knew that the Australian team was using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.

And not even after Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner were tarred and feathered in the town square did the interest subside. Outrage was diluted by time into regret and curiosity, but there was a permanence to the damage done.

This next chapter was inevitable and in the end it was Usman Khawaja who put his hand up and first told his story, one now corroborated by his good mate Warner. The floodgates may well now open, and civil war could be at hand.

Khawaja's version, which has trickled out gradually over the course of four days, is only barely revelatory. The notion that knowledge of the sandpaper plot went beyond the banned trio is not new, stands to reason and has been hinted at consistently almost from day one.

Bancroft himself back in 2021 insinuated with only a degree of subtlety that the great conspiracy extended beyond he, Smith and Warner. It was Bancroft's comments that prompted the indignant statement from the bowlers, which Khawaja claims further enraged Warner.

Given what Khawaja and Warner have now shared publicly, you can only imagine the atmosphere inside that dressing room. Fractured relationships may have been held together by shared on-field goals, but once that field is no longer shared, all bets are off.

The wider reaction has been curious. Some have pointed blame at Khawaja, which is unsurprising and something he likely expected.

It seems that in going first he is seeking to clear the runway for Warner to eventually tell his tale in greater, potentially more scathing detail. Whether Khawaja has done this out of pure friendship, a form of penance or a little of both is something only he will know, but arguing he is simply trying to make a buck from a book is an oversimplification.

Darren Lehmann rejected Usman Khawaja's claims, but said ball tampering had been widespread in international cricket. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Darren Lehmann, meanwhile, the coach at the time and the only other person to suffer any significant repercussions, rejected some of Khawaja's assertions but offered up the fact that ball tampering had been "going on for 150 years" by "everyone in the world".

The substance of Khawaja's claims have not sparked any great backlash or rebuttal, but the timing, source and medium of them have drawn ire. And from all of that combined, much can be gleaned.

The greatest sin committed by the Australian cricket team in Cape Town in 2018 — or at least the sin that cost them the most — was taking the Australian public for fools.

Lehmann was, of course, correct when he said that ball tampering had been around forever and that basically everybody did it. Performed with the correct amount of tact it could be passed off as one of the game's "dark arts", and even those who did get caught generally only received fines or very minor suspensions.

As you could sense in Lehmann's tone, this was not as much of a taboo inside Australian cricket, even down to the dog-eat-dog ranks of grade cricket, as it was to the uninitiated who, quite justifiably, simply saw cheating as cheating and not part of some wider unspoken code.

In any case, before Cape Town most Australians were comforted by the belief that they were above such a thing. That Test match permanently shattered illusions. Mints and fingernails are one thing, but something as blatant and guileless as sandpaper? Not only were we ball tamperers, we were incredibly bad at it too.

Then came the first cover-up. Not the one Khawaja has allegedly lifted the lid on, but the instinctive, reflexive lie that came from Cricket Australia and the players on the day, when it was claimed that the contraband in Bancroft's pocket was a piece of sticky tape covered with "granules" from the pitch.

As ever, the cover-up was worse than the crime. The cavalier hubris of the whole affair, from conception to execution to deception, stung our sense of Australian exceptionalism and prompted an exceptional punishment.

Steve Smith breaks down speaking to media at Sydney International Airport upon his return from South Africa. (AAP: Brendan Esposito)

Eight years on and with a perpetual war of words seemingly pending, it's hard to see how many lessons have been learned. "Ball tampering is bad" may be the extent of them.

Trying to wring the truth out of this mess may forever prove impossible, arguably by design. Khawaja said he was stunned that at no point during the investigation was he questioned or approached in any way. Indeed, if your goal is to ascertain what everybody knew, it does seem counterproductive not to simply ask everybody what they knew.

We have received hints at the truth, raised eyebrows and winking "no comments". Even Khawaja's recollections are in the main broad enough to avoid direct accusation, and therefore responsibility.

If everyone is ball tampering, then is anyone really ball tampering? If everyone knew about it, then who do you actually blame for it? At this point we're left with Joe Pesci in JFK, screaming at us about mysteries wrapped in riddles inside enigmas. "Even the ball tamperers don't know who did it! Don't you get it?"

And all the while Australians, who have always cared less for a case of whodunnit and more about the irreparable breach of trust, are still being played for fools.

Usman Khawaja (far right) says David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were the victims of the saga. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

Khawaja says Bancroft, Smith and Warner are the greatest victims and his point is valid. They suffered unprecedented consequences for not entirely unprecedented acts. If they did indeed carry the can for their equally implicated teammates then they have right to feel beyond aggrieved.

But the sense of loss felt by Australians was what justified those consequences at the time and what is fuelling the emotion of today. Rightly or wrongly, some element of our national identity will always be attached to our men's Test cricket team and the wounds that remain stem from a feeling of betrayal.

Nothing we have learned this week helps to mend those wounds. Yet more cover-ups, more accusations, more denials, more quasi-confessions. The water is only muddier, the deeds of the past worth less, and the worst, surely, still yet to come.

World.title: Focus on Sheffield Shield as Test selection comes to the crunch
World.content:
Potential Australia Test players will start their auditions this Wednesday when a full round of Sheffield Shield matches begin.

Two more Shield rounds follow before the first Test against New Zealand begins in Perth on December 9.

It is likely the squad for the first few Tests will be named some time after this week's matches and before the following round of matches in late November.

The Test squad will assemble in Perth on December 3, and with the bowling unit relatively settled, the interest lies in who gets selected in Australia's spluttering batting line-up.

Australia confirmed Marnus Labuschagne would not be considered for Test selection this summer against New Zealand. (Getty Images: Grant Pitcher/Gallo Images)

The next one or two Sheffield Shield rounds could answer some of the questions that were posed when Australia gave up a one-nil lead in South Africa to eventually lose the final two Tests, the series and the number one Test ranking.

The most pressing issue is the name of the number three batter following Marnus Labuschagne's disappointing tour of South Africa.

Since returning to the national side at the beginning of last year's Ashes series, the Queenslander has made just 426 runs in 10 Tests at an average of 23.66.

Labuschagne's return of zero and four during the third Test in Cape Town was the final straw for most commentators, and Australia's chairman of selectors, George Bailey, confirmed he would not be considered for the four-Test series against New Zealand this summer.

Cooper Connolly is the incumbent number seven in the Australian Test side. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone, file photo)

Labuschagne's ousting could mean Western Australia's Cooper Connolly retains his spot in the side, having got the gig at Cape Town when Steve Smith sat out because of his neck injury.

Connolly has been selected to play for Australia in the three one-day internationals against England, with the first on Friday, and so will not be playing in the Shield this week.

Western Australia's next Shield match against Tasmania in Perth, which starts on November 23, will give him some red-ball match practice if he is named in the squad.

If not Connolly, who else could come into the Test side?

Jack Clayton of the Queensland Bulls is scoring a mountain of runs and putting his name forward as a possible Test batter. (Getty Images: Mark Brake)

Apart from Shield enthusiasts, not many people would have heard of 27-year-old Queenslander Jack Clayton, but he is the hot player this season and one who has been endorsed for Test selection by his former state teammate, Usman Khawaja.

The number four has scored 303 runs in three Shield matches this year at an average of 75.75 and moreover has scored runs in every game with a recent 104 and two 50s.

He has another opportunity to push his claim when Queensland takes on Tasmania in Brisbane this week.

Oliver Davies of New South Wales is leading the Sheffield Shield run-scorers list after three matches. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Aggressive New South Wales opener Oliver Davies is at the top of the Shield batting charts with 332 runs at 66.40

However, 253 of those runs came in one innings in the first Shield match of the season and since then the 26-year-old has posted just one other significant score of 52.

His opening partner, discarded Test batter Sam Konstas, continues to push his name forward, with 229 runs at 76.33, including a century, a 50 and a one-day ton.

Sam Konstas of the NSW Blues is hoping to revive his Test career. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The pair will be part of the NSW side to play South Australia this week at Cricket Central in Sydney's Silverwater.

Victorian youngsters Campbell Kellaway and Oliver Peake are often talked up, and while neither have set the Shield alight this season, they have another chance against WA come Wednesday.

Oliver Peake of Victoria is one of the young Victorian batters tipped for higher honours. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Of the older campaigners, 33-year-old former Test players NSW's Kurtis Patterson and Western Australia's Cameron Bancroft are both in the runs, but will their ages work against them?

The jury is still out on NSW's 34-year-old Nic Maddinson, who was surprisingly called up for two Tests in South Africa after missing all of last season's Sheffield Shield while recovering from testicular cancer treatment.

Nic Maddinson was a surprise recall for the first two Tests against South Africa, but was dropped for the decider. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

And what of the batting order and most pressingly the number three position after Labuschagne's axing?

Moving Steve Smith up to three seems the obvious solution and the one most pundits are calling for.

His average of 65.22 from 30 innings at first drop is better than at any other spot in the line-up, but he has only batted there once since 2017, scoring 17 against England in Perth last year.

Steve Smith has returned to his home in New York while he recovers from a neck injury. (AP: Themba Hadebe)

Then there is the issue of his dodgy neck joint that flared up in South Africa, which he is now resting at his New York home.

Smith is expected to return for NSW's match against Queensland on November 22 at the SCG.

Cameron Green is another option for first drop.

Like his fellow Western Australian, Connolly, Green will miss this week's round of matches as part of the Australian squad for the one-day series.

The big watch on Green is his bowling fitness following an abdominal injury prior to the South African Tests.

Cameron Green returned to the Australian side for the third Test against South Africa as a batter only after suffering an abdominal injury. (AP: Halden Krog)

He returned in Cape Town as a batter only and continues to build up his bowling loads in training.

He could bowl in the one-dayers, otherwise his only opportunity to prove his match fitness will be the Shield match against Tasmania.

If Green can bowl, it is hard to see Tasmania's Beau Webster returning to number seven.

Webster was dropped for the third Test at Cape Town after taking just one wicket in his previous four Tests and scoring 81 runs at 13.50.

Western Australia's Josh Inglis would seem to be a lock to stay in the team after his first innings century at Cape Town batting at five.

Matthew Renshaw starred for Australia during the series against South Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

Queenslander Matthew Renshaw's solid return to the opening position at Cape Town helps Inglis's cause.

Both Inglis and Renshaw are in the one-day squad but will get another shot at four-day cricket the following week.

Sheffield Shield matches are so often the forgotten cricket fixtures of the summer, but right now they are of crucial importance.

Sheffield Shield matches Wednesday, November 11:

New South Wales v South Australia, Sydney

Victoria v Western Australia, Melbourne

Queensland v Tasmania, Brisbane

Tech.title: David Ellison says AI could be the ‘biggest creative unlock in modern history’
Tech.content:
During Paramount Skydance’s latest earnings call, CEO David Ellison said “it’s hard to imagine” AI won’t have a bigger impact on the film industry than CGI. In response to a question about the company’s outlook for AI, Ellison said:

“I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early 90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.”

Ellison gave Terminator as an example, describing how it cost $4 million to make, but “if you wanted to make that picture today, shot for shot, it’s $60 to 70 million.” He went on to suggest AI might be able to help with that: “We think these tools will help unlock more original storytelling by being able to make the budgets more digestible to be able to take that amount of risk.”

Ellison said AI will “significantly” reshape Paramount Skydance’s business, saying the company has been developing its own AI tools. As a result of those tools, Ellison claims, “content will be easier to produce, projects across the organization will speed up, and how we work will transform.” He emphasized that “all of this makes the value of premium IP and live events more valuable, not less.”

Ellison also noted that “in a world of AI slop, we think there will always be a premium for truly hand-crafted storytelling.” He added, “We also continue to believe that artificial intelligence is a tool for artists and will never be a replacement for them.”

Tech.title: What could China get from Jensen Huang?
Tech.content:
It’s difficult to overstate Nvidia’s power in today’s AI landscape. The company’s chips are the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built, and demand has consistently outpaced supply for years. Nvidia has also been an influential investor in a wide range of up-and-coming AI companies in recent years, with about $99 billion worth of equity investments in frontier AI labs, neoclouds, infrastructure companies, and more. Its chief executive has even become close with President Donald Trump.

This is why, as both cofounder and longtime CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry.

Huang is in hot water after news broke of his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen) is an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider and a top Nvidia customer. Questions are swirling around how the affair may have influenced Huang’s reported push to sell advanced chips to China — and potentially even influenced President Trump’s own decisions surrounding AI export controls.

Jensen Huang would be a valuable target for a foreign adversary with sights on the American AI industry

US officials believe the Megaspeed executive is a foreign intelligence asset that has funneled information straight to the Chinese government, per The New York Times — in particular, officials reportedly believe that Megaspeed is related to a convoluted web of Chinese companies working together to access chips in bulk and perhaps even illegally get some of those chips into China. Alibaba is reportedly one of Megaspeed’s top customers.

“It’s not entirely surprising that the CEO of arguably one of the most important, if not the most important, AI chip companies is the target of some sort of intelligence-gathering from countries like China,” Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at CSET, said in an interview with The Verge, adding that an alleged spy would potentially be interested in “better understanding what the US government is thinking on export controls,” as well as gathering information on Huang’s conversations with the Trump administration, attempting to influence policy, and gathering information on trade secrets like “who’s buying Nvidia’s chips, who’s getting them first, what’s coming next in terms of AI chips.”

Megaspeed’s sister company, headquartered in Malaysia, spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, the Times reported, citing trade records from trade platform ImportGenius. The transaction sizes were outside the norm for a small company, particularly when Nvidia chips are so difficult to get.

”Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job”

Nvidia spokespeople had said Huang’s relationship with the Megaspeed executive was strictly business. Their interactions were described as “not unusual or unexpected” in statements to the press. Nvidia’s line was, “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job.”

But at some point, their relationship became personal. In June 2024, just before Megaspeed became an Nvidia customer, photos show the two with other AI executives at a bar in Taipei after a local trade show; the following year, they reportedly had a business dinner in Taipei with others as well. But in private, according to US officials cited by the Times, the two’s relationship raised alarm bells for the US government — they had reportedly been surveilling the Megaspeed executive for months, if not longer, and that’s how it came out that she was in close contact with Huang.

The revelation is particularly concerning because of Huang’s lobbying role. He’d been trying to convince the Trump administration and Congress to loosen export controls for sending advanced semiconductors to China, ostensibly so that Nvidia could sell more chips. We now know this was happening around the same time that Huang was spotted at the Taiwan dinner with Alice Huang in May 2025, according to Culper Research, which shorted Nvidia’s stock earlier this year. That dinner occurred shortly after Nvidia had shared the Trump administration’s new restrictions on its China-specific H20 chips in April.

Just a couple months after the Taiwan dinner, Huang reportedly met with Trump in the Oval Office in July 2025 to plead his case for loosening export restrictions on Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors. Days later, the company announced that the administration had blessed sales of its H20 chips to China. Huang had argued that spreading American chips to China would help establish US technology as the standard, rather than allowing for Chinese chips to grow, according to The New York Times. After setbacks earlier in the second Trump term in export policy to China, Huang began speaking with then-White House AI czar David Sacks in 2025, who became the key advocate for Nvidia’s view that selling American chips to China would be beneficial, the Times reported.

By October 2025, Huang was lobbying Trump to allow Nvidia to sell more advanced chips to China, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, per the Times; but after Trump considered the proposal, he ultimately decided not to move forward. (That same month, Huang hired an external PR firm known for handling sex scandals, Wired reported.)

Months later, in December 2025, Trump changed course slightly, allowing Nvidia to sell H20 chips to a greenlit list of “approved customers” in China, with the US government taking a 25 percent cut of those sales. The same rules would apply to other US chipmakers, he wrote on Truth Social at the time.

“It is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions”

CSET’s Dohmen said that during the past two years, the US has seen a light loosening of AI export control regulations under the Trump administration, driven partly by Huang’s own lobbying. But it’s important to note, she said, that “even without any kind of intelligence operations from the Chinese side, it is in Nvidia’s interest and in Jensen Huang’s interest to lobby for looser export control restrictions.” Any restrictions by definition stifle Nvidia’s business expansion and cut off potential sales to help it grow its already stunning market cap — which is currently about $4.25 trillion, second only to Apple.

Huang’s relationship with Trump is also particularly relevant here. The president lavished praise on Huang during a speech last year, saying that until recently, he hadn’t even heard of Nvidia, and then he wanted to break it up. But after meeting Huang, he said, he understood why it would be difficult to re-create the company he’d built. More recently, Huang put Trump on speakerphone when the president called him during an appearance onstage at the All-In Summit, publicly displaying his close access to the Oval Office.

This past spring, a classified memo — the writing of which was overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, per the Times — circulated among Trump administration officials ahead of the president’s trip to China in May, warning of the Megaspeed executive’s alleged involvement in surveillance on behalf of China’s Ministry of State Security. Her reported goal was to learn about advanced AI chips in the US and try to influence them being made available to China on a large scale. Asked if he had known about the memo reviewed by Rubio at a press briefing on Monday, Trump said, “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.” Earlier in the briefing, he said he was unaware of the alleged spy connection ahead of his trip to China.

Huang was initially left off the list of executives joining Trump on the trip, but the president later asked him to join. Trump had been briefed about a year ago that US intelligence believed the Megaspeed executive to be a China intelligence operative, according to the Times, and that she had a close relationship with a US citizen who turned out to be Nvidia’s CEO. At the time, he reportedly chose not to take action.

So far, the allegations haven’t affected Huang’s future at Nvidia. He’ll continue to lead the company during the investigation. Trump has also stood by him since news broke of the affair, telling reporters this past weekend, “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”

Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised”

On Sunday, Huang wrote an internal memo to Nvidia employees — some of which are his own family members — writing, “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” He then addressed Nvidia’s board, partners, and shareholders, adding that he is “fully committed” to leading the company and “will work to earn back your confidence.” This weekend, Nvidia’s board of directors launched an independent investigation into the national security allegations. Huang will not have control over the participants in the investigation, and Nvidia said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello wrote in a note on Monday that Morningstar “can’t rule out the investigation fading away and Nvidia returning to business as usual,” particularly since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” There’s also the fact that Huang’s Nvidia struck deals in August with six large financial institutions to provide more than $500 billion in financing for the buildout of AI data centers and other infrastructure, and as the US-China AI race intensifies, those are high-stakes agreements.

“It’s unclear to us what these partnerships and financing deals would look like with a different Nvidia CEO,” Colello wrote. “Costs of capital may rise for future investments if perhaps the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals.” Morningstar still maintained a very high uncertainty rating for the company, with Colello writing that it’s possible US approval of Nvidia to sell H20 chips to China will be revoked and that the company could ostensibly be sanctioned as well.

Trump told reporters on Sunday that Huang should remain CEO of Nvidia and that he would “certainly take him” on his next trip to China. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump told reporters. “He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.”

Tech.title: Here’s what Trump said he knew about Jensen Huang
Tech.content:
When were you first informed that there was an issue with Jensen Huang and the affair? What was presented to you at the time?

I would say that when I heard about it, first of all, I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person. I’ve known him a long time. It’s the largest, by value, the largest or one of the largest companies in the world. He did that with a chip. When you think about it, you’ve got a chip that’s 10 years advanced, can’t be… the Blackwell can’t even be copied. He’s an amazing guy.

I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem. I believe he’s suffering greatly. I read his statement. And I believe he’s suffering greatly. Moreso because of his family. His wife who he loves and his family. But he is definitely suffering.

Just to follow up on the, “When were you first told of these potential issues with Mr. Huang?” You didn’t answer that question.

Well I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago.

When is that?

We’ll look into it. I know the FBI’s looking into it in terms of something else. I think that he’ll be in good shape.

…

Are you going to bring up the case of Jensen Huang with President Xi when you visit with him next week?

No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man. He built a great company. American company. I think he’s a very honorable guy. I feel very confident that he’ll be in good shape.

Sticking with Jensen Huang, when you went to China earlier this year in May, did you know about these alleged ties to the spy then?

No, I didn’t hear about it then. But a lot of people have heard about it. And Jensen totally denies that. I asked him today, because I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling alright, how are you doing… and I asked him about that. He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy. I asked him that question, did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said, I had no idea that she was a spy. And I really believe him.

…

I want to put a finer point on when exactly you were made aware of the intelligence around Jensen Huang.

Oh, I’d have to check. But this has been going on…

But there are reports that Secretary Rubio put an intelligence memo out last year. Did you read that memo?

I’d certainly check with the intelligence people. It could have been mentioned. Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.

Tech.title: Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang
Tech.content:
The leather-jacketed CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, spurring an investigation by his company and intense discussions worldwide. Recent reporting noted that since last year, US intelligence reports had identified Alice Huang (no relation) as not only the exec for an AI compute company renting access to Nvidia GPUs, but also a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security.

In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies, including the “neoclouds” like Coreweave who have been some of its biggest customers. So far, Nvidia and Jensen Huang have said that they have “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” but that hasn’t settled things as the investigation continues.

Tech.title: The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
Tech.content:
At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction?

Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.

Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying

The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.

At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom.

And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.

There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.

The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.

When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

Tech.title: Apple’s $50 Intelligence Usage Packs extend access to some AI features
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After publishing a support article in early September outlining usage limits for some Apple Intelligence features, the company has updated Logic Pro with an option to “Buy More Usage” for a one-time purchase price of $49.99, as spotted by 9to5Mac. It has a built-in AI assistant to do things like “start a new song, set up a vocal track from a single prompt, or refine an active project.”

These Intelligence Usage Packs, as Apple calls them, will allow users to continue accessing certain Apple Intelligence features that have usage limits because they rely on cloud-based AI models from OpenAI or Google Gemini. The Usage Packs can only be used by the Apple Account that purchased them (Family Sharing isn’t supported) and, as Apple explains on its website, any unused additional usage will roll over from month to month, but will expire 12 months after it was purchased.

For Logic Pro, Apple says the usage limit is “impacted by the complexity of conversations you have with the assistant.” Users finding themselves running out of access can find the option to buy an Intelligence Usage Pack in the Intelligence Features > Show Usage section of the app’s main menu. Currently, only Logic Pro has the option to buy more usage, but it’s expected to be added to other Apple Creator Studio apps this month, including Pixelmator Pro, Final Cut Pro, Motion, plus Pages, Keynote, and Numbers that are getting access to Apple’s AI chatbot.
