Tech.title: Anthropic reportedly plans to move forward with IPO plans
Tech.content:
In Brief

Launching a major tech IPO would seem risky right now, shortly after one of Nasdaq’s biggest sell-offs and amid revelations that a CEO central to the AI boom had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But that isn’t deterring Anthropic, which is moving ahead with its listing plans, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Anthropic plans to set a valuation range this week and begin trading on Thursday or Friday of next week, the Journal reported.

Investors will look to Anthropic’s valuation to gauge the strength of the AI boom. Some institutional investors are now pushing for a valuation below the $1.5 trillion target discussed as recently as last week, a figure that was itself considerably below the $2 trillion floated a few months ago, the report said.

OpenAI, Anthropic’s main rival, was reportedly valued at $1.25 trillion last week after the ChatGPT maker raised $11 billion in fresh capital, short of the $20 billion it had initially sought.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang reportedly engaged a PR firm with a history of handling  high-profile sex scandals a year ago
Tech.content:
In Brief

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang hired Heller Inc., a crisis communications firm known for handling sex scandals, at least a year before he publicly acknowledged an extramarital affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, Wired reported.

Heller Inc. founder Risa Heller has advised prominent men through personal scandals and sexual misconduct accusations, according to a 2023 New York Magazine profile. Her reported clients include former congressman Anthony Weiner, celebrity chef Mario Batali, and former New Yorker writer Jeffrey Toobin.

Wired also reported that Nvidia’s internal communications team was told to copy Heller Inc. on press inquiries about Huang shortly after an October 2025 New York Times report about whether Nvidia was helping Chinese companies evade U.S. chip export restrictions.

The Times reported that Megaspeed, a then little-known Singapore-based data center company with ties to China, had acquired nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips. It described Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, the woman later linked to Jensen Huang, standing next to him at a Taipei gathering of Nvidia customers.

Heller and Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

On Sunday, Nvidia published a statement from Huang acknowledging an affair with a former Megaspeed executive, though he didn’t name Alice Huang. Nvidia’s board separately announced an independent investigation, citing reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Tech.title: Hotel giant Wyndham exposed customer data after app security lapse
Tech.content:
Hotel and resort giant Wyndham has acknowledged a cybersecurity incident after a good-faith security researcher discovered a bug that allowed anyone to access customers’ personal information.

Security researcher Robert Wiggins at What Security exclusively told TechCrunch that he found a password inside the source code of Wyndham’s Android app, which granted access to an internal company database, hosted by tech company Salesforce.

Wiggins told TechCrunch that the credential exposed personal information including customer names, email addresses, and Wyndham member numbers. The database also stores customer login tokens (called JWTs) that keep customers logged-in to their apps without having to repeatedly enter their own passwords. The database also contained Wyndham files and documents.

According to Wiggins, the database had millions of entries, but he was unable to determine an accurate number of exposed customer records. Wyndham touts some 129 million enrolled rewards members.

The researcher said Wyndham has no way to report security flaws, and asked for TechCrunch’s help in alerting the company. Soon after TechCrunch made contact with Wyndham’s cybersecurity staff, the exposed credential was revoked, preventing any further access to the database.

“Our team has taken steps to address the issue,” a Wyndham spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Our security teams have no evidence of any unauthorized access,” the statement added, without providing any further details about the claim.

Wyndham’s spokesperson would not say, when asked, whether the company had the technical means, such as server logs, to determine if anyone had access to the customer database prior to Wiggins’ discovery.

TechCrunch also asked Wyndham whether it planned to notify customers whose information was exposed, or disclose the incident to U.S. regulators, such as filing a notice with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, as public companies are required to do for material cybersecurity incidents. Wyndham would not say.

Wyndham’s spokesperson also would not say for how long the password was embedded in its customer app, or how Wyndham plans to ship a long-term fix for the app.

App and software developers generally avoid including passwords or credentials in publicly released software and apps — a process known as “hardcoding” — as anyone with a copy of the software can extract the password and use it to access its associated server or database. Given the simplicity with which credentials can be abused by anyone, many cases of hardcoded credentials are automatically scored with a maximum vulnerability severity rating.

For Wiggins, this is his second public discovery of hardcoded credentials in two weeks, after finding a near-identical vulnerability in Applebee’s app that exposed customer data. Wiggins relied on AI tools for both discoveries, which make it easier to identify simple security weaknesses, such as hardcoded credentials, by scouring thousands of lines of decompiled app code every second.

When asked about Wyndham’s response, Wiggins told TechCrunch that he was glad the company fixed the issue, but noted that without visibility into any past activity, someone with malicious intent could have leaked large amounts of customers’ personal information.

The company would not say whether it planned to set up a vulnerability disclosure program to allow outside security researchers and hackers to privately report security vulnerabilities.

Michael Francess, Wyndham’s cybersecurity director who responded to the incident, told TechCrunch that researchers can alert [email protected] with details of potential security issues. The company’s spokesperson would not say whether it plans to change its website to allow researchers to alert the company.

This is the latest known security incident at Wyndham in recent years. In 2024, a security researcher found several Wyndham hotel check-in desks were running remote-access spyware that was leaking screenshots of guest records and booking information to the open web.

Soon after our reporting, the spyware app found on the hotel computers, called pcTattletale, was hacked and its banks of customer data stolen, forcing the company’s owner, Bryan Fleming, to shut down the company. Fleming, a former resident of Michigan, was later arrested by federal authorities and convicted of making, selling, and advertising unlawful spyware.

Tech.title: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
Tech.content:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.

Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.

NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA. We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. pic.twitter.com/oTaJyL7S2R — Culper (@CulperResearch) May 13, 2026

In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”

Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.

Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.

Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

Tech.title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
Tech.content:
Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.

Securities lawyers were already moving. At least four firms, including Schall, Brown & Schwartz and Levi & Korsinsky, announced investigations Monday into whether Nvidia misled investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects them to have plenty of company.

“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview Monday morning, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of the day. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Bartlett was right, in fact. A case surfaced Monday afternoon in the Northern District of California, where Nvidia is headquartered.

Rosen Law Firm, a New York-based plaintiffs’ firm that specializes in securities class actions, filed it on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor who made seven purchases totaling roughly $20,500 this year, according to a schedule attached to the complaint. (Rosen was lead counsel in a $250 million settlement with Alibaba and ranks among the most active filers of such cases.) The proposed class covers anyone who bought Nvidia securities between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, and the suit names both Nvidia and Huang.

The complaint accuses them of misleading investors about Huang’s ties to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center outfit where Alice Huang was considered a top exec, and it points to three statements as proof: Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo’s late-October claim that Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected,” the company’s even earlier claim that it found “no evidence of diversion” of its chips, and Jensen Huang’s Oct. 30 comment to Bloomberg that Nvidia’s dealings with Megaspeed were “normal and not unusual.”

All three were false or misleading, the suit says, because Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang. Kistenmacher is asking for unspecified damages, interest and attorneys’ fees, and he wants a jury trial.

While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation may turn up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, Rizzo really did tell the Times that the relationship was “not unusual or unexpected.” Rizzo separately told another outlet, The Hill, that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Of course, the world now knows that was not true. Worse, the Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.

From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.

The Kistenmacher complaint makes the same argument.

Bartlett predicted a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. This early lawsuit relies on that theory, and Monday’s drop of $7.97 per share, or 4.27%, gives the attorneys involved a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.

That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.

Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.

A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)

There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubts the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, but the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.

It’s worth underscoring that neither law firm announcements nor this newly filed complaint is a sign of a strong case. Plaintiffs’ firms are quick to publish these notices when they see an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has suffered the biggest loss. Kistenmacher said in his filing that he’s willing to serve as lead plaintiff, but the court will ultimately choose among the competing investors. No doubt they’ll materialize soon.

Tech.title: Fervo now has $12B in orders for its geothermal power tech
Tech.content:
Geothermal company Fervo couldn’t have picked a better time to deliver its first power plants.

In its third-quarter earnings report, released Monday, the company said it now has $11.9 billion worth of contracted revenue on the books, up from $7.2 billion last quarter.

Fervo has been hitting its deadlines recently, which undoubtedly has helped to drive orders.

As hyperscalers scour the earth for electricity to power their AI data centers, Fervo is on track to complete a 396 megawatt power plant for Google by the end of 2028. The geothermal company connected its first 100 megawatt power plant to the grid earlier this year.

Both projects are built at Cape Station in Utah, a resource that could generate 8.4 gigawatts of electricity. Previously, experts told Fervo the site could only produce about 4 gigawatts.

The Google project, now called Cape Google 400, will be grid connected, co-founder and CEO Tim Latimer said in an earnings call Monday. The arrangement means that Google can draw power from the deal and sell it to other customers if it’s not ready to use it.

“We built Cape Station on our schedule. Google can develop a potential data center on their schedule, and neither party is waiting on the other,” he said.

Latimer’s statement also underlines an advantage that geothermal has over competing generating sources like large nuclear or natural gas power plants — the phased nature of its construction.

Fervo’s newer wells are deeper and hotter, each capable of generating 15 megawatts gross power, and several are linked together into what the company calls a GeoBlock. The first completed GeoBlock generated 33 megawatts, while recent ones hit 50 megawatts. They’re sized to match the demand of a typical data center hall, so hyperscalers can bring them online as they’re completed.

As a business, Fervo is still in the early stages. It ended the quarter with an operating loss of $43.7 million, though it holds cash and cash equivalents of $1.9 billion and long-term debt of $301.6 million, which should give it plenty of runway.

Much will depend on the company bringing down the cost of its power plants. While hyperscalers are hungry for power today, they may not always be as price-indiscriminate.

Yet if Fervo can deliver on its promises, it could end up winning on price. The first phase of its Cape Station project cost $7,000 per kilowatt of capacity, the company said. The cost for its Google project is $5,500 per kilowatt, a significant drop that suggests Fervo is on the right path. With subsidies, that’s about equivalent to a new natural gas power plant running on fuel that costs $6 per million BTUs. Still about twice what natural gas costs today, but trending closer to where it needs to be.

But if Fervo can hit its long-term target of $3,000 per kilowatt, it could significantly undercut natural gas power, even at today’s prices. That’s a pretty ambitious target, but the company has made significant strides in just a few years. No wonder Google is getting in early.

Tech.title: YouTube streaming data returns to Billboard charts, ending major disagreement
Tech.content:
YouTube is officially returning to the Billboard charts, ending a disagreement over how music streams should count toward chart rankings.

Announced Monday, YouTube is set to resume sharing its streaming data with Billboard in 2027. The decision follows recent changes to Billboard’s chart formula, which now gives more weight to ad-supported streams.

The disagreement began in December 2025, when YouTube said it would stop sharing its streaming data with Billboard. The company argued that the chart formula favored paid subscriptions while not giving enough credit to fans who listen for free with ads.

At the time, Lyor Cohen, YouTube’s global head of music, criticized the system in a blog post, saying it didn’t reflect how people listen to music today.

“Billboard uses an outdated formula that weights subscription-supported streams higher than ad-supported. This doesn’t reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don’t have a subscription. Streaming is the primary way people experience music, making up 84% of U.S. recorded music revenue,” Cohen wrote.

Under Billboard’s previous formula, 1,000 paid streams counted the same as 2,500 ad-supported streams. YouTube felt this gave too much importance to paid listening, especially when millions of fans discover and support artists through free streaming.

Billboard has now updated its formula, reducing the gap between the two types of streams. Under the new system, 1,000 paid streams will equal 1,500 ad-supported streams when calculating album consumption units, compared with 2,500 under the previous formula. Paid streams will still count for more, but free streams will now have a bigger impact on chart positions.

YouTube’s return could make a difference for many artists, especially independent musicians and those with large international fan bases. Music videos, live performances, lyric videos, and other content on the platform help artists reach new audiences. With YouTube’s data back in the mix, more of that activity will now count toward their Billboard performance.

For Billboard, getting YouTube’s data back also means having a more complete picture of how people listen to and discover music. With so many fans using the platform, leaving its streams out meant missing a major part of music consumption.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang’s Troubles Leave the AI Industry Reeling
Tech.content:
No executive has pulled the strings in the artificial intelligence era quite like Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang. He parlayed the boom into incredible wealth, became a close confidant of President Donald Trump, and emerged as a prominent voice in US-China relations. That now all stands in the balance.

Over the last few days, Huang’s status as an AI titan has come under scrutiny amid an admission that he had an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company whom US intelligence services concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia’s board of directors said that the company would launch an investigation into the incident. Huang, the company said, “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it.” Huang earned $36 million last year, owned about 3.5 percent of Nvidia as of March, according to a corporate filing—which also noted that Huang is an at-will employee who can be let go anytime without severance.

How exactly the investigation shakes out, and what it means for Huang’s future at the company, remains to be seen. But the incident at least puts his position at risk, and raises questions about how the industry will respond.

“He’s the person who decides who gets the chips and who doesn't,” says David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School who tracks the chip industry.

Nvidia, which Huang cofounded in 1993, controls 90 percent of the market for chips used in training frontier AI models. With those chips in short supply, Huang has the power to determine which areas of AI get a boost next. Nvidia has also bankrolled much of the AI buildout, investing billions in the very companies buying its chips, such as OpenAI and Anthropic. When Elon Musk wants to build a new data center, Yoffie says, he can put in a call to Huang.

Internally, Huang closely manages even small details at Nvidia, responds to emails from any one of its roughly 60,000 staffers, and raises his voice to get points across, according to current and former employees. He’s a regular on cable TV and at tech conferences, where he’s been trying to deflate concerns about an AI market bubble and boost the positioning of his company.

But Nvidia has no other executive anywhere close to Huang’s prominence, and no apparent potential successor. “We have no idea who would replace him,” Yoffie says. “You put someone new into that position, if you're a customer, who knows what that's going to mean.”

Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, says that Huang has played such an important role—and become so close to the president—that he has become load-bearing for the entire US AI industry.

“On the one hand, Huang is irreplaceable. He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution,” Fedasiuk says. But he says that the company, which is indispensable to the AI industry, has to come first.

“He has to be replaceable as the CEO of the world's largest company, at $4 trillion in capex.”

Nvidia shares fell more than 4 percent on Monday, even as broader stock market indices rose.

The board’s investigation will most likely focus on whether Huang violated any company policies, Yoffie says. But the FBI could also investigate whether laws were broken, and Congress may decide to look into whether Huang’s affair influenced the US government’s policy on selling chips to China.

Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Waymo Said It Fixed Its School Bus Problem. The US Government Says It Didn’t Work
Tech.content:
The US government is examining whether Waymo’s recall of software involved with a series of school bus passing incidents last fall actually fixed the safety issue.

The formal investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration will determine whether the company’s supposed software fix succeeded in preventing its robotaxis from improperly passing stopped school buses with red lights on and their stop arms extended—indicators that the buses were picking up and dropping off students. It is illegal to pass these stopped school buses in all 50 states.

According to a filing, Waymo issued a fix for the software issue in mid-November and a voluntary recall a month later. But the government says that the majority of school bus issues occurred after that date.

Earlier this year, a report from the National Transportation Safety Board, the US’s independent safety agency, found that another school bus passing incident occurred in mid-January, several weeks after the supposed software fix. The NTSB is also investigating the school bus passing issue.

In a written statement, Waymo spokesperson Dana Gallagher said the company has “made significant improvements to vehicle behavior around school buses” and that it has not been cited for passing school buses since March—months after the mid-December software recall. She wrote that Waymo looks “forward to continuing [its] engagement on recall processes for AV software that continues to learn and improve.”

Late last year, WIRED reported, the Austin, Texas, school district even helped set up a half-day data collection event for Waymo’s vehicles, coordinating with the self-driving vehicle developer to bring school buses and stop-arm signals to an empty parking lot so that the company could collect information to help train its vehicles to avoid the illegal street maneuver. The data collection event occurred after Waymo had issued its software fix and voluntary recall. Still, the incidents continued.

In years past, recall queries like this one have led to civil penalties, some of them costing automakers and software developers tens of millions of dollars.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang Hired a PR Firm Known for Handling Sex Scandals Last Year
Tech.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang began working with a crisis communications firm known for handling public scandals a year before he admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. The firm, Heller, has handled Huang’s behind-the-scenes communications since at least October 2025, according to two sources familiar with the matter.

Risa Heller, the firm’s founder, has built a reputation as a fixer for powerful men facing allegations of sexual misconduct and other personal controversies, according to a 2023 New York magazine profile. Her past clients and people who have sought her advice include former congressman Anthony Weiner, chef Mario Batali, and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller also handles corporate communications and issues unrelated to personal controversies for its clients.

Heller’s public relations consultants were initially believed to be hired for matters related to Huang’s personal life, including his family’s philanthropic endeavors, according to people familiar with the arrangement. The firm frequently communicated with Huang and his daughter Madison, a product marketing director at Nvidia who has become an increasingly prominent figure within the company, sources tell WIRED. It’s not clear whether Heller’s early work with the Huang family involved Huang’s affair.

Got a Tip? Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who has information to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact WIRED reporters securely on Signal at ChaoticGoode.12 & Peard33.24

In 2024, Huang began appearing in public with a woman who goes by Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed, according to The New York Times. Megaspeed was created when it split off from a Chinese gaming and cloud computing firm in 2023, a few months after the US government began restricting exports of advanced semiconductors to China, including those developed by Nvidia. A subsidiary of Megaspeed later became a major buyer of Nvidia chips.

In early October 2025, Jensen Huang’s business dealings with Megaspeed and his connection to Alice became public in a lengthy New York Times report, which alleged that the US Commerce Department was investigating whether the company was helping Chinese firms evade American export controls through its subsidiaries.

The report caused tensions to rise within Nvidia’s top ranks, and Jensen was rankled by the story, according to sources. By the end of that month, Nvidia’s internal communications teams had been instructed to include Heller’s firm on any press inquiries about Huang, whether personal or professional, according to people familiar with the matter.

When reached by email, a representative for Heller referred WIRED to Nvidia. Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

US intelligence officials have determined that Alice (who has no known relation to Jensen) is a spy working for the Chinese government, according to the Times. Nvidia initially said that Jensen’s interactions with Alice were part of routine business with clients. But on Sunday, Huang acknowledged that his relationship with her was romantic in nature. In an email to Nvidia staff, he said he owed them and his family an apology. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced it is opening an independent investigation into Jensen’s activities. It said it has no reason to believe that national security or confidential Nvidia information has been compromised.

Before founding her firm, Risa Heller worked for Jane Harman, then a Democratic congresswoman from California, and later served as Democratic senator Chuck Schumer’s New York City press secretary. Nvidia’s head of public policy communications, John Rizzo, also previously worked for Schumer, serving as his deputy communications director.

Tech.title: King Arthur Baking Sourdough Sidekick Review: Rising to the Occasion
Tech.content:
Instead, I followed the directions in the included Quick Start Guide booklet, which indicated that I simply needed to fill the water reservoir and flour hopper, set the current day and time (and the day and time I wanted the starter to be ready—you can choose up to seven days ahead; I chose seven), add a little bit of existing starter, and press “Auto Mode.” Almost immediately, a torrent of flour released from the hopper and began mixing into my seed starter with the stirring paddle. (King Arthur recommends keeping a portion of your starter in the fridge in case things go wrong, and I second this suggestion.)

Oddly, no water was dispensed in this process, so post-mixing, my starter was now in the form of an under-hydrated ball. Over the next few days, it became a larger, drier ball until I finally decided to remove the crock to add a couple of tablespoons of water; as I did, I noticed the reservoir was still at its maximum fill line.

I decided I should probably download the app, where I noticed the Sidekick indicated it needed a firmware update. After the update, the Sidekick began dispensing water during mixing, but I realized I really should have followed the instructions in the main instruction booklet, which calls for using a scale to properly calibrate the amounts of water and flour the machine dispenses.

Theoretically, you should only have to do this once, which is good because it’s an irritatingly lengthy and fiddly process. However, my next attempt (remember when I mentioned saving some starter in the fridge?) went much better, properly dispensing 30 grams each of water and flour each day and initiating a stirring cycle every two hours. It starts with a loud beep, then the paddle begins a loud mechanical whir, and for the first few days this can be quite startling, especially if you’re in the same room when it happens.

Photograph: Kat Merck

You can bypass the every-two-hours stirring cycle via the onboard controls, but since the stirring’s purpose is to knock down the starter’s volume and reincorporate any unconsumed flour, I kept it on. (For what it’s worth, I did think the paddle, an update from the Sidekick’s first design, did a pretty good job of incorporating all of the flour and water each time it mixed.)

Note that, in part due to the regular mixing and the lack of discard (Auto Mode will prompt you to discard after a week, while Ratio and Custom modes, detailed below, will have discard reminders), your finished starter in the Sidekick may not look as traditionally puffy or bubbly as you may be used to. You can disable stirring, or you can go on scent—it should smell tangy and indisputably fermented. As the many online Sidekick adherents often say, “Trust the process.” Some online users recommended adding a few teaspoons of more nutritionally dense rye flour to the (presumably all-purpose) flour in the hopper, which is supposed to supercharge the starter’s growth, but I admit I didn’t notice much of a difference in appearance, smell, or performance between an all-purpose starter and a rye-boosted starter.

Tech.title: New Hulu Doc ‘Get Huge’ Shows the Deadly Toll of Looksmaxxing
Tech.content:
Before Clavicular, before Androgenic, before the Tate brothers, before bonesmashing and frame-mogging and the manosphere and looksmaxxing entered the online lexicon, there was Tony Huge.

A 44-year-old former model turned lawyer turned bodybuilder turned supplement impresario, Huge fled the United States for Thailand to escape legal pressure on his company from the Food and Drug Administration and to build out a “harem” of young, nubile Thai women. With his bulky frame, his sex-and-drugs-fueled lifestyle, and his motto “a day natty [natural] is a day wasted,” Huge became an icon for what was then the fledgling biohacking community. He amassed a huge following of disaffected, lonely young men, some of whom moved to Thailand to live with him. Then, some of them started dying.

Huge is one of the main focuses of Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death, a bone-chilling documentary series hitting Hulu on November 10. Directed by Stacey Lee and executive-produced by the journalist Jennings Brown, Get Huge kicks off with the untimely death of “Leo and Longevity,” aka Laith Abdallah Algaz, a biohacker and penis enlargement influencer who was found deceased in Huge’s home in January 2023.

What follows, however, is not a typical true-crime documentary. It’s a dizzying investigation into the hedonistic, self-destructive, and often deadly world of self-optimization, in which dudes inject themselves with pig’s brains and liquified gold, alliances shift at the drop of a hat, and you’re only as good as your last high-performing Instagram Reel. (A warning, spoilers for Get Huge follow.)

Since 2023, Huge has opened up his Pattaya, Thailand, home to the Get Huge team, offering “full transparency” into what Lee refers to as “this 24/7 performance of being a man.”

“It was, ‘Here’s my harem, here’s my other men that I’m leading, here’s my muscles, here’s my drugs,’” she says. But as her crew got further and further into the filmmaking process, it became clear that what was going on behind the scenes—not just the turmoil within Huge’s inner circle but also the hangers-on dropping like flies around him—was far more interesting.

“Therein lies the problem for the young kid watching at home who is watching this as a blueprint for their life. They can't discern what's real and what's not,” Lee says. “Even I was having trouble discerning what was real and what’s not.”

In some respects, Get Huge is about the rise of looksmaxxing, the wildly popular and dangerous online self-optimization movement popularized by manosphere influencers such as Clavicular and Androgenic. (The filmmakers say Clavicular participated in initial talks with the producers to participate in the documentary but ultimately declined; Androgenic plays a small but key role in the series.)

Tech.title: Ford Just Proved Its EV Battery Health Barely Degrades After 5 Years
Tech.content:
Real-world battery life for phones, laptops and other electronic devices can diminish over years of use, but does the same happen to electric cars after thousands of miles and hundreds of recharges? According to data published by Ford this week: Yes, but not as badly as you might fear.

The automaker published a report analyzing the battery state of health of more than 36,000 Mustang Mach-E electric SUVs sold to customers across the US and Canada during the initial 2021 model year. After more than five years on the road — and an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven — the fleet averaged 92% battery health.

I call that impressive, but not totally surprising. That battery durability data is largely in line with what I’ve seen reported across the industry by other automakers and independent analysts.

Why should you care about a 5-year-old car?

One of the biggest concerns of early EV adopters a decade ago (also shared by fence-sitters today) is long-term reliability. The battery is by far the most expensive component of an electric car, and owners want to know their shiny new EV will last as long as the combustion car it replaces.

Battery longevity is particularly important as more used EVs enter the market. Many experts (myself included) have touted pre-owned and off-lease EV deals as a way to bypass the electric-car price premium, but shoppers may be hesitant to roll the dice on higher-mileage vehicles. Many fear a used EV won’t meet their range needs or, worse, could blindside them with an expensive battery replacement.

Ford’s study is another data point that could help allay those worries.

The high-mileage club

Ford examined more than 36,000 individual vehicles delivered to customers across all 50 US states and Canada during the EV’s first year of sales. A little more than five years later, the automaker says that around 95% of vehicles surveyed retained between 87% and 97% of their battery health (an average of 92%) across the entire 2021 fleet after an estimated 2 billion cumulative miles driven.

A healthier battery retains more of its advertised range per charge. Antuan Goodwin/CNET

Better battery health means an EV keeps delivering more of its advertised range as the odometer climbs. The 2021 Mustang Mach-E rolled off the assembly line with an EPA-estimated range between 211 and 305 miles, depending on the spec, which means that owners lost around 16 to 24 miles of range over time, according to my back-of-the-napkin math.

That said, there’s no beating the chemistry. Around 2,000 vehicles in the group crossed the 100,000-mile mark, retaining around 91% health. A smaller subset of about 30 drivers reached 200,000 miles in their Mach-Es, with an average battery health of 88%. More miles, it seems, means more wear.

At the extreme anecdotal end of the spectrum, one owner put more than 400,000 miles on his original battery — though Ford didn’t state the specific health of that 2022 Mach-E.

In line with independent reports

An independent study published by Aviloo earlier this year adds credence to Ford’s reported numbers. An Austrian EV battery diagnostics firm analyzed over 500,000 EVs from 20 global brands to measure battery degradation — at 50,000, 100,000 and 150,000 kilometers — finding that many popular models maintained over 90% battery health at high mileage.

A used car is a great way to bypass the EV price premium, but it’s important the battery continues to perform as the miles add up. Antuan Goodwin/CNET

Tesla’s Model Y, which competes directly with the Mach-E, was found to hold around 90.3% battery health at 150,000 kilometers (93,205 miles). Aviloo reported that the Volkswagen ID4 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 showed 90.6% and 92.8% retention, respectively, over the same surveyed mileage. The first-generation Nissan Leaf — a much older EV with a smaller battery — showed more degradation at 86.3%, an unfortunate double whammy given its shorter initial range.

The future and the Fathom

According to Ford’s engineers and battery chemists, the Mach-E’s battery was designed to last at least 10 years, adding that the 2021 models in the study use an older nickel-cobalt-manganese, or NCM, chemistry.

Ford’s new Universal Electric Vehicle platform, which will underpin the upcoming Fathom small electric pickup, will use a newer lithium iron phosphate chemistry. That will come with unique charging needs and different battery management calibration than its Class of 2021. The UEV architecture is also built around robust bidirectional charging, so we’ll have to check back in five or so years to see how using your car to power your home affects long-term battery health.

Tech.title: AI-Driven Tech Layoffs Could Trigger a 1.6 Million Job Recession
Tech.content:
When Meta began laying off 8,000 people in May, it felt like an omen. Meta, the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, had seen several high-profile failures, from the death of the metaverse to its multibillion-dollar court setbacks. The Magnificent Seven — the tech giants that drive US stock market gains — seemed to hit a plateau over the last year, as more investors expressed concern about a potential AI bubble.

A wave of recent tech layoffs and buyouts reveals a growing volatility in the tech industry, as major companies restructure to cut costs and redirect spending toward AI. In just the last few weeks, Google extended its voluntary buyout program to select employees in five countries, and the graphic design platform Canva reduced its staff by 22%, laying off or relocating 1,271 employees.

Companies that have laid off or offered buyouts to 1,000 or more employees this year include Microsoft (60,000), Oracle (21,000), Amazon (17,000 in addition to 14,000 in 2025), Uber (3,300) and Netflix (1,000). According to the TrueUp tech layoffs tracker, layoffs are accelerating faster than last year, with over 200,000 workers reduced so far in 2026. The cuts aren’t limited to struggling companies, but are affecting profitable organizations with strong revenues.

More from CNET

The dominant factor behind layoffs has been AI. Companies have spent billions of dollars on the technology, plus a terrifying $3.2 trillion (with a “T”) that, Goldman Sachs says, doesn’t show up on balance sheets. With current returns failing to justify the massive scale of capital expenditure, companies are slashing labor costs and relying on AI to offset the resulting productivity losses.

While the US isn’t officially in a recession (yet), there are growing fears that mass layoffs could spread to other sectors, such as retailers and financial companies, creating a large wave of workforce reductions in the country. Analysts warn that if job losses extend beyond the tech industry, it could result in another 1.6 million people being laid off, bringing the formal unemployment rate closer to recession-level.

A precarious job market

With several economic pressures at play — inflation, higher interest rates and rising energy and computing costs — buyouts and layoffs allow company executives to reduce operating expenses while investing heavily in AI infrastructure, automation and specialized technical talent. That hasn’t worked out in all cases. A handful of companies, including Salesforce and Ford, ended up rehiring or hiring new people after AI-driven layoffs.

Even companies currently reducing their workforce, such as Canva, appear to be offering friendly terms, potentially to avoid burning bridges. As part of its severance package, Canva gave outgoing employees $10,000 grants, MacBooks, six months of salary and a year of healthcare. For many workers without a union contract, that will be the best-case scenario if the economy goes south.

Canva’s terms for departing employees are both exceedingly generous and a window into modern tech:

* Six months salary

* A year healthcare

* A year of LinkedIn premium

* A $10k grant to start a business

* Keep your MacBook https://t.co/Hqdegdb8Ek pic.twitter.com/pKuj8lJDvB — Mark Di Stefano (@MarkDiStef) November 3, 2026

Job instability, stagnant wages and rising prices have been the norm for several years, arguably since the last major US recession in 2020, at the start of the pandemic. Given that recessions historically occur about every six years (regardless of which party is in the White House), a larger downturn could be on the horizon, especially if an AI market correction triggers further stock declines and widespread layoffs. If high-cost data centers lose clients and major IPOs falter, enterprises will likely slash spending and jobs as the promise of AI-driven efficiency fades.

So far, layoffs don’t appear to be spreading to other industries, and overall job cuts are the lowest since 2022. But the job market has become increasingly precarious, especially for younger workers, according to Lisa Countryman-Quiroz, CEO of JVS Bay Area, a workforce nonprofit.

For example, entry-level hires are down by a third in the most AI-exposed occupations since 2021, which could affect sectors like retail and finance —typical entry-level gateways for many young people. Household wages aren’t keeping up with expenses, and many job seekers have found themselves unemployed for more than six months. “While we may or may not see broadening layoffs, I’m concerned about the erosion of stable career pathways,” Countryman-Quiroz said. The one bright spot seems to be in healthcare, with 42,000 jobs added last month.

AI, tech and the midterms

The 2026 midterm elections could also indirectly affect tech layoffs, mainly due to changes in the political and regulatory environment around AI and data centers. In the lead-up to the midterms, the backlash against data centers and tech billionaires became a pressing issue for candidates. Campaigns around data center moratoriums helped some Democratic candidates, including Gina Hinojosa, the surprise gubernatorial winner in Texas, where Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has his home and business headquarters.

Pausing new data center construction will be a shot in the arm for communities protesting the drain of AI infrastructure on local resources. But any slowdown in the buildout could also reduce demand for construction, chip suppliers or technical roles tied to AI expansion.

The midterm elections also affected financial markets, with technology and AI-linked stocks falling as investors worried that Democrats might impose new guardrails on AI. A weaker market can often make companies more cautious about hiring, capital spending and staffing, which could exacerbate cost-cutting pressures and lead to more layoffs and buyouts.

Countryman-Quiroz suggested that Congress could address AI’s disruption by investing in more job training, especially in growing areas like healthcare. “Current federal funding is only sufficient to train about 200,000 workers per year, a fraction of what’s needed,” she said. “Workforce development has historically enjoyed bipartisan support, so there is an opportunity for both parties to work together on solutions.”

Tech.title: iOS 27.3 Could Bring More Audio Intelligence and the Redesigned Health App Soon
Tech.content:
Apple launched the first public beta of iOS 27.3 on Monday, about two months after the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro lineup and iOS 27. The headliner here is the return of the new Health app: After briefly testing the redesigned Health app in an early iOS 27.2 beta, Apple has put the app back in the recent beta cycle.

Apple historically releases an iOS update in December, so I expect iOS 27.3 to land on iPhones later this year.

CNET/Apple

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only on something other than your primary device. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.3, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short, so it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

More from CNET

Also, since this isn’t the final version, there could be more features to land on your iPhone when Apple releases 27.3.

Here are some features developers and beta testers can try now in the first iOS 27.3 beta.

The revamped Health app is back

The redesigned Health app returns in the iOS 27.3 beta after Apple tested the feature in the iOS 27.2 beta process. Developers and beta testers can explore the refreshed app and see things like a new Longevity tab and your Health Age.

Apple wrote online that we can expect the redesigned Health app to land on devices later this year.

Explore Live Rewind and Siri Recap

Live Rewind on the Apple Watch generates a transcription of what was said during the last 15 seconds. Apple/Screenshot by CNET

If developers and beta testers have an Apple Watch that is running the watchOS 27.3 beta as well as an iPhone running the iOS 27.3 beta, those folks can test out Apple’s Live Rewind and Siri Recap in Audio Intelligence.

Live Rewind allows you to pull up a text transcript of a conversation in the past 15 seconds on your Apple Watch, and Siri Recap can automatically give you a summary of meetings, conversations and other events. Live Rewind snippets are replaced by new audio and then deleted, and Siri Recaps delete themselves after seven days if you don’t manually delete them sooner. However, you can also save both of these in the Siri app and export them to the Notes or Journal apps on your iPhone.

While both Live Rewind and Siri Recap are automatically deleted over time, I’m uncomfortable with the ability to save snippets or recaps, which raises concerns about people recording my conversations without my knowledge. Even if Audio Intelligence just summarizes what I said, I still find both features creepy.

And while I recognize the utility for certain groups of people, I also think it’s better to just, y’know… talk to someone instead of asking your watch what they just said.

Gym Strength comes to Fitness Plus

In addition to the revamped Health app, developers and beta testers who subscribe to Fitness Plus (which costs $10 per month) can also access a new gym experience called Gym Strength. It’s designed to provide folks with personalized four-week strength training plans that take into account someone’s goals, experience level and schedule.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets and weights in order to help you meet your goals. And if you’re unfamiliar with an exercise, you can also watch video tutorials to see how to perform that exercise.

Siri AI can perform more actions and comes to more languages

Siri AI gets a huge update in the iOS 27.3 beta. The feature can now do more actions in supported apps, like Apple Music and Messages. For example, if you go into Apple Music, you can ask Siri to create a playlist for you, and in Messages, you can ask Siri to schedule, edit or unsend messages. If you open an app and ask Siri what it can do in the app, the digital assistant should give you some examples of its capabilities.

The beta also brings Siri AI to traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish and Norwegian.

New StandBy mode features

StandBy mode also gets an upgrade in the iOS 27.3 beta. In the beta, you can add full weather and calendar slides to the mode and choose from more colors.

StandBy mode gets a few new apps in the iOS 27.3 beta. CNET/Apple

Apple introduced StandBy mode alongside iOS 17, and it was one of my favorite iPhone features. I’m happy Apple is finally showing it some love and adding more features and capabilities so it feels more like a home or desk hub.

Adaptive Dark Mode comes to Safari

If you’re a fan of dark mode, the iOS 27.3 beta has a treat for you. The beta gives you a new setting in Safari called Adaptive Dark Mode. When enabled, it forces dark mode onto webpages in Safari that may not have a dark mode option otherwise.

Here’s where to find the option.

1. Tap Settings.

2. Tap Apps.

3. Tap Safari.

4. Tap Adaptive Dark Mode.

5. Tap On.

Adaptive Dark Mode in the iOS 27.3 beta makes most web pages in Safari support Dark Mode. CNET/Apple

Those are a few of the new features developers can try now with the first beta of iOS 27.3. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.3 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices before the end of the year.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27.2, why you may have missed iOS 27.1 and our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

Tech.title: Anthropic Introduces New Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 AI Models
Tech.content:
Anthropic took the wraps off yet another set of AI models on Monday, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, which are ready to use and make substantial improvements over their predecessors. While an average user may not see the benefits of the latest models, Anthropic says they’re best for the “most ambitious, open-ended work.”

The new Claude models show greatly improved metrics in areas like coding (don’t they all?), reasoning, vision, cybersecurity and biology. The latter of which have strong safeguards against misuse in the Fable model, which give Anthropic enough confidence to release it to the public.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors and are available at lower prices — a trend we’ve continued to see lately with most new AI model releases.

More from CNET

Anthropic dropped a series of benchmarks showing off how much better the new models are compared with the previous ones. And generally, they’re impressive. Fable 5.2 outperforms Fable 5.1 in one agentic coding benchmark at 49.1% versus 32.4% at “Xhigh effort,” bringing a meaningful distance in performance. As far as cybersecurity benchmarks are concerned, Mythos 5.2 scores a jump from 61.7% to 76.3% — a rather impressive jump — if you’re using the model to its fullest potential.

Anthropic says Claude Mythos 5.2 is its most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. The new model is capable of catching more vulnerabilities and is better at reproducing and fixing them. That said, Mythos 5.2’s cybersecurity features are locked to a specific group right now: Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program.

The company boasted about enhanced capabilities in the latest model improvements in mathematics, science and engineering. It also says that testers of Fable 5.2 found the new model more capable of more ambiguous tasks that require abstract reasoning when it came to research and analysis.

Anthropic makes a big deal about the alignment of Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Alignment tracks whether and how the intention of the (human) user is executed by the model. And as agentic AI becomes more prevalent, there are more stories of AI deciding to go out of its way to complete a task, even with devastating consequences. Fable 5.2 includes guardrails that block risky cybersecurity activities — like penetration testing and exploit generation — and advanced biology capabilities.

Eligible Claude subscribers will get one to three Fable resets this week based on how long they’ve subscribed.

Tech.title: New Paramount Plus and HBO Max Bundle to Arrive Early Next Year
Tech.content:
Skydance, the company formed by the combination of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, intends to launch a Paramount Plus and HBO Max streaming bundle in early 2027. The announcement was shared in a letter to shareholders on Monday ahead of the media giant’s third-quarter earnings call. It marks the first earnings presentation since the merger between Paramount Skydance and WBD was finalized in October.

This past March, then-Paramount CEO (now Skydance CEO) David Ellison said the plan is to merge both streaming services together into a single app. According to today’s announcement, the first step is to roll out a bundled offering as the company integrates the two platforms into one. “As we work toward a fully unified offering, we will phase in changes based on consumer feedback so we can continue to drive healthy financial growth through the transition,” the letter said. With the bundle, customers should expect a new movie to drop between the two platforms “every two weeks, on average.”

Additionally, Skydance unveiled the three new divisions under its reorganized banner: Skydance Studios, Skydance Direct-to-Consumer and Skydance TV. The studios department will oversee film and TV productions, while the DTC division manages the streaming businesses, and the Skydance TV umbrella covers its cable and broadcast networks such as CBS, Food Network, Comedy Central, Nickelodeon, CNN and TNT.

More from CNET

Paramount Plus is home to CBS content, as well as streaming originals like MobLand, Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender, Tulsa King and Yellowjackets. The streamer also carries Paramount Pictures theatrical releases such as Top Gun: Maverick. HBO Max’s library is full of HBO hits, Warner Bros. classics, DC shows and films like Lanterns, and live sports from TNT and TBS.

Tech.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 to Cross Historic One Light-Day Milestone on Nov. 18
Tech.content:
NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft is on track to set another historic record as its mission approaches the half-century mark. On Nov. 18 at 5:16 a.m. ET, the probe will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, a journey of nearly five decades that places it farther from our planet than any human-made object in history.

It’s quite an accomplishment for a spacecraft built in the mid-1970s One light-day is the distance that light travels in a single day at the speed of light, which is approximately 186,282 miles per second. That translates to 25.9 billion kilometers or about 16.1 billion miles in a single day. At an average human walking speed of 3 mph, it would take a human 612,015 years to walk that distance.

Fortunately, Voyager 1 has been traveling a bit faster than that. It currently zips along the cosmos at a steady 37,763 mph, a speed it achieved in 1980 after a gravity-assisted Saturn flyby. It has been flying at that speed ever since.

More from CNET

A journey wrought with peril

Voyager 1 has traveled a long way with the help of gravity-assisted speed boosts from Jupiter and Saturn in 1979 and 1980. NASA

The historic milestone isn’t without its drama. Voyager 1 has been in space for nearly half a century, and in that time, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory has done everything it can to extend the life of Voyager 1. That includes troubleshooting issues, performing maintenance and shutting down various systems to save power and extend the spacecraft’s life-span.

Several of those efforts took place in 2026. The team running Voyager 1 spent weeks shutting down three devices and powering on three low-power alternatives to reduce overall power usage. This initiative, which was internally called The Big Bang, was also performed on Voyager 2. The transition was completed in early September, giving Voyager 1 more time with its dwindling power supply while also keeping it warm enough to continue operating in the frigid conditions of interstellar space.

It was a tricky maneuver that required the team to simultaneously turn multiple instruments on and off. The difficulty of the maneuver was amplified by the fact that it took almost a full day for any signal to reach Voyager and another full day for Voyager to send a signal back, with hours of downtime while the spacecraft performed the operations.

All of this took place several months after Voyager 1 experienced a sudden drop in power, which necessitated shutting off one of its three remaining instruments still in operation. Voyager 1 now has only two instruments still in operation.

The end of an era

Making it a whole light-day away from Earth is likely going to be Voyager 1’s final milestone while it still has enough power to communicate with Earth. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators. They are essentially nuclear-powered batteries that generate energy by converting the steady heat from decaying plutonium-238.

When Voyager 1 first launched, its radioisotope thermoelectric generators produced about 470 watts of power. But plutonium-238 doesn’t last forever, and after 50 years in space, the RTGs now produce about 215 watts of power, with an average loss of about 4 watts per year. Most of that power is used to keep Voyager 1 up and running, which is why NASA has shut down eight of the 10 instruments that Voyager had when it launched.

At its current rate of usage and decay, Voyager 1 is expected to shut down its final science instrument in the 2030s and will eventually lose communication with Earth in 2036 due to insufficient power to send back a radio signal.

The same fate is expected for Voyager 2, Voyager 1’s twin, which has also spent half a century in space. While it is labeled the sequel, Voyager 2 actually launched 16 days before Voyager 1, and the two have spent nearly identical amounts of time traversing the cosmos. Thanks to its slower speed and trajectory, it likely won’t reach the one light-day distance until after its instruments shut down.

Thanks to the vastness of space, Voyager 1 will lose all of its power before it hits its next milestone, which is the beginning of the Oort Cloud, a vast, icy shell of comets at the edge of our solar system. It’ll take about 300 years for Voyager 1 to make it there.

Thanks to the near-perfect vacuum of outer space, Voyager 1 will continue to fly at its current speed even after it shuts down entirely. So it’ll still hit that milestone; it just won’t be able to phone home to tell us about it.

Tech.title: How to Use AI Tools Like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude to Prep for a Job Interview
Tech.content:
ChatGPT’s voice mode lets you run a spoken mock interview and hear follow-up questions in real time. Oscar Wong/Getty Images

For job seekers, the job interview can feel like an endurance test of their skills and personality.

It’s enough to make a person yearn for the simpler days of newspaper ads and in-person handshakes. But alas, we find ourselves immersed in the era of smart homes and Bluetooth-enabled blueberry mint vapes. But AI offers one practical advantage: a way to rehearse before the real thing.

A chatbot can play the role of a hiring manager, ask questions likely to come up for a specific job and tell you — bluntly, if you want — where your answers fall flat. That makes AI chatbots some of the more practical interview prep tools available, especially since you can rehearse as many times as you need without leaning on a friend’s patience. These chatbots can also help you research the company, prepare stories that answer common behavioral questions and get a rough sense of what the role should pay.

More from CNET

Here are a couple of ways you can leverage AI tools to ace your next job interview.



Match your background to each role

How you look in a job interview matters. Even if you’re sitting at home pantsless and just woke up from a nap, you gotta look the part on Zoom.

You can ask ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude to generate Zoom backgrounds that showcase your understanding of and affinity for the company culture.

Gemini created these backgrounds for my theoretical job interviews with Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Google, Netflix and more.

Some of them turned out a little better than others, but you get the idea.

Created by Rachel Kane using Gemini AI

Know your worth

Some states, like California, have made it all but mandatory for employers to post the salary range for jobs they post as vacant. Even if you might know the salary range of the job going into the interview, the topic of compensation is always best approached with as much information as possible.

I asked Google’s Gemini AI to reference Glassdoor listings, public earnings, expenditure announcements, shareholder communications, and online media results for the salary ranges of the CEOs at Meta, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Netflix, and Alphabet and to provide me with salary ranges for mid-level marketing professionals at those companies.

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Gemini then gave me a five-year growth schedule, where it laid out how I could begin to make more money by leveraging my sign-on bonus in the first year, my vesting stock in the second, a raise in the third, a title change in the fourth and a big promotion in the fifth (very idealistic, but it could happen).

Gemini also provided more information on how each of those companies typically structures your compensation — whether it’s an all-cash salary, one with built-in bonuses, or employee stock options. It’s important to have this information when you’re asked about the salary you expect.

You’re more awesome than you think

Most guides on how to land a gig suggest that job seekers research the company, its culture and what the role entails. But honestly, job seekers are already investing a tremendous amount of time applying to open positions and going through multiple rounds of interviews.

What’s more important is your ability to effectively explain why you’re perfect for the job.

For my hypothetical marketing role, I used Claude to research the CMOs at those companies, including their social posts and their teams’ major priorities. I asked the AI tool to give me some one-word anchors for interview talking points, cross-referenced to elements of my resume that would be directly applicable.

It gave me some keywords to bring up, and how to relate them back to my own resume, listed out CEOs’ vision and products, told me which company could be my biggest opportunity and best fit and why — and how to express that in an interview:

Claude/Screenshot by CNET

Practice the interview

Nerves are normal in a high-stakes communication like a job interview. You’re trying to appear interested but not desperate, competent but not cocky, and decide on a salary requirement you won’t live to regret.

One way to get your mind right for the job interview and take the edge off could be using an AI tool to run through some sample interview questions with you.

Several online platforms offer features that let you run a trial before your interview, including Final Round AI, which offers real-time interview transcription and support, mock interviews and resume building. Another platform, Yoodli, focuses on AI-powered communication coaching to improve both verbal and nonverbal delivery and offers AI roleplays. You can also talk with Gemini Live and get real-time responses.

In my case, I asked ChatGPT via the voice chat feature to pretend it was the hiring manager for a job at a fictitious company that sells subscription dog-sitting services, and to act as if it was unimpressed by my resume to give me a challenge and desensitize me to the worst-case scenario.

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

ChatGPT/Screenshot by CNET

While the text chat was more of a critique of my resume, bless its sweet little machine algorithm, ChatGPT in voice chat was way too nice to even get into character for this challenge, no matter how I prompted it.

AI tools can be effective options for job seekers who don’t feel comfortable reaching out to someone in their network to help them prepare. Always keep in mind, however, that AI tools come with pitfalls, including issues related to data collection, bias and inconsistent messaging.

Use AI to prepare, but don’t let it fake your performance. AI doesn’t replace genuine networking, and the guiding principle should be to stay authentic.

Tech.title: Bluetooth Core 7.0 Speeds Are Set to Quadruple in 2027, Especially for Audio
Tech.content:
Wireless tech is about to get a whole lot snappier. On Thursday, the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, the trade association that oversees Bluetooth, officially unveiled Bluetooth High Data Throughput, a flagship upgrade set to arrive as part of the Bluetooth Core 7.0 standard. The revision supercharges Bluetooth Low Energy by pushing maximum bit rates to 7.5Mbps, effectively quadrupling the throughput of the existing LE 2M technology. Compatible devices are slated to hit store shelves starting in 2027.

That’s good news for phone users, tablet havers, laptop groupies, smart speaker stans and more. Bluetooth is still the most popular medium-to-short-range wireless standard for connecting devices. But this is a big rollout, and the changes will start with premium wireless, such as earbuds, with other applications following.

Those other applications could include spatial computing, exchanging AI-related info with local devices, connecting to health wearables and a host of smart home applications, like playing Spotify through an Amazon Echo Studio or dimming a smart bulb.

More from CNET

“In practical terms, a smartwatch could sync hours of sensor-rich training data to a phone in seconds. A smart home product could complete a firmware update with little visible downtime,” Damon Barnes, Director of Technical Marketing at the Bluetooth Special Interest Group, told CNET. “Smart glasses and other AI-enabled devices could exchange more data with a companion device or the cloud. And in audio, the additional capacity can support richer experiences, including high-resolution, lossless, surround, and spatial audio.”

A representative from the Bluetooth Special Interest Group didn’t respond to a request for comment.

What makes Bluetooth HDT so speedy?

The biggest change in this update is a new physical layer for Bluetooth. Layers are like different sections of the Bluetooth protocol, and the physical layer is the bedrock of the standard, the foundational layer involved in transmitting and receiving data signals.

Improvements in the physical layer can have very significant effects on all Bluetooth communications. In this case, new modulation schemes let the physical layer handle data more efficiently and transmit more data at once, which is why the speed increases are so significant.

These improvements also make the new standard more efficient, saving battery life in many applications. So your smart lock may last longer before you need to exchange the AA batteries, earbuds won’t need to go back in the case as fast, and so on.

When and what you can expect with Bluetooth HDT

We know the first flagship devices are expected to appear with the technology in early 2027, but don’t have an exact date.

Barnes also told use that since the update is starting with wireless audio, the first devices to see it will be headphones, earbuds and speakers.

With protocol changes like this, it can take some time for new products to reach the market, and manufacturers may take a long time, even years, to adopt it.
